Citrate synthase is trimethylated on a single lysine by CSKMT, a modification opposed by oxaloacetate, and the deacetylase SIRT3 tunes several of these enzymes according to nutrient state. Loss of individual factors causes mitochondrial disease, paraganglioma, or Friedreich ataxia, placing this step upstream of oxidative energy metabolism rather than within it.
Several citric acid cycle enzymes need maturation and regulation before working, setting cycle capacity. Aconitase and succinate dehydrogenase require iron-sulfur clusters from mitochondrial machinery including frataxin and ISCU, and SDHAF chaperones flavinylate and assemble succinate dehydrogenase, while CSKMT trimethylates citrate synthase and SIRT3 deacetylates enzymes according to nutrient state. Defects cause mitochondrial disease, paraganglioma or Friedreich ataxia.—Mitochondria must prepare and regulate the enzymes of their central energy-generating cycle before it can run, setting how much oxidative energy metabolism cells can support according to nutrient state. Defects in this preparatory layer cause inherited mitochondrial disease, hereditary paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma tumours, and Friedreich ataxia, a neurodegenerative disorder with cardiomyopathy.

Diseases associated with surfactant metabolism (7)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Defective pro-SFTPC causes SMDP2 and RDS
originalSurfactant protein C is made by alveolar type II cells as a propeptide that must fold, traffic through the secretory pathway and be proteolytically trimmed before the mature hydrophobic peptide joins the lipid film that lowers surface tension and keeps alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration. Mutations that disrupt folding, routing or processing of pro-SFTPC produce a dominant disease mechanism in which the misfolded proprotein is retained in type II cells rather than simply being absent. The retained precursor triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, reactive oxygen species generation and autophagy, injuring and killing the cells that renew the alveolar epithelium. The result is impaired surfactant homeostasis with floccular material filling alveoli, seen as interstitial lung disease and as respiratory distress in newborns.
Surfactant protein C is produced by alveolar type II cells as a propeptide that must fold, traffic and be processed before joining the lipid film that prevents alveolar collapse. Mutations disrupting this cause misfolded pro-SFTPC to be retained, triggering ER stress, reactive oxygen species and autophagy that injure type II cells. Impaired surfactant homeostasis results, presenting as interstitial lung disease and neonatal respiratory distress.—In the lungs, alveolar type II cells produce the surfactant that keeps air sacs from collapsing at the end of each breath. Inherited mutations cause a dominant disease in which a faulty precursor is retained, stressing and killing the cells that renew the alveolar lining. Surfactant homeostasis fails, presenting as interstitial lung disease in children and adults and as respiratory distress in newborns.
Defective CSF2RB causes SMDP5
originalAlveolar macrophages clear and recycle pulmonary surfactant, and they depend on GM-CSF signalling through a receptor built from an alpha subunit (CSF2RA) and a shared beta subunit (CSF2RB) to acquire that capacity. Loss-of-function mutations in the beta subunit cause pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 5, also called hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, in which macrophages fail to take up and degrade surfactant lipid and protein; the alveoli fill with floccular surfactant material, gas exchange deteriorates, and respiratory failure follows. The surfactant components involved here — the hydrophobic proteins SFTPB and SFTPC, the collectins SFTPA1, SFTPA2 and SFTPD, and SFTA3 — are secreted by type II pneumocytes to lower alveolar surface tension and support innate defence, then internalised by macrophages via clathrin-coated vesicles. The pathway therefore links haematopoietic cytokine signalling to lung lipid homeostasis rather than to surfactant synthesis itself.
Alveolar macrophages need GM-CSF signalling through a receptor of CSF2RA and CSF2RB subunits to clear surfactant. Loss-of-function CSF2RB mutations cause hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (surfactant metabolism dysfunction 5), where surfactant lipids and proteins secreted by type II cells are not taken up and degraded, filling alveoli and causing respiratory failure. The pathway links cytokine signalling to lung lipid homeostasis rather than surfactant synthesis.—In the lungs, alveolar macrophages clear and recycle surfactant, an ability that depends on a blood-cell growth factor signal. Inherited loss causes hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, in which air sacs fill with uncleared surfactant material, gas exchange deteriorates and respiratory failure follows, often in childhood. This links haematopoietic cytokine signalling and innate lung defence to lung lipid balance rather than to surfactant production.
Defective pro-SFTPB causes SMDP1 and RDS
originalSurfactant protein B is a small hydrophobic peptide, cleaved from a larger precursor in alveolar type II cells, that lets phospholipid films spread across the air-liquid interface and lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse at end-expiration. When SFTPB is mutated, the mature peptide is lost and the pathway of surfactant assembly fails at two points: lamellar bodies form abnormally and the SFTPC precursor is left partially processed and inactive, so floccular lipoprotein material accumulates in air spaces instead of a functional film. The result is pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 1, a rare disorder of surfactant homeostasis, and a severe respiratory distress syndrome that presents in newborns and premature infants and is typically fatal without transplantation. This biology links intracellular processing of a secreted proprotein to alveolar mechanics and neonatal lung function.
Surfactant protein B, a hydrophobic peptide processed from a precursor in alveolar type II cells, spreads phospholipid films and lowers surface tension to prevent alveolar collapse. SFTPB mutations abolish it, causing abnormal lamellar bodies, incompletely processed SFTPC and accumulation of floccular material. The result is surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 1, a severe neonatal respiratory distress syndrome usually fatal without transplantation.—In the lungs, alveolar type II cells produce surfactant that spreads across the air sacs and prevents their collapse at the end of each breath. Inherited loss of a key surfactant component causes pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 1, with abnormal material filling the air spaces. This produces severe respiratory distress in newborns and premature infants that is typically fatal without lung transplantation.
Defective CSF2RA causes SMDP4
originalAlveolar macrophages clear and recycle pulmonary surfactant, and they can only do so when GM-CSF signalling licenses their maturation and catabolic function. The receptor is a heterodimer of a ligand-binding alpha subunit and a shared signalling beta subunit; loss-of-function mutations in the alpha subunit gene block this input, so surfactant lipids and the surfactant proteins A, B, C and D accumulate in alveoli instead of being taken up and degraded. The resulting disorder, pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 4 or hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, fills airspaces with floccular lipoproteinaceous material and impairs gas exchange, presenting as progressive hypoxaemic lung disease in children. The same surfactant components maintain alveolar surface tension and innate defence, so their mishandling links macrophage growth-factor signalling to respiratory failure, with misfolded proprotein forms provoking ER stress, oxidative stress and autophagy in alveolar epithelium.
Alveolar macrophages require GM-CSF signalling, via a receptor of ligand-binding alpha and shared beta subunits, to mature and degrade surfactant. Loss-of-function alpha subunit mutations block this, so surfactant lipids and proteins A-D accumulate, causing hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 4) with progressive hypoxaemic lung disease in children. Misfolded surfactant proproteins also provoke ER stress, oxidative stress and autophagy in alveolar epithelium.—In the lungs, alveolar macrophages need a blood-cell growth factor signal to mature and clear surfactant. Inherited loss of this input causes pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 4, a hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis in which air sacs fill with uncleared material, impairing gas exchange and causing progressive low-oxygen lung disease in children. It links macrophage growth signalling to respiratory failure and alveolar epithelial stress.
Defective SLC34A2 causes PALM
originalAlveolar type II cells recycle phosphate from the airspace for surfactant synthesis, and they do so through the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter NaPi-2b encoded by SLC34A2, which moves divalent phosphate across the apical membrane together with three sodium ions in an electrogenic step driven by the sodium gradient. The same transporter operates, less abundantly, in intestinal, pancreatic, prostatic and renal epithelia, where it contributes to dietary and systemic phosphate handling. When SLC34A2 function is lost, phosphate liberated in alveolar fluid is no longer cleared and precipitates with calcium as microscopic calcium phosphate concretions, producing pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis. Affected individuals are often asymptomatic for years before a slowly progressive decline in gas exchange and lung compliance, which can end in respiratory failure. This links a single epithelial transport activity to surfactant metabolism and to the prevention of ectopic mineralisation in the lung.
SLC34A2 encodes NaPi-2b, an electrogenic sodium-phosphate cotransporter that lets alveolar type II cells recover phosphate from airspaces for surfactant synthesis, and also functions in intestinal and other epithelia. Loss of function leaves phosphate in alveolar fluid, where it precipitates as calcium phosphate microliths, causing pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis. Patients are often asymptomatic for years before slowly progressive decline in gas exchange and respiratory failure.—In the lungs, alveolar type II cells recycle a mineral nutrient from the air sacs for surfactant production; the same activity contributes to mineral handling in intestine, pancreas, prostate and kidney. Inherited loss causes pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, in which tiny mineral stones fill the air sacs. Affected people are often symptom-free for years before slowly declining gas exchange and lung compliance lead to respiratory failure.
Defective ABCA3 causes SMDP3
originalAlveoli stay open at the end of each breath because type II epithelial cells secrete a phospholipid-rich surfactant that lowers surface tension, and ABCA3 is the lipid transporter that loads that material into lamellar bodies, the secretory organelles from which surfactant is released. It moves phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol, the dominant surfactant lipids, from the endoplasmic reticulum membrane into the limiting membrane of the lamellar body, where they are packaged with the surfactant proteins. When ABCA3 is defective, lamellar bodies fail to mature and surfactant is deficient or abnormal, producing pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3: fatal respiratory distress in full-term newborns in severe cases, and chronic childhood interstitial lung disease in milder ones. This places the transporter at the centre of alveolar lipid handling and neonatal lung function.
ABCA3 is a lipid transporter in alveolar type II cells that moves phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol into lamellar bodies, where surfactant is packaged with its proteins to lower surface tension. When defective, lamellar bodies fail to mature and surfactant is deficient, causing surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3. Severe cases cause fatal neonatal respiratory distress, milder ones chronic childhood interstitial lung disease.—Alveoli stay open at the end of each breath because type II cells of the lung secrete surfactant from specialised storage organelles. When loading of these organelles fails, surfactant is deficient or abnormal, causing pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3: fatal respiratory distress in full-term newborns in severe cases and chronic childhood interstitial lung disease in milder ones.
Defective SFTPA2 causes IPF
originalSurfactant protein A2 is one of the pulmonary collectins secreted by alveolar type II cells into the airway, where it helps organise surfactant lipids at the air-liquid interface, regulates surfactant turnover, and opsonises inhaled microbes for clearance. Mutations that disturb the folding of SFTPA2 prevent its secretion: the misfolded protein is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than reaching the alveolar lumen, so its contribution to surfactant homeostasis is lost and the type II cell bears a chronic burden of unfolded protein. The consequence is familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, in which repeated alveolar epithelial injury drives progressive scarring, breathlessness and declining gas exchange, typically fatal from respiratory failure within a few years of diagnosis. This links defective SFTPA2 to alveolar epithelial secretory failure as an initiating event in interstitial lung disease.
Surfactant protein A2 is a collectin secreted by alveolar type II cells that organises surfactant lipids, regulates turnover and opsonises inhaled microbes. Folding mutations trap SFTPA2 in the endoplasmic reticulum, preventing secretion and imposing chronic unfolded protein stress on type II cells. This causes familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, with repeated epithelial injury, progressive scarring and fatal respiratory failure within years.—In the lungs, alveolar type II cells secrete surfactant components that organise the air-liquid interface, regulate surfactant turnover and help clear inhaled microbes. Inherited mutations that block secretion burden these cells and cause familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, with progressive scarring, breathlessness and declining gas exchange, typically fatal from respiratory failure within a few years of diagnosis. Alveolar epithelial injury is the initiating event.

Diseases of nucleotide metabolism (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Defective PNP disrupts phosphorolysis of (deoxy)guanosine and (deoxy)inosine
originalPurine nucleoside phosphorylase normally strips the sugar from inosine, deoxyinosine, guanosine and deoxyguanosine, releasing hypoxanthine or guanine for salvage back into nucleotides and clearing the products of nucleic acid turnover. When the enzyme is defective, this phosphorolysis step fails and its substrates build up; deoxyguanosine is rephosphorylated to dGTP, which poisons ribonucleotide reductase and blocks DNA synthesis in dividing cells. T lymphocytes, with their high deoxynucleoside kinase activity and demanding proliferative programme, are the most vulnerable, so loss of activity produces a profound T cell deficiency with variable B cell involvement, recurrent infection, and in many patients neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The disorder sits alongside adenosine deaminase deficiency as an inborn error of purine catabolism causing combined immunodeficiency, and illustrates how a single salvage reaction supports lymphoid development.
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase removes the sugar from inosine, guanosine and their deoxy forms, releasing bases for salvage. When defective, substrates accumulate and deoxyguanosine becomes dGTP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and blocks DNA synthesis. T lymphocytes are most vulnerable, so deficiency causes profound T cell immunodeficiency with recurrent infection, often with neurological impairment and autoimmunity, paralleling adenosine deaminase deficiency.—Recycling of nucleic acid breakdown products normally supports lymphocyte development. When this step is defective, toxic byproducts build up in dividing cells, and T lymphocytes are most vulnerable, causing profound T cell deficiency with variable B cell involvement, recurrent infections and often neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The disorder is an inborn error of nucleotide metabolism causing combined immunodeficiency in children.
Defective ADA disrupts (deoxy)adenosine deamination
originalAdenosine deaminase converts adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine, the committed step that lets cells dispose of purine nucleosides through the salvage and degradation route toward uric acid. When ADA activity is lost, this deamination step fails and the unprocessed substrates accumulate, with deoxyadenosine being phosphorylated to dATP that poisons ribonucleotide reduction and DNA synthesis. Developing thymocytes and lymphocytes are the cells least able to tolerate this, so the consequence of defective (deoxy)adenosine deamination is severe combined immunodeficiency, with profoundly reduced T, B and NK cells, recurrent infection from infancy, and additional skeletal, neurological and pulmonary features reflecting the enzyme's ubiquitous expression. The disorder is treatable by enzyme replacement, transplantation or gene therapy, making it a model for how a single metabolic clearance reaction sustains adaptive immunity.
Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine for purine disposal. When lost, deoxyadenosine accumulates and is phosphorylated to dATP, which blocks ribonucleotide reduction and DNA synthesis, especially in developing lymphocytes. The result is severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T, B and NK cells and skeletal, neurological and pulmonary features, treatable by enzyme replacement, transplantation or gene therapy.—Clearance of nucleoside breakdown products is essential for immune development. When it fails, toxic byproducts poison developing thymocytes and lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency with very low T, B and NK cells and recurrent infections from infancy, plus skeletal, neurological and lung features. The disorder is treatable by enzyme replacement, bone marrow transplantation or gene therapy, making it a model for how metabolism sustains adaptive immunity.
Defective APRT disrupts adenine salvage
originalAdenine released by polyamine synthesis and nucleic acid turnover is normally recycled rather than degraded, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase performs that salvage step by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto free adenine to give AMP. When the enzyme is defective, this purine salvage route fails and adenine is instead oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to the highly insoluble metabolite 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as crystals in urine and renal tissue. The clinical consequence is APRT deficiency: radiolucent kidney stones, crystalline nephropathy, and progressive renal failure that can recur after transplantation unless xanthine oxidoreductase is inhibited. The biology sits within purine metabolism, where salvage pathways spare the energetic cost of de novo nucleotide synthesis, and it illustrates how loss of a single recycling enzyme causes disease through toxic accumulation of the unsalvaged substrate rather than through nucleotide shortage.
Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase salvages free adenine by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP to make AMP. When defective, adenine is oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which crystallises in urine and kidney. APRT deficiency therefore causes radiolucent kidney stones, crystalline nephropathy and renal failure that can recur after transplant unless xanthine oxidoreductase is inhibited, reflecting toxic accumulation rather than nucleotide shortage.—Recycling of a nucleic acid building block normally spares the energetic cost of making new ones. When recycling fails, the unrecycled material is converted to an insoluble product that crystallises in urine and kidney tissue, causing radiolucent kidney stones, crystalline nephropathy and progressive kidney failure. The disease can recur after kidney transplantation unless treated with a drug that blocks the toxic conversion.
Defective HPRT1 disrupts guanine and hypoxanthine salvage
originalPurine bases released by nucleic acid turnover are normally recycled rather than discarded, and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase is the enzyme that does it, transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto hypoxanthine to make IMP and onto guanine to make GMP. Loss of this salvage activity forces the cells to depend entirely on energetically costly de novo purine synthesis, while the unsalvaged bases are oxidized by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to urate. The consequences in humans are striking: partial deficiency produces gout and urate nephropathy from overproduction, and near-complete deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan disease, with hyperuricaemia, dystonia, cognitive impairment and compulsive self-injurious behaviour reflecting the particular reliance of basal ganglia dopaminergic neurons on purine recycling. The pathway links nucleotide economy to neurodevelopment and to renal handling of uric acid.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase salvages hypoxanthine and guanine into IMP and GMP using PRPP. Without it, cells rely on costly de novo purine synthesis and unsalvaged bases are oxidised to urate. Partial deficiency causes gout and urate nephropathy, while near-complete deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan disease with hyperuricaemia, dystonia, cognitive impairment and self-injury, reflecting basal ganglia dependence on purine recycling.—Recycling of nucleic acid building blocks spares the energy cost of making new ones, and basal ganglia neurons depend particularly on it. Partial loss causes gout and kidney disease from hyperuricaemia, while near-complete loss causes Lesch-Nyhan disease, with dystonia, cognitive impairment and compulsive self-injurious behaviour. The process links nucleotide economy to neurodevelopment and to kidney health.

Diseases of the urea cycle (8)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
OTC main chain variants cause OTC deficiency
originalOrnithine transcarbamylase performs the second step of the urea cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, condensing ornithine with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline and thereby committing waste nitrogen to disposal as urea. Amino acid substitutions in the main chain of the enzyme underlie ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common inherited urea cycle disorder and the only X-linked one. When the enzyme cannot process carbamoyl phosphate, ammonia accumulates in blood, producing encephalopathy, cerebral oedema, coma and death in severely affected newborns. Mutations fall along a severity gradient: those striking catalytic or substrate-binding residues abolish activity and present neonatally, while changes at surface or domain-interface positions leave partial function and surface later, often triggered by protein load, illness or catabolic stress. The pathway connects hepatic nitrogen handling to neurological health, and management relies on nitrogen scavengers and dietary protein restriction.
Ornithine transcarbamylase condenses ornithine with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline, the second urea cycle step in mitochondria. Amino acid substitutions cause ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common and only X-linked urea cycle disorder, with hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, coma and neonatal death. Catalytic-site mutations abolish activity and present neonatally, while surface or interface changes cause later, stress-triggered disease, managed by nitrogen scavengers and protein restriction.—In the liver, waste nitrogen from protein breakdown is disposed of through a dedicated cycle. Inherited defects at its second step cause the most common inherited nitrogen-disposal disorder, and the only X-linked one, with hyperammonaemia causing encephalopathy, brain swelling, coma and death in severely affected newborns. Milder forms appear later, triggered by protein load, illness or catabolic stress, and are managed with nitrogen scavengers and protein restriction.
CPS1 variants cause CPS1 deficiency
originalCarbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of the urea cycle in the liver mitochondrial matrix, condensing ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP into carbamoyl phosphate so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea. Loss-of-function variants in CPS1 cause an autosomal recessive deficiency in which ammonia accumulates, presenting as catastrophic neonatal hyperammonaemia or as later crises provoked by catabolic stress, infection or protein load; untreated episodes produce cerebral oedema and irreversible neurological injury. The enzyme requires allosteric activation by N-acetylglutamate, so truncating mutations upstream of the C-terminal activator-binding domain abolish activity, while missense changes in the bicarbonate and carbamate phosphorylation domains or the integrating domain that channels carbamate between active sites destabilise folding and reduce catalysis. Severity tracks with residual activity, linking this single enzymatic step to whole-body nitrogen homeostasis.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 catalyses the first, rate-limiting urea cycle step in liver mitochondria, forming carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia, bicarbonate and ATP. Recessive CPS1 variants cause hyperammonaemia, neonatal or stress-triggered, with cerebral oedema and neurological injury. The enzyme needs N-acetylglutamate activation; truncations upstream of its binding domain abolish activity, while missense changes in catalytic or channelling domains impair folding, and severity tracks residual activity.—In liver mitochondria, the first and rate-limiting step of nitrogen disposal fails in an autosomal recessive disorder. Patients present with catastrophic neonatal hyperammonaemia or with later crises provoked by catabolic stress, infection or protein load, and untreated episodes cause brain swelling and irreversible neurological injury. Severity tracks residual activity, linking this single step to whole-body nitrogen balance.
NAGS variants cause NAGS deficiency
originalNitrogen from amino acid breakdown leaves the body as urea, and the urea cycle only runs if its first enzyme is switched on by an allosteric activator. N-acetylglutamate synthase makes that activator in the mitochondrial matrix, condensing acetyl-CoA with glutamate to give N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory cofactor of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Loss-of-function variants in NAGS abolish activator production, so carbamoyl phosphate is never formed and the cycle cannot begin. The result is N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency, a rare recessive urea cycle disorder presenting with hyperammonemia, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and encephalopathy, often in the newborn period, with low citrulline and risk of permanent neurological damage or death if untreated. It is distinctive among urea cycle defects in responding to carbamylglutamate, a stable analogue of the missing activator that restores flux.
N-acetylglutamate synthase makes N-acetylglutamate from acetyl-CoA and glutamate in mitochondria, the obligatory activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I that starts the urea cycle. Loss-of-function NAGS variants prevent carbamoyl phosphate formation, causing a rare recessive disorder with neonatal hyperammonaemia, vomiting, seizures, encephalopathy and low citrulline. Uniquely among urea cycle defects, it responds to carbamylglutamate, a stable activator analogue.—In the liver, disposal of nitrogen from amino acid breakdown depends on an activating cofactor made in mitochondria. Its inherited absence causes a rare recessive nitrogen-disposal disorder presenting with hyperammonaemia, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and encephalopathy, often in newborns, with risk of permanent neurological damage or death. Uniquely among such disorders, it responds to oral treatment with a stable replacement for the missing activator.
ASL variants cause argininosuccinate aciduria
originalArgininosuccinate lyase performs the fourth step of the urea cycle, splitting argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea and so that the cycle's arginine supply is regenerated. Loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding this homotetrameric enzyme cause argininosuccinic aciduria, a recessive urea cycle disorder in which argininosuccinate accumulates and ammonia is not cleared. Severe neonatal presentations bring hyperammonemia, encephalopathy and respiratory alkalosis, while milder late-onset disease may declare itself only under catabolic stress or infection. Because the active site is formed at subunit interfaces, different mutant alleles can partially complement one another within a tetramer and leave residual activity, which helps explain the wide clinical spectrum. Beyond ammonia detoxification, the reaction also supplies arginine for nitric oxide synthesis, a likely contributor to the hypertension and neurological features seen in patients.
Argininosuccinate lyase splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate, the fourth urea cycle step that disposes of nitrogen and regenerates arginine. Recessive variants cause argininosuccinic aciduria, with neonatal hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and respiratory alkalosis or milder stress-triggered disease. Intersubunit active sites allow allelic complementation and residual activity, and reduced arginine for nitric oxide synthesis may contribute to hypertension and neurological features.—In the liver, the fourth step of nitrogen disposal also regenerates an amino acid used elsewhere in the body. Inherited recessive loss causes a disorder with hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and respiratory alkalosis in severe newborn cases, while milder late-onset disease appears under catabolic stress or infection. Reduced supply of a vessel-relaxing signal likely contributes to the hypertension and neurological features seen in patients.
OTC leader sequence variants cause OTC deficiency
originalOrnithine transcarbamylase catalyses the second step of the urea cycle inside mitochondria, condensing carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to make citrulline so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea. The enzyme is encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes, so it must be imported: a 33-residue N-terminal leader sequence directs the precursor across the mitochondrial membranes and is proteolytically removed on arrival. Variants that alter this leader are a recognised cause of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common inherited urea cycle disorder and X-linked in inheritance. Such mutations can destabilise the transcript, lower protein levels, and prevent correct mitochondrial targeting and maturation, leaving the mature enzyme absent from the matrix. The result is hyperammonaemia with orotic aciduria, and in severe neonatal presentations encephalopathy, illustrating how a failure of protein targeting alone can disable an entire metabolic route.
Ornithine transcarbamylase forms citrulline from carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine in mitochondria, the second urea cycle step, and is imported using a 33-residue N-terminal leader that is cleaved on arrival. Variants in this leader cause X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency by destabilising transcripts, lowering protein and preventing mitochondrial targeting. The result is hyperammonaemia with orotic aciduria and severe neonatal encephalopathy.—In liver mitochondria, the second step of nitrogen disposal requires that a nuclear-encoded component be delivered into the organelle. Inherited variants disrupting this delivery cause the most common inherited nitrogen-disposal disorder, which is X-linked, producing hyperammonaemia with abnormal urinary acid excretion and, in severe newborn cases, encephalopathy. It illustrates how failed protein targeting alone can disable an entire metabolic route.
ASS1 variants cause citrullinemia
originalArgininosuccinate synthase carries out the third step of the urea cycle, joining citrulline to aspartate in an ATP-dependent condensation to form argininosuccinate, and it is the point at which loss-of-function variants produce type 1 citrullinemia. The enzyme works in the cytosol of hepatocytes, with lower activity in kidney, and its output feeds both nitrogen disposal as urea and the endogenous supply of arginine for downstream uses such as nitric oxide synthesis. Missense changes typically destabilise folding or the citrulline and aspartate binding sites, while nonsense, frameshift and splice-site variants remove the protein altogether; the common G390R allele is recurrent among more than a hundred catalogued mutations. The result is hyperammonemia with raised plasma citrulline, glutamine and orotic acid and low arginine, and in severe neonatal presentations lethargy, vomiting, seizures, coma and death from ammonia-driven encephalopathy.
Argininosuccinate synthase joins citrulline and aspartate into argininosuccinate using ATP, the third urea cycle step, mainly in hepatocyte cytosol, also supplying arginine for nitric oxide synthesis. Loss-of-function variants, including the recurrent G390R among over a hundred, cause type 1 citrullinaemia. Patients have hyperammonaemia with high citrulline, glutamine and orotic acid and low arginine, with severe neonatal lethargy, seizures, coma and death.—In liver cells, and to a lesser extent kidney, the third step of nitrogen disposal fails in a recessive disorder caused by more than a hundred inherited variants, including a recurrent one. Patients develop hyperammonaemia with abnormal blood amino acid levels, and severe newborn presentations bring lethargy, vomiting, seizures, coma and death from encephalopathy. The step also supports the body's supply of an amino acid used for vascular signalling.
ARG1 variants cause hyperargininemia
originalThe final step of the urea cycle is carried out by cytosolic arginase 1, which hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, completing nitrogen disposal and regenerating the ornithine that re-enters the cycle. The enzyme is most abundant in liver, with lower activity in kidney and red cells. Loss-of-function variants in ARG1 cause arginase 1 deficiency, or hyperargininemia, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism in which plasma and cerebrospinal arginine accumulate. Affected children typically present after infancy with progressive spastic paraparesis, developmental regression, seizures and growth failure, a neurological course distinct from the other urea cycle disorders because severe hyperammonemia is uncommon. Treatment relies on protein restriction and nitrogen-scavenging agents. This biology links amino acid catabolism and ureagenesis to arginine availability for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis.
Cytosolic arginase 1, abundant in liver, hydrolyses arginine to urea and ornithine, completing the urea cycle. Recessive ARG1 variants cause hyperargininaemia, with arginine accumulating in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid. Unlike other urea cycle disorders, severe hyperammonaemia is uncommon; children develop progressive spastic paraparesis, developmental regression, seizures and growth failure, treated with protein restriction and nitrogen scavengers.—In the liver, and to a lesser extent kidney and red blood cells, the final step of nitrogen disposal fails in an autosomal recessive inborn error. Affected children typically present after infancy with progressive spastic paraparesis, developmental regression, seizures and growth failure, a neurological course distinct from other nitrogen-disposal disorders because severe hyperammonaemia is uncommon. Treatment relies on protein restriction and nitrogen-scavenging drugs.
SLC25A15 variants cause hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinemia syndrome
originalThe urea cycle spans two compartments, so ornithine made in the cytosol must be carried into mitochondria and the citrulline made there must be carried out. SLC25A15 is the mitochondrial inner-membrane antiporter that performs this exchange, and loss-of-function variants in it cause hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome. Without transport, ornithine accumulates in the cytosol while the matrix is starved of it, leaving carbamoyl phosphate to condense with lysine into homocitrulline and stalling nitrogen disposal; ammonia rises, producing episodic encephalopathy, protein intolerance, spastic paraparesis and developmental impairment. A related carrier, SLC25A2, overlaps in function and partially buffers the defect, which helps explain the variable age of onset and severity. The biology sits at the intersection of amino acid metabolism, mitochondrial solute transport and detoxification of waste nitrogen, and the resulting disorder is managed like other urea cycle defects.
SLC25A15 exchanges cytosolic ornithine for mitochondrial citrulline across the inner membrane, linking the urea cycle's two compartments. Loss-of-function variants cause hyperornithinaemia-hyperammonaemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome: matrix ornithine shortage leads carbamoyl phosphate to react with lysine, forming homocitrulline, and ammonia rises. Patients have episodic encephalopathy, protein intolerance, spastic paraparesis and developmental impairment, partly buffered by SLC25A2.—In the liver, nitrogen disposal spans the cytosol and mitochondria and requires exchange between them. Inherited loss causes a recessive syndrome with episodic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, protein intolerance, spastic paraparesis and developmental impairment, and a partially redundant transporter explains variable age of onset and severity. The condition sits at the intersection of amino acid metabolism and detoxification and is managed like other nitrogen-disposal disorders.

Diseases of branched-chain amino acid catabolism (11)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Isovaleric acidemia
originalLeucine catabolism proceeds through a mitochondrial flavoenzyme, isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, which dehydrogenates isovaleryl-CoA to 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA while reducing FAD; loss of this single step causes isovaleric acidemia, one of the classic organic acidemias. Blocked flux backs up isovaleryl-CoA, which is diverted into isovaleric acid, 3-hydroxyisovalerate, isovalerylglycine and isovalerylcarnitine that accumulate in blood and urine and give affected infants the characteristic odour of sweaty feet. Presentation ranges from neonatal metabolic crisis with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis, hyperammonaemia and seizures to a milder intermittent or nearly asymptomatic course, with poor correlation between mutation and severity. Because the defect lies in branched-chain amino acid breakdown feeding acetyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, catabolic stress and protein load provoke decompensation, and management rests on leucine restriction plus glycine and carnitine conjugation to clear the accumulated acyl groups.
Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial flavoenzyme in leucine catabolism, converts isovaleryl-CoA to 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA, and its loss causes isovaleric acidemia. Accumulated isovaleryl-CoA is diverted into isovaleric acid, glycine and carnitine conjugates, producing a sweaty-feet odour. Presentation ranges from neonatal crisis with acidosis, hyperammonaemia and seizures to mild intermittent disease, provoked by catabolic stress, and is managed with leucine restriction plus glycine and carnitine.—Breakdown of a dietary branched-chain amino acid in mitochondria is blocked in a classic organic acidaemia of infancy. Toxic byproducts accumulate in blood and urine, giving affected infants a characteristic sweaty-feet odour. Presentation ranges from neonatal metabolic crisis with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis, hyperammonaemia and seizures to milder intermittent courses, provoked by catabolic stress or protein load and managed by dietary restriction and supplements.
Loss-of-function mutations in DBT cause MSUD2
originalThe branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex commits leucine, isoleucine and valine to oxidative breakdown, and mutations that destroy the integrity of its E2 core subunit cause the maple syrup urine disease subtype known as MSUD2. The complex is built from E1 decarboxylase subunits, the dihydrolipoyl transacylase E2 component encoded by DBT, and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase; E2 carries the lipoyl groups that accept the acyl intermediate and pass reducing equivalents on, so loss of functional DBT stalls the whole complex regardless of intact E1. Branched-chain amino acids and their ketoacids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and risk of cerebral oedema. Management relies on dietary restriction of these amino acids, placing this step at the centre of branched-chain amino acid catabolism and nitrogen handling.
The branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex commits leucine, isoleucine and valine to oxidation, and mutations disrupting its DBT-encoded E2 transacylase cause MSUD2. E2 carries lipoyl groups that accept acyl intermediates, so its loss stalls the complex despite intact E1. Branched-chain amino acids and ketoacids accumulate, causing sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and cerebral oedema, managed by dietary restriction.—Breakdown of dietary branched-chain amino acids fails in a subtype of maple syrup urine disease. The accumulating amino acids and their byproducts reach toxic levels in blood, urine and brain, producing sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and risk of brain swelling, typically in newborns. Management relies on lifelong dietary restriction of these amino acids, placing this step at the centre of protein catabolism.
H139Hfs13* PPM1K causes a mild variant of MSUD
originalBranched-chain amino acids from dietary protein are disposed of by oxidative decarboxylation of their ketoacid derivatives, a committed and irreversible step performed by the mitochondrial branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex built from BCKDHA and BCKDHB (E1), DBT (E2) and the shared DLD (E3). The products feed acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, and when the complex fails, leucine, isoleucine and valine and their ketoacids accumulate to neurotoxic levels, producing the encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and characteristic sweet-smelling urine of maple syrup urine disease. Complex activity is switched off by inhibitory phosphorylation of the E1 beta subunit and switched back on by the mitochondrial phosphatase PPM1K, which removes that mark. A frameshift truncating PPM1K destabilises the phosphatase, leaves the dehydrogenase locked in its phosphorylated inactive state, and causes a mild, variant form of the disease that is corrected by restoring wild-type phosphatase.
The mitochondrial branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex irreversibly decarboxylates branched-chain ketoacids, feeding the citric acid cycle; failure causes maple syrup urine disease with encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and sweet-smelling urine. Activity is switched off by E1 phosphorylation and restored by the phosphatase PPM1K. A PPM1K frameshift destabilises the phosphatase, locking the complex inactive and causing a mild variant corrected by restoring wild-type phosphatase.—Disposal of dietary branched-chain amino acids in mitochondria is a committed step whose failure produces maple syrup urine disease, with neurotoxic accumulation, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and sweet-smelling urine. The step is switched on and off according to nutritional and hormonal state. A particular inherited defect in this switching causes a mild, variant form of the disease, showing that regulation as well as catalysis matters clinically.
Loss-of-function mutations in DLD cause MSUD3/DLDD
originalDihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase is the shared E3 subunit of three mitochondrial alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, so recessive loss-of-function mutations in it disable branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase at once. The resulting deficiency presents with lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, branched-chain amino acids and urinary alpha-keto acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because the branched-chain complex is affected, the condition is classed with maple syrup urine disease, but its pleiotropic biochemistry sets it apart from defects in the complex's own catalytic subunits, the E1 alpha and beta chains and the E2 transacylase. Mechanistically the E3 component reoxidizes the lipoamide arm after decarboxylation, passing electrons to NAD+; without it, oxidative decarboxylation stalls and both amino acid catabolism and entry of carbon into the citric acid cycle fail. Compound heterozygosity is common and residual activity predicts severity poorly.
Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase is the shared E3 subunit of branched-chain ketoacid, alpha-ketoglutarate and pyruvate dehydrogenase complexes, reoxidising lipoamide and reducing NAD+. Recessive mutations disable all three, causing lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, branched-chain amino acids and alpha-keto acids, and neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Classed with maple syrup urine disease, it differs biochemically, and residual activity predicts severity poorly.—A shared component of several mitochondrial energy-producing complexes is lost in a recessive disorder that disables multiple metabolic routes at once. Patients present with lactic acidosis, accumulation of branched-chain amino acids and organic acids, progressive neurological deterioration and sometimes liver involvement. It is classed with maple syrup urine disease, but its broader biochemistry sets it apart, and residual activity predicts severity poorly.
3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency
originalLeucine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a biotin-dependent carboxylation step, and loss of that step defines 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, the most common organic aciduria found by newborn screening at roughly one in 50,000 births. The enzyme converts 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA as the fourth reaction of leucine catabolism, and is built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries a covalently attached biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity. Recessive mutations in either subunit destabilise the complex, impair catalysis, or block biotinylation, so leucine-derived intermediates spill over into 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine. Outcomes vary widely: most affected individuals remain mildly affected or asymptomatic, while a small fraction present in the neonatal period with metabolic decompensation and severe neurological injury.
3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme of leucine catabolism, converts 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA using MCCC1 (biotin-carrying) and MCCC2 (carboxyltransferase) subunits. Recessive mutations in either impair the enzyme, so intermediates spill into 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine. It is the commonest organic aciduria on newborn screening; most individuals are mild or asymptomatic, few have severe neonatal decompensation.—In mitochondria, a vitamin-dependent step in breakdown of a dietary branched-chain amino acid is lost in the most common organic aciduria found by newborn screening, around one in 50,000 births. Inheritance is recessive. Outcomes vary widely: most affected individuals remain mildly affected or asymptomatic, while a small fraction present in the neonatal period with metabolic decompensation and severe neurological injury.
Mitochondrial short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase deficiency 1
originalShort-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase deficiency is an inborn error of mitochondrial metabolism caused by loss-of-function mutations in ECHS1, the hydratase that adds water across the double bond of short-chain enoyl-CoA intermediates. The enzyme serves two converging routes: the hydration step of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, and the degradation of branched-chain amino acids, where its preferred substrate is the valine-derived methylacrylyl-CoA and it also acts on the leucine intermediate 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA while binding but barely turning over the isoleucine-derived tiglyl-CoA. When the enzyme is absent, reactive methylacrylyl-CoA and related acyl-CoA species accumulate and damage mitochondrial proteins, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with basal ganglia lesions, epilepsy, cardiac involvement and severe developmental and neurological regression. The disorder illustrates how a single hydratase step links amino acid catabolism to cellular energy supply and to metabolite detoxification in the brain.
ECHS1 is a mitochondrial hydratase acting in fatty acid beta-oxidation and branched-chain amino acid breakdown, preferring valine-derived methylacrylyl-CoA. Loss-of-function mutations cause short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase deficiency, in which reactive acyl-CoA species accumulate and damage mitochondrial proteins. Patients develop Leigh-like encephalopathy with basal ganglia lesions, epilepsy, cardiac involvement and neurological regression, linking amino acid catabolism to brain energy supply.—This inborn error of mitochondrial metabolism disrupts both fat burning and breakdown of dietary branched-chain amino acids. Reactive byproducts accumulate and damage mitochondria, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with basal ganglia lesions, epilepsy, cardiac involvement and severe developmental and neurological regression in infants and children. It illustrates how one step links amino acid breakdown to energy supply and detoxification in the brain.
Loss-of-function mutations in BCKDHA or BCKDHB cause MSUD
originalBranched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine are degraded by a mitochondrial multienzyme complex whose first, committed step is oxidative decarboxylation of their transaminated keto acids. That reaction is carried out by the E1 heterotetramer built from BCKDHA and BCKDHB subunits docked onto the DBT transacylase core. Severe loss-of-function mutations in either E1 subunit disrupt subunit interfaces or the hydrophobic core, so the complex fails to assemble and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase activity is lost. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing classic maple syrup urine disease with its characteristic sweet-smelling urine, neonatal encephalopathy, cerebral oedema and, untreated, death; management depends on lifelong dietary restriction. Mutations at BCKDHA define MSUD type 1A and those at BCKDHB type 1B, the latter accounting for roughly a third of cases.
The first committed step of branched-chain amino acid breakdown, oxidative decarboxylation of keto acids, is performed by the E1 heterotetramer of BCKDHA and BCKDHB on the DBT core. Severe mutations in either subunit disrupt assembly and abolish activity, causing classic maple syrup urine disease with sweet-smelling urine, neonatal encephalopathy, cerebral oedema and death if untreated. BCKDHA defines type 1A, BCKDHB type 1B.—Breakdown of dietary branched-chain amino acids fails in classic maple syrup urine disease, an inherited disorder of newborns. Toxic accumulation in blood, urine and brain produces sweet-smelling urine, neonatal encephalopathy, brain swelling and, untreated, death; management depends on lifelong dietary restriction. Defects in two different components define subtypes 1A and 1B, the latter accounting for roughly a third of cases.
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase deficiency
originalLoss of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase activity leaves the cell unable to brake catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine, and the resulting shortage of these amino acids causes a neurological disorder with impaired intellectual development, microcephaly and autistic features. Normally the kinase phosphorylates serine residues on the E1 alpha subunit of the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, switching off the irreversible oxidative decarboxylation step that commits branched-chain ketoacids to degradation; this sets how much of the dietary supply is spared for protein synthesis and neurotransmitter-related metabolism. When the kinase is inactivated, the complex, built from the E1 alpha and beta subunits with the E2 transacylase and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, runs unrestrained, and branched-chain amino acids fall in plasma, tissue and urine. It is the mirror image of maple syrup urine disease, and symptoms respond to dietary branched-chain amino acid supplementation.
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase phosphorylates the E1 alpha subunit to switch off irreversible branched-chain ketoacid degradation, sparing leucine, isoleucine and valine for protein synthesis. When the kinase is lost, the complex runs unrestrained and branched-chain amino acids fall in plasma and tissue. This mirror image of maple syrup urine disease causes intellectual disability, microcephaly and autistic features that respond to dietary supplementation.—Inherited loss of a brake on breakdown of dietary branched-chain amino acids causes a neurological disorder with impaired intellectual development, microcephaly and autistic features, because these essential nutrients become depleted in plasma, tissues and urine. Normally the brake spares dietary supply for protein synthesis and brain metabolism. The condition mirrors maple syrup urine disease, and symptoms respond to dietary amino acid supplementation.
Beta-ketothiolase deficiency
originalBeta-ketothiolase deficiency, also called alpha-methylacetoacetic aciduria, is an inherited error of branched-chain amino acid and ketone body metabolism caused by loss of the mitochondrial enzyme ACAT1. Normally ACAT1 performs the thiolytic cleavage of 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA into propionyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA, the final step of isoleucine catabolism, and also handles acetoacetyl-CoA during ketone body utilisation. Mutations that destabilise the protein or abolish its activity cause isoleucine intermediates and their organic acid derivatives to accumulate in blood and urine, the diagnostic hallmark. Affected children typically present between six and eighteen months with ketoacidotic crises, vomiting, lethargy and occasionally coma, often provoked by infection or fasting; neonatal onset is unusual. As in other branched-chain metabolic disorders, genotype predicts severity poorly, and management rests on avoiding catabolic stress.
Beta-ketothiolase deficiency, or alpha-methylacetoacetic aciduria, results from loss of mitochondrial ACAT1, which cleaves 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA into propionyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA in isoleucine catabolism and also handles acetoacetyl-CoA in ketone utilisation. Isoleucine-derived organic acids accumulate diagnostically. Children usually present between six and eighteen months with infection- or fasting-triggered ketoacidotic crises, and management avoids catabolic stress.—An inherited mitochondrial error of amino acid and ketone body metabolism causes characteristic organic acids to accumulate in blood and urine. Affected children typically present between six and eighteen months with ketoacidotic crises, vomiting, lethargy and occasionally coma, often provoked by infection or fasting; neonatal onset is unusual. Genotype predicts severity poorly, and management rests on avoiding catabolic stress.
3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency
originalValine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a reactive thioester intermediate, and the loss of the hydrolase that clears it defines 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. HIBCH normally catalyses the fifth step of valine catabolism, hydrolysing 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA to free 3-hydroxyisobutyrate and coenzyme A so the pathway can continue toward methylmalonate semialdehyde and eventually succinyl-CoA. When the enzyme is defective, the unhydrolysed acyl-CoA accumulates and, like the upstream intermediates that build up in ECHS1 deficiency, behaves as a reactive electrophile that modifies cysteine residues in proteins such as those of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. The clinical result is a Leigh-like encephalopathy: psychomotor regression, developmental delay, neurodegeneration and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions. It illustrates how a single branched-chain amino acid catabolic step protects the brain's energy metabolism from its own intermediates.
HIBCH hydrolyses 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA to 3-hydroxyisobutyrate and CoA, the fifth step of mitochondrial valine catabolism. In recessive HIBCH deficiency, the reactive acyl-CoA accumulates and, as in ECHS1 deficiency, modifies protein cysteines including those of pyruvate dehydrogenase. The result is Leigh-like encephalopathy with psychomotor regression, developmental delay, neurodegeneration and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions.—Breakdown of a dietary branched-chain amino acid in mitochondria produces a reactive intermediate that must be cleared, and inherited loss of clearance causes an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. The accumulated intermediate damages the brain's energy machinery, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with psychomotor regression, developmental delay, neurodegeneration and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions in infants and children.
3-methylglutaconic aciduria
originalLeucine, once its carbon skeleton is broken down, passes through a mitochondrial hydratase step that converts 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA, feeding the amino acid's carbons into ketone body and acetyl-CoA production. The enzyme AUH carries out this fifth reaction of leucine catabolism, and loss-of-function mutations that destabilise or inactivate it cause the autosomal recessive disorder 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. Blocking the step backs up the pathway, so 3-methylglutaconic acid, 3-methylglutaric acid and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid accumulate and spill into the urine, where they serve as the diagnostic signature. Clinical severity is unpredictable, ranging from an incidental biochemical finding to metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and coma, a spread that reflects how much residual enzyme activity remains and how heavily a given tissue depends on leucine oxidation for energy.
The mitochondrial hydratase AUH converts 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to HMG-CoA, the fifth step of leucine catabolism feeding ketone body and acetyl-CoA production. Recessive loss-of-function mutations cause 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, with 3-methylglutaconic, 3-methylglutaric and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acids accumulating in urine. Severity ranges from incidental finding to acidosis, encephalopathy and coma, depending on residual activity and tissue reliance on leucine oxidation.—Breakdown of a dietary branched-chain amino acid in mitochondria, feeding carbon toward ketone bodies and energy production, fails in an autosomal recessive organic aciduria recognised by its urinary signature. Clinical severity is unpredictable, ranging from an incidental laboratory finding to metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and coma, depending on residual activity and on how heavily tissues rely on this route for energy.

Gene Silencing by RNA (6)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Post-transcriptional silencing by small RNAs
originalSmall RNAs give cells a sequence-specific way to shut off messages that have already been made, tuning the output of hundreds of genes and enforcing the developmental and stress programmes that microRNAs control. An Argonaute protein loaded with a microRNA or siRNA guide scans mRNAs for complementarity; when the match is exact, AGO2, the only human Argonaute with endonuclease activity, slices the target, while imperfect pairing instead represses translation and speeds deadenylation and decay. AGO1, AGO3 and AGO4 lack cleavage activity and work only through this second route. The TNRC6 scaffolds bind Argonaute and recruit the deadenylase and decapping machinery that carries out the silencing, concentrating the complex in cytoplasmic foci. The same guide-directed recognition can also feed back on chromatin to silence transcription. Loss of this post-transcriptional silencing deregulates proliferation and differentiation, and Argonaute-microRNA circuits are broadly disturbed in cancer.
Argonaute proteins loaded with microRNA or siRNA guides silence complementary mRNAs, tuning hundreds of genes and enforcing developmental and stress programmes. With exact pairing AGO2, the only slicing human Argonaute, cleaves the target, while imperfect pairing represses translation and accelerates decay via TNRC6 scaffolds recruiting deadenylase and decapping machinery in cytoplasmic foci. Loss deregulates proliferation and differentiation, and these circuits are disturbed in cancer.—Small RNA-guided silencing lets cells switch off messages that have already been made, tuning hundreds of genes and enforcing developmental and stress programmes in humans and other animals. It is essential for orderly proliferation and differentiation, which become deregulated when it is lost. These silencing circuits are broadly disturbed in cancer, making the process relevant to tumour biology and to therapeutic gene silencing.
Small interfering RNA (siRNA) biogenesis
originalLong double-stranded RNA, whether from a virus or from transcribed repeats and transposons in the genome, is converted here into the short guides that silence matching transcripts. siRNA biogenesis is the entry point of RNA interference, giving cells a sequence-specific way to suppress parasitic nucleic acids and providing the basis for experimental and therapeutic gene knockdown. DICER1 cleaves the duplex into 21-25 nucleotide products while bound to TARBP2 or PRKRA within a RISC-loading complex, and the duplex is handed to an Argonaute protein; of the four human Argonautes, AGO2 is the one with slicer activity and is found largely on the cytosolic face of the rough endoplasmic reticulum as well as in the nucleus. The passenger strand is discarded, and the translin-associated nuclease pair TSN and TSNAX contributes to processing the discarded RNA.
siRNA biogenesis, the entry point of RNA interference, converts long double-stranded RNA from viruses, repeats or transposons into short guides that silence matching transcripts, underpinning experimental and therapeutic knockdown. DICER1 with TARBP2 or PRKRA cuts duplexes into 21-25 nucleotide products and loads them onto Argonaute, chiefly slicer-competent AGO2. The passenger strand is discarded, with TSN and TSNAX helping process it.—Long double-stranded RNA from viruses, or from transcribed repeats and transposons in the genome, is turned into short guides that silence matching transcripts. This entry point of RNA interference gives cells a sequence-specific defence against parasitic genetic elements and viruses, and it underlies experimental and therapeutic gene knockdown, including approved small interfering RNA medicines.
PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) biogenesis
originalGerm cells must keep transposons from mobilising in the genome they pass to the next generation, and piRNA biogenesis supplies the small RNAs that enforce that silence. Long precursor transcripts are made by RNA polymerase II from piRNA clusters, individual transposons and intergenic regions, then processed without Dicer: the mitochondrial phospholipase D PLD6 generates mature 5' ends, an exonuclease trims the 3' end, and HENMT1 adds a 2'-O-methyl mark that stabilises the 26-30 nucleotide product. Loaded PIWI proteins split the labour, with PIWIL1 and PIWIL2 acting in cytoplasmic cleavage and a ping-pong amplification loop, while PIWIL4 with TDRD9 enters the nucleus to direct DNA methylation of target loci. Tudor-domain partners, the helicase MOV10L1, MAEL and chaperone activity organise these complexes in germ granules. Loss of the pathway derepresses L1 elements and arrests spermatogenesis, causing male infertility.
In germ cells, piRNA biogenesis supplies small RNAs that keep transposons silent: Pol II precursor transcripts are processed without Dicer: PLD6 forms 5' ends, an exonuclease trims 3' ends and HENMT1 methylates them. PIWIL1 and PIWIL2 cleave targets and amplify piRNAs in a ping-pong loop, while PIWIL4 with TDRD9 directs nuclear DNA methylation, organised by Tudor proteins and MOV10L1. Loss derepresses L1 elements, causing male infertility.—Germ cells must stop transposons from mobilising in the genome they pass to the next generation, and small RNAs made in germ cells enforce that silence in the male germline. Loss of this process reactivates mobile elements and arrests sperm production, causing male infertility, which shows its importance for fertility and for the integrity of inherited genomes.
MicroRNA (miRNA) biogenesis
originalMicroRNAs are short RNAs that tune the output of most human genes, and their biogenesis is the multi-step route from a transcribed hairpin to a loaded silencing complex. The pathway sets how strongly hundreds of mRNAs are translated and degraded, shaping differentiation, proliferation and stress responses; loss of the processing machinery is embryonically lethal, and its disruption is a recurrent feature of tumours. RNA polymerase II generates a primary transcript whose hairpin is cropped in the nucleus by DROSHA with its partner DGCR8, exported by Exportin-5 in a Ran-GTP-dependent step, and cut by DICER1 with TARBP2 or PRKRA to a short duplex. One strand is discarded and the guide strand is retained by an Argonaute protein, of which AGO2 alone can slice highly complementary targets, forming the effector complex that directs post-transcriptional silencing.
MicroRNA biogenesis converts transcribed hairpins into silencing complexes that tune translation and decay of many mRNAs, shaping differentiation, proliferation and stress responses; its loss is embryonically lethal and its disruption common in tumours. DROSHA-DGCR8 crops primary transcripts in the nucleus, Exportin-5 exports them, and DICER1 with TARBP2 or PRKRA cuts duplexes. Argonaute retains the guide strand, with AGO2 alone able to slice.—Short regulatory RNAs tune the output of most human genes, shaping differentiation, proliferation and stress responses. Their production is essential: losing the processing machinery is lethal in embryos, and its disruption is a recurrent feature of tumours. The process therefore links gene regulation to development and cancer and underlies sequence-specific post-transcriptional control throughout the body.
tRNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA or tRNA-related fragment, tRF) biogenesis
originalTransfer RNAs are not only adaptors for translation; they are also substrates for regulated cleavage that yields tRNA-derived small RNAs, and this biogenesis route is how cells convert a stress signal into a new class of regulatory RNA. Longer tRNA halves arise from a single cut in or near the anticodon loop, while shorter fragments come from cleavage closer to the 5' or 3' end, and 3' trailers left over from precursor maturation persist as their own species. Among the ribonucleases implicated are the secreted, endocytosed angiogenin, which cuts the anticodon loop under starvation and other stresses, the double-strand-specific DICER1, and ELAC2, which releases 3' trailers from particular tRNA precursors. Production is induced by hypoxia, oxidative stress, nutrient deprivation, hormones and viral infection, linking tRNA metabolism to translational repression, stress granule formation and gene silencing.
Transfer RNAs can be cleaved into tRNA-derived small RNAs, converting stress signals into regulatory RNAs. Anticodon cuts yield tRNA halves, cuts nearer the ends yield shorter fragments, and 3' trailers from precursor processing persist; angiogenin cleaves anticodon loops under starvation and stress, and DICER1 and ELAC2 contribute. Hypoxia, oxidative stress, nutrient deprivation, hormones and viruses induce production, linking tRNA metabolism to translational repression, stress granules and silencing.—Under stress, cells generate small regulatory RNAs by cleaving transfer RNAs, converting a stress signal into a new layer of gene control. Production rises with low oxygen, oxidative stress, nutrient deprivation, hormones and viral infection, linking these conditions to reduced protein synthesis, stress granule formation and gene silencing. The process matters for cell survival under stress and has been implicated in cancer and neurodegeneration.
Transcriptional regulation by small RNAs
originalSmall RNAs are best known for silencing messenger RNAs in the cytoplasm, but the same machinery also works in the nucleus, where it can switch target genes on or off at the level of transcription itself. Argonaute proteins loaded with microRNAs are carried across the nuclear envelope by importin-8 and by RAN-dependent import of the shuttling scaffold TNRC6A, then engage chromatin and RNA polymerase II at loci whose sequences match the guide RNA. The outcome depends on the chromatin marks recruited: DNA cytosine methylation with histone H3 lysine-9 and lysine-27 methylation accompany transcriptional gene silencing, whereas H3 lysine-4 methylation accompanies RNA activation, which is why core histones and the full polymerase II complex accompany the Argonautes here. Nuclear small RNAs have additionally been linked to alternative splicing choices and to the response to DNA double-strand breaks, extending guide-RNA specificity into genome maintenance.
Small RNA machinery also acts in the nucleus to switch genes on or off transcriptionally. MicroRNA-loaded Argonautes are imported by importin-8 and RAN-dependent TNRC6A import, then engage chromatin and RNA polymerase II at complementary loci. DNA methylation with H3K9 and H3K27 methylation accompanies silencing, whereas H3K4 methylation accompanies RNA activation, and nuclear small RNAs also influence alternative splicing and the double-strand break response.—Small RNA guides usually silence messages in the cytoplasm, but in the nucleus of human cells they can switch target genes on or off at the level of transcription. This nuclear role extends guide-RNA specificity to gene activation, silencing, alternative splicing choices and the response to DNA breaks, linking small RNAs to genome maintenance and suggesting routes for therapeutic gene activation.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression (12)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
ERCC6 (CSB) and EHMT2 (G9a) positively regulate rRNA expression
originalOnly about half the ribosomal RNA gene copies in a nucleus are transcriptionally active at any time, and this pathway describes how ERCC6 (CSB) and the histone methyltransferase EHMT2 (G9a) keep that active fraction switched on, setting the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth. CSB is recruited through TTF1 bound at the Sal box terminator of rRNA repeats and brings in G9a, which dimethylates histone H3 lysine 9 across the transcribed region; CBX3 (HP1gamma) reads that mark and reinforces polymerase I output, a loop that persists only while transcription continues. The accompanying nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase components, including CHD3/CHD4, HDAC1/2, MTA and RBBP4/7 subunits, act on the same chromatin to shape rRNA gene state. Loss of CSB function deregulates polymerase I transcription and contributes to the growth failure and neurodegeneration of Cockayne syndrome.
ERCC6 (CSB) and the methyltransferase G9a keep the active fraction of rRNA genes switched on, setting ribosome biogenesis capacity. CSB is recruited via TTF1 at rDNA terminators and brings G9a, which dimethylates H3K9 across transcribed regions; HP1gamma reads this and reinforces polymerase I output while transcription continues. NuRD-type components also act there, and CSB loss contributes to Cockayne syndrome growth failure and neurodegeneration.—Only about half of the ribosomal RNA gene copies in a nucleus are active at any time, and keeping that fraction switched on sets the cell's capacity for ribosome production and growth. Loss of this function deregulates ribosome production and contributes to the growth failure and neurodegeneration of Cockayne syndrome, an inherited disorder that also features photosensitivity and premature ageing.
NoRC negatively regulates rRNA expression
originalRibosome production is expensive, and cells keep only a fraction of their hundreds of rRNA gene copies transcriptionally active; the nucleolar remodeling complex is how the rest are shut down and kept that way. TIP5 (BAZ2A) partnered with the ATP-dependent remodeller SNF2H repositions the promoter nucleosome into a silent configuration, guided to rDNA by a promoter-associated noncoding RNA bound through its TAM domain and by an interaction with transcription termination factor TTF-I at a promoter-proximal site. Recruitment of SIN3-associated HDAC1 and HDAC2 removes histone acetylation, and DNMT1 and DNMT3B together with the methyl-CpG reader MBD2 impose heritable CpG methylation, locking copies off across cell divisions. The silenced state opposes the RNA polymerase I machinery and its SL1/UBTF initiation factors listed here, setting rRNA output, nucleolar organisation and genomic stability of the repeat array; loss of this restraint accompanies unchecked growth in cancer.
The nucleolar remodelling complex silences surplus rRNA gene copies. TIP5 with the remodeller SNF2H, guided by promoter-associated noncoding RNA and TTF-I, repositions the promoter nucleosome into a silent state, while SIN3-HDAC1/2 deacetylate histones and DNMT1, DNMT3B and MBD2 impose heritable CpG methylation. This opposes polymerase I initiation, governing rRNA output, nucleolar organisation and repeat stability; its loss accompanies cancer growth.—Ribosome production is costly, so cells keep only a fraction of their many ribosomal RNA gene copies active and silence the rest stably across cell divisions. This restraint sets ribosome output, nucleolar organisation and the genomic stability of the repeat array in the nucleolus. Loss of this restraint accompanies unchecked growth in cancer, linking nucleolar silencing to tumour proliferation.
DNA methylation
originalCytosine methylation is the chemical mark that lets a cell keep a stable record of which genes it should not express, and it is copied to daughter cells at each division. Three active methyltransferases transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine to cytosine, mostly in CG dinucleotides: DNMT1 acts on hemimethylated sites generated by replication and so maintains existing patterns, while DNMT3A and DNMT3B, aided by the catalytically inactive DNMT3L, place new marks during the genome-wide remethylation that follows early embryonic and germline erasure. UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated DNA and modified histones and recruits DNMT1 to replicating chromatin, which explains why core histones accompany the enzymes here and links methylation to histone marks. Methylated promoters and CG islands are silenced, supporting imprinting, X inactivation and repression of repeats; aberrant patterns and DNMT3A mutations are recurrent in cancer and overgrowth syndromes.
Cytosine methylation records which genes should stay silent and is inherited through divisions. DNMT1, recruited by UHRF1 to hemimethylated DNA after replication, maintains patterns, while DNMT3A and DNMT3B with inactive DNMT3L establish new marks after embryonic and germline erasure, linking methylation to histone marks. Methylated promoters support imprinting, X inactivation and repeat repression, and aberrant methylation and DNMT3A mutations occur in cancer and overgrowth syndromes.—Chemical marking of DNA lets cells keep a stable, heritable record of genes to keep off, copied at each division and re-established after erasure in early embryos and germ cells. It supports genomic imprinting, X-chromosome inactivation and repression of repetitive elements. Aberrant patterns are recurrent in cancer, and inherited or acquired defects cause overgrowth syndromes and contribute to blood cancers such as acute myeloid leukaemia.
PRC2 methylates histones and DNA
originalPolycomb Repressive Complex 2 lays down the initiating mark of heritable gene silencing, trimethylating lysine 27 of histone H3 to keep developmental regulators off in cells where they do not belong. This is how lineage decisions are made stable and inherited through division; its loss or hyperactivity underlies developmental syndromes and cancers, and gain-of-function EZH2 mutations drive lymphoma. The catalytic subunit EZH1 or EZH2 works only within a core containing EED and SUZ12, with RBBP4/RBBP7 and accessory factors such as JARID2, AEBP2, MTF2 and the PHF1/PHF19 Polycomb-like proteins shaping recruitment to CpG-rich, unmethylated promoters; EZHIP restrains catalysis. The resulting H3K27me3 is read by PRC1, which ubiquitinates H2A and locks in repression. PRC2 also associates with DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B, linking histone methylation to CpG DNA methylation and longer-term epigenetic memory.
Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 trimethylates histone H3 lysine 27 to keep developmental regulators heritably silent, stabilising lineage decisions; its dysregulation causes developmental syndromes and cancers, including EZH2-driven lymphoma. EZH1 or EZH2 functions with EED and SUZ12, with accessory factors guiding recruitment to CpG-rich promoters and EZHIP restraining activity. PRC1 reads H3K27me3, and PRC2 associates with DNA methyltransferases for longer-term memory.—Heritable gene silencing keeps developmental regulators off in cells where they do not belong, making lineage decisions stable through cell division during embryonic development. Its loss or overactivity underlies developmental overgrowth syndromes and cancers, and gain-of-function mutations drive lymphoma, making it a cancer drug target. It also connects to longer-term epigenetic memory across cell generations.
Regulation of endogenous retroelements by KRAB-ZFP proteins
originalRoughly half the human genome is retroelement-derived, and keeping those sequences transcriptionally silent is the job of the KRAB zinc finger protein family, the largest group of transcription regulators encoded by our genome. Each KRAB-ZFP uses its zinc finger array to recognise a particular class of transposable element, and the family has expanded in step with retroelement invasion, an evolutionary arms race in which younger elements are bound by fewer factors. Silencing is executed through the scaffold TRIM28, which binds the KRAB domain, is SUMOylated via UBE2I and SUMO2, and recruits effectors: the histone H3K9 trimethyltransferase SETDB1 with its partner ATF7IP, heterochromatin protein HP1, and the NuRD deacetylase complex built on HDAC1/2, MTA and CHD3/4 subunits. The resulting heterochromatin protects genome stability, especially in early embryos and germ cells, and its loss permits retrotransposition, aberrant transcription and innate immune activation.
