KRAB zinc finger proteins, the largest human transcription regulator family, silence the retroelements that make up half the genome, each recognising particular transposon classes in an evolutionary arms race. Their KRAB domain binds TRIM28, which after SUMOylation recruits SETDB1-ATF7IP for H3K9 trimethylation, HP1 and NuRD deacetylases. The resulting heterochromatin protects genome stability in embryos and germ cells; its loss allows retrotransposition and innate immune activation.—Roughly half the human genome derives from retroelements, and keeping them transcriptionally silent protects genome stability, especially in early embryos and germ cells. The largest family of transcription regulators in our genome has expanded in an evolutionary arms race with these elements. Loss of silencing permits retrotransposition, aberrant transcription and innate immune activation, with consequences for development and disease.
TET1,2,3 and TDG demethylate DNA
originalActive removal of DNA methylation lets cells erase an epigenetic mark rather than wait for it to be diluted by replication, and it is how imprints are erased in primordial germ cells and how the paternal genome is demethylated in the zygote. The TET dioxygenases oxidize 5-methylcytosine stepwise to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine; thymine DNA glycosylase then excises the formyl- and carboxyl-modified bases, leaving an abasic site that base excision repair restores to unmodified cytosine. The oxidized intermediates are themselves abundant marks in embryonic stem cells and neurons, where TET1 expression tracks neuronal activity, while TET3 acts in oocytes and zygotes. TET2 predominates in haematopoietic stem cells and behaves as a tumour suppressor, its loss-of-function mutations being recurrent in myeloid malignancy. The pathway thus links chromatin state, developmental reprogramming and DNA repair chemistry.
Active DNA demethylation erases methylation without replication, removing imprints in primordial germ cells and demethylating the paternal zygotic genome. TET dioxygenases oxidise 5-methylcytosine stepwise, and thymine DNA glycosylase excises formyl and carboxyl forms for base excision repair to restore cytosine. Intermediates are abundant in stem cells and neurons; TET3 acts in oocytes, and TET2, a myeloid tumour suppressor, is often mutated in leukaemia.—Active erasure of DNA marks lets cells reset their epigenetic state, as when parental imprints are erased in primordial germ cells and the paternal genome is reprogrammed in the zygote. The process is prominent in embryonic stem cells, in neurons, where it tracks neuronal activity, and in oocytes. In blood stem cells it acts as a tumour suppressor, and its loss is recurrent in myeloid malignancies.
Formation of WDR5-containing histone-modifying complexes
originalWDR5 is a scaffolding hub that nucleates chromatin-modifying assemblies, and this pathway covers how those complexes are built. WDR5 joins RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 to form the WRAD module that licenses and positions the six KMT2 methyltransferases (KMT2A-D, SETD1A, SETD1B), which deposit mono-, di- and trimethylation on histone H3 lysine 4 at active promoters and enhancers. Complex-specific partners diversify targeting: MEN1 and the protease TASP1 with KMT2A/B, KDM6A, NCOA6, PAXIP1 and PAGR1 with KMT2C/D, and CXXC1 with WDR82 in the SET1 complexes. WDR5 also sits in the GCN5/PCAF-ATAC and KAT8-NSL acetyltransferase complexes, linking H3K4 methylation to histone acetylation. This machinery sets Hox gene expression during embryonic patterning and lineage specification; germline loss causes chromatinopathies such as Kabuki and Wiedemann-Steiner syndromes, and KMT2A rearrangement drives mixed lineage leukemia, making the WDR5 interface a drug target.
WDR5 scaffolds chromatin-modifying complexes, forming the WRAD module with RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 that enables six KMT2/SET1 methyltransferases to methylate H3K4 at promoters and enhancers, with complex-specific partners directing targeting. WDR5 also joins ATAC and NSL acetyltransferase complexes. This machinery controls Hox expression and lineage specification; mutations cause Kabuki and Wiedemann-Steiner syndromes, and KMT2A rearrangements drive mixed lineage leukaemia.—This chromatin machinery activates gene expression during embryonic patterning and lineage specification, notably setting body-plan gene expression. Inherited loss causes chromatin-related developmental disorders such as Kabuki and Wiedemann-Steiner syndromes, and rearrangement of one component drives mixed lineage leukaemia, an aggressive blood cancer of children and adults. Its central scaffold is pursued as a cancer drug target.
SIRT1 negatively regulates rRNA expression
originalRibosome production is the cell's largest biosynthetic commitment, so rRNA transcription must track nutrient supply; SIRT1 provides that link by negatively regulating rRNA expression when energy is scarce. Acting as an NAD-dependent histone deacetylase, SIRT1 senses a high NAD/NADH ratio during glucose limitation and, together with nucleomethylin (RRP8) and the H3K9 methyltransferase SUV39H1, forms a nucleolar silencing complex that deacetylates and dimethylates histone H3 on ribosomal DNA chromatin. Recognition of pre-existing H3K9me2 by the complex allows the repressive mark to spread across adjacent nucleosomes, closing the rDNA repeats to the RNA polymerase I machinery represented here by TBP and the SL1 subunits TAF1A-TAF1D. The result is coordinated restraint of ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation under metabolic stress, a form of energy-dependent nucleolar silencing linked to caloric restriction responses, nucleolar stress signalling and cellular ageing.
SIRT1, an NAD-dependent deacetylase, represses rRNA transcription when energy is scarce. Sensing a high NAD/NADH ratio during glucose limitation, it forms a nucleolar complex with nucleomethylin and SUV39H1 that deacetylates and dimethylates H3K9 on rDNA, with the mark spreading across nucleosomes to block polymerase I and SL1. This restrains ribosome biogenesis and growth under metabolic stress, linked to caloric restriction and ageing.—Ribosome production is the cell's largest biosynthetic commitment, so it must track nutrient supply. When energy is scarce, as during sugar limitation, cells silence their ribosome-producing genes in the nucleolus, restraining growth and proliferation. This energy-dependent nucleolar silencing is linked to responses to caloric restriction, nucleolar stress signalling and cellular ageing, connecting metabolism with longevity.
Regulation of endogenous retroelements by the Human Silencing Hub (HUSH) complex
originalRetrotransposons and integrated retroviral DNA are transcriptionally silenced by the Human Silencing Hub, a three-subunit complex of MPP8, Periphilin and TASOR that keeps young LINE-1 elements, some HIV proviruses and other intronless foreign sequences switched off. This surveillance protects genome stability and limits insertional mutagenesis, and it is also why therapeutic transgenes and viral vectors are often epigenetically shut down. Recognition works partly through nascent transcripts bound by Periphilin and partly by reading existing H3K9 trimethylation, after which the methyltransferase SETDB1 with its partner ATF7IP, together with EHMT1/EHMT2, marks surrounding nucleosomes; the chromatin remodeller MORC2 compacts the locus. Components of the nuclear RNA exosome targeting complex, including MTREX, ZCCHC8 and RBM7, link the silenced transcripts to degradation. Long exons of host genes are sensitive, while introns confer protection, making transcript architecture the discriminating signal for self versus non-self DNA.
The Human Silencing Hub of MPP8, Periphilin and TASOR silences young LINE-1 elements, some HIV proviruses and other intronless foreign sequences, protecting genome stability and explaining transgene silencing. It recognises nascent transcripts and existing H3K9me3, recruiting SETDB1-ATF7IP and EHMT1/2 to methylate nucleosomes and MORC2 to compact chromatin, while nuclear exosome targeting factors degrade transcripts. Introns protect host genes, so transcript architecture distinguishes self from non-self.—Retrotransposons and integrated retroviral DNA, including some HIV proviruses, are kept silent in human cells, protecting genome stability and limiting insertional mutagenesis. This surveillance distinguishes foreign from self DNA based on transcript architecture. It also explains why therapeutic transgenes and viral gene therapy vectors are often shut down, making it relevant to HIV latency and gene therapy design.
B-WICH complex positively regulates rRNA expression
originalRibosome production sets the pace of cell growth, and this chromatin-remodelling route raises output by opening the rDNA repeats so that RNA polymerase I can transcribe them efficiently. The B-WICH assembly, built around the ATP-dependent remodeller SMARCA5 with BAZ1B, nuclear myosin MYO1C, actin, DDX21, DEK, MYBBP1A, ERCC6 and SF3B1, binds active ribosomal RNA genes and also the polymerase III-transcribed 5S rRNA and 7SL RNA genes. By sliding nucleosomes and recruiting histone acetyltransferases such as EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, it converts the surrounding histones to an acetylated, transcriptionally permissive state that favours loading of the SL1 promoter-selectivity factor (TAF1A-TAF1D with TBP) and the Pol I catalytic core. The result is coordinate control of rRNA and signal recognition particle RNA synthesis, linking nucleolar activity to growth signals, with GSK3B among the kinases modulating the response.
The B-WICH chromatin remodelling complex, built around SMARCA5 with BAZ1B, nuclear myosin, actin, DDX21, ERCC6 and others, opens rDNA repeats to boost RNA polymerase I transcription and also binds 5S rRNA and 7SL RNA genes. By sliding nucleosomes and recruiting acetyltransferases such as EP300 and KAT2A/B, it creates permissive chromatin favouring SL1 and polymerase I loading, linking nucleolar output to growth signals, modulated by GSK3B.—Ribosome production sets the pace of cell growth, and opening the chromatin of ribosomal genes raises their output. This process coordinates production of ribosomal RNAs and of the RNA in the particle that targets secreted proteins, linking nucleolar activity to growth signals in proliferating cells. It ties nutrient and growth-factor cues to the cell's biosynthetic capacity.
MLL4 and MLL3 complexes regulate expression of PPARG target genes in adipogenesis and hepatic steatosis
originalFat cells are made by a transcriptional programme in which the nuclear receptor pair PPARG and RXRA, once bound by lipid ligands, switches on the genes of lipid uptake, storage and droplet formation. Here that switch is coupled to chromatin: the related histone H3K4 methyltransferases KMT2C and KMT2D, with their shared complex subunits ASH2L, RBBP5, WDR5, DPY30, PAXIP1, PAGR1, NCOA6 and the H3K27 demethylase KDM6A, are recruited to PPARG:RXRA sites and deposit activating marks, while Mediator, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators are exchanged for NCOR1/NCOR2-HDAC3 corepressors. The output genes define the adipocyte — adiponectin, FABP4, CD36, perilipins, LPL, DGAT2, SCD, PNPLA2 and LIPE — and also drive thermogenic brown fat and hepatocyte triglyceride synthesis. Loss of the methyltransferase activity blocks adipogenesis and protects against diet-induced hepatic steatosis, the first step toward fatty liver disease, steatohepatitis and cirrhosis.
Adipocyte formation is driven by ligand-bound PPARG and RXRA, which activate genes for lipid uptake, storage and droplets. KMT2C and KMT2D H3K4 methyltransferase complexes, including KDM6A, are recruited to these sites to deposit activating marks, while coactivators replace NCOR-HDAC3 corepressors. Targets include adiponectin, FABP4, CD36, perilipins and LPL, also in brown fat and liver; losing methyltransferase activity blocks adipogenesis and protects against hepatic steatosis.—Fat cells arise through a programme that switches on genes for fat uptake, storage and droplet formation, and the same programme drives heat-producing brown fat and fat synthesis in liver cells. Blocking it prevents fat cell formation and protects against diet-induced fatty liver, the first step toward fatty liver disease, steatohepatitis and cirrhosis, linking it to obesity and metabolic liver disease.
Regulation of endogenous retroelements by Piwi-interacting RNAs (piRNAs)
originalTransposable elements are a standing threat to germline genome integrity, and piRNA-guided silencing of endogenous retroelements is how germ cells keep them quiet across generations. Short PIWI-interacting RNAs, generated from transposon and non-coding transcripts and amplified by successive rounds of cleavage, load onto PIWI proteins and find their targets by base-pairing with nascent or mature transcripts, triggering either co-transcriptional or post-transcriptional repression. In the transcriptional arm represented here, PIWIL4 engages nascent retroelement RNA and, through SPOCD1 and C19orf84, recruits de novo DNA methylation machinery including DNMT3A and its cofactor DNMT3L, together with nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase activity and BAF-type chromatin remodellers acting on the surrounding histones. This imprinting of methylation during the perinatal window of germ cell reprogramming establishes lasting retroelement repression; its loss derails spermatogenesis, and SPOCD1 mutations cause male infertility.
PIWI-interacting RNAs, produced and amplified from transposon and non-coding transcripts, guide PIWI proteins to silence retroelements in germ cells across generations. In the transcriptional arm, PIWIL4 engages nascent retroelement RNA and, through SPOCD1 and C19orf84, recruits DNMT3A and DNMT3L along with deacetylase and BAF remodelling activity. This establishes lasting methylation during perinatal reprogramming; its loss disrupts spermatogenesis, and SPOCD1 mutations cause male infertility.—Transposable elements threaten germline genome integrity, and male germ cells keep them silent across generations using small guide RNAs. Lasting silencing is imprinted during the perinatal window of germ cell reprogramming. Its loss derails sperm production, and inherited mutations in one component cause male infertility, showing the importance of this process for fertility and heritable genome stability.

RNA Polymerase I Transcription (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
RNA Polymerase I Promoter Opening
originalRibosome production begins with transcription of the rRNA genes by RNA polymerase I, and before that polymerase can be loaded the nucleosomal rDNA promoter must be made accessible. This opening step sets how many rRNA genes are active, and therefore the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth, which is why it is tuned to nutrient and proliferative signals and is deranged in cancer and in ribosomopathies. The upstream binding factor UBTF binds and bends promoter DNA, displacing histones to create a nucleosome-free region; its phosphorylation, with MAPK3 among the kinases implicated, governs productive engagement with the polymerase I initiation complex. Core histones of all four classes represent the chromatin being remodelled, while MBD2 and PHF6 act on the repressive side, keeping a fraction of rDNA repeats silent. The output is an initiation-competent promoter rather than any metabolic product.
Before RNA polymerase I can transcribe rRNA genes, the nucleosomal rDNA promoter must be opened, setting how many genes are active and thus ribosome biogenesis capacity, a step tuned to growth signals and disturbed in cancer and ribosomopathies. UBTF binds and bends promoter DNA, displacing histones, with phosphorylation, partly by MAPK3, controlling engagement. MBD2 and PHF6 keep some repeats silent.—Ribosome production starts with transcription of ribosomal RNA genes, and opening their chromatin sets how many genes are active and therefore the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth. This step is tuned to nutrient and proliferative signals, and it is deranged in cancer and in ribosomopathies, inherited disorders of ribosome production such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.
RNA Polymerase I Transcription Initiation
originalRibosome production begins with transcription of the rRNA genes, and RNA polymerase I transcription initiation is the step that sets how many ribosomes a cell will build — a rate that scales directly with growth, and one that is raised in proliferating and tumour cells. At the rDNA promoter the selectivity factor SL1, built from TBP with the Pol I-specific TAF1A–TAF1D subunits, forms a platform together with the architectural activator UBTF; phosphorylation of UBTF and the adaptor RRN3 then license loading of the multisubunit polymerase, whose POLR1 catalytic core shares several small subunits with Pol II and Pol III. Initiation output is tuned by reversible acetylation of the basal machinery through the KAT2A/KAT2B acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC1/HDAC2 within NuRD-type chromatin remodelling complexes, while the terminator-binding factor TTF1 links promoter events to rDNA chromatin state and nucleolar organisation.
RNA polymerase I transcription initiation sets ribosome production, rising in proliferating and tumour cells. At the rDNA promoter, the SL1 factor of TBP and TAF1A-TAF1D forms a platform with UBTF; UBTF phosphorylation and the adaptor RRN3 license polymerase loading. Output is tuned by KAT2A/KAT2B acetylation opposed by HDAC1/2 in NuRD complexes, while TTF1 links promoter events to rDNA chromatin and nucleolar organisation.—Starting transcription of ribosomal RNA genes sets how many ribosomes a cell builds, a rate that scales directly with growth and is raised in proliferating and tumour cells. Output is tuned by reversible chromatin modification, linking promoter activity to nucleolar organisation. This makes the step central to growth control and a target of interest in cancer therapy.
RNA Polymerase I Transcription Termination
originalRibosome production begins with RNA polymerase I making a single long precursor rRNA in the nucleolus, and transcription of that gene must be stopped cleanly at the end of the repeat so the polymerase can be recycled and the transcript released. In this termination step the DNA-binding factor TTF1 occupies a terminator element downstream of the rRNA gene and stalls the elongating enzyme; the release factor PTRF/CAVIN1 then acts on the paused complex to free both the nascent pre-rRNA and polymerase I from the template. The gene set accordingly includes the full polymerase I catalytic core and its shared subunits, the SL1 promoter-selectivity complex with TBP and the TAF1 proteins, the nucleolar activator UBTF, and TFIIH components that couple this transcription to repair. Output here sets the ceiling on ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation.
RNA polymerase I transcription of precursor rRNA in the nucleolus must terminate cleanly to release the transcript and recycle the enzyme. TTF1 binds a downstream terminator and stalls the polymerase, and PTRF/CAVIN1 releases both the nascent pre-rRNA and polymerase I. Components include the polymerase I core, SL1 with TBP and TAF1 proteins, UBTF and TFIIH factors linking transcription to repair, together setting ribosome biogenesis and growth.—Ribosome production starts in the nucleolus with transcription of a long ribosomal RNA precursor, which must end cleanly so the transcribing machinery can be recycled and the transcript released. Clean termination sets the ceiling on ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation, and it also connects ribosomal gene transcription to DNA repair, making it relevant to rapidly growing cells.
RNA Polymerase I Promoter Escape
originalRibosome production begins with rRNA transcription, and promoter escape by RNA polymerase I is the step where an assembled initiation complex commits to processive synthesis. Cells tune this step to match ribosome supply to growth demand, so it sits at the heart of nucleolar function and of growth control; its dysregulation accompanies rapid proliferation in cancer and underlies ribosomopathies. The polymerase I catalytic core with its specific subunits engages rDNA through the SL1 complex of TBP and TAF1A/TAF1B/TAF1C together with the activator UBTF, and the initiation factor RRN3 dissociates as the enzyme clears the promoter and enters elongation, unlike polymerase II initiation there is no requirement for ATP-driven promoter melting. Shared small polymerase subunits, TFIIH components including CDK7-cyclin H and the helicases ERCC2/ERCC3, chromatin-bound histones and PHF6 provide the nucleolar chromatin context in which escape occurs.
Promoter escape by RNA polymerase I is the step where the rDNA initiation complex commits to processive rRNA synthesis, tuned to match ribosome supply to growth; dysregulation accompanies cancer and ribosomopathies. The polymerase engages rDNA via SL1 and UBTF, and RRN3 dissociates as it enters elongation, without ATP-driven promoter melting. TFIIH components, histones and PHF6 provide the nucleolar chromatin context.—Ribosome production begins with ribosomal RNA transcription, and the point at which it commits to productive synthesis is tuned to match ribosome supply to growth demand. This sits at the heart of nucleolar function and growth control; its dysregulation accompanies rapid proliferation in cancer and underlies ribosomopathies, inherited disorders of ribosome production affecting blood formation and development.

RNA Polymerase III Transcription (6)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
RNA Polymerase III Chain Elongation
originalRNA polymerase III makes the short, abundant, untranslated RNAs a cell needs constantly dash tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others dash and chain elongation is the productive phase in which the enzyme, having opened its promoter and escaped initiation, processively extends the transcript to its termination signal. Because tRNA and 5S rRNA supply are set here, the output of this polymerase scales with ribosome production and growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and other neurodevelopmental disease, while activating lesions raise its output in cancer. The sixteen-subunit enzyme is built from a catalytic core of the largest and second-largest subunits together with subunits shared with the other nuclear polymerases, plus a Pol III-specific subcomplex that handles promoter opening and RNA cleavage. Alternative forms of one subunit distinguish enzyme variants with differing gene preferences and a role in cytosolic DNA sensing.
RNA polymerase III elongation processively extends transcripts of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other small RNAs to termination, setting supplies that scale with ribosome production and growth. The sixteen-subunit enzyme has a catalytic core, subunits shared with other polymerases and a specific subcomplex for promoter opening and RNA cleavage. Subunit mutations cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, activating lesions occur in cancer, and one variant senses cytosolic DNA.—Cells continually need large amounts of small untranslated RNAs for protein synthesis and RNA processing, and this productive transcription phase sets their supply, scaling with ribosome production and growth. Inherited defects cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and other neurodevelopmental disorders, while activating changes raise output in cancer. Variant forms also contribute to sensing of foreign DNA in the cytosol during viral infection.
RNA Polymerase III Transcription Initiation From Type 1 Promoter
originalRibosome production depends on a steady supply of 5S ribosomal RNA, and this is the route by which RNA polymerase III is loaded onto the 5S rRNA gene, the classic type 1 promoter with its internal control region. Assembly is strictly ordered: the nine-zinc-finger factor TFIIIA binds the internal promoter first, creating a platform for the multisubunit TFIIIC complex, which in turn positions a TBP-containing TFIIIB built around BRF1 and BDP1 upstream of the start site; TFIIIB then recruits the polymerase itself, whose catalytic core (POLR3A, POLR3B) is completed by subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Output from this pathway sets the ceiling on ribosome assembly and is tied to growth control, and mutations in polymerase III subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and impair innate sensing of cytosolic DNA.
RNA polymerase III is loaded onto the 5S rRNA gene, a type 1 promoter with an internal control region, in strict order: TFIIIA binds first, TFIIIC follows, and TFIIIB containing TBP, BRF1 and BDP1 is positioned upstream to recruit the polymerase with catalytic POLR3A and POLR3B. This sets the ceiling on ribosome assembly, and polymerase III mutations cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and impair cytosolic DNA sensing.—Ribosome production depends on a steady supply of a small ribosomal RNA, and starting its transcription sets a ceiling on ribosome assembly and cell growth. Inherited defects in the transcribing machinery cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, which impair brain white matter development, and weaken innate immune sensing of foreign DNA in the cytosol, increasing susceptibility to severe viral infection.
RNA Polymerase III Transcription Termination
originalRNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs in bulk tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others and this step ends each round of synthesis, freeing the transcript and the DNA template so the enzyme can recycle onto a new gene. Termination is driven almost entirely by the polymerase itself: a run of thymidines on the non-template strand is enough to destabilise the elongation complex, without the dedicated release factors or extensive cis-elements that other polymerases require. The seventeen-subunit enzyme is represented here in full, including subunits shared with polymerases I and II and the alternative catalytic-region paralogues POLR3G and POLR3GL. Released nascent transcripts bearing 3' oligo-U are captured by the La protein SSB, which protects them from exonucleolytic trimming and guides folding and maturation. Output from this machinery sets the ceiling on translational capacity and cell growth.
RNA polymerase III termination ends synthesis of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other small RNAs, releasing transcript and template so the enzyme can recycle. A thymidine run on the non-template strand suffices to destabilise the elongation complex, without dedicated release factors. The seventeen-subunit enzyme includes POLR3G paralogues, and the La protein SSB binds 3' oligo-U ends to protect and guide maturation, together setting translational capacity.—Cells constantly need large amounts of small structural RNAs, and ending each round of their synthesis frees the transcribing machinery to start again. This recycling sets the ceiling on translational capacity and cell growth, scaling with proliferation. Defects in the responsible machinery cause neurodevelopmental disorders affecting brain white matter, while its overactivity accompanies tumour growth.
RNA Polymerase III Abortive And Retractive Initiation
originalRNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs constantly — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others — so the rate at which it commits to productive synthesis sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and ribosome production. This step describes what happens immediately after the enzyme opens promoter DNA: the polymerase repeatedly synthesises and releases very short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent transcript, before it escapes the promoter and elongates processively. Promoter recognition upstream of this depends on distinct assembly factors for the different promoter classes — the multisubunit TFIIIC complex with TFIIIA at 5S genes, TBP-associated BRF1 and BDP1 at tRNA genes, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex and ZNF143 at U6-type type 3 promoters. The La protein binds the uridylate-rich 3' ends of the released products. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies oncogenic growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.
After RNA polymerase III opens promoter DNA, it repeatedly makes and releases short abortive oligonucleotides before escaping into processive elongation, a commitment that limits production of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA and other small RNAs and thus protein synthesis. Upstream recognition uses TFIIIA and TFIIIC at 5S genes, BRF1-BDP1 at tRNA genes and BRF2 with SNAPc and ZNF143 at type 3 promoters. Deregulation accompanies cancer, and subunit mutations cause leukodystrophy.—Cells constantly need small structural RNAs, and how readily their transcription commits to productive synthesis sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and ribosome production. Deregulated output accompanies oncogenic growth in tumours, and inherited defects in the responsible machinery cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, a childhood disorder of brain white matter development with motor and cognitive impairment.
RNA Polymerase III Transcription Initiation From Type 3 Promoter
originalA handful of small non-coding RNAs, notably the spliceosomal U6 snRNA, are made by RNA polymerase III from gene-external promoters that look more like those of polymerase II genes than like classical tRNA promoters. Initiation from these metazoan-specific type 3 promoters supplies the U6 and related transcripts on which pre-mRNA splicing and other RNA processing depend, so the cell's capacity to mature its own messages is set here. Recognition begins at the proximal sequence element by the five-subunit SNAPc complex (SNAPC1-SNAPC5), which cooperates with the polymerase III-specific TFIIIB variant built on BRF2, BDP1 and TBP bound at a TATA box; together they load the seventeen-subunit polymerase, whose core shares several small subunits with polymerases I and II. Upstream enhancer elements add POU2F1 at an octamer motif and the zinc-finger factor ZNF143 at the SPH element to raise output.
RNA polymerase III transcribes U6 snRNA and related RNAs from gene-external type 3 promoters resembling polymerase II promoters, supplying RNAs needed for pre-mRNA splicing. The SNAPc complex binds the proximal sequence element and cooperates with a TFIIIB variant of BRF2, BDP1 and TBP at the TATA box to load the seventeen-subunit polymerase. Enhancer-bound POU2F1 and ZNF143 increase output.—A handful of small non-coding RNAs essential for messenger RNA splicing are made from a distinct, animal-specific class of gene promoters, setting the cell's capacity to mature its own messages. This supply underpins gene expression in all proliferating and specialised cells, and its regulation links cell growth to the splicing capacity on which every tissue depends.
RNA Polymerase III Transcription Initiation From Type 2 Promoter
originalTransfer RNAs and other short non-coding RNAs are made by RNA polymerase III, and type 2 promoters are the internal A-box/B-box arrangement found in tRNA and Alu-type genes. Initiation here begins with the multisubunit TFIIIC complex binding the two internal boxes directly, without needing the TFIIIA zinc-finger factor required at 5S rRNA promoters. TFIIIC then recruits TFIIIB, built from BRF1, BDP1 and TBP, which positions the polymerase over the start site; once TFIIIB is stably engaged, it alone can sustain repeated rounds of transcription. The seventeen-subunit enzyme includes catalytic POLR3A and POLR3B plus subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Output from this system sets the cell's translational capacity, is tuned to growth and nutrient signals through mTOR and MYC, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and related neurodevelopmental disease.
Transcription of tRNA and Alu-type genes by RNA polymerase III uses type 2 promoters with internal A and B boxes. TFIIIC binds these boxes directly, without TFIIIA, and recruits TFIIIB (BRF1, BDP1, TBP), which positions the polymerase and alone sustains repeated transcription rounds. Output sets translational capacity, is tuned by mTOR and MYC, and subunit mutations cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and neurodevelopmental disease.—Transfer RNAs and other short non-coding RNAs are needed in bulk, and starting their transcription sets the cell's translational capacity. Output is tuned to growth and nutrient signals and is raised in cancers driven by growth-promoting oncogenes. Inherited defects in the machinery cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and related neurodevelopmental disease, affecting brain white matter development in children.

Batch 03 · under "Hemostasis"

Coagulation pathway (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Initiation of coagulation cascade
originalBlood clotting begins when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor to plasma, and this initiation phase produces the first small burst of thrombin that primes the rest of the cascade. Tissue factor (F3) sits on fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, normally held in a cryptic, low-activity state; phosphatidylserine exposure and thiol-disulfide rearrangement convert it to its procoagulant form, where it binds factor VII/VIIa with high affinity and the complex cleaves factors IX and X to their active proteases. Cofactors FV and FVIII, von Willebrand factor and prothrombin carry the signal forward, while TFPI, antithrombin and protein S restrain it, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans, glypicans and perlecan provide the surface on which inhibition is accelerated. Unrestrained or ectopic tissue factor activity, including on tumour- and sepsis-derived vesicles, drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation; deficiency of FVIII or FIX causes haemophilia.
Coagulation is initiated when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor, normally cryptic on fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, which binds factor VIIa and activates factors IX and X to generate an initial thrombin burst. Cofactors carry the signal forward while TFPI, antithrombin and protein S on heparan sulfate proteoglycans restrain it. Ectopic tissue factor drives thrombosis and DIC, and FVIII or FIX deficiency causes haemophilia.—Blood clotting begins when injury or inflammation exposes a procoagulant signal on cells around blood vessels, such as fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, producing an initial burst that primes the clotting cascade. Unrestrained or misplaced activity, including on vesicles shed by tumours or during sepsis, drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation, while deficiency of downstream clotting factors causes haemophilia.
FXIIa, PKa-dependent activation of coagulation pathway
originalThe contact system feeds into clotting when factor XII autoactivates on a surface: FXIIa converts factor XI to XIa, and plasma kallikrein, generated from prekallikrein bound to high molecular weight kininogen, can also activate factor IX directly, so this FXIIa- and kallikrein-dependent route amplifies fibrin formation while linking coagulation to kinin-driven inflammation. It is not needed for ordinary haemostasis — people lacking factor XII or prekallikrein do not bleed — yet it drives pathological thrombus growth, and factor XII deficiency is associated with protection from venous thrombosis while C1 inhibitor deficiency raises thrombotic risk. That dissociation makes the system an attractive antithrombotic target. Assembly occurs at the platelet surface, where the GPIb-IX-V complex provides a docking platform that concentrates these zymogens; by contrast, factor XI loss does cause bleeding, placing FXI at the junction of the contact and canonical cascades.
In the contact system, surface-autoactivated factor XII activates factor XI, and kallikrein from kininogen-bound prekallikrein can activate factor IX, amplifying fibrin formation and linking coagulation to kinin inflammation. It is dispensable for haemostasis yet drives pathological thrombosis, making it an attractive antithrombotic target, while C1 inhibitor deficiency raises risk. Assembly occurs on platelet GPIb-IX-V, and factor XI deficiency, unlike factor XII deficiency, causes bleeding.—A plasma surface-contact system feeds into blood clotting and links it to inflammation. It is not needed for ordinary haemostasis, since people lacking its initiating factors do not bleed, yet it drives pathological thrombus growth; its deficiency is associated with protection from venous thrombosis, while deficiency of its inhibitor raises thrombotic risk. This makes it an attractive antithrombotic drug target, with platelets providing the assembly surface.
Amplification and propagation of coagulation cascade
originalOnce tissue factor has generated a trace of thrombin at a wound, the amplification and propagation phases turn that trace into a burst large enough to clot blood. Thrombin feeds back to activate factors XI, VIII and V on the activated platelet surface, where the tenase complex (FIXa with FVIIIa) makes FXa and the prothrombinase complex (FXa with FVa) cleaves prothrombin, so fibrinogen is converted to cross-linked fibrin and the platelet plug is stabilised. Phosphatidylserine exposure, which requires the scramblase ANO6, and von Willebrand factor binding through the GPIb-IX-V receptor provide the procoagulant membranes and platelet adhesion. Antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and the protein C/protein S system restrain the burst; loss of factor VIII or IX causes haemophilia, while defective inhibition predisposes to thrombosis.
In amplification and propagation, initial thrombin activates factors XI, VIII and V on platelets, where tenase (FIXa-FVIIIa) produces FXa and prothrombinase (FXa-FVa) cleaves prothrombin, generating cross-linked fibrin that stabilises the plug. ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine exposure and von Willebrand factor binding via GPIb-IX-V support this. Antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and protein C/S restrain it; FVIII or FIX loss causes haemophilia, defective inhibition thrombosis.—After injury, an initial trace of clotting activity is amplified into a burst large enough to clot blood, stabilising the platelet plug at the wound with a fibrous mesh. Activated platelets provide the surface for this amplification, and natural inhibitors restrain the burst. Loss of key clotting factors causes haemophilia A and B, while defective inhibition predisposes to venous thrombosis.
Fibrin formation
originalFibrin formation is the final structural step of blood coagulation, converting soluble plasma fibrinogen into the insoluble meshwork that seals a wounded vessel and gives a clot its mechanical strength. Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from the fibrinogen chains, releasing monomers that self-assemble into protofibrils and then thick fibers in a three-dimensional network; activated factor XIII, a transglutaminase, covalently cross-links the fibers in a calcium-dependent manner so the clot resists premature mechanical and enzymatic breakdown. Platelet integrin αIIbβ3 binds the network, linking aggregation to clot retraction and stability. The same module carries the brakes: antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and other serpins neutralize thrombin, while protein C restrains upstream cofactors, so fibrin deposition stays local. Deficiency of fibrinogen or factor XIII causes bleeding and poor wound healing, whereas loss of the inhibitory arm predisposes to thrombosis.
Fibrin formation converts soluble fibrinogen into an insoluble meshwork that seals wounds and strengthens clots. Thrombin removes fibrinopeptides so monomers assemble into fibers, which calcium-dependent factor XIIIa cross-links against breakdown, and platelet alphaIIb-beta3 binds the network for retraction. Antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and protein C keep deposition local; fibrinogen or factor XIII deficiency causes bleeding, while losing inhibition predisposes to thrombosis.—Clot formation ends with the conversion of a soluble plasma protein into an insoluble meshwork that seals a wounded vessel and gives the clot mechanical strength, linking platelet aggregation to clot retraction. Built-in brakes keep clotting local. Inherited deficiency of the structural or stabilising components causes bleeding and poor wound healing, whereas loss of the inhibitory arm predisposes to thrombosis.

Platelet activation, signaling and aggregation (12)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Platelet degranulation
originalWhen a vessel is injured, platelets not only plug the breach but empty their storage granules into it, and platelet degranulation is that secretory event. The released cargo amplifies platelet recruitment, supports coagulation, and initiates wound repair; loss of granule content or of the machinery that releases it causes bleeding disorders such as gray platelet and storage pool disease. Alpha granules supply adhesive and clotting proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen chains, factor V, thrombospondin and multimerin, along with protease inhibitors of the serpin family and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family members that drive angiogenesis and fibrosis. P-selectin and CD63 move to the surface as granule membranes fuse, marking activation. Fusion itself depends on SNARE and regulatory proteins including STXBP2, VTI1B, RAB27B and SYTL4, while integrin alphaIIb-beta3 and the cytoskeletal proteins talin, kindlin-3 and filamin couple activation to secretion.
Platelet degranulation releases granule cargo at vessel injury to amplify platelet recruitment, support coagulation and initiate repair; defects cause gray platelet and storage pool disease. Alpha granules supply von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, factor V, serpins and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF, while P-selectin and CD63 appear on the surface. Fusion depends on SNARE and regulatory proteins, coupled to integrin activation.—When a blood vessel is injured, platelets plug the breach and release the contents of their storage granules, amplifying platelet recruitment, supporting clotting and starting wound repair, including new vessel growth and fibrosis. Loss of granule content or of the release machinery causes bleeding disorders such as gray platelet syndrome and storage pool disease, and some immune disorders share the same secretory defects.
GRB2:SOS provides linkage to MAPK signaling for Integrins
originalIntegrins report the state of the extracellular matrix to the cell interior, and this step is how that report reaches the MAP kinase cascade: GRB2 with its exchange factor SOS1 couples an adhesion complex to Ras, converting matrix attachment into proliferative and survival signalling. The context is the activated platelet or adherent cell, where fibrinogen chains, fibronectin and von Willebrand factor engage the ITGA2B/ITGB3 receptor whose cytoplasmic tail is held by talin, with RAP1A/RAP1B and the adaptor APBB1IP acting upstream to bring the receptor into its high-affinity state. Clustering activates focal adhesion kinase (PTK2) and SRC, which phosphorylate sites that recruit the GRB2:SOS pair; loss of this linkage leaves cells attached but unable to translate adhesion into growth-factor-like ERK output, a requirement for anchorage-dependent growth, migration and platelet aggregation.
GRB2 and SOS1 couple integrin adhesion complexes to Ras, converting matrix attachment into MAP kinase proliferative and survival signals. In activated platelets, fibrinogen, fibronectin and von Willebrand factor engage talin-bound ITGA2B/ITGB3, activated upstream via RAP1 and APBB1IP. Clustering activates FAK and SRC, which recruit GRB2-SOS; without this link, cells remain attached but lack ERK output needed for anchorage-dependent growth, migration and aggregation.—In activated platelets and other adherent cells, attachment to the surrounding matrix or a clot is converted into growth, survival and migration signals. This link underlies anchorage-dependent growth, cell migration and platelet aggregation during haemostasis; without it, cells remain attached but cannot translate adhesion into proliferative signalling, a property relevant to tissue repair and to how cancer cells escape anchorage requirements.
Thrombin signalling through proteinase activated receptors (PARs)
originalThrombin, the protease at the end of the coagulation cascade, also acts as a hormone-like signal by cleaving proteinase-activated receptors on the cell surface, and this route is how a clotting signal becomes a cellular response. In platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, making it central to haemostasis and to arterial thrombosis; the same receptors mediate thrombin's effects on endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Activation is irreversible and unusual: thrombin clips the receptor N-terminus, and the new tethered ligand folds back to activate the receptor, which then couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling. Beta-arrestins terminate and redirect signalling, while Src and ERK link receptor activation to growth and differentiation responses. PAR1 is the dominant human thrombin receptor, with PAR4 contributing at higher concentrations.
Thrombin cleaves proteinase-activated receptors, unmasking a tethered ligand that irreversibly activates them, turning a clotting signal into cellular responses. In platelets this drives shape change, secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, central to haemostasis and arterial thrombosis, and it also acts on endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Gq and G12/13 coupling activates PLC beta, calcium, PKC and Rho, while beta-arrestins terminate signalling; PAR1 dominates, with PAR4.—The final protease of the clotting cascade also acts as a hormone-like signal on cells, turning a clotting event into a cellular response. In platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion and aggregation, making it central to haemostasis and arterial thrombosis such as heart attack, and it also affects endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Its receptor is an antiplatelet drug target.
Thromboxane signalling through TP receptor
originalThromboxane A2 is the platelet-derived eicosanoid that drives aggregation and vasoconstriction, and its actions all run through the TP receptor, the target of the antiplatelet drug class that blocks it. Signalling through TP shapes haemostasis, and its overactivity contributes to thrombosis, hypertension and bronchoconstriction, while pharmacological interruption of thromboxane production or receptor engagement is standard cardiovascular prophylaxis. TP exists as two splice variants differing in their cytoplasmic tails, one first described in platelets and placenta and the other in endothelium. Ligand binding couples the receptor to Gq-family alpha subunits, stimulating phospholipase C and raising intracellular calcium to trigger shape change and granule release; coupling to G13 instead activates Rho and Rac for cytoskeletal remodelling. The assortment of beta and gamma subunits here reflects the combinatorial heterotrimers available to this G protein-coupled receptor.
Thromboxane A2, a platelet eicosanoid, drives aggregation and vasoconstriction through the TP receptor, contributing to thrombosis, hypertension and bronchoconstriction, and blocking its production or receptor is standard cardiovascular prophylaxis. TP has two splice variants differing in their tails. Gq coupling activates phospholipase C and calcium for shape change and granule release, while G13 activates Rho and Rac for cytoskeletal remodelling.—A platelet-derived lipid signal drives platelet aggregation and blood vessel constriction, and its overactivity contributes to thrombosis, hypertension and airway constriction. Interrupting its production or blocking its receptor is standard cardiovascular prevention with widely used antiplatelet therapy. Receptor variants found in platelets, placenta and endothelium link this signal to haemostasis and vascular tone.
GP1b-IX-V activation signalling
originalPlatelets stick to a damaged vessel wall before they do anything else, and the GPIb-IX-V complex is the receptor that makes that first contact possible. Its four subunits (GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9 and GP5) bind von Willebrand factor immobilised on exposed subendothelial collagen, an interaction that works best under the high shear of arterial flow and tethers a resting platelet long enough for firm adhesion and activation to follow. Loss or defect of the complex causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, with giant platelets and bleeding; inappropriate engagement at a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque drives the arterial thrombi behind heart attack and stroke. Signalling from the cytoplasmic tail runs through filamin A to the actin cytoskeleton and recruits Src, PI3K regulatory subunit and 14-3-3, while the receptor also docks thrombin for presentation to protease-activated receptors, amplifying activation.
The platelet GPIb-IX-V complex (GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9, GP5) binds von Willebrand factor on exposed subendothelial collagen under high arterial shear, tethering platelets for adhesion and activation. Its loss causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome with giant platelets and bleeding, while engagement at ruptured plaques drives heart attack and stroke. Its tail signals via filamin A, Src, PI3K and 14-3-3, and it presents thrombin to PARs.—Platelets first stick to a damaged vessel wall through a receptor complex that tethers them under the high shear of arterial blood flow, allowing firm adhesion and activation to follow. Its loss causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, with giant platelets and bleeding, while inappropriate engagement at ruptured atherosclerotic plaques drives the arterial thrombi behind heart attack and stroke.
Disinhibition of SNARE formation
originalPlatelet granule release requires that syntaxin-4 on the plasma membrane be freed from a clamp before it can pair with vesicle SNAREs, and this disinhibition of SNARE formation is the switch that licenses fusion. Munc18-3 (STXBP3) binds syntaxin-4 in a closed conformation that cannot enter a fusion complex; conventional protein kinase C isoforms activated downstream of thrombin, collagen and other platelet agonists phosphorylate the pair and release the constraint, allowing syntaxin-4 to assemble with SNAP and VAMP partners and drive exocytosis of dense granule and alpha granule contents. The result is amplified recruitment and aggregation of platelets at a site of vascular injury, so the step sits at the interface of agonist signal transduction and regulated secretion. Related Munc18-syntaxin control governs insulin granule and immune cell granule release, and defective granule secretion produces bleeding tendency.
Platelet granule release requires freeing syntaxin-4 from Munc18-3 (STXBP3), which holds it closed and unable to form SNARE complexes. Conventional PKC isoforms activated by thrombin, collagen and other agonists phosphorylate the pair, letting syntaxin-4 assemble with SNAP and VAMP partners to drive dense and alpha granule exocytosis, amplifying aggregation. Similar control governs insulin and immune granule release, and defective secretion causes bleeding.—Platelets release granule contents at sites of vascular injury, and a licensing step governs whether that release can occur, amplifying recruitment and aggregation of further platelets. It sits at the interface of platelet stimulation and regulated secretion. Related control governs hormone release from pancreatic beta cells and granule release from immune cells, and defective granule secretion produces a bleeding tendency.
GPVI-mediated activation cascade
originalPlatelets stick to exposed collagen at a damaged vessel wall largely through GPVI, and the activation cascade it triggers converts that contact into shape change, granule release and aggregation — the first step of haemostasis and a driver of arterial thrombosis. GPVI pairs with the FcR gamma chain, whose ITAM is phosphorylated by the Src-family kinases Fyn and Lyn, recruiting Syk and assembling a signalosome around the transmembrane adaptor LAT and the cytosolic adaptor SLP-76 (LCP2), much as immune receptors do in T and B cells. Syk output runs through PI3K subunits and PLC-gamma2 to calcium mobilisation and protein kinase C, while VAV exchange factors drive Rac, RhoA and CDC42 for cytoskeletal remodelling; SHP-1 and SHP-2 tune the response. The related receptor CLEC-2, ligated by podoplanin, feeds into the same machinery. Loss of GPVI gives a mild bleeding tendency, and its blockade is pursued as antithrombotic therapy.
Collagen binding by platelet GPVI triggers shape change, secretion and aggregation, initiating haemostasis and driving arterial thrombosis. GPVI pairs with FcR gamma, whose ITAM is phosphorylated by Fyn and Lyn to recruit Syk and assemble a LAT-SLP-76 signalosome, leading through PI3K and PLC-gamma2 to calcium and PKC, and through VAV to Rac, RhoA and CDC42. CLEC-2 shares this machinery; GPVI blockade is an antithrombotic strategy.—Platelets stick to exposed matrix at a damaged vessel wall, and the activation this triggers drives shape change, granule release and aggregation, the first step of haemostasis and a driver of arterial thrombosis. The signalling resembles immune receptor activation in T and B cells. Because loss gives only a mild bleeding tendency, its blockade is pursued as a safer antithrombotic therapy.
p130Cas linkage to MAPK signaling for integrins
originalWhen an integrin engages an extracellular matrix ligand, the adhesion it forms must be converted into a growth and motility signal, and this is the branch that carries it to the MAP kinase cascade. Clustering of the platelet integrin αIIbβ3 on fibrinogen, fibronectin or von Willebrand factor, stabilised on the cytoplasmic side by talin and the Rap1 GTPases with their effector RIAM, assembles a focal adhesion kinase–Src complex. Src-dependent phosphorylation of the docking protein p130Cas creates binding sites for the adaptor Crk, and the resulting Cas–Crk module couples adhesion to Ras–ERK activation and to Rac-driven cytoskeletal remodelling. The output is spreading, migration and, in platelets, firm aggregation and clot retraction; loss of the integrin or its activation machinery causes bleeding disorders, while the same signalling axis is exploited by invasive tumour cells.
This branch converts integrin-matrix adhesion into MAP kinase growth and motility signals. Platelet alphaIIb-beta3 clustering on fibrinogen, fibronectin or von Willebrand factor, stabilised by talin, Rap1 and RIAM, assembles a FAK-Src complex that phosphorylates p130Cas to recruit Crk, coupling adhesion to Ras-ERK and Rac. Outputs include spreading, migration, aggregation and clot retraction; defects cause bleeding, and tumour cells exploit the axis.—When platelets and other cells attach to matrix or a clot, this adhesion is converted into growth and motility signals. The outcome is spreading, migration and, in platelets, firm aggregation and clot retraction. Loss of the platelet adhesion receptor or its activation machinery causes bleeding disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while invasive tumour cells exploit the same signalling to spread.
ADP signalling through P2Y purinoceptor 12
originalPlatelets release ADP from their dense granules when they are activated, and ADP acting back on the P2Y12 receptor is what converts a weak, reversible clump into a stable thrombus. This amplification loop is required for aggregation triggered by every other platelet agonist fcollagen, thrombin, thromboxane, adrenaline, serotonin f and it is the target of the thienopyridine antiplatelet drugs used after coronary stenting; loss-of-function variants cause a bleeding tendency. P2RY12 couples to Gi, so agonist binding releases an inhibitory alpha subunit that lowers adenylate cyclase output and cAMP, relieving protein kinase A restraint on cytoplasmic calcium, while the liberated beta-gamma dimer engages its own effectors. The many G protein alpha, beta and gamma subunits here represent the interchangeable heterotrimer components through which this receptor, and Gi-coupled receptors generally, act. Downstream consequences include granule secretion, thromboxane generation and integrin activation.
ADP released from platelet dense granules acts on the P2Y12 receptor to convert reversible clumps into stable thrombi, required for aggregation by all agonists and targeted by thienopyridine drugs after stenting; loss-of-function variants cause bleeding. P2RY12 couples to Gi, lowering adenylate cyclase output and cAMP to relieve PKA restraint on calcium, while beta-gamma acts separately. Effects include secretion, thromboxane generation and integrin activation.—Activated platelets release a nucleotide that acts back on them to convert a weak, reversible clump into a stable thrombus. This amplification is required for aggregation triggered by every other platelet stimulus and is the target of widely used antiplatelet drugs given after coronary stenting. Inherited loss causes a bleeding tendency, while its activity contributes to arterial thrombosis such as heart attack.
Arachidonate production from DAG
originalArachidonic acid, the precursor of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, can be liberated not only from phospholipids but also from diacylglycerol, and this route additionally generates the principal endocannabinoid of the nervous system. Diacylglycerol lipases alpha and beta hydrolyse DAG produced by phosphoinositide breakdown – in platelets this DAG is almost entirely arachidonate-bearing – to yield 2-arachidonoylglycerol, an agonist of cannabinoid receptor 1 that mediates retrograde suppression of neurotransmitter release at synapses. Monoacylglycerol lipase, together with the serine hydrolases ABHD6 and ABHD12, then degrades 2-AG to glycerol and free arachidonate, terminating cannabinoid signalling and feeding the eicosanoid pool. The balance between synthesis and hydrolysis sets endocannabinoid tone and links lipid second-messenger signalling to inflammation, pain and neuroprotection; loss of ABHD12 causes a neurodegenerative disorder with ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.
Diacylglycerol lipases alpha and beta hydrolyse arachidonate-rich DAG to produce 2-arachidonoylglycerol, the main brain endocannabinoid, which acts on CB1 to suppress synaptic neurotransmitter release. Monoacylglycerol lipase, ABHD6 and ABHD12 degrade 2-AG to glycerol and arachidonate, ending signalling and supplying eicosanoid precursors. This balance links lipid signalling to inflammation, pain and neuroprotection; ABHD12 loss causes neurodegeneration with ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.—This process liberates precursors of inflammatory lipid mediators and produces the brain's principal endocannabinoid, which suppresses neurotransmitter release at synapses. The balance sets endocannabinoid tone, linking lipid signalling to inflammation, pain and neuroprotection, with platelets as another important site. Inherited loss of one degrading activity causes a neurodegenerative disorder with ataxia, hearing loss, cataract and retinitis pigmentosa.
ADP signalling through P2Y purinoceptor 1
originalADP released from platelet dense granules acts as an autocrine amplifier of haemostasis, and the P2Y1 purinoceptor is the arm of that response that starts shape change and the first, reversible wave of aggregation. It works with the Gi-coupled P2Y12 receptor, the target of clopidogrel and related antithrombotics; both must be engaged for full, irreversible aggregation and thrombus stabilisation, so loss of either leaves a bleeding tendency while excess signalling favours arterial thrombosis. P2Y1 couples to Gq family alpha subunits (GNAQ, GNA11, GNA14, GNA15) with a wide range of beta and gamma partners, mobilising calcium from internal stores. Downstream, p38 MAP kinase and Src-family signalling converge on cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonic acid for thromboxane synthesis and recruiting further platelets. The pathway therefore links nucleotide sensing to integrin activation, granule secretion and clot formation.
Platelet-released ADP acts on the P2Y1 receptor to initiate shape change and reversible aggregation, working with P2Y12, the clopidogrel target; both are needed for irreversible aggregation, so loss causes bleeding and excess favours arterial thrombosis. P2Y1 couples to Gq-family subunits to mobilise stored calcium, and p38 and Src signalling activate cytosolic phospholipase A2 for thromboxane synthesis, linking nucleotide sensing to integrin activation and clotting.—Platelets release a nucleotide that acts back on them to start shape change and the first, reversible wave of aggregation, working alongside a second receptor targeted by widely used antithrombotic drugs. Both arms are needed for full, irreversible aggregation and thrombus stabilisation, so loss of either causes a bleeding tendency, while excess signalling favours arterial thrombosis such as heart attack and stroke.
Adrenaline signalling through Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor
originalAdrenaline acting on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors is the arm of catecholamine signalling that damps rather than drives cAMP production. The three receptor subtypes encoded here couple preferentially to Gi/Go heterotrimers, so agonist binding inhibits adenylate cyclase and lowers cyclic AMP, while the released G protein subunits also regulate potassium and calcium channels. The physiological consequences are broad: suppression of insulin secretion and promotion of glucagon release from pancreatic islets, contraction of gastrointestinal sphincters, platelet aggregation, and presynaptic autoinhibition of noradrenaline release at sympathetic and central synapses. That last negative feedback loop is why alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and dexmedetomidine lower sympathetic outflow and blood pressure and produce sedation and analgesia, and why the subtypes differ in their vascular versus neuronal contributions to autonomic tone.
Adrenaline acting on three alpha-2 adrenergic receptor subtypes couples to Gi/Go to inhibit adenylate cyclase and lower cAMP, while released subunits regulate potassium and calcium channels. Effects include suppressed insulin and increased glucagon secretion, gastrointestinal sphincter contraction, platelet aggregation and presynaptic autoinhibition of noradrenaline release. This feedback explains how clonidine and dexmedetomidine reduce sympathetic outflow, blood pressure and produce sedation.—Stress-hormone and sympathetic nerve signalling through this damping receptor arm suppresses pancreatic beta-cell secretion and promotes alpha-cell secretion, contracts gut sphincters, promotes platelet aggregation, and provides presynaptic feedback that limits sympathetic nerve output. That feedback is why drugs acting here lower blood pressure and produce sedation and pain relief, used in hypertension and in anaesthesia and intensive care.

Platelet homeostasis (5)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Elevation of cytosolic Ca2+ levels
originalRaising cytosolic Ca2+ is the switch that converts agonist binding into a functional response in non-excitable cells, and in platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation during haemostasis. Two sources are combined. Phospholipase C-generated IP3 opens the ER channels ITPR1-3 to discharge internal stores; the resulting drop in store content is sensed by STIM1, which gathers at ER-plasma membrane contacts and gates the ORAI1/ORAI2 pore to produce store-operated Ca2+ entry that both sustains signalling and refills the store. Independently, ligand- and receptor-operated routes admit Ca2+ directly: the ATP-gated P2X family, with P2X1 prominent in platelets, and TRPC3/6/7 channels. Loss of STIM1 or ORAI1 function produces immunodeficiency and impaired platelet and lymphocyte activation, while excessive entry favours thrombosis, placing this step at the centre of secretion, adhesion and calcium-dependent enzyme control.
Rising cytosolic calcium converts agonist binding into responses in non-excitable cells, driving platelet shape change, secretion, integrin activation and aggregation. IP3 opens ER channels to release stores; STIM1 senses depletion and gates ORAI1/ORAI2 for store-operated entry, while P2X and TRPC channels admit calcium directly. STIM1 or ORAI1 loss causes immunodeficiency and impaired platelet activation, while excessive entry favours thrombosis.—This ion-signalling step converts receptor stimulation into function in non-excitable cells: in platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion and aggregation during haemostasis, and in lymphocytes it drives immune activation. Inherited loss causes immunodeficiency with impaired platelet and lymphocyte activation, while excessive signalling favours thrombosis, placing this step at the centre of secretion, adhesion and cellular activation.
Reduction of cytosolic Ca++ levels
originalCalcium signals must be terminated as sharply as they are generated, and this pathway is how a cell clears calcium from its cytosol after a transient. Pumps of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum family reload internal stores, plasma membrane calcium ATPases extrude calcium against its gradient using ATP, and sodium/calcium exchangers move it out in exchange for inbound sodium, a lower-affinity but high-capacity route that dominates in cardiac myocytes. Calmodulin senses the rising ion and stimulates the plasma membrane pumps, giving feedback control over the recovery phase; sorcin modulates calcium handling in excitable cells. Restoring resting calcium sets the rate of muscle relaxation, resets neuronal excitability and secretory cells for the next stimulus, and prevents the sustained overload that triggers protease and phospholipase activation and cell death. Failure contributes to heart failure, arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.
After a calcium transient, cells clear cytosolic calcium using SERCA pumps to refill stores, plasma membrane calcium ATPases, and high-capacity sodium/calcium exchangers dominant in cardiac myocytes. Calmodulin stimulates the membrane pumps for feedback control, and sorcin modulates handling in excitable cells. Restoring resting calcium sets muscle relaxation, resets neurons and secretory cells and prevents overload-induced death; failure contributes to heart failure, arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.—After every signalling transient, cells must restore resting conditions sharply, and this recovery sets the rate of muscle relaxation, especially in the heart, resets neuronal excitability and prepares secretory cells for the next stimulus. It also prevents the sustained overload that triggers cell death. Failure contributes to heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.
Prostacyclin signalling through prostacyclin receptor
originalHealthy vascular endothelium releases prostacyclin continuously, and its action at the Gs-coupled prostacyclin receptor PTGIR keeps platelets quiescent and vessels relaxed. This signalling is the principal brake on spontaneous thrombosis: receptor engagement raises cAMP, activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and blocks the rise in cytoplasmic calcium that platelet activation and granule secretion require, while smooth muscle relaxation lowers vascular tone. The genes here are PTGIR together with the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit GNAS and a full complement of beta and gamma subunits that form the heterotrimer transducing receptor occupancy to adenylate cyclase. The output opposes thromboxane A2, the other major eicosanoid arm, and the set point between them governs bleeding versus clotting tendency. Loss of prostacyclin tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension and to the thrombotic risk seen when prostanoid synthesis is pharmacologically shifted.
Endothelial prostacyclin acting on the Gs-coupled receptor PTGIR keeps platelets quiescent and vessels relaxed, the main brake on spontaneous thrombosis. Via GNAS and beta-gamma subunits, it activates adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP and PKA activity to block the calcium rise needed for platelet activation, and relaxes smooth muscle. It opposes thromboxane A2, and loss of prostacyclin tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension and thrombotic risk.—Healthy blood vessel lining continuously releases a signal that keeps platelets quiet and vessels relaxed, serving as the main brake on spontaneous thrombosis. The balance between this protective arm and a platelet-derived prothrombotic signal governs bleeding versus clotting tendency. Loss of this tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension and to the thrombotic risk seen with anti-inflammatory drugs that shift the balance.
Platelet sensitization by LDL
originalCirculating low-density lipoprotein does not by itself trigger platelets, but at normal plasma concentrations it lowers their threshold for activation, so that thrombin, collagen or ADP produce a larger aggregation response. This sensitization links dyslipidaemia to the prothrombotic tendency seen in atherosclerosis. The apolipoprotein B component of LDL is recognised by ApoER2 (LRP8), a splice variant of the apolipoprotein E receptor family, whose engagement recruits the Src-family kinase Fgr and leads to phosphorylation of p38 MAP kinase on its activation loop. Active p38 phosphorylates cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonate for thromboxane production and amplifying granule release and aggregation. The signal is self-limiting: LDL also promotes PECAM-1 signalling, which recruits the phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 together with protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes to dephosphorylate p38 and terminate the primed state.
At normal plasma levels, LDL lowers platelet activation thresholds, enhancing aggregation to thrombin, collagen or ADP and linking dyslipidaemia to atherosclerotic thrombosis. ApoB binds ApoER2 (LRP8), recruiting Fgr and activating p38 MAP kinase, which phosphorylates cytosolic phospholipase A2 to release arachidonate for thromboxane. LDL also triggers PECAM-1 signalling, recruiting SHP-1, SHP-2 and PP2A to dephosphorylate p38 and end priming.—Circulating blood lipid particles at normal plasma levels do not trigger platelets but lower their activation threshold, so that injury signals produce larger aggregation responses. This sensitisation links abnormal blood lipids to the prothrombotic tendency of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease. The effect is self-limiting, because the same particles also engage a counteracting restraint that ends the primed state of the platelet.
cGMP effects
originalcGMP made by guanylate cyclases in response to nitric oxide or natriuretic peptides is the messenger that relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelets and tunes neuronal excitability, and this pathway covers what happens once it has been made. Its central reader is cGMP-dependent protein kinase, present as the smooth-muscle PRKG1 and the epithelial and neuronal PRKG2, which phosphorylates targets that lower cytosolic calcium: IRAG1 in complex with the IP3 receptor ITPR1 to curb calcium release from internal stores, and large-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels built from KCNMA1 with beta subunits to hyperpolarise the membrane. Signal duration is set by phosphodiesterases that hydrolyse cGMP, among them PDE5A, whose pharmacological inhibition sustains vasodilation and is used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Loss of this braking arm favours vasoconstriction and excessive platelet aggregation.
cGMP produced in response to nitric oxide or natriuretic peptides relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelets and tunes neuronal excitability. cGMP-dependent kinases PRKG1 and PRKG2 lower cytosolic calcium by phosphorylating IRAG1 with the IP3 receptor and activating BK potassium channels. Phosphodiesterases such as PDE5A terminate signalling, and PDE5 inhibitors treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension; loss favours vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation.—A messenger produced in response to vessel-relaxing signals relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelets and tunes neuronal excitability, and this process covers how its signal acts and is ended. Drugs that prolong the signal sustain vasodilation and are used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Loss of this braking arm favours blood vessel constriction and excessive platelet aggregation.

Cell surface interactions at the vascular wall (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Tie2 Signaling
originalBlood vessels need a signal that tells endothelial cells to stay quiescent, stay attached to each other, and survive, and the Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase encoded by TEK provides it. Angiopoietin-1 and angiopoietin-4 bind and trigger receptor autophosphorylation, while angiopoietin-2 acts largely as a competing ligand that loosens this restraint and primes vessels for sprouting or regression; the balance between them governs vascular stability, permeability, and angiogenic remodelling during development, wound healing, and tumour growth. Phosphorylated Tie2 becomes a docking platform: SHC1, GRB2 with SOS1 and the PTPN11 phosphatase route signals to RAS proteins and the MAP kinase cascade, while p85 regulatory and p110 catalytic PI3K subunits drive AKT-dependent endothelial survival. Loss or mutation of this axis underlies venous malformations, and its dysregulation contributes to sepsis-associated vascular leak and tumour vasculature.
The endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase Tie2 (TEK) signals vessels to remain quiescent, connected and alive. Angiopoietin-1 and -4 activate it, while angiopoietin-2 competes, priming sprouting or regression, balancing vascular stability, permeability and angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumours. Phosphorylated Tie2 recruits SHC1, GRB2-SOS1 and PTPN11 for MAP kinase signalling and PI3K for AKT survival; mutations cause venous malformations.—Blood vessels need a signal telling endothelial cells to stay quiescent, attached to each other and alive. The balance of this signal governs vascular stability, permeability and remodelling during development, wound healing and tumour growth. Inherited defects underlie venous malformations, and its dysregulation contributes to blood vessel leak in sepsis and to abnormal tumour vasculature, making it relevant to vascular and cancer therapy.
Basigin interactions
originalBasigin (CD147) is an immunoglobulin-superfamily transmembrane glycoprotein on epithelial and many other cell surfaces that acts both as an adhesion receptor and as an obligatory chaperone for membrane transporters. Its interactions matter because they set the surface level of the monocarboxylate transporters that export lactate from glycolytic cells, and because basigin engagement on neighbouring fibroblasts drives matrix metalloproteinase production and angiogenic VEGF signalling, a combination that supports tumour invasion and metastasis. Partners here include the MCT lactate/pyruvate carriers, the heavy chain 4F2hc with its LAT-family amino acid exchangers, Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunits, caveolin-1, beta1 integrin pairs, and cyclophilin A, which binds the N-terminal Ig-like domain. Homophilic contacts between basigin molecules on apposed cells, plus binding to L1CAM and MAG, link this hub to adhesion, energy metabolism, migration and development.
Basigin (CD147) is an immunoglobulin-superfamily glycoprotein acting as an adhesion receptor and chaperone for transporters, setting surface levels of lactate-exporting monocarboxylate transporters. Engagement on fibroblasts induces metalloproteinases and VEGF, supporting tumour invasion and metastasis. Partners include 4F2hc with amino acid exchangers, Na+/K+-ATPase beta, caveolin-1, beta1 integrins, cyclophilin A, L1CAM, MAG and basigin itself, linking adhesion, metabolism, migration and development.—A cell-surface adhesion hub on epithelial and many other cells supports export of metabolic waste from highly glycolytic cells such as tumour cells, and drives neighbouring fibroblasts to produce matrix-degrading enzymes and promote new blood vessels, supporting tumour invasion and metastasis. It also contributes to cell adhesion, energy metabolism, migration and nervous system development, and is studied as a cancer target.
PECAM1 interactions
originalPECAM-1/CD31 is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor concentrated at endothelial cell junctions and present on platelets and leukocytes, where its interactions govern leukocyte transendothelial migration, T cell activation, platelet responses and angiogenesis. It engages partners both homophilically, through its extracellular Ig domains, and heterophilically, including with the integrin alphaV/beta3 pair. Its main signalling role is inhibitory: Src-family kinases such as SRC, FYN, LYN, LCK and YES1 phosphorylate tyrosines in the cytoplasmic ITIM motifs, creating docking sites for the SH2-domain phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 and the inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which damp immunoreceptor and integrin signalling and limit PLCgamma-dependent activation. This restraint sets thresholds for platelet aggregation and immune cell activation, while junctional PECAM-1 contributes to endothelial barrier maintenance and mechanosensing of shear stress, linking the receptor to vascular inflammation and thrombosis.
PECAM-1 (CD31), an immunoglobulin-superfamily receptor at endothelial junctions and on platelets and leukocytes, governs transendothelial migration, T cell activation, platelet responses and angiogenesis through homophilic and integrin binding. Src-family kinases phosphorylate its ITIMs, recruiting SHP-1, SHP-2 and SHIP1 to dampen immunoreceptor and integrin signalling. This sets activation thresholds, while junctional PECAM-1 maintains the barrier and senses shear, linking it to inflammation and thrombosis.—An adhesion receptor concentrated at junctions between endothelial cells, and present on platelets and white blood cells, governs leukocyte migration across vessel walls, T cell activation, platelet responses and new vessel growth. Its signalling is mainly restraining, setting thresholds for platelet aggregation and immune activation, while at junctions it maintains the endothelial barrier and senses blood flow shear, linking it to vascular inflammation and thrombosis.

Batch 04 · under "Cellular responses to stress"

Cellular response to chemical stress (12)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Detoxification of Reactive Oxygen Species
originalAerobic metabolism unavoidably produces superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants, and detoxification of reactive oxygen species is the set of enzymes that converts them to water and oxygen before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA. The same chemistry sets the amplitude and duration of peroxide signalling, so these enzymes both protect cells and shape redox-sensitive responses; their failure contributes to oxidative stress in neurodegeneration, inflammation and ageing. Three superoxide dismutases act in distinct compartments — cytosol, mitochondrial matrix and extracellular space — and hand hydrogen peroxide to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins. Thioredoxins and glutathione reductase, with their NADPH-dependent reductases, regenerate the reduced peroxidases each cycle.
