Also represented are the sources: NADPH oxidase subunits and endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductases that generate peroxide deliberately, plus copper chaperones that load superoxide dismutase with its metal cofactor.
Aerobic metabolism generates superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and a set of enzymes converts these oxidants to water and oxygen before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA while also shaping peroxide signalling. Compartment-specific superoxide dismutases pass peroxide to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins, which thioredoxin and glutathione reductase systems regenerate using NADPH. NADPH oxidases, ER oxidoreductases and copper chaperones are included; failure contributes to neurodegeneration, inflammation and ageing.Aerobic metabolism generates superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and a set of enzymes converts these oxidants to water and oxygen before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA, while also setting the strength and duration of peroxide signalling. Compartment-specific superoxide dismutases pass hydrogen peroxide to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins, which NADPH-dependent thioredoxin and glutathione reductase systems regenerate. NADPH oxidases and ER oxidoreductases generate peroxide, and copper chaperones load dismutases with metal.Every aerobic cell relies on this defence to keep the oxidative by-products of respiration from damaging its membranes, proteins and genetic material, while also shaping redox-dependent signalling. It operates inside the cell, in mitochondria and in the extracellular space. Its failure contributes to oxidative stress in neurodegenerative disease, chronic inflammation and ageing, and immune cells that deliberately produce oxidants depend on the same balance.
Regulation of HMOX1 expression and activity
originalHeme oxygenase 1 breaks down heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, and because heme is both a cofactor and a pro-oxidant, how much of this enzyme a cell makes is tightly controlled. Its induction is one of the standard cytoprotective responses to oxidative stress, hypoxia, heavy metals, inflammation and hemolysis, limiting tissue injury; loss of the enzyme in humans causes a rare syndrome of hemolysis, endothelial damage and inflammation. Control runs mainly through antioxidant response elements in the promoter, where small MAF partners such as MAFK dimerize either with NFE2L2 to drive transcription or with the heme-sensing repressor BACH1 to silence it, so that rising heme itself relieves repression. Beyond transcription, the enzyme works as a dimer anchored in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane until the intramembrane protease HM13 releases a soluble form that reaches cytosol, mitochondria and nucleus.
Heme oxygenase 1 degrades heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and iron, and is induced as a cytoprotective response to oxidative stress, hypoxia, metals, inflammation and hemolysis; its loss in humans causes hemolysis, endothelial damage and inflammation. Its promoter is controlled by small MAF proteins pairing with activating NFE2L2 or the heme-sensing repressor BACH1. The ER-anchored dimer can be released by the protease HM13 as a soluble form.Heme oxygenase 1 cleaves heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, removing a pro-oxidant cofactor as part of a cytoprotective stress response. At antioxidant response elements, small MAF proteins pair either with NFE2L2 to activate its gene or with the heme-sensing repressor BACH1 to silence it, so rising heme relieves repression. The enzyme acts as an ER-anchored dimer until intramembrane proteolysis releases a soluble form.Cells throughout the body mount this cytoprotective response when faced with oxidative stress, low oxygen, heavy metal exposure, inflammation or the breakdown of red blood cells, limiting tissue injury. It is especially important in blood vessels, liver, spleen and the macrophages that handle released blood pigment. People who lack this activity develop a rare syndrome of haemolysis, endothelial damage and severe inflammation.
NFE2L2 regulates pentose phosphate pathway genes
originalCells meeting oxidative stress need NADPH, and the transcription factor NRF2 supplies it by turning up the pentose phosphate pathway. Acting with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements, and recruiting the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, NRF2 induces glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase in the oxidative branch, plus transketolase and transaldolase in the non-oxidative branch. The result reroutes glucose away from glycolysis toward NADPH production, which regenerates reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and toward ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. This coupling of redox sensing to central carbon metabolism supports survival during electrophilic and oxidant challenge, and is exploited by tumours: constitutive NRF2 activation sustains the reducing power and biosynthetic precursors that proliferating cancer cells require, and contributes to chemotherapy and radiation resistance.
Under oxidative stress the transcription factor NRF2, with a small MAF partner and the coactivators CREBBP and EP300, induces oxidative and non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway enzymes such as G6PD, PGD, transketolase and transaldolase. This diverts glucose toward NADPH, which regenerates glutathione and thioredoxin, and toward ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides. Tumours with constitutive NRF2 activation exploit this for growth and chemotherapy and radiation resistance.Under oxidative stress the transcription factor NRF2, partnered with a small MAF protein at antioxidant response elements and recruiting the acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, induces pentose phosphate pathway enzymes: glucose-6-phosphate and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenases plus transketolase and transaldolase. This diverts glucose from glycolysis toward NADPH, which regenerates reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and toward ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis, coupling redox sensing to central carbon metabolism.Cells facing oxidant or electrophilic challenge redirect their sugar metabolism to build up reducing power and nucleotide precursors, improving their survival under stress. In normal tissues this protects against chemical and oxidative injury. Tumours with permanently switched-on stress defences exploit the same programme to fuel rapid proliferation and to resist chemotherapy and radiation, making it relevant to cancer treatment failure.
Regulation of NFE2L2 gene expression
originalNFE2L2 (NRF2) is the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, and how much of it a cell makes sets the ceiling on its stress defences; tumours that raise it gain resistance to oxidants and chemotherapy, while too little leaves tissues vulnerable to oxidative and electrophilic injury. Beyond the familiar control of NRF2 protein stability, transcription of the gene itself is regulated, and this is where antioxidant capacity is wired into other signalling routes. MYC, the NF- innerB subunit p65 with p50, and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain act at its promoter, and NRF2 with its small MAF partner feeds back on its own gene, while CREBBP and EP300 supply histone acetyltransferase and coactivator function. The result couples proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to the size of the cellular antioxidant response.
NRF2 is the master antioxidant and detoxification transcription factor, and its level sets cellular stress defence, with excess aiding tumour resistance and deficiency leaving tissues vulnerable. Beyond protein stability, the NFE2L2 gene itself is transcriptionally regulated by MYC, NF-kappa-B p65/p50 and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain, with NRF2-MAF autoregulation and CREBBP/EP300 coactivation. This couples proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to antioxidant capacity.Transcription of the NFE2L2 gene, encoding the antioxidant master regulator NRF2, is controlled separately from NRF2 protein stability and sets the ceiling on cellular stress defences. MYC, the NF-kappaB p65/p50 dimer and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain act at its promoter, NRF2 with a small MAF partner autoregulates its own gene, and CREBBP and EP300 provide acetyltransferase coactivation, coupling proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to antioxidant capacity.The overall capacity of a cell to defend itself against oxidants and toxic chemicals depends on how strongly its master stress-defence programme is expressed. Tumours that boost it become resistant to oxidative stress and chemotherapy, whereas tissues with too little are vulnerable to oxidative and chemical injury. This control ties stress resistance to proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals in growing and inflamed tissues.
NFE2L2 regulating TCA cycle genes
originalThe stress-responsive transcription factor NFE2L2 (NRF2) is best known for switching on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also reshapes central carbon metabolism, and its control of tricarboxylic acid cycle genes is one arm of that metabolic reprogramming. Here NFE2L2 drives expression of IDH1 and ME1, two NADPH-generating dehydrogenases that link citrate and malate metabolism to reductive biosynthesis and to regeneration of glutathione and thioredoxin. The effect is to couple the cell's response to oxidative and electrophilic stress with the supply of reducing equivalents and of carbon skeletons for lipid and nucleotide synthesis. In tumours with constitutive NFE2L2 activation, typically through loss of its KEAP1-dependent degradation, this same wiring supports anabolic growth and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, making TCA-linked gene regulation a point where redox homeostasis and proliferative metabolism meet.
Beyond antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NFE2L2 reprograms central metabolism by inducing the TCA-linked NADPH-generating enzymes IDH1 and ME1. This links stress responses to reducing equivalents for glutathione and thioredoxin regeneration and to carbon skeletons for lipid and nucleotide synthesis. In tumours with constitutive NFE2L2 activation, often through loss of KEAP1-dependent degradation, this wiring supports anabolic growth and chemotherapy and radiation resistance.Beyond inducing antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NFE2L2 reprograms central carbon metabolism by driving expression of IDH1 and ME1, NADPH-generating dehydrogenases acting on isocitrate and malate. This couples the response to oxidative and electrophilic stress with the supply of reducing equivalents for regenerating glutathione and thioredoxin and of carbon skeletons for lipid and nucleotide synthesis, linking redox homeostasis to anabolic metabolism.Cells under oxidative or chemical stress reshape their central energy metabolism to supply reducing power and the building blocks for membranes and DNA. In normal tissues this helps them survive toxic insults. In tumours whose stress-defence programme is permanently switched on, the same rewiring supports rapid anabolic growth and resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, where redox balance and proliferation meet.
NFE2L2 regulating inflammation associated genes
originalThe stress-responsive transcription factor NFE2L2 is best known for switching on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also sets the tone of inflammatory gene expression, and this arm of its activity links redox state to immune signalling. Acting at antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with a small MAF partner, NFE2L2 recruits the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300 to remodel chromatin at target promoters, among them the monocyte chemoattractant CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Output is context-dependent: NFE2L2 can drive such genes directly while also restraining NF-kB-driven inflammation indirectly, partly through heme oxygenase-1. Loss of this control contributes to chronic inflammatory and oxidative-stress-associated disease, including airway and vascular inflammation, and explains why NFE2L2 activators are pursued as anti-inflammatory as well as cytoprotective agents.
Beyond antioxidant defence, the transcription factor NFE2L2 shapes inflammatory gene expression by binding antioxidant response elements with a small MAF partner and recruiting CREBBP and EP300 to promoters such as the chemokine CCL2. Its effects are context-dependent, as it can also restrain NF-kB-driven inflammation partly through heme oxygenase-1. Loss of this control contributes to chronic airway and vascular inflammation, motivating NFE2L2 activators as anti-inflammatory agents.Besides antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NFE2L2 tunes inflammatory gene expression, linking cellular redox state to immune signalling. Bound with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements, it recruits the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300 to remodel chromatin at chemokine promoters such as CCL2. Its effect is context-dependent: it can activate such genes directly while indirectly restraining NF-kB-driven inflammatory transcription, partly through induction of heme oxygenase-1.Beyond protecting cells from oxidants, the cellular stress-defence programme shapes inflammatory responses, linking a cell's redox state to immune signalling and the recruitment of monocytes. Its effects are context-dependent, sometimes promoting and sometimes restraining inflammation. Loss of this control contributes to chronic inflammatory and oxidative-stress-associated disease, including airway and vascular inflammation, which is why drugs that activate it are pursued as anti-inflammatory agents.
NFE2L2 regulating MDR associated enzymes
originalThe transcription factor NRF2 (NFE2L2) does more than defend cells against oxidative and electrophilic stress: by driving expression of drug efflux transporters it also sets how much of a xenobiotic a cell retains. This arm of its programme, in which NFE2L2 regulates multidrug resistance-associated enzymes and transporters, explains why tumours with constitutive NRF2 activity survive chemotherapy that should kill them. NFE2L2 partners with a small Maf protein such as MAFK on antioxidant response elements and recruits the coactivators CREBBP and EP300 to acetylate histones and open those promoters. Among the induced targets are ATP-binding cassette pumps: ABCC1 and ABCC3, which export glutathione and drug conjugates, and ABCG2, a broad efflux pump, alongside ABCF2, linked to platinum resistance in ovarian cancer. The same circuitry that provides cytoprotection in normal tissue therefore becomes a liability in treated cancer.
NRF2 also controls how much xenobiotic a cell retains by inducing drug efflux transporters, explaining why tumours with constitutive NRF2 activity resist chemotherapy. With a small Maf partner such as MAFK and the coactivators CREBBP and EP300, it activates ATP-binding cassette pumps including ABCC1 and ABCC3, which export glutathione and drug conjugates, ABCG2, and ABCF2, linked to ovarian cancer platinum resistance. Cytoprotection thus becomes a liability in treated cancer.The transcription factor NRF2 controls how much xenobiotic a cell retains by inducing drug efflux transporters and multidrug-resistance enzymes. Bound with a small Maf protein such as MAFK at antioxidant response elements, it recruits CREBBP and EP300 to acetylate histones and open target promoters. Induced targets include the ATP-binding cassette pumps ABCC1 and ABCC3, which export glutathione and drug conjugates, the broad efflux pump ABCG2, and ABCF2.In normal tissues the cellular stress-defence programme helps cells expel toxic foreign chemicals, contributing to protection against environmental toxins. In tumours where this programme is permanently switched on, the same capacity lets cancer cells pump out chemotherapy drugs and survive treatment, as in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. A mechanism that is protective in healthy tissue thus becomes a major liability in treated cancer.
GSK3B and BTRC:CUL1-mediated-degradation of NFE2L2
originalNFE2L2 (NRF2) is the transcription factor that switches on antioxidant and detoxification genes, so how fast it is destroyed sets the cell's capacity to handle oxidative and electrophilic stress. Alongside the better-known KEAP1-CUL3 route, a second disposal route operates through the SCF ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and the substrate receptor BTRC. GSK3B phosphorylates a DSGIS motif in the Neh6 domain of NFE2L2, after priming phosphorylation of nearby serines, creating the phosphodegron that BTRC recognises; polyubiquitination then targets NFE2L2 to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here. Because PI3K/AKT signalling inhibits GSK3B, this branch couples growth-factor and insulin signalling to stabilised NFE2L2 and heightened stress-response output, and its loss in tumours contributes to the constitutive NRF2 activity that supports chemoresistance.
Besides the KEAP1-CUL3 route, NFE2L2 is degraded through an SCF ubiquitin ligase of CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and BTRC. GSK3B phosphorylates a primed DSGIS motif in the Neh6 domain, creating a phosphodegron for BTRC, and polyubiquitination sends NFE2L2 to the 26S proteasome. Because PI3K/AKT inhibits GSK3B, growth-factor and insulin signalling stabilise NFE2L2, and loss of this branch in tumours supports chemoresistance.The degradation rate of the transcription factor NFE2L2 sets cellular capacity for oxidative and electrophilic stress responses, and besides KEAP1-CUL3 a second route uses an SCF ubiquitin ligase of CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and the receptor BTRC. Its loss in tumours contributes to constant activation of stress defences, which helps cancer cells resist chemotherapy.
Regulation of BACH1 activity
originalBACH1 is a broadly expressed transcriptional repressor that sets the threshold for the oxidative stress response: partnered with small Maf proteins such as MAFK, it occupies Maf recognition elements at antioxidant and heme-handling genes, most notably heme oxygenase-1, and keeps them silent until heme accumulates or oxidants rise. Controlling how much BACH1 protein and activity a cell carries therefore shapes redox balance, heme turnover, erythroid and immune gene programmes, and, in disease, ischemic angiogenesis and the metastatic behaviour of breast cancer cells. Regulation runs through two routes represented here. An SCF-type ubiquitin ligase built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 with the substrate receptors FBXL17 or SKP2, together with ubiquitin supplied by UBB, UBC and the ribosomal fusion precursors, marks BACH1 for proteasomal degradation. In parallel, microRNAs including miR-155 and let-7 family members limit BACH1 message output.
BACH1 is a transcriptional repressor that, with small Maf proteins such as MAFK, silences antioxidant and heme-handling genes like heme oxygenase-1 until heme or oxidants rise, influencing redox balance, immune and erythroid programmes, ischemic angiogenesis and breast cancer metastasis. Its abundance is controlled by an SCF ubiquitin ligase with FBXL17 or SKP2 that targets it for proteasomal degradation. MicroRNAs including miR-155 and let-7 also limit BACH1 expression.The transcriptional repressor BACH1, partnered with small Maf proteins such as MAFK, occupies Maf recognition elements at antioxidant and heme-handling genes such as heme oxygenase-1, keeping them silent until heme or oxidants rise. BACH1 abundance is limited by an SCF ubiquitin ligase of SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 with the receptors FBXL17 or SKP2, which targets it for proteasomal degradation, and by microRNAs such as miR-155 and let-7.Present in most tissues, this repressor sets the threshold at which cells activate their oxidative stress defences and handle breakdown of blood pigment. Its abundance influences redox balance and red blood cell and immune gene programmes. In disease it affects new blood vessel formation after ischaemic injury and the metastatic spread of breast cancer cells, making its control relevant to vascular and cancer biology.
NFE2L2 regulating ER-stress associated genes
originalNRF2 is best known as the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also converges on the transcriptional arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, and this branch describes its control of ER-stress-associated targets. The central output is ATF4, a stress-induced transcription factor that lets cells survive hypoxia, amino acid limitation and accumulation of unfolded protein by turning on adaptive metabolic and chaperone genes; under sustained stress the same factor tips the balance toward apoptosis. ATF4 also drives serine and glycine biosynthesis, one reason tumour cells including non-small cell lung cancer depend on it. Transcription here requires NRF2 heterodimerised with a small MAF partner on antioxidant response elements, together with the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, linking redox sensing to proteostasis and to cancer cell stress tolerance.
NRF2 also controls ER stress-associated targets, chiefly ATF4, which helps cells survive hypoxia, amino acid limitation and unfolded protein but promotes apoptosis under sustained stress. ATF4 also drives serine and glycine synthesis, on which tumours such as non-small cell lung cancer depend. This transcription requires NRF2 with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements and the coactivators CREBBP and EP300, linking redox sensing to proteostasis.Beyond antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NRF2 controls targets of the ER stress response, notably ATF4. Under sustained stress the same response can tip cells toward death. Tumour cells, including non-small cell lung cancer, depend on this link for stress tolerance and for making the amino acids they need to grow.
NFE2L2 regulating anti-oxidant/detoxification enzymes
originalWhen reactive oxygen species or electrophiles accumulate, the transcription factor NRF2 escapes degradation, enters the nucleus and switches on a battery of cytoprotective genes; this arm of the antioxidant response is what allows cells to survive oxidative and xenobiotic insult, and its loss sensitises tissues to inflammation, chemical injury and degeneration, while its constitutive activation in tumours confers drug resistance. NRF2 binds antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins, with BACH1 acting as a competing repressor and the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300 supplying coactivator function. The induced programme spans glutathione synthesis and recycling (GCLC, GCLM, GSR), cystine import through SLC7A11, glutathione transferase-mediated phase II conjugation, quinone reduction by NQO1, heme catabolism by HMOX1, and thioredoxin- and peroxiredoxin-based peroxide removal. ATF4 coupling links this response to integrated stress signalling.
When reactive oxygen species or electrophiles accumulate, NRF2 escapes degradation and activates cytoprotective genes; loss sensitises tissues to inflammation and injury, while constitutive activation confers tumour drug resistance. Its loss sensitises tissues to inflammation, chemical injury and degeneration. NFE2L2 regulating tumorigenic genes
originalNRF2, encoded by NFE2L2, is best known as the stress-responsive transcription factor that switches on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but when it is constitutively stabilised — as in tumours with KEAP1 loss or NFE2L2 mutation — the same factor drives a pro-tumorigenic transcriptional programme. This arm of NRF2 output supports cancer cell survival, growth-factor autonomy and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, and its activation marks aggressive lung and other epithelial cancers. Acting as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins such as MAFK and recruiting the coactivators CREBBP and EP300, with SP1 contributing to promoter occupancy, NRF2 induces anti-apoptotic BCL2 and BCL2L1, mitogens including AREG, EGF and PDGFA, and components of NOTCH1 signalling. The result couples cytoprotection to proliferation and developmental signalling, so that a defence pathway becomes a driver of tumour progression rather than a barrier to it.

Cellular Senescence (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Oxidative Stress Induced Senescence
originalReactive oxygen species, whether generated by mitochondrial dysfunction downstream of oncogenic RAS or by prolonged interferon-beta exposure, can push a cell into an irreversible proliferative arrest, and oxidative stress induced senescence is the route by which that happens. It is a tumour-suppressive barrier: cells that sustain oxidative damage withdraw permanently from the cycle rather than propagate it, at the cost of accumulating senescent cells in ageing tissue. Oxidised thioredoxin releases MAP3K5 (ASK1), which activates the MKK3/MKK6-p38 and MKK4/MKK7-JNK arms; p38 substrates MAPKAPK2/3 and MAPKAPK5 phosphorylate BMI1 and p53 respectively, while JNK-driven AP-1 induces the H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B. Both converge on de-repression of the CDKN2A locus by evicting Polycomb complexes, raising p16INK4A to block CDK4/6-mediated RB inactivation and p14ARF to stabilise p53 against MDM2.

Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP)
originalCells that have permanently exited the cell cycle do not fall silent; they secrete a program of cytokines, chemokines and growth-factor binding proteins known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. This secretome reinforces the arrest in the cell that makes it, recruits immune cells to clear damaged cells, and—when it persists—drives chronic inflammation, tissue ageing, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and growth of neighbouring premalignant cells. Here the transcriptional control is the focus. DNA damage signalling raises CDKN1A, which restrains CDK2 and leaves the APC/C ubiquitin ligase with its FZR1 activator competent to degrade the histone methyltransferases EHMT1 and EHMT2, de-repressing the silenced IL6 and CXCL8 promoters. Oncogenic RAS–MAPK signalling activates CEBPB, which cooperates with NF-kappa-B subunits at the same promoters, while IL6–STAT3 and IL1A feed back to sustain output. AP-1 components FOS and JUN drive IL1A and IGFBP7, and INK4/CIP-family inhibitors lock in the arrest.

Oncogene Induced Senescence
originalCells that acquire a strong oncogenic signal, typically hyperactive RAS/RAF/ERK output or unrestrained E2F activity following loss of RB1, respond by permanently withdrawing from the cell cycle rather than proliferating. This oncogene-induced senescence is one of the body's first barriers to tumour formation, and its failure allows an initiating mutation to expand into a growing lesion. The response converges on the CDKN2A locus, whose two distinct products enforce arrest by separate routes: p16INK4A blocks CDK4 and CDK6 so RB1 stays hypophosphorylated and E2F target genes remain silent, while p14ARF destabilises MDM2 and thereby stabilises TP53 and its arrest programme. ERK-phosphorylated ETS1 and ETS2 drive p16INK4A transcription, ID1 opposes them, and related inhibitors including p15INK4B contribute. A microRNA-24/Argonaute arm sets a translational ceiling on both transcripts, tuning how readily cells commit to arrest.

Formation of Senescence-Associated Heterochromatin Foci (SAHF)
originalCells that have sustained irreparable DNA damage or critically short telomeres exit the cell cycle for good, and the assembly of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci is how that exit is made permanent. Each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin bearing H3K9 methylation, with telomeric and centromeric regions pushed to the periphery, and proliferation-promoting genes driven by E2F are locked in a silent state. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 stages at PML nuclear bodies before relocating to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and remodelling chromatin; linker H1 variants, HMGA proteins and loss of lamin B1 accompany the structural reorganisation. Formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, with CDKN1A enforcing the arrest. This chromatin endpoint underlies tumour suppression by senescence and contributes to the altered nuclear architecture of aged tissue.

Cellular response to heat stress (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Regulation of HSF1-mediated heat shock response
originalCells meet heat, oxidative insult and proteotoxic stress by switching on a transcriptional programme that makes more chaperones, and the control of HSF1-mediated heat shock response determines when that switch is thrown and how quickly it is turned off again. Keeping HSF1 inactive under normal conditions matters as much as activating it: chronic activation supports tumour cell proteostasis, while blunted induction leaves neurons vulnerable to aggregated protein. HSP70 family members and their DNAJ and BAG co-chaperones bind HSF1 and hold it monomeric, a repression relieved when unfolded substrates compete for them; trimerisation, nuclear import through the nuclear pore complex with the carrier HIKESHI, and DNA binding follow. Kinases including GSK3B and the ERK1/2-MAPKAPK2 axis, together with SIRT1-dependent deacetylation and ubiquitin-mediated turnover, tune the amplitude and duration of the response.
Heat, oxidants and proteotoxic stress trigger an HSF1-driven chaperone transcriptional programme whose on and off timing is tightly regulated; chronic activation supports tumour proteostasis, while weak induction leaves neurons vulnerable to aggregates. Attenuation phase
originalThe heat shock response must be switched off as well as on, and the attenuation phase is how cells terminate it once chaperone capacity again matches the load of unfolded protein. Sustained HSF1 activity is costly and, left unchecked, supports the proteostasis addiction seen in tumours, while premature shutdown leaves damaged proteins unresolved. Attenuation proceeds by several converging routes: newly made HSPA1A/HSPA1B and DNAJB1, no longer occupied by exposed hydrophobic surfaces, bind HSF1 trimers and silence them; HSP90 complexes with FKBP4 and PTGES3 favour the inactive state; HSBP1 engages the trimer and blocks DNA binding and transactivation; and acetylation by the p300/CBP acetyltransferases reduces HSF1 occupancy at heat shock elements. Trimers then leave the promoter and revert to monomers. Downstream chaperone products such as HSPB1, HSPH1 and SERPINH1 mark the response being wound down.

HSF1 activation
originalCells respond to heat, oxidants, and other proteotoxic insults by mounting the heat shock response, and HSF1 activation is the switch that turns it on. Without it, misfolded proteins accumulate unchecked and cells die under stress; constitutive activation instead supports the proteotoxic tolerance of tumour cells, making this a target in cancer. HSF1 sits in cytoplasm and nucleus as an inactive monomer held in check by chaperones including HSP90 and HSP70 family members; stress releases it, and it trimerises, accumulates in the nucleus, and binds heat shock elements to drive transcription of chaperones and co-chaperones such as DNAJB1, HSPB1, HSPH1 and ubiquitin. Feedback is built in: newly made chaperones, together with HSBP1, return HSF1 to the monomeric state, while acetylation and deacetylation, translation elongation factor and RNA-binding inputs, and RPA-mediated promoter access tune the amplitude of the response.

Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) (5)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
XBP1(S) activates chaperone genes
originalWhen unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the IRE1 arm of the unfolded protein response splices XBP1 mRNA to produce an active transcription factor, and the spliced product then drives a broad expansion of ER folding and processing capacity. This is the adaptive, pro-survival output of ER stress signalling: cells that cannot mount it fail at secretion-heavy tasks such as antibody production, insulin secretion and collagen deposition, and tip instead toward apoptosis. Spliced XBP1 binds the CCACG half of ER stress response elements together with the CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, inducing chaperones and co-chaperones (DNAJB9, DNAJB11, DNAJC3, HYOU1), oxidoreductases (PDIA5, PDIA6), degradation components for terminally misfolded substrates (EDEM1, SYVN1), translocon-associated and trafficking factors (SSR1, SERP1, SRPRA, SEC31A, KDELR3), plus WFS1, whose loss causes Wolfram syndrome.

When it fails these cells cannot sustain secretion and tend to die. Loss of one of its targets causes Wolfram syndrome, a disorder of juvenile diabetes and neurodegeneration.
ATF6 (ATF6-alpha) activates chaperone genes
originalWhen misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, one arm of the unfolded protein response cleaves ATF6-alpha and releases its cytosolic bZIP fragment to the nucleus, where it turns on the chaperone genes that restore folding capacity. This transcriptional output is what lets secretory cells such as plasma cells, hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells expand their ER and survive heavy client protein loads; when it fails, chronic ER stress pushes cells toward apoptosis. The activated fragment recognises the CCACG motif of ER stress response elements and works together with the heterotrimeric CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, whose three subunits are represented here, to drive targets including the ER chaperones BiP (HSPA5), GRP94 (HSP90B1) and calreticulin, as well as XBP1 and the stress regulators ATF4 and CHOP, linking adaptive folding capacity to cell fate decisions.

CREB3 factors activate genes
originalThe CREB3/OASIS family of membrane-anchored transcription factors couples the secretory pathway to gene expression, allowing tissues with heavy secretory loads to expand their capacity. Each member sits in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane through a transmembrane segment, carrying a bZIP dimerization and DNA-binding module plus an activation domain on the cytosolic side. When these factors move to the Golgi they are cleaved in turn by the resident proteases MBTPS1 and MBTPS2, a regulated intramembrane proteolysis event that frees the cytosolic fragment to enter the nucleus and switch on target genes. Individual members act in distinct tissues: CREB3L1 in osteoblast collagen secretion, CREB3L2 in cartilage, CREB3L3 in hepatic lipid and acute-phase gene control, with CREBRF opposing this output. Several are induced by ER stress but, unlike ATF6, do not sense unfolded protein via BiP release. Loss of CREB3L1 causes osteogenesis imperfecta.

ATF4 activates genes in response to endoplasmic reticulum stress
originalWhen misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, translation of the transcription factor ATF4 rises and it switches on a transcriptional programme that either restores proteostasis or commits the cell to death. This arm of the unfolded protein response, acting downstream of PERK-mediated eIF2alpha phosphorylation, drives expression of the ER-associated degradation factor HERPUD1, the amino acid biosynthetic enzyme asparagine synthetase, the growth regulator IGFBP1, the inflammatory mediators IL-8 and MCP-1, and the pro-apoptotic factor CHOP (DDIT3), with ATF3 providing feedback. Chronic activation contributes to secretory cell loss in diabetes and neurodegeneration.

ATF6B (ATF6-beta) activates chaperones
originalOne arm of the unfolded protein response reads the folding load in the endoplasmic reticulum and answers it by making more chaperones, and ATF6B is the weaker of its two transcription factors. There the sequential proteases MBTPS1 (S1P) and MBTPS2 (S2P) clip it, freeing a cytoplasmic fragment carrying a bZIP domain and a nuclear localisation signal that enters the nucleus and drives chaperone and ER-quality-control genes. Because it activates transcription only weakly and heterodimerises with the stronger ATF6, it can dampen rather than amplify the response, tuning how much secretory capacity a stressed cell builds.

Batch 05 · under "Axon guidance"

Signaling by ROBO receptors (8)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Regulation of commissural axon pathfinding by SLIT and ROBO
originalAxons that connect the two halves of the nervous system must cross the midline exactly once, and SLIT–ROBO signalling is the switch that makes a single crossing possible. Before crossing, commissural axons are drawn to the floor plate by Netrin-1 acting on the DCC receptor, while ROBO3 dampens the repulsive receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 so that midline-derived SLIT1, SLIT2 and SLIT3 are ignored; the secreted cue NELL2, read through ROBO3, keeps growth cones steered toward the midline from the motor column side. Once inside the floor plate, SLIT-bound ROBO associates with DCC and silences the attractive netrin response, ROBO3 is downregulated and alternatively spliced, and the axon is expelled contralaterally and barred from re-crossing. SRC-family kinase activity couples these receptors to cytoskeletal remodelling. Loss of ROBO3 underlies horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, in which hindbrain axons fail to cross.

After crossing, SLIT-bound ROBO silences DCC attraction and ROBO3 is downregulated, preventing re-crossing; ROBO3 loss causes horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis.SLIT-ROBO signalling lets a growing axon cross a source of repellent cue exactly once. This ensures correct left-right wiring of motor and sensory circuits. When it fails, hindbrain axons do not cross, causing horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, in which affected people cannot move their eyes sideways and develop a curved spine.
ROBO receptors bind AKAP5
originalAxon guidance receptors of the ROBO family steer growing axons away from midline Slit sources, and their cytoplasmic tails can be coupled to local kinase and phosphatase activity through a scaffold. The binding of AKAP5 to ROBO2 and to the ROBO3.1 isoform brings protein kinase A, protein kinase C and the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin into the immediate vicinity of the receptor, so that guidance signalling is read out alongside cAMP and calcium cues rather than in isolation. PKC recruited in this way phosphorylates ROBO3.1. Such anchoring is the general strategy AKAP proteins use to confine broadly acting kinases to defined membrane microdomains, and in neurons it links receptor engagement at the growth cone to cytoskeletal remodelling and decisions about midline crossing. The downstream consequences of the ROBO-AKAP5 interaction itself remain undefined, with the complex demonstrated in brain tissue.

SLIT2:ROBO1 increases RHOA activity
originalGuidance cues steer growing axons and restrain cell motility by reshaping the actin cytoskeleton, and this branch of SLIT-ROBO signalling does so by raising RHOA activity. When SLIT2 binds the ROBO1 receptor, the receptor engages the unconventional myosin MYO9B and blocks its RHOA GTPase-activating function; with GTP hydrolysis on RHOA suppressed, the active GTP-bound pool rises. The consequence is ROCK activation and phosphorylation of the myosin regulatory light chain, generating the actomyosin contractility that cranial motor neuron axons require to follow SLIT cues correctly. The same output limits cell migration and invasion, and loss of this restraint has been linked to increased invasiveness of lung cancer cells. It illustrates how a receptor can raise small GTPase activity by inhibiting an inhibitor rather than recruiting an exchange factor.
In one branch of SLIT-ROBO signalling, SLIT2 binding to ROBO1 inhibits the RHOA GTPase-activating function of the myosin MYO9B, raising active RHOA. This activates ROCK and myosin light chain phosphorylation, producing the actomyosin contractility cranial motor axons need to follow SLIT cues, and limiting cell migration, with loss linked to lung cancer invasiveness. The same response restrains the migration and invasion of other cell types. Loss of this restraint has been linked to increased invasiveness of lung cancer cells, connecting developmental guidance to tumour spread.
Regulation of cortical dendrite branching
originalCortical neurons acquire their input capacity by elaborating dendritic arbors, and this branching programme sets how many synapses a pyramidal cell can receive and therefore how cortical circuits are wired. The same secreted guidance cue family that repels growing axons is reused here for a constructive purpose: SLIT1 binds the transmembrane receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 on cortical dendrites and, instead of causing retraction, promotes the formation of new branch points. The cytoplasmic adaptor NCK2 couples activated ROBO to the actin regulatory machinery and is required for the branching response, illustrating how the interpretation of a guidance signal depends on which effector is engaged in which compartment. Disturbed regulation of cortical dendrite branching yields simplified arbors and altered connectivity of the kind associated with neurodevelopmental and intellectual disability phenotypes, placing this signalling within cytoskeletal control of neuronal morphogenesis.
Cortical pyramidal neurons elaborate dendritic arbors that set how many synapses they receive, and the axon-repelling cue SLIT1 is reused here to promote branching. SLIT1 binding to ROBO1 and ROBO2 on dendrites, with the adaptor NCK2 coupling ROBO to actin regulators, creates new branch points rather than retraction. Disturbed dendrite branching yields simplified arbors and altered connectivity associated with neurodevelopmental and intellectual disability phenotypes.Dendritic branching reuses a guidance cue system that normally repels axons. Branching sets how cortical circuits are wired. When it is disturbed, neurons develop simplified arbors and altered connectivity of the kind associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual disability.
Regulation of expression of SLITs and ROBOs
originalSLIT ligands and their ROBO receptors steer growing axons away from inappropriate territory, most visibly at the midline, and set the paths of commissural projections, so the amount of each protein a neuron displays at a given moment determines how it responds to guidance cues. This pathway covers how those levels are set, at every step from gene to functional receptor. LIM-homeodomain factors such as LHX2, LHX3, LHX4, LHX9 and ISL1, together with HOXA2, drive ROBO and SLIT transcription in a cell-type-dependent way; the RNA-binding protein MSI1 boosts translation of ROBO3 mRNA, with ribosomal subunits, cap-binding and nonsense-mediated decay components supplying the translational machinery. Protein abundance is then tuned by ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP33 which stabilises ROBO1, while dystroglycan and a collagen IV chain anchor secreted SLITs where they are needed. Misregulation contributes to axon guidance defects and to invasive behaviour in cancer.

Activation of RAC1
originalGrowing axons decide whether to cross the midline, and RAC1 activation is how a repulsive guidance cue is converted into remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton at the growth cone. A low level of RAC1 activity sustains axon outgrowth, so the pathway is less an on-off switch than a set point that shapes where a growth cone advances and where it turns away; loss of this control produces midline crossing errors and mispatterned commissural tracts. SLIT2 binding to the ROBO1 receptor exposes cytoplasmic motifs that recruit the adaptors NCK1 or NCK2, which bring the dual-specificity exchange factors SOS1 and SOS2 to the membrane, where they load GTP onto RAC1. Active RAC1 then engages PAK family serine/threonine kinases, linking receptor occupancy to actin and adhesion dynamics, and placing this repulsion step within broader Rho-family control of cell shape and motility.

Inactivation of CDC42 and RAC1
originalGrowing axons steer by retracting from repellent cues, and this branch of SLIT–ROBO signalling provides the switch that does it: inactivation of CDC42 and RAC1 collapses the actin-based protrusions at the leading edge of a growth cone. Repulsive guidance of commissural and cortical axons, midline crossing decisions, and the positioning of neurons during cortical development all depend on it, and disruption of SRGAP-family genes is associated with intellectual disability and defective neuronal migration. Mechanistically, SLIT2 binding to ROBO1 exposes a cytoplasmic motif that recruits SLIT/ROBO-specific GAPs, SRGAP1–3 and the Vilse/CrossGAP orthologue ARHGAP39, which stimulate GTP hydrolysis on CDC42 and RAC1 and so return these small GTPases to their inactive GDP-bound state. Lowering Rho GTPase activity withdraws the filopodial and lamellipodial drive, linking a receptor at the membrane to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

Role of ABL in ROBO-SLIT signaling
originalGrowing axons are steered away from the midline when the secreted cue SLIT binds ROBO receptors, and the ABL kinases sit at the point where that repellent signal is converted into cytoskeletal change. This determines whether commissural axons cross the midline once or recross inappropriately, and the same receptor-kinase axis is reused in epithelial polarity and in tumour cell migration. ABL1 and ABL2 act in two directions at once: they phosphorylate effectors that reorganise the growth cone, and they phosphorylate ROBO1 itself, tuning how sensitive the receptor remains to further SLIT. Their partners span both major cytoskeletal systems, with the cyclase-associated proteins CAP1 and CAP2 governing actin filament turnover and CLASP1/CLASP2 acting on microtubule plus ends, so filopodial collapse and microtubule behaviour are coordinated rather than controlled separately.

Sema4D induced cell migration and growth-cone collapse
originalSema4D binding to plexin-B1 reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, driving endothelial cell migration in angiogenesis while causing growth cones of responding neurons to collapse and retract, so the same ligand steers vessel and axon guidance in opposite directions depending on context. Plexin-B1 acts as a receptor whose cytoplasmic tail recruits the RhoA-specific exchange factors ARHGEF11 and ARHGEF12 and binds the small GTPase RND1, and in endothelium its association with ERBB2 couples receptor occupancy to RhoA, RhoB and RhoC activation. Active RhoA engages ROCK1 and ROCK2, which phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains such as MYL9 and MYL12B and activate LIM kinases; the resulting non-muscle myosin II contractility builds stress fibres, stabilizes focal adhesions and integrin-mediated adhesion in migrating cells, or in neurons collapses the peripheral actin network. This branch is Rho-dependent and distinct from the R-Ras-directed arm of plexin signalling.
Sema4D binding to plexin-B1 remodels actin, promoting endothelial migration in angiogenesis but collapsing neuronal growth cones. ROCK then phosphorylates myosin light chains and activates LIM kinases, generating myosin II contractility, stress fibres and stable adhesions, a Rho-dependent branch distinct from R-Ras plexin signalling.Sema4D binding to plexin-B1 reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, driving cell migration or growth cone collapse depending on context. It therefore shapes vascular patterning and axon guidance during development, with the outcome depending on the cell type that receives it.
Other semaphorin interactions
originalSemaphorins are guidance cues that tell migrating cells and growing axons where not to go, and plexins are their principal receptors; beyond the canonical class 3 to plexin-A route, a broad set of other semaphorin interactions couples transmembrane and GPI-anchored semaphorins to plexins of the A, B, C and D subfamilies and to non-plexin partners. These contacts steer axon repulsion and fasciculation, vascular patterning, bone remodelling and immune cell behaviour. Specificity comes from the receptor combination: SEMA4D acting through CD72 on B cells, SEMA4A and SEMA6 family members engaging plexin-A receptors, SEMA7A signalling through integrin alpha1/beta1 rather than a plexin, and SEMA6D working with the TREM2-TYROBP adaptor pair in myeloid cells. SEMA3E-PLXND1 restricts endothelial sprouting. Loss of these cues produces miswired circuits, disordered vessel branching and altered immune activation.

SEMA3A-Plexin repulsion signaling by inhibiting Integrin adhesion
originalGrowing axons are steered as much by being pushed away as by being pulled, and Sema3A repulsion is the classic example: the secreted cue binds neuropilin-1, which pairs with a plexin-A family receptor to transduce the signal and collapse the growth cone. The route described here works by switching off substrate adhesion, so a neurite loses traction on the extracellular matrix and turns away; the same logic restrains migration of non-neuronal cells. Plexin GAP activity toward R-Ras lowers integrin affinity for ligand, while Rnd1 and Rac1 gate plexin activation and cytoskeletal remodelling, FARP2 acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and Src-family and Fes kinases relay phosphorylation. Talin and the lipid kinase PIP5K1C link the output to focal adhesion assembly. Disrupting it misroutes axons and disturbs wiring of the peripheral and central nervous systems.

Sema4D mediated inhibition of cell attachment and migration
originalSemaphorin 4D acting through plexin-B1 tells a cell to let go and turn away, converting an extracellular guidance cue into loss of integrin-mediated adhesion and collapse of the leading edge. This repulsive signalling shapes axon guidance and growth cone steering, and the same receptor pair is co-opted in vascular and tumour settings, where plexin-B1 partners with the receptor tyrosine kinase MET. Ligand binding allows Rnd1 to engage plexin-B1 and switch on its intracellular GTPase-activating domain, which lowers active R-Ras; the resulting drop in PI3K and Akt output relieves inhibition of GSK-3beta, which phosphorylates and inactivates the microtubule assembly factor CRMP2. In parallel, recruitment of p190RhoGAP transiently reduces RhoA-GTP, and Rac1 activity is redirected, so that actin and microtubule dynamics at the periphery favour retraction rather than protrusion.

Sema3A PAK dependent Axon repulsion
originalGrowing axons are steered as much by repulsion as by attraction, and Sema3A is one of the classic repellents: growth cones that meet it collapse and turn away, which is how sensory and cortical projections are kept out of inappropriate territory and how peripheral nerve and dendrite patterning is set. Signal reception requires neuropilin-1 as the ligand-binding subunit together with a plexin-A family receptor, and the PAK-dependent arm of the response converts that binding into actin disassembly. Rac1 recruited to the receptor complex activates group I PAK kinases, which phosphorylate LIMK1; LIMK1 in turn phosphorylates cofilin, blocking its actin-severing and depolymerising activity and remodelling filaments in the collapsing growth cone. Src-family and Fes kinases and HSP90 chaperones support signal transmission. Loss of this route leaves axons insensitive to a major guidance cue and mistargeted.

CRMPs in Sema3A signaling
originalGrowing axons steer by retracting from repellent cues, and the collapsin response mediator proteins are the cytosolic step that converts one such cue, Sema3A, into a change in the growth cone cytoskeleton. Sema3A binds a receptor made of neuropilin-1 together with a plexin-A, and the plexin's cytoplasmic tail holds CRMP family members (CRMP1 and the related DPYSL proteins) close to the kinases that modify them. Sequential phosphorylation by Fyn-recruited Cdk5 with its neuronal activator p35, by Fes, and by GSK3beta strips CRMPs of their ability to bind tubulin heterodimers, so microtubule assembly stalls and F-actin depolymerises, collapsing the growth cone and turning the axon away. This axon guidance and neuronal differentiation machinery patterns cortical and sensory projections, and CRMP phosphorylation by the same kinases is a recurring feature of neurodegenerative and regenerative failure in injured nerves.

CHL1 interactions
originalCHL1, a close homolog of L1, is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor on subsets of neurons and glia that supports neuronal survival, neurite extension and the steering of growing axons. Unlike other L1 family members it does not bind itself homophilically, so its signalling depends on partners: contactin-6 in trans, beta1-containing integrin heterodimers engaged through RGD and DGEA motifs in its Ig domains, and neuropilin-1, through which it converts secreted Semaphorin-3A into a repulsive turning or collapse response in the growth cone. Its cytoplasmic tail contacts ankyrin, linking adhesion to the spectrin cytoskeleton, and a chaperone interaction is also part of its handling at the membrane. These contacts translate extracellular guidance cues into cytoskeletal change during nervous system wiring, and CHL1 loss is associated with abnormal axon targeting and neurodevelopmental deficits.
CHL1 is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor on neurons and glia that supports neuronal survival, neurite extension and axon steering. Recycling pathway of L1
originalGrowth cones advance by gripping the substrate at the front and letting go at the back, and the recycling of the adhesion molecule L1 is how that asymmetry is maintained. L1CAM links immobile extracellular ligands to retrograde actin flow through ERM proteins such as ezrin, radixin and moesin, so that cytoskeletal movement is converted into forward traction; without this, axon outgrowth and neuronal migration fail, and L1CAM mutations cause X-linked hydrocephalus and corpus callosum agenesis. A tyrosine-based sorting motif in the L1 cytoplasmic tail is read by the AP-2 clathrin adaptor only when unphosphorylated, so SRC-mediated phosphorylation retains L1 at the peripheral membrane while dephosphorylation at the central domain licenses clathrin- and dynamin-dependent endocytosis. Internalized L1 is then carried anterogradely along microtubules, with kinesin motors and shootin-1, back to the leading edge for reuse.
Growth cones advance by gripping the substrate at the front and releasing at the back, an asymmetry maintained by recycling the adhesion molecule L1CAM, which couples extracellular ligands to retrograde actin flow via ERM proteins. NrCAM interactions
originalNrCAM is an L1-family adhesion receptor that helps axons find their targets and helps assemble the specialized membrane domains of myelinated nerve, including the node of Ranvier; it is also needed for normal eye development, and its loss is associated with axon guidance and lens defects. Its interactions fall into three groups. Through a cytoplasmic ankyrin-binding segment it couples the adhesive surface to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton, clustering receptors at nodes. A C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffolds of the SAP97/SAP102/PSD-95 family, linking NrCAM into postsynaptic and submembrane protein networks. Extracellularly it binds the GPI-anchored contactin axonin-1/TAG-1 to promote neurite outgrowth, and partners with neuropilin-2 in the receptor complex that converts class 3 semaphorin cues into repulsive axon turning. Together these contacts make NrCAM a bridge between guidance signalling and cytoskeletal organisation.

An ankyrin-binding segment couples it to the spectrin cytoskeleton, and a PDZ-binding motif engages SAP97, SAP102 and PSD-95 scaffolds. It also contributes to synaptic organisation. It is needed for normal eye development, and its loss is associated with axon guidance errors and lens defects.
Interaction between L1 and Ankyrins
originalL1 family adhesion molecules are anchored to the underlying membrane skeleton through ankyrins, and this link determines where adhesion and excitability machinery sit on a neuron's surface. Ankyrin-G, ankyrin-B and ankyrin-R bind the cytoplasmic tails of L1CAM, neurofascin and NrCAM and tether them, together with voltage-gated sodium channels and KCNQ2/KCNQ3 potassium channels, to spectrin-actin networks built from alpha and beta spectrins. Coupling restrains lateral diffusion in the plasma membrane and strengthens homophilic adhesion, which in turn supports axon guidance, branching and synaptogenesis of cortical inhibitory neurons, and concentrates sodium channels at axon initial segments and nodes of Ranvier so that action potentials initiate and propagate reliably. Mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and spastic paraplegia, while ankyrin and channel defects underlie epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia and hereditary spherocytosis.

This restrains diffusion and strengthens adhesion, supporting axon guidance, branching and inhibitory neuron synaptogenesis, and concentrates sodium channels at axon initial segments and nodes for reliable action potentials. Neurofascin interactions
originalNeurofascin is an L1-family immunoglobulin adhesion molecule whose interactions organize specialized axonal membrane domains, and this adhesive biology is what allows nodes of Ranvier and axo-glial junctions to form and hold together so that saltatory conduction works. Distinct isoforms act on either side of the junction: the neuronal 186 kDa form clusters at nodes with NrCAM and is anchored to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton through ankyrin, while the glial 155 kDa form works with contactin and its associated protein CNTNAP1 to build the paranodal septate-like junction with the myelinating cell. A C-terminal class I PDZ-binding motif recruits syntenin-1, linking adhesion to intracellular scaffolding and trafficking, and the presence of doublecortin reflects the roles these contacts play in axon subcellular targeting, neurite outgrowth and synapse formation during neural development. Disruption of these contacts causes paranodal disorganization and conduction failure, and neurofascin is an autoantigen in inflammatory neuropathy.

Signal transduction by L1
originalThe adhesion molecule L1CAM does more than glue neurons together: it acts as a receptor that converts contact with the extracellular environment into decisions about axon growth, guidance and cell migration. This signalling underlies neurite extension and pathfinding during nervous system development, and loss-of-function mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and related syndromes with corticospinal tract and corpus callosum defects. On the cell surface L1 partners with beta1- and beta3-containing integrins, triggering Src-family kinase activity, the exchange factor VAV2, RAC1 and PAK1, and thence the MEK1/2-ERK1/2 cascade that drives motility and outgrowth. L1 also serves as an obligate co-receptor with neuropilin-1 for semaphorin 3A-induced growth cone collapse, so the same molecule can mediate repulsion or, through homophilic trans binding, attraction. Association with FGFR1 and casein kinase 2 phosphorylation add further layers of control.

Netrin-1 signaling (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Netrin mediated repulsion signals
originalGrowing axons are steered by the same guidance cue in opposite directions depending on which receptor they display, and netrin-mediated repulsion is the arm that turns netrin-1 into a turning-away signal. It shapes the trajectories of commissural and other projecting neurons, and the same receptors act in vascular patterning and as regulators of cell survival, since UNC5 family members are dependence receptors that trigger death when unoccupied by ligand. Netrin binding to UNC5A-D promotes phosphorylation within the receptor's ZU-5 domain, with Src-family kinase activity and the phosphatase SHP2 relaying the signal to the actin cytoskeleton of the growth cone. Long-range repulsion additionally requires cooperation with DCC, whose cytoplasmic domain pairs with UNC5, whereas UNC5 alone suffices at short range. Loss of this steering causes misrouted commissures and defective neural wiring.

DSCAM interactions
originalDSCAM and its paralogue DSCAML1 are immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptors on the neuronal surface, and their interactions guide growing axons and set the spacing of neurites and cell bodies in the developing nervous system. Both engage in homophilic binding, cell to cell, which mediates self-recognition and the repulsion that keeps sister branches and like neurons from overlapping; loss of this activity disrupts dendritic tiling and retinal mosaic arrangement. DSCAM also cooperates with the netrin receptor DCC in responding to the secreted guidance cue netrin-1, linking adhesive contact to the attractive turning of commissural axons at the midline. The gene lies in the chromosome 21 region associated with Down syndrome, though a direct causal contribution remains unproven. Overall this is cell-surface adhesion feeding into axon pathfinding, lamina targeting and the wiring precision of neural circuits.

Role of second messengers in netrin-1 signaling
originalGrowing axons steer by reading guidance cues, and netrin-1 is one of the strongest attractants for commissural axons crossing the midline of the developing spinal cord. Whether a growth cone turns toward or away from netrin depends on the second messengers it generates, so this signalling sets the wiring of long-range connections; loss of the pathway leaves axons unable to reach their targets, and the netrin receptor DCC is also mutated in congenital mirror movements and corpus callosum agenesis. Netrin binding to DCC engages phospholipase C gamma, aided by phosphatidylinositol transfer, to produce IP3 and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores while diacylglycerol directly gates TRPC3 and TRPC6; store depletion recruits other TRPC channels, and the resulting calcium influx at the growth cone, tuned by cyclic nucleotide levels, determines attraction versus repulsion.

DCC mediated attractive signaling
originalGrowing axons steer toward sources of netrin-1, and DCC is the receptor that converts that gradient into attraction, guiding commissural axons across the midline and wiring the two halves of the nervous system together. Loss of this attractive signalling leaves midline crossing incomplete, as seen in congenital mirror movements and agenesis of the corpus callosum. DCC itself has no catalytic activity; instead the kinases FAK, Src and Fyn associate with its cytoplasmic tail and, on netrin binding, phosphorylate it and recruit adaptors such as NCK1 and DOCK1. These feed the Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 and the exchange factor TRIO, while WASL and the actin-binding ABLIM proteins remodel filaments in the growth cone. The output is asymmetric actin polymerisation and filopodial extension on the netrin-facing side, turning a diffusible cue into directed growth-cone motility.

EPH-Ephrin signaling (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
EPHB-mediated forward signaling
originalEphB receptors bound by membrane-anchored ephrin-B ligands on a neighbouring cell signal into the receptor-bearing neuron, and this forward signalling shapes dendritic spines during central nervous system development. It converts contact between cells into synapse formation: filopodia become motile, find a partner, shorten, and mature into mushroom-shaped spines, with NMDA receptor subunits recruited to the new postsynaptic site. The output is cytoskeletal. Clustered receptors engage Src-family kinases and focal adhesion kinase, and recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as intersectin and kalirin that load CDC42 and RAC1; these drive Arp2/3-dependent actin branching and PAK signalling, while a parallel RHOA-ROCK-LIMK arm phosphorylates cofilin to stabilise existing filaments. Loss of this signalling leaves spines immature and synapses sparse, and the same receptors guide axons and set tissue boundaries elsewhere.

Ephrin signaling
originalEphrin signaling is bidirectional: when a B-type ephrin on one cell meets an EPH receptor on another, the receptor transmits a forward signal and the ligand itself transmits a reverse signal back into its own cell. This two-way readout of cell-cell contact steers growth cones, sets tissue boundaries, and shapes dendritic spines; loss of it misroutes corpus callosum and retinal axons and, for ephrin-B1, produces craniofrontonasal developmental defects. Reverse signaling works two ways. Src-family kinases including FYN and SRC phosphorylate conserved tyrosines on the ephrin cytoplasmic tail, recruiting the adaptor NCK2 and, through GIT1, ARHGEF7 and PAK kinases, converting the contact into RAC1-dependent actin and myosin light chain remodeling. Alternatively the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages scaffolds such as syntenin, coupling adhesion to junctional and synaptic organization rather than to kinase output.

EPH-ephrin mediated repulsion of cells
originalContact between an EPH receptor-bearing cell and an ephrin-bearing cell usually ends in withdrawal rather than sticking, and this contact-dependent repulsion is how growth cones, axon branches and migrating cells are steered away from inappropriate territory. It patterns retinotopic maps, guides commissural and corticospinal axons, keeps tissue boundaries sharp, and its loss produces mis-wired projections and disordered cell segregation. Because the trans-cellular EPH-ephrin interaction is of high affinity, adhesion must be actively dismantled: transmembrane and secreted proteases including ADAM10 and matrix metalloproteinases cleave the ligand or receptor, gamma-secretase components process the remaining stub, and clathrin- and AP-2-dependent endocytosis with dynamin internalises intact receptor-ligand complexes. Src-family kinases transmit the signal, while RAC1 activated through TIAM1 and VAV exchange factors drives the actin remodelling that collapses the growth cone and retracts the membrane.

EPHA-mediated growth cone collapse
originalGrowing axons steer by retreating from repulsive cues, and ephrin-A binding to EPHA receptors is one of the main signals that makes a growth cone collapse and pull back. This repulsion keeps axons out of territories rich in ephrin-A and is how topographic maps, such as the retinal projection onto the superior colliculus, acquire their graded order; losing it produces mistargeted projections. Ligand engagement clusters EPHA receptors and recruits Src-family kinases, which phosphorylate and switch the exchange factor ephexin (NGEF) toward RHOA activation while Cdc42 and Rac1 signalling falls. Active RHOA drives ROCK1 and ROCK2 to phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains, and non-muscle myosin II contracts the actin network faster than it can extend. The net shift from protrusion to contraction disassembles filopodia and lamellipodia, converting a receptor-ligand contact into directed axon retraction.

Gastrulation (10)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) during gastrulation
originalGastrulation requires that epiblast cells in the primitive streak stop behaving as an epithelium and leave it, and this epithelial-mesenchymal transition is how mesoderm is generated; an incomplete version of the same programme delivers definitive endoderm. Posterior signals, prominently FGF acting through FGFR1 along with WNT, NODAL and BMP, converge on the primitive streak transcription factors EOMES and TBXT, which switch on SNAI1. SNAI1 then represses the genes that hold the epithelium together, including E-cadherin, occludin and claudins, so that junctions dissolve, cells detach from the basement membrane and ingress, and a mesenchymal expression programme with N-cadherin takes over. Without it the germ layers cannot be laid down. The same transcriptional switch is redeployed in carcinoma cells, where TGF-beta-driven loss of E-cadherin underlies invasion and metastasis, making this early developmental step a template for tumour cell dissemination.

Formation of lateral plate mesoderm
originalDuring gastrulation the primitive streak produces mesodermal subsets with distinct fates, and the lateral plate mesoderm is the population that goes on to build heart, limbs, blood, and the linings of the body cavity and gut. Its induction depends on Hedgehog signals, SHH and IHH, arriving from the adjacent endoderm to switch on the forkhead factor FOXF1, which marks the tissue once specified. FOXF1 then drives BMP4 expression, and BMP4 with FOXF1 turns on GATA4; BMP4 sustains FOXF1 while GATA4 reinforces its own transcription and that of BMP4, creating a self-maintaining loop that locks in lateral identity before downstream differentiation genes are engaged. Because this territory gives rise to cardiac and vascular progenitors, disturbance of the loop underlies congenital heart and diaphragm defects, and the same signals are used to derive these lineages from pluripotent stem cells.

Formation of axial mesoderm
originalEarly in gastrulation, cells ingressing at the anterior primitive streak form the axial mesoderm, or chordamesoderm, the midline tissue that becomes the prechordal plate, head process and notochord. This midline is the embryo's organizing rod: it stiffens the body axis, patterns neural tube and somites through secreted Sonic Hedgehog, and later persists as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc, whose degeneration underlies disc disease. NODAL signalling through SMAD2 and SMAD3 cooperates with the pioneer factor FOXH1, with TEAD factors and their coactivator YAP1 released from Hippo restraint, and with the mesodermal factor TBXT to switch on FOXA2, which in turn drives notochord genes such as NOTO and SHH. WNT input via CTNNB1 with LEF1 and TCF7 positions this programme along the axis, coupling germ layer specification to midline identity.

Formation of the anterior neural plate
originalThe earliest step in building a brain is the specification of the anterior neural plate, the rostral epiblast territory that will fold into a neural tube and give rise to forebrain and midbrain; failure of neural tube closure produces spina bifida and related congenital defects of the central nervous system. Anterior character depends on BMP signalling being held off by inhibitors from the anterior visceral endoderm, after which OTX2, ZIC2 and POU-domain factors including POU3F1 and POU5F1 act on an upstream enhancer to switch on SOX2 in the neuroepithelium. SOX1, PAX6, ZEB2 and ZNF521 accompany this transition from pluripotency, as NANOG and POU5F1 expression is resolved. The sharp limit with the posterior neural plate is set by reciprocal repression between high anterior OTX2 and posterior GBX2, fixing the midbrain-hindbrain boundary and the regional identity of later brain development.

Formation of definitive endoderm
originalDuring gastrulation, epiblast cells ingressing through the anterior primitive streak become definitive endoderm, the germ layer that gives rise to the gut tube and its derivative organs including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. Its specification is driven by high NODAL signalling, which acts through SMAD2 and SMAD3 with SMAD4 to induce EOMES, MIXL1 and goosecoid; EOMES in turn switches on FOXA2, SOX17 and the GATA4/GATA6 pair that define endodermal identity and license later organ-specific programmes. Unlike prospective mesoderm, these progenitors retain E-cadherin rather than switching to N-cadherin, avoiding a full epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and instead remodelling adhesion so they can intercalate into an epithelial sheet; CDH1 together with the chemokine receptor CXCR4 is the usual way the population is isolated. WNT input via CTNNB1 and TCF7L2 patterns the streak alongside brachyury. Directing stem cells through this step is the starting point for making hepatocytes and insulin-producing beta cells.

Somitogenesis
originalSomitogenesis is the periodic segmentation of the vertebrate embryo's paraxial mesoderm into somites, the blocks of mesenchyme that give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis; its failure produces congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Segment size and spacing arise from a clock-and-wavefront arrangement, in which a molecular oscillator in presomitic mesoderm meets gradients of WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling that set the determination front. The oscillator is built from Notch-pathway negative feedback: HES7 represses its own transcription, and the glycosyltransferase LFNG, induced through NOTCH1/RBPJ, feeds back to dampen Notch, with DLL1 and DLL3 ligands shaping the response. At the front, TBX6 and MSGN1 drive MESP2, which turns on EPHA4 for boundary formation and RIPPLY2 to extinguish TBX6. Rapid proteasomal turnover keeps these short-lived regulators oscillating.

Germ layer formation at gastrulation
originalGastrulation converts a single-layered epiblast into the three germ layers, and germ layer formation at this stage sets out the body plan: everything from notochord and heart to gut endoderm traces back to cells that ingress through the primitive streak. NODAL signalling through SMAD2, SMAD3 and SMAD4, with the chromatin reader TRIM33, acts together with BMP4 and WNT-driven beta-catenin/TCF7-LEF1 input to position the streak posteriorly and to switch on the first mesendoderm transcription factors, TBXT and EOMES. These, with FOXH1, MIXL1 and GSC, specify mesoderm and definitive endoderm while shutting down the pluripotency network of POU5F1, SOX2 and NANOG. Mesoderm emerges by epithelial-mesenchymal transition; endoderm uses a partial, more plastic version. Failure of streak formation arrests the embryo before any organ lineage exists.

Specification of the neural plate border
originalBetween the future brain and the future skin, a strip of ectoderm is set aside that will become the neural crest and the cranial placodes; specifying this neural plate border is what allows vertebrates to build a peripheral nervous system, craniofacial skeleton, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, lens, inner ear and olfactory epithelium. The territory is defined positionally by intermediate levels of BMP and FGF with a graded WNT input, so that BMP4, FGF4 and WNT3A acting through beta-catenin and TCF7L1 place cells between neural and epidermal fates rather than in either. Within that domain a combination of transcription factors, including GBX2, TFAP2A and its paralogues, PAX3, PAX7, MSX1, DLX5 and ZIC1, cross-regulate into a self-reinforcing border identity while pluripotency factors are resolved. No single gene marks the border; failure here underlies neurocristopathies and craniofacial malformation.

Formation of intermediate mesoderm
originalThe intermediate mesoderm is the strip of embryonic mesoderm that gives rise to the entire urogenital system — gonads, nephric ducts, ureteric epithelium and metanephric mesenchyme — so its specification determines whether kidneys and reproductive tracts form at all, and defects here underlie renal agenesis and urogenital malformation. It is carved out along the medial-lateral axis by graded BMP signalling, high in lateral plate and low in paraxial mesoderm, while Wnt, FGF and retinoic acid gradients set its position along the head-to-tail axis. OSR1 and LHX1 mark the territory first, followed by the paralogous transcription factors PAX2 and PAX8, which act in a mutually reinforcing loop with the earlier factors. FOXC1 and FOXC2 expressed in neighbouring paraxial mesoderm repress LHX1 and OSR1 and so confine the domain. The same cues are used to direct human pluripotent stem cells toward kidney lineages in vitro.

Formation of the posterior neural plate
originalEarly in development the dorsal epiblast thickens into the neural plate, the sheet that folds into the neural tube and becomes the entire central nervous system; incomplete closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Formation of the posterior neural plate specifies the caudal half of that sheet, which gives rise to the hindbrain and anterior spinal cord, and it is built differently from the anterior half: rather than arising directly from epiblast, its caudal portion derives from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors in which WNT and FGF signalling, via WNT3A and FGF8, drive SOX2 through a dedicated posterior enhancer while TBX6 pulls sister cells toward paraxial mesoderm. Maternal to zygotic transition (MZT) (5)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Chromatin modifications during the maternal to zygotic transition (MZT)
originalAfter fertilization the embryo must erase the chromatin states it inherited from egg and sperm and build one capable of supporting its own transcription; these chromatin modifications during the maternal to zygotic transition accomplish that reprogramming. Both pronuclei lose DNA methylation, by different routes: in the paternal genome cytosine deamination and base excision repair, aided by TET3-mediated oxidation of 5-methylcytosine, replace modified bases with unmodified cytosine, while in the maternal genome DPPA3 blocks TET3 recruitment and displaces UHRF1 so that DNMT1-dependent maintenance methylation fails and demethylation occurs passively through cleavage divisions. In parallel, histone demethylases of the KDM5 and KDM6 families trim inherited H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, opening developmental loci. The result is the progressively accessible chromatin that permits zygotic genome activation, before methylation and repressive marks are re-imposed around implantation; failure impairs preimplantation development and imprint handling.

M-decay: degradation of maternal mRNAs by maternally stored factors
originalAn oocyte enters fertilization loaded with transcripts it made during oogenesis, and clearing them on schedule is what allows the embryo to switch from maternal to its own gene products. M-decay is the arm of this clearance carried out by factors the mother already stored in the egg, as opposed to later degradation driven by zygotic products; when it fails, oocytes arrest, zygotes stall at early cleavage and fertility is lost. Two adaptors set the timing: ZFP36L2 acts in the maturing oocyte and BTG4 after fertilization, each recruiting the multisubunit CCR4-NOT deadenylase, whose CNOT7/CNOT8 and CNOT6/CNOT6L nucleases shorten poly(A) tails and commit messages to decay. BTG4 links the complex to poly(A)-binding protein and the eIF4 cap-binding machinery, coupling translation to turnover. In parallel, DICER1-derived endogenous siRNAs guide AGO2 to slice complementary maternal mRNAs. Oocyte-specific factors such as NOBOX, ZP2 and PADI6 mark the transcripts and cellular context involved.

Zygotic genome activation (ZGA)
originalThe embryo begins life transcriptionally silent, relying on maternal mRNA and protein; zygotic genome activation is the switch by which the newly formed embryonic genome starts transcribing for itself, and without it development arrests within the first few cleavages. It follows extensive epigenetic remodelling of both pronuclei, including DNA demethylation and changes in histone methylation and acetylation, and proceeds in a minor wave at the one-cell stage and a major wave around the eight-cell stage in humans. DUX4, whose expression is promoted by DPPA2 and DPPA4, binds promoters of early embryonic genes such as ZSCAN4, LEUTX, DUXA and KDM4E and recruits coactivators including CREBBP and EP300 to activate them; it also drives bidirectional transcription from endogenous retroviral long terminal repeats and pericentric satellite repeats, the latter contributing to chromocenter formation. Clearance of maternal transcripts by the uridylyltransferases TUT4 and TUT7 accompanies the handover to embryonic control.
