Z-decay: degradation of maternal mRNAs by zygotically expressed factors
originalAfter fertilization the embryo must dismantle the stockpile of messages it inherited from the oocyte, and zygotic decay is the arm of that clearance carried out by factors the zygotic genome itself switches on. Timely removal of maternal transcripts allows the embryo to hand control of gene expression to its own genome; when it fails, transcript levels stay abnormal, development stalls and infertility follows. The uridine tail recruits PABPN1, which in turn brings in the 3'-to-5' exoribonuclease DIS3L2 to destroy the transcript, linking deadenylation, uridylation and exonucleolytic decay into one maternal-to-zygotic transition programme.

originalSperm package nearly all of their DNA with protamines rather than histones, achieving extreme compaction at the cost of a transcriptionally silent, epigenetically bare genome. Immediately after fertilization the male pronucleus must be rebuilt into ordinary chromatin using histones supplied by the oocyte, and this protamine-to-nucleosome exchange is what makes the paternal genome decondense, become permissive for transcription, and participate in the first embryonic divisions. Arginine methylation of H3.3 by METTL23 supports its incorporation. The reprogrammed chromatin established here sets the paternal epigenome inherited by the embryo, and defects contribute to fertilization failure.

MITF-M-regulated melanocyte development (9)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Regulation of MITF-M dependent genes involved in metabolism
originalThe melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation genes: it also sets how much oxidative metabolism a melanocyte or melanoma cell runs. By inducing PPARGC1A, the coactivator that coordinates mitochondrial biogenesis and respiratory gene expression, MITF pushes cells toward oxidative phosphorylation rather than glycolysis, and this axis helps explain why some melanomas survive targeted BRAF inhibition while low-MITF, low-PPARGC1A tumours are more invasive and drug-tolerant. MITF also raises expression of SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase that couples metabolic state to transcription and, through deacetylation of substrates including the p300 acetyltransferase, supports proliferation and opposes senescence. Together these targets make MITF a node linking lineage identity to cellular energetics, oxidative stress tolerance and melanoma phenotype switching.

originalMelanocytes depend on the transcription factor MITF-M not only to build pigment but to stay alive, and this branch of its output is the survival programme: MITF drives anti-apoptotic targets including BCL2, BCL2A1 and the IAP family member BIRC7, so melanoblasts survive migration and colonisation of the skin during development and melanocytes persist afterwards. Loss of this activity causes pigment cell death and depigmentation phenotypes, while its persistence in melanoma supports tumour cell survival and resistance to therapy. MITF also induces DICER1, linking it to microRNA processing, and one of its own targets, the TRPM1 intronic microRNA miR-211, acts with Argonaute proteins and TNRC6 scaffolds in silencing complexes to shape downstream gene expression. Repressive input comes through POU3F2 and the SIN3A-HDAC1 corepressor, tuning how much survival signal the lineage receives.

The result is cytoskeletal remodelling, altered attachment to matrix and a mesenchymal-like, migratory character. Because high MITF-M marks proliferative melanoma and low MITF-M marks quiescent invasive cells, this repressive output links a lineage transcription factor to metastatic behaviour and to resistance against targeted therapy.

originalMITF-M is the melanocyte-specific master transcription factor, and beyond pigmentation it directs a set of target genes that keep proliferating melanocytes and melanoma cells genomically stable. Losing MITF by RNA interference allows DNA damage to accumulate and pushes cells into senescence, whereas MITF suppression driven by ATF4 and translational reprogramming produces a reversible cell cycle arrest without senescence. The pathway therefore links lineage identity to replication licensing, genome integrity and proliferative lifespan, and is central to how melanoma cells switch between proliferative and invasive, dedifferentiated states.

Regulation of MITF-M dependent genes involved in invasion
originalThe melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation: it sets how mobile and invasive a melanocytic cell is. Through targets such as the adhesion molecule CEACAM1, the actin-nucleating formin DIAPH1 and the purine-metabolic enzyme GMPR, MITF tunes cell-cell adhesion and the state of the actin cytoskeleton, and it also feeds into epithelial-mesenchymal-transition programmes via SNAI2. This matters most in melanoma, where cells switch between an MITF-high proliferative, differentiated state and an MITF-low invasive state; the level of MITF activity therefore helps determine whether tumour cells divide locally or migrate and metastasise, and it influences response to targeted therapy. The same transcriptional control underlies normal melanoblast migration during development, linking lineage identity to motility rather than treating them as separate programmes.

originalThe melanocyte master regulator MITF-M does not simply promote growth; its target gene output shifts with its own activity level, and the cell cycle genes it controls explain why. At intermediate activity MITF drives proliferation by inducing mitotic and G1/S machinery including CDK2, cyclin D1, cyclin B1, CDC25B and PLK1, plus the receptor tyrosine kinase MET; when activity falls, cells dedifferentiate, slow their cycle and become invasive, and when it rises too far the CDK inhibitors p21 and p16 impose arrest. This rheostat behaviour is central to melanocyte biology and to melanoma, where phenotype switching between proliferative and invasive states tracks MITF levels independently of pigmentation output. originalThe melanocyte transcription factor MITF-M is best known for driving pigmentation genes, but it also runs a second programme that builds and acidifies the degradative compartments of the cell. originalSkin, hair and eye colour depend on a melanocyte transcriptional programme driven by the M-isoform of MITF, which switches on the enzymes and structural proteins that build and move melanosomes. Developmental Lineage of Mammary Gland Alveolar Cells
originalMilk-secreting alveolar cells arise during pregnancy from hormone receptor-negative luminal progenitors of the mammary gland, the alternative fate to the ductal epithelium that lines the gland's branching ducts. This lineage decision is what allows lactation: without alveolar commitment and expansion there is no secretory compartment to synthesise and release milk. Fate choice is set by the interplay of Notch, WNT and hormone receptor signalling, with loss of Notch input pushing progenitors toward alveolar identity, and prolactin acting through its receptor and downstream STAT signalling to drive alveolar differentiation and milk protein production. Neighbouring myoepithelial cells contribute by modulating Notch ligand availability. After weaning, most alveolar cells are cleared by involution, but a surviving pool of alveolar precursors self-renews and reconstitutes the secretory tissue in later pregnancies, linking this programme to mammary stem cell hierarchy and to breast cancer subtype origins.

Developmental Lineage of Mammary Gland Myoepithelial Cells
originalThe basal layer of the mammary epithelium supplies its own committed progenitors, and the myoepithelial lineage arising from them gives the gland its contractile capacity: spindle-shaped cells wrapped around ducts and alveoli that squeeze milk toward the nipple in response to oxytocin, so that lactation fails without them. These cells sit between luminal cells and the basement membrane, which they help deposit, and their continuous sheath also acts as a barrier restraining luminal outgrowth. Specification toward this fate is driven by strong EGF receptor stimulation, and the ligands represented here — amphiregulin, EGF and TGF-alpha — are the inputs that set that signal intensity during ductal morphogenesis and organoid differentiation. Myoepithelial progenitors are normally unipotent, but after loss of luminal cells, EGFR together with Notch and Wnt signalling licenses them to regenerate the luminal compartment.

originalThe pancreas begins as two buds of foregut endoderm, and this developmental lineage traces how definitive endoderm formed at gastrulation is patterned along the body axes and directed into multipotent pancreatic progenitor cells that will later give rise to acinar, ductal and islet endocrine cells, including insulin-producing beta cells. The growth factors here act as those instructive cues: fibroblast growth factors including FGF10 from the mesenchyme sustain progenitor proliferation and expansion of the buds, alongside FGF2, FGF4, FGF7 and EGF. Failure of this specification step underlies pancreatic agenesis and neonatal diabetes, and the same cues are used to make beta cells from stem cells in vitro.

originalThe islets of Langerhans arise during development from duct-like bipotent trunk progenitors of the pancreas, and this step describes their passage into a committed endocrine mid-progenitor state that still retains the capacity to make alpha, beta, delta, gamma and epsilon cells. Whether a trunk progenitor takes the ductal or the endocrine route is decided largely by its mechanical environment, which is why the matrix proteins dominate here. Fibronectin and vitronectin engage integrin alpha5beta1, promote cell spreading and sustain a YAP1-NOTCH mechanosignalling axis that represses endocrine commitment, while fibrillar collagens and laminins favour confinement, relieving that repression so NEUROG3 can rise and progenitor markers such as SOX9 and ONECUT1 fall. EGF signalling likewise restrains NEUROG3 induction. Understanding these cues underpins efforts to direct stem cells toward insulin-producing beta cells for diabetes therapy.

originalThe outer skin surface between hair follicles and glands is continuously rebuilt by keratinocytes that move upward through defined layers, and this differentiation programme produces the cornified barrier that blocks pathogen entry and water loss. Stem cells in the basal layer self-renew and generate transit amplifying cells, which divide several times before committing to a spinous, then granular, then corneocyte fate; corneocytes discard nuclei and organelles to become flattened, cross-linked squames that are shed and replaced throughout life. Each transition depends on cues from the surrounding microenvironment, with epidermal growth factor signalling favouring basal proliferation and delaying commitment, so that the balance between renewal and terminal differentiation sets epidermal thickness and turnover. Disruption of this balance underlies barrier-defective skin disease, impaired wound repair, and keratinocyte-derived tumours.

Developmental Lineage of Mammary Stem Cells
originalMammary glands arise from non-neural surface ectoderm, and the mammary stem cells derived from that ectoderm are the founders of the ductal tree, capable of regenerating a functional gland and of giving rise to both luminal and myoepithelial progeny. This developmental lineage traces that transition, from embryonic surface ectoderm to basal-residing mammary stem cells (also described as bipotent progenitors), which in the adult human breast are rare and concentrated in the ducts of terminal ductal lobular units. Their behaviour underlies placode and bud formation, pubertal ductal outgrowth, pregnancy-associated remodelling, and, when misregulated, the stem-like compartments implicated in breast cancer. FGF10 signalling through its epithelial receptor is one of the better-conserved inputs generating and maintaining these cells, acting alongside Wnt/beta-catenin, Hedgehog, Notch and ovarian hormone signalling in mammary specification.

Differentiation of Circulating Monocytes
originalCirculating monocytes arise in the bone marrow from myeloid progenitors, egress to the blood in a CCR2-dependent manner, and survive there only a day or two before either dying or entering tissues to become monocyte-derived macrophages and dendritic cells. Their differentiation sustains innate defence: classical CD14-high monocytes phagocytose and kill bacteria, non-classical CD16-high monocytes patrol the vasculature and respond to nucleic acids and viruses, with an intermediate antigen-presenting state between them. The two cytokines represented here set the fate and tone of this output: macrophage colony-stimulating factor drives survival, proliferation and mononuclear phagocyte differentiation through its receptor CSF1R, while interferon gamma from T and NK cells licenses classical activation, raising antigen presentation and antimicrobial capacity. Too little of this axis leaves monocyte and macrophage compartments depleted; excess drives the inflammatory monocyte influx seen in atherosclerosis, autoimmunity and chronic infection.

originalPancreatic ductal cells form the single-layered epithelium that lines the branching duct tree and carries acinar secretions and bicarbonate to the gut; their developmental lineage traces back through bipotent trunk progenitors, which also yield endocrine progenitors, to the multipotent pancreatic progenitors of the early bud. Duct shape changes with calibre, from cuboidal to high columnar, and apical cilia and microvilli mark the mature cell. The genes here are the matrix side of that programme: fibrillar collagens together with fibronectin and vitronectin build the interstitial stroma around growing ducts, while the laminin chains and their assembled trimers, with collagen IV-type partners, form the basement membrane that polarises the epithelium and positions trunk progenitors for duct versus endocrine choice. Adhesion to this matrix via integrin engagement guides branching morphogenesis, and disturbed duct identity underlies cystic disease and ductal adenocarcinoma with its dense desmoplastic matrix.

originalDuring the branching morphogenesis stage of pancreatic development, committed but still undifferentiated epithelial precursors in the growing ductal tree must be kept proliferating until a subset is released to become hormone-producing endocrine cells. This transcriptional programme sets that balance, and its disruption limits beta cell number, an origin of neonatal diabetes and pancreatic hypoplasia. ONECUT1 sustains expression of ONECUT3 and HNF1B, which maintain the epithelial progenitor state and duct formation, while NEUROG3 induction marks the commitment of individual cells to the endocrine lineage. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators, with the acetyltransferases CREBBP, EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, drives the repressor HES1 to restrain NEUROG3 and hold neighbouring cells as progenitors, so that lateral inhibition rations differentiation across the branching epithelium.

originalThe pancreas begins as a pair of buds of endoderm whose cells are already committed to become the exocrine acini, ducts and islets, and this transcriptional programme is what specifies and maintains that early precursor state. Much of it is inferred from mouse embryology, where loss of the founding factors causes pancreatic agenesis or severe hypoplasia; in humans, mutations in the same genes underlie pancreatic and beta-cell developmental disorders, including diabetes arising from failed islet formation. HNF1B, ONECUT1 and PDX1 act in the nascent bud, and together with mesenchymal FGF10 signalling they drive expression of a second tier that includes PTF1A, ONECUT3, NR5A2 and NKX6-1. These downstream factors begin to separate the acinar and endocrine fates, so the network functions as the hierarchical link between endodermal patterning and later hormone- and enzyme-producing cell identity.

AKT-mediated inactivation of FOXO1A
originalGrowth factor and insulin signalling suppresses a stress- and starvation-driven transcriptional programme, and AKT-mediated inactivation of FOXO1A is the step that accomplishes it. In the absence of signalling, FOXO1 shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm with enough nuclear residence to drive genes for gluconeogenesis, autophagy, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis; once insulin or growth factors activate the AKT isoforms downstream of PI3K, the kinases phosphorylate FOXO1 at several sites, promoting 14-3-3 binding and its exclusion from the nucleus, so the programme is switched off. This is the branch of insulin action that lowers hepatic glucose output and permits growth and survival, and its loss of control contributes to insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia. Because FOXO1 restrains proliferation, constitutive AKT activity in tumours keeps this tumour-suppressive factor cytoplasmic and inert.

originalPancreatic endocrine cells arise from a transient population of progenitors that switch on neurogenin 3, and this transcriptional programme is what commits those cells away from duct and acinar fates toward the hormone-producing islet lineages. Without it no beta, alpha, delta or PP cells form; loss-of-function mutations in humans cause congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea with permanent neonatal diabetes, and the same programme is the target of efforts to make beta cells from stem cells. NEUROG3 acts as a short-lived pioneer factor that directly induces a second tier of regulators, including PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and the zinc-finger factor INSM1, which together consolidate endocrine identity, drive exit from the cell cycle, and bias progenitors toward particular hormone subtypes. The pathway illustrates how a brief pulse of one factor is converted into a stable differentiated state.

Kidney development (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Nephron development
originalThe nephron is the filtering and reabsorbing unit of the kidney, running from glomerulus through proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal segments to the collecting duct, and its formation during fetal life sets the number of nephrons a person will ever have. Nephron development begins where ureteric bud tips meet metanephric mesenchyme: WNT9B from the bud induces progenitors to aggregate and express WNT4, driving a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into renal vesicles, while a self-renewing progenitor pool is maintained in parallel. The vesicle is polarized from the outset, with WT1 acting proximally to repress PAX2 and permit podocyte formation, and LHX1 and POU3F3 specifying distal segments and loop elongation. HNF1B then activates Notch components DLL1, JAG1 and LFNG plus IRX1/IRX2 as the comma- and S-shaped bodies form, and HNF4A supports proximal tubule identity. Defective versions of this programme underlie congenital kidney malformation and reduced nephron endowment.

Formation of the nephric duct
originalThe kidney and much of the male reproductive tract descend from a single epithelial tube, and this pathway covers how that nephric duct is carved out of intermediate mesoderm. Cells of the nephrogenic cord epithelialise in response to signals from adjacent somites and surface ectoderm, forming the duct of the pronephros and then the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, from whose caudal end the ureteric bud emerges to branch into the adult metanephric kidney. Positional cues from retinoic acid acting via HOXB4 set where this occurs, while PAX2 and PAX8 with LHX1 mark early renal progenitors; LHX1 and GATA3 sustain each other in a self-reinforcing loop that drives duct differentiation and switches on targets such as EMX2, ID4, nephronectin and the receptor tyrosine kinase RET. RET responds to GDNF from metanephric mesenchyme, and nephronectin engages integrin alpha8beta1, coupling duct to mesenchyme. Failure here produces renal agenesis and other congenital urinary tract anomalies.

Formation of the ureteric bud
originalThe permanent kidney begins when a single outgrowth, the ureteric bud, sprouts from the nephric (Wolffian) duct into the adjacent metanephric mesenchyme; that bud goes on to form the ureter, branches to build the collecting duct tree, and induces nephrons at its tips. Getting the number and position of buds right determines final nephron endowment, and errors produce renal agenesis, duplex or multicystic dysplastic kidneys and other congenital urinary tract anomalies. Batch 07 · under "Signaling by Receptor Tyrosine Kinases"

Signaling by MET (10)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
MET interacts with TNS proteins
originalThe receptor tyrosine kinase MET, activated by hepatocyte growth factor, controls epithelial cell scattering, wound closure and invasive growth, and its coupling to tensin proteins at focal adhesions links that signal to how a cell grips and pulls on its substrate. At adhesion sites MET associates with tensin family members whose expression tends to be reciprocal: TNS4 stabilises the receptor and favours motility, while TNS3 predominates in less migratory states. Because tensins bridge the cytoplasmic tail of beta-1 integrin to the actin cytoskeleton, this interaction places growth factor signalling directly onto the adhesion machinery that determines migration speed and direction. Elevated TNS4 accompanies MET-driven invasion in carcinomas, making this branch of MET signalling relevant to metastatic behaviour rather than to proliferation alone.

MET activates PI3K/AKT signaling
originalHepatocyte growth factor binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase MET triggers a survival and growth response, and one major branch of it runs through PI3K to AKT. This arm supports epithelial cell survival, motility and tissue regeneration in liver, kidney and skin, and is a principal reason MET-driven tumours resist apoptosis and invade. Activated MET autophosphorylates and recruits GRB2, which brings the multi-site adaptor GAB1 to the receptor; MET then phosphorylates GAB1 to create docking sites for the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1. The associated PIK3CA catalytic subunit converts PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, recruiting AKT for activation and thereby suppressing pro-apoptotic effectors and promoting mTOR-dependent growth. MET amplification or activating mutation, or excess HGF in the stroma, keeps this signal on and is targeted by MET kinase inhibitors.

MET Receptor Activation
originalTurning on the MET receptor tyrosine kinase is a two-step affair, and this pathway covers both: the proteolytic maturation of hepatocyte growth factor and the ligand-driven dimerization of MET itself. The output is a signal that drives epithelial cell survival, scattering, motility and branching morphogenesis, and that underpins liver and placental development as well as wound repair and tissue regeneration. HGF is secreted as an inert single-chain precursor and must be cleaved by a membrane-anchored serine protease such as hepsin or by the extracellular activator HGFAC; the Kunitz-domain inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restrain those proteases and so set how much active ligand is available. Mature HGF engages the SEMA and PSI domains of MET, promoting receptor pairing and trans-autophosphorylation that both raises kinase activity and creates docking sites for adaptors. Excessive MET activation is a recurrent driver of invasive carcinoma.

MET activates PTK2 signaling
originalHepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor makes cells move, and the route from receptor to movement runs through focal adhesion kinase. MET activates PTK2 signaling only when PTK2 is engaged simultaneously by MET and by integrins contacting the extracellular matrix, so the pathway couples a soluble growth factor cue to the adhesive state of the cell; SRC phosphorylation is required for PTK2 to reach full activity. The matrix side is supplied by fibronectin, fibrillar and fibril-associated collagens and the laminin chains that build basement membranes, read out through collagen- and laminin-binding integrins that pair alpha subunits with beta1. The output is adhesion turnover and directed migration, as in wound epithelialisation and branching morphogenesis, and the same axis drives invasion and metastasis when MET is amplified or HGF is supplied by tumour stroma.

MET receptor recycling
originalAfter hepatocyte growth factor binds MET, the activated receptor is internalised rather than simply switched off, and its route through the endosomal system determines how long and how strongly it signals. Recycling of MET back to the plasma membrane sustains ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 output, supporting the motility, scattering and invasive growth responses that HGF elicits in epithelial cells and that are hijacked in carcinoma progression. Endocytosed receptor is sorted by the adaptor GGA3 through RAB4A/RAB4B-marked early recycling endosomes and returned to the surface with help from ARF6, while adaptors GRB2, GAB1 and the CRK/CRKL pair remain bound and continue to relay signals from the endosome itself. Diverting MET toward degradation instead of recycling shortens the response, so this trafficking step acts as a control point on receptor tyrosine kinase signal duration.

MET activates STAT3
originalHepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase triggers one branch of downstream signalling in which STAT3 is recruited and activated, linking a growth factor cue at the cell surface to changes in transcription that drive scattering, morphogenesis and invasive growth. STAT3 docks at a phosphorylated tyrosine in the MET carboxy-terminal tail, directly or via a scaffold, and is itself phosphorylated on Y705, which allows dimerization, nuclear entry and target gene expression; SRC activity contributes to this phosphorylation, and continued signalling from endosomes after MET internalization sustains it. The output is anchorage-independent proliferation and increased motility, which is why this axis is scrutinized in carcinomas where MET is amplified or HGF is produced in an autocrine loop. In normal physiology the same route supports epithelial repair, liver regeneration and branching morphogenesis.

MET activates RAP1 and RAC1
originalHepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase reshapes the cytoskeleton and makes epithelial cells move, and this branch of MET signalling is how that happens: activation of the small GTPases RAP1 and RAC1. The output is cell scattering, lamellipodium formation, spreading and integrin-dependent adhesion, processes used in wound healing, liver regeneration and embryonic morphogenesis, and hijacked by carcinomas for invasion and metastasis. Mechanistically, the activated receptor recruits GRB2 and the scaffolding adaptor GAB1, whose phosphorylated tyrosines bind the SH2/SH3 adaptors CRK and CRKL. These adaptors in turn dock guanine nucleotide exchange factors at the membrane: RAPGEF1 loads GTP onto RAP1A and RAP1B to strengthen adhesion, while DOCK7 acts on RAC1 to drive actin polymerisation at the leading edge. Sustained signalling through this axis is a feature of MET-amplified tumours.

MET activates RAS signaling
originalHepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase drives the proliferation, survival, scattering and morphogenesis of epithelial cells, and much of that output runs through RAS. This branch describes how activated MET converts receptor phosphorylation into GTP loading on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, and thence into sustained ERK activity that reprogrammes gene expression for motility and growth. The receptor does not contact RAS directly: phosphotyrosines on MET recruit the adaptors GRB2 and SHC1, or scaffolds such as RANBP9, which in turn bring in the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 to catalyse GDP-to-GTP exchange. Signalling continues from endosomes after receptor internalisation, and binding of MUC20 or RANBP10 to MET dampens the response. Constitutive activity of this axis, through MET amplification or mutation, sustains invasive growth in carcinoma and is a target of kinase inhibitor therapy.

Drug-mediated inhibition of MET activation
originalMET is a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by hepatocyte growth factor to drive cell scattering, motility, invasive growth and survival, and it becomes oncogenic when amplified or mutated so that it signals excessively or without ligand. Because MET activation also emerges as an escape route in tumours treated against related receptors such as EGFR, blocking it matters both as a primary therapy and as a way to overcome acquired resistance. Pharmacological inhibition of MET activation covers the two ways this axis is drugged: monoclonal antibodies that intercept HGF or occupy the receptor ectodomain and prevent ligand-induced dimerisation, and small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors that block catalytic activity and downstream phosphorylation. The outcome is loss of MET autophosphorylation and of the adaptor recruitment that would otherwise feed proliferative and invasive signalling in solid tumours carrying MET-driven lesions.

MET activates PTPN11
originalHepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase drives epithelial cell scattering, motility, wound repair and morphogenesis, and the same axis is hijacked in carcinomas where MET is amplified or mutated. One branch of that output runs through the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN11 (SHP2). Activated, autophosphorylated MET recruits GRB2, which brings in the multisubstrate adaptor GAB1; GAB1 in turn docks PTPN11 at the receptor complex, where it becomes tyrosine phosphorylated after HGF stimulation. PTPN11 recruited in this way sustains ERK1/2 activation downstream of MET and supports recruitment and activation of sphingosine kinase, linking receptor engagement to lipid second messenger production and cell scattering. The phosphatase also acts back on MET itself, dephosphorylating receptor tyrosines, so this arm both propagates and limits growth factor signalling toward proliferation and migration.

Signaling by VEGF (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Neuropilin interactions with VEGF and VEGFR
originalNeuropilins are short-tailed cell-surface receptors that bind selected VEGF family ligands and hand them to the signalling VEGF receptors, so this set describes how ligand presentation tunes endothelial responsiveness during blood and lymphatic vessel growth. NRP1 captures the heparin-binding isoform VEGF-A165 along with VEGF-B and PlGF-2, while NRP2 additionally binds VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, and both associate laterally with KDR (VEGFR-2) or FLT1 (VEGFR-1) to raise their affinity for particular ligands rather than to signal by their own kinase activity, since they have none. The consequence is isoform-selective control of endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting, with NRP1 weighted toward arterial and angiogenic vessels and NRP2 toward veins and lymphatics. Loss of neuropilin function disrupts vascular patterning in development, and the same co-receptor interface is exploited in tumour angiogenesis and targeted by anti-angiogenic strategies.

VEGFR2 mediated cell proliferation
originalEndothelial cells divide in response to VEGF, and this is the branch of VEGFR2 signalling that drives that proliferation — the basis of angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation, and the target of anti-VEGF drugs. VEGFA binding to the KDR receptor triggers Src-dependent phosphorylation of the receptor tail, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting inositol trisphosphate opens IP3 receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium that, with calmodulin, cooperates with diacylglycerol to activate conventional protein kinase C isoforms. PKC then feeds into the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK cascade, either by phosphorylating Raf directly or by acting on Ras itself — here through relief of GTPase-activating protein restraint rather than exchange-factor recruitment. Sphingosine kinase and PDPK1 add further lipid and kinase input, linking the same receptor to survival as well as growth.

VEGF binds to VEGFR leading to receptor dimerization
originalBlood and lymphatic vessels grow where endothelial cells receive a vascular endothelial growth factor signal, and that signal begins with ligand binding to a VEGF receptor and the receptor pairing up. The step initiates cascades that drive endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and it is the point at which tumours recruit their own blood supply and the target of anti-angiogenic drugs. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC and VEGFD engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences; receptors mainly form homodimers, though FLT1-KDR heterodimers occur. KDR carries most angiogenic signalling in vivo, FLT1 acts largely as a modulating or decoy receptor, and FLT4 specifies lymphatic endothelium. Loss or dysregulation underlies vascular malformations, lymphoedema and pathological neovascularisation in retinopathy and cancer.

originalWhen VEGF acts on VEGFR2, one of the immediate consequences is that blood vessels dilate and leak, and this arm of VEGFR2 signalling explains how that happens. EGFR interacts with phospholipase C-gamma
originalGrowth factor binding to the EGF receptor does more than switch on kinase cascades; one branch of its output runs through phospholipid turnover, and that is what this pathway captures. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once tyrosine phosphorylated at the membrane, PLCG1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, so a single receptor event raises cytosolic calcium released from internal stores and activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling in epithelia, and inappropriate output from this arm contributes to the growth and invasiveness of EGFR-driven carcinomas.

GRB2 events in EGFR signaling
originalThis is the step that converts a ligand-bound, autophosphorylated EGF receptor into active RAS, and it is the canonical textbook route from a growth factor at the cell surface to proliferation. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises the receptor and triggers phosphorylation of its cytoplasmic tail. The adaptor GRB2 docks on those phosphotyrosines through its SH2 domain while holding the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 through its SH3 domains, so receptor binding delivers SOS1 to the plasma membrane next to HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, where it promotes GDP-to-GTP exchange. Output feeds the MAP kinase cascade and downstream transcriptional programmes for growth and survival. Because the link is so direct, activating EGFR or RAS mutations drive lung, colorectal and other carcinomas, and determine whether receptor-blocking therapy can work.

EGFR downregulation
originalGrowth factor receptors must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this pathway describes how ligand-activated EGFR is removed from the cell surface and destroyed so that signalling is limited in strength and duration. Loss of this braking system leaves the receptor chronically active, a route to transformation exploited by many epithelial tumours. After EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin or another ligand triggers autophosphorylation, the RING ubiquitin ligase CBL is recruited directly and through GRB2 and attaches ubiquitin to the receptor. The adaptor SH3KBP1 (CIN85) links CBL to endophilins, which bend membranes during clathrin-coated pit formation, while EPS15 and epsin read the ubiquitin mark and HGS/STAM sort the cargo into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation rather than recycling. Phosphatases such as PTPN12 and Sprouty proteins add further negative feedback on receptor and downstream kinase output.

SHC1 events in EGFR signaling
originalLigand-bound EGFR has to convert a phosphotyrosine signal into RAS activation, and the adaptor SHC1 provides one of the two routes by which it does so. SHC1 docks on phosphorylated receptor tails through its SH2 and PTB domains, becomes tyrosine phosphorylated itself, and then recruits GRB2 together with the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1; SOS1 loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, launching the MAPK cascade that drives proliferation, survival and epithelial migration. The pathway can be triggered by any of the receptor's ligands, including EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and HB-EGF, several of which are shed from the membrane by proteolysis. Because this is the principal mitogenic output of EGFR, activating mutations in the receptor or in RAS lock it on and are among the commonest drivers of lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers.

originalGrowth factor stimulation of the EGF receptor must be converted into a lipid signal if a cell is to activate the AKT survival and growth arm, and assembly of the GAB1 signalosome is how that conversion happens. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or HB-EGF — activates EGFR, which binds GRB2; GRB2 in turn brings in the scaffold GAB1, and GAB1 recruits the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1 together with the catalytic subunit PIK3CA. The assembled complex phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, triggering AKT-dependent proliferation and resistance to apoptosis. GAB1 also docks the phosphatase PTPN11 and links to SRC-family kinase activity, itself restrained by CSK and the adaptor PAG1, while paxillin ties the complex to adhesion signalling. Excessive flux through this node is a recurring feature of EGFR-driven cancers.

Nuclear signaling by ERBB4
originalThe receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4 can act directly in the nucleus as well as at the cell surface, and nuclear signaling by ERBB4 is how neuregulin ligands are converted into changes in gene expression rather than kinase cascades alone. Neuregulin or EGF-family binding to juxtamembrane-A isoforms triggers ectodomain shedding by ADAM17, followed by gamma-secretase cleavage (presenilins with nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN) that liberates a soluble intracellular domain into the cytosol. This fragment shuttles transcription factors into the nucleus and serves as their co-factor: with TAB2 and the corepressor NCOR1 it suppresses astrocytic genes such as GFAP and S100B in neural precursors, with STAT5A it drives beta-casein transcription during lactation, and with estrogen receptor it promotes progesterone receptor and CXCL12 expression. Competing WW-domain partners YAP1 and the tumour suppressor WWOX set whether the fragment reaches the nucleus, linking this axis to mammary differentiation and breast cancer.

Downregulation of ERBB4 signaling
originalSignalling through the ERBB4 receptor tyrosine kinase, one of the EGF receptor family, is terminated by ubiquitin-dependent destruction of the receptor and its cleavage fragments, and this downregulation sets how much growth-factor input from neuregulins a cell converts into proliferation, differentiation or nuclear gene regulation. Excessive or unopposed ERBB4 signalling contributes to tumour growth, while the same restraint shapes heart and nervous system development where ERBB4 acts. WW-domain motifs in the receptor's cytoplasmic tail recruit the NEDD4-family E3 ligases WWP1, ITCH and NEDD4, which attach ubiquitin to intact ERBB4 and to its membrane-anchored and soluble intracellular cleavage products, routing them to proteasomal and lysosomal degradation. Ubiquitination of the soluble fragment limits the pool that can enter the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-regulator. Binding by these ligases does not require receptor activation, and SRC-mediated phosphorylation modulates the outcome.

ERBB2 Regulates Cell Motility
originalGrowth factor receptors of the ERBB family do more than drive proliferation: when ERBB2 partners with EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4 after ligand binding, it also steers where a cell goes. This motility arm matters for epithelial wound closure and morphogenesis, and its hyperactivation in ERBB2-amplified breast cancer contributes to invasion and metastasis rather than growth alone. Ligands such as EGF, betacellulin, heregulins and HB-EGF trigger receptor dimerisation and phosphorylation, creating a docking site for MEMO1. MEMO1 in turn holds active RHOA and its effector DIAPH1, a formin, at the plasma membrane, so that actin polymerisation and microtubule capture are coordinated at the leading edge. The result is directed lamellipodial protrusion and stabilised cell polarity, linking receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling and migration.

Downregulation of ERBB2:ERBB3 signaling
originalGrowth signalling through the ERBB2:ERBB3 heterodimer has to be switched off as well as switched on, and this negative feedback arm sets how much ERBB3 remains available at the cell surface. Neuregulin binding to ERBB3 and pairing with ERBB2 activates AKT; the same AKT activity phosphorylates and stabilises the deubiquitinase USP8, which reverses self-ubiquitination of the E3 ligase RNF41. Stabilised RNF41 then ubiquitinates ERBB3 and sends it for degradation, so receptor output limits its own duration. When RNF41 levels are low, ERBB3 persists on the membrane and sensitivity to neuregulin rises. Loss of this brake contributes to sustained PI3K/AKT signalling in breast and other epithelial cancers, where ERBB3 retention is one route to resistance against ERBB2-directed therapy, making receptor turnover part of the control of proliferation and survival.

PLCG1 events in ERBB2 signaling
originalGrowth factor receptors of the ERBB family can steer cells toward motility and calcium-dependent responses rather than simply proliferation, and the PLCG1 arm of ERBB2 signalling is how that branch is engaged. Once recruited and activated, PLCG1 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C. The output feeds into actin remodelling, cell migration and secretion, and contributes to the invasive behaviour of ERBB2-amplified breast tumours. Because this route depends on heterodimer formation rather than ERBB2 alone, it illustrates how receptor partner choice determines which second messengers a growth signal produces.

Drug-mediated inhibition of ERBB2 signaling
originalERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose amplification drives an aggressive subset of breast and gastric cancers, and blocking it is one of the clearest successes of targeted cancer therapy. Two drug classes converge on this receptor: small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib, which occupy the ATP-binding site and shut down catalytic activity, and monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab, which bind the extracellular domain to prevent dimerisation and promote receptor downregulation. Loss of signalling removes the proliferative and survival input normally relayed to PI3K/AKT and MAPK cascades. The accompanying chaperone machinery, HSP90 with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, stabilises ERBB2 and is itself a drug target, while ERBIN binds the receptor and restrains its signalling. Resistance commonly arises through kinase-domain mutation or bypass activation of related receptors.

originalWhen ERBB2 heterodimerizes with EGFR or ERBB4 after growth factor binding, phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails become docking sites for the adaptor GRB2, and this is the step that converts ligand binding into RAS-dependent proliferation. GRB2 arrives bound to SOS1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, which in turn switches on RAF and the downstream MAP kinase cascade controlling cell cycle entry, growth and survival. The ligands feeding into this route are the EGF-family and neuregulin growth factors, so the same adaptor step serves epithelial proliferation, cardiac and neural development, and wound repair. Because ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancers raises the number of signalling-competent dimers, GRB2 recruitment is a principal route by which these tumours sustain constitutive MAP kinase output, and it underlies resistance when RAS is mutated downstream.

originalPTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that becomes active downstream of ERBB2, linking growth factor receptor engagement at the plasma membrane to proliferation, migration and survival signalling in epithelial cells. Signaling by Insulin receptor (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Insulin receptor recycling
originalAfter insulin binds its receptor and the complex is internalised, the cell must decide the fate of both partners, and insulin receptor recycling is the route that destroys the hormone while returning the receptor to the cell surface. This sets how long a cell stays insulin-responsive and how quickly circulating insulin is cleared, so it bears directly on insulin sensitivity and on the resistance seen in type 2 diabetes. The vacuolar ATPase, represented here by the full complement of V0 and V1 subunits, pumps protons into the endosome; the resulting acidic pH releases insulin from the receptor, and the freed hormone is degraded by insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin D. Phosphatases such as PTP1B and PTPRF strip phosphates from the receptor's activated kinase domain, terminating downstream signalling and restoring a ligand-free receptor to the plasma membrane for another round of stimulation.
After insulin-receptor internalisation, recycling destroys insulin and returns the receptor to the surface, setting how long cells stay insulin-responsive and how fast insulin is cleared, relevant to type 2 diabetes. This sets how long a cell stays responsive and how quickly the circulating hormone is cleared, mainly in liver and other target tissues. It therefore bears directly on hormone sensitivity and on the resistance seen in type 2 diabetes.
Signal attenuation
originalInsulin signalling must be switched off as well as on, and signal attenuation is the step that returns a stimulated cell to baseline after an insulin pulse. Once ligand and receptor dissociate inside the endosome and insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen, endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphate from the activated insulin receptor and from its docking substrates. Dephosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 releases the adaptors and exchange factors they recruit — GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 — so the complexes that feed the ERK arm through MAPK1 and MAPK3 fall apart, and the adaptor GRB10 contributes further negative regulation of the receptor. Loss of this shutdown leaves growth and metabolic signalling running without a hormonal cue, while excessive attenuation blunts insulin action and contributes to insulin resistance, making it part of how glucose homeostasis is kept responsive.

IRS activation
originalInsulin's message gets past the receptor only through a docking protein, and IRS activation is that step: the activated insulin receptor recruits IRS1 or IRS2 and phosphorylates them on multiple tyrosines, converting them into membrane-associated scaffolds that assemble downstream effectors. This is what couples insulin binding to PI3K-dependent glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, and to the Ras-MAP kinase arm controlling growth and gene expression. IRS1 engages the receptor's juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain, with its PH domain anchoring it to membrane phospholipids, then releases once phosphorylated so that SH2-containing partners can bind. GRB10 competes at the receptor and dampens the output, one of several brakes on the pathway. Loss or serine-phosphorylation-driven inactivation of IRS proteins underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, making this node the main site where metabolic signalling is tuned.

Batch 08 · under "DNA Repair"

DNA Damage Reversal (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
ALKBH2 mediated reversal of alkylation damage
originalAlkylating agents, whether environmental or endogenous, leave methyl adducts such as 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine on DNA bases, where they block base pairing and stall replication. ALKBH2-mediated reversal of alkylation damage erases these lesions directly, without excising the base or breaking the backbone, so no repair patch or strand gap is ever created. ALKBH2 is an iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase, a human counterpart of bacterial AlkB, that hydroxylates the offending methyl group; the unstable intermediate collapses and releases formaldehyde, regenerating the unmodified base. Longer adducts such as 1-ethyladenine are removed the same way, yielding acetaldehyde. Acting mainly on double-stranded DNA and enriched at replication foci, this repair route protects genome integrity and shapes cellular sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy.
Alkylation damage such as 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine blocks base pairing and stalls replication. ALKBH2, an iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase related to bacterial AlkB, hydroxylates the methyl group so it leaves as formaldehyde, restoring the base directly without excision or strand breakage; ethyl adducts leave as acetaldehyde. Working mainly on double-stranded DNA at replication foci, it protects genome integrity and influences sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy.Methyl adducts such as 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine block base pairing and stall replication. A dioxygenase dependent on iron(II) and 2-oxoglutarate hydroxylates the offending alkyl group directly on duplex DNA; the unstable intermediate collapses, releasing formaldehyde from a methyl group or acetaldehyde from an ethyl group and regenerating the unmodified base, with no base excision, strand incision or repair patch.—
ALKBH3 mediated reversal of alkylation damage
originalAlkylating agents, whether environmental or endogenous, leave methyl adducts on DNA bases that block base pairing and stall replication. Direct reversal by ALKBH3 erases two of the most damaging of these, 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine, restoring the unmodified base in a single oxidative step rather than excising and resynthesising the strand. The enzyme is an iron(II)- and alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase that hydroxylates the offending methyl group so it falls away as formaldehyde; an ethyl adduct is released as acetaldehyde. Because ALKBH3 works best on single-stranded DNA, repair of duplex substrates requires the ASCC complex, whose ASCC3 helicase unwinds the damaged region while ASCC1 and ASCC2 target the activity to sites of alkylation damage. This chemistry contributes to alkylation tolerance and shapes how tumour cells respond to methylating chemotherapy.

MGMT-mediated DNA damage reversal
originalAlkylating agents, whether endogenous metabolites or chemotherapy drugs, can transfer a methyl group to the O6 position of guanine, creating a base that pairs ambiguously with both cytosine and thymine and therefore seeds G:C to A:T transition mutations at the next round of replication. Direct reversal by MGMT removes this lesion before it is copied, restoring guanine in a single step without excising the base or nicking the backbone. The protein accepts the methyl group onto an active-site cysteine and is thereby inactivated, so each molecule acts only once and the cell's capacity is set by how much of it is present. Silencing of the gene by promoter hypermethylation is common in glioma and other tumours, raising mutational load but also sensitising those tumours to alkylating chemotherapy such as temozolomide, which makes this repair route a prognostic and predictive marker in oncology.

MGMT reverses it directly by transferring the methyl group to its own active-site cysteine, which inactivates the protein so repair capacity depends on protein amount. The protein is inactivated by the transfer, so each molecule acts stoichiometrically, once.—

Base Excision Repair (10)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
APEX1-Independent Resolution of AP Sites via the Single Nucleotide Replacement Pathway
originalAbasic sites arise constantly in DNA, both spontaneously and as intermediates left behind by glycosylases that excise damaged bases, and they must be cleaned up before replication turns them into mutations or strand breaks. This branch of base excision repair resolves them without the usual AP endonuclease step: NEIL1 and NEIL2, bifunctional glycosylases with beta/delta lyase activity, incise the strand and leave a 3' phosphate and a 5' deoxyribose phosphate. DNA polymerase beta trims the 5'dRP but is blocked by the 3' phosphate, so the phosphatase activity of PNKP must restore a 3'-hydroxyl before a single replacement nucleotide can be inserted and the nick sealed by the XRCC1-scaffolded LIG3 complex. The route matters for handling oxidative lesions, including those generated by OGG1, and for limiting mutagenesis in transcribed and replicating DNA.
Abasic sites, formed spontaneously or by glycosylases removing damaged bases, must be processed before they cause mutations or breaks. In this AP-endonuclease-independent branch of base excision repair, the bifunctional glycosylases NEIL1 and NEIL2 incise the strand, leaving 3' phosphate and 5' deoxyribose phosphate ends. PNKP removes the 3' phosphate, DNA polymerase beta trims the 5'dRP and inserts one nucleotide, and XRCC1-LIG3 seals the nick, limiting mutagenesis from oxidative lesions.Abasic sites are resolved without an AP endonuclease step. A single replacement nucleotide is then inserted and the nick sealed by a scaffolded ligase complex.—
Cleavage of the damaged purine
originalThe first committed step of base excision repair is removal of a chemically damaged purine base from DNA, and this is where that cleavage happens: DNA glycosylases hydrolyse the N-glycosidic bond, releasing the damaged base and leaving an abasic site for downstream endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps. It matters because oxidation and alkylation of guanine and adenine are constant products of respiration and environmental exposure, and unrepaired 8-oxoguanine mispairs with adenine to fix G:C to T:A transversions. OGG1 excises 8-oxoguanine, MUTYH removes the adenine misinserted opposite it, MPG handles alkylated and deaminated purines, and NEIL3 acts on further oxidised lesions. Histones place the reaction in chromatin, while the shelterin components mark telomeric DNA as a distinct substrate. Loss of MUTYH causes an inherited polyposis and colorectal cancer predisposition.

OGG1 removes 8-oxoguanine, MUTYH removes adenine mispaired opposite it, MPG handles alkylated and deaminated purines, and NEIL3 acts on further oxidised lesions, operating in chromatin and at telomeres. The reaction proceeds on nucleosomal DNA.—
Cleavage of the damaged pyrimidine
originalOxidation and deamination constantly damage the pyrimidine bases of DNA, and the first committed step of base excision repair is removal of the damaged base by a glycosylase that recognises it. Cleavage of the damaged pyrimidine is carried out here by uracil DNA glycosylases UNG and SMUG1, the thymine and mismatch glycosylases TDG and MBD4, and the oxidised-pyrimidine enzymes NTHL1 and the NEIL family, which hydrolyse the N-glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site for downstream incision, gap filling and ligation. Without this step, deaminated cytosine and oxidised bases are read as mutations, driving C-to-T transitions and cancer predisposition. The presence of histones and of shelterin components such as TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2 reflects that this chemistry operates on nucleosomal DNA and is needed at telomeres, where guanine and pyrimidine oxidation threatens chromosome-end integrity.

The chemistry operates within nucleosomal DNA and at telomeric repeats bound by protective complexes.—
Displacement of DNA glycosylase by APEX1
originalBase excision repair begins when a DNA glycosylase recognises a damaged or mismatched base and cuts it out, leaving an abasic site. These glycosylases bind their product tightly, so the abasic site must be handed off rather than simply released, and this step is that handoff: the AP endonuclease APEX1 displaces the bound glycosylase and takes possession of the lesion before cleaving the backbone for downstream repair synthesis. The arrangement protects the cell from the abasic site itself, which is mutagenic and blocks replication if left exposed. The glycosylases involved cover the common chemistries of DNA damage "" oxidised guanine and thymine, alkylated purines, uracil from cytosine deamination or misincorporation, and mismatches opposite oxidised bases "" and inherited defects in this repair route, such as MUTYH deficiency, predispose to colorectal adenomas and cancer. The step couples lesion recognition to strand incision and keeps repair intermediates channelled from one enzyme to the next.

This handoff shields the mutagenic, replication-blocking abasic site and channels intermediates between enzymes. PCNA-Dependent Long Patch Base Excision Repair
originalBase excision repair removes damaged and abasic bases, and when the 5' end of the resulting nick cannot be trimmed by a simple one-nucleotide patch, the cell switches to long-patch repair using the replication machinery. This PCNA-dependent branch keeps oxidative and alkylation damage from becoming mutations or strand breaks, and it operates most readily in S phase, when replication factors are abundant. After the AP endonuclease APEX1 incises the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta adds the first nucleotide and displaces the intractable 5' abasic sugar phosphate; the clamp loader RFC loads PCNA, and polymerase delta or epsilon extends strand-displacement synthesis with RPA coating the displaced flap. FEN1 excises that flap and DNA ligase I seals the patch. The same clamp, clamp loader and polymerases serve genome replication, so this route links damage repair directly to replicative synthesis.

This links repair of oxidative and alkylation damage to the replication machinery.When the 5' sugar-phosphate remnant at an incised abasic site resists one-nucleotide replacement, repair switches to a long patch that borrows replication machinery. Abasic sugar-phosphate removal via the single-nucleotide replacement pathway
originalWhen a damaged or mismatched base is excised by a DNA glycosylase, the DNA is left with an abasic site whose sugar-phosphate remnant must be cleared before the gap can be filled; this is the short-patch, single-nucleotide replacement arm of base excision repair. Without it, abasic sites and their 5'-deoxyribose phosphate residues persist as blocking, mutagenic lesions that stall replication and drive base substitutions, which is why this chemistry underlies genome stability against oxidative and alkylation damage. APEX1 displaces the glycosylase from its product and incises the backbone on the 5' side of the base-free deoxyribose, creating a nick with a 3'-hydroxyl. DNA polymerase beta is then recruited to the resulting gap and uses its lyase activity to release the 5'dRP group, leaving a clean single-nucleotide gap for fill-in synthesis and ligation.

Recognition and association of DNA glycosylase with site containing an affected pyrimidine
originalBase excision repair begins when a DNA glycosylase scans duplex DNA, flips out an aberrant base and prepares it for removal, and this step covers recognition of damaged or mismatched pyrimidines in particular. It is the cell's main defence against the constant chemical erosion of bases by oxidation, deamination and alkylation, and its failure drives point mutation and cancer predisposition, as seen with germline defects in the uracil- and thymine-directed glycosylases. Uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation is handled by UNG and SMUG1, mismatched thymine at CpG sites by TDG and MBD4, and oxidised pyrimidines by NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes, while OGG1 addresses oxidised purines. Because lesions must be found within chromatin, core histones and the telomere-binding shelterin proteins are part of the context in which recognition occurs, linking this repair step to nucleosome packaging and telomere maintenance.
