POLB-Dependent Long Patch Base Excision Repair
originalBase excision repair removes damaged or inappropriate bases, and when the resulting gap cannot be sealed after a single nucleotide is added, the cell switches to a long-patch route that displaces and trims a short flap before ligation. This variant keeps oxidative and alkylation damage from persisting as single-strand breaks, which otherwise collapse replication forks and drive mutation and genome instability. After APEX1 incises the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta performs strand-displacement synthesis of roughly two to ten nucleotides; FEN1 cleaves the displaced flap and DNA ligase I seals the nick. PARP1 and PARP2 detect the break and synthesise poly(ADP-ribose) to recruit and coordinate these factors, while PARG and ADPRS reverse that modification so the repair machinery can be released. The same damage-sensing step is what PARP inhibitors exploit therapeutically.
When a single-nucleotide patch cannot complete base excision repair, a long-patch route displaces and removes a short flap, preventing persistent single-strand breaks. After APEX1 incision, polymerase beta synthesises about two to ten nucleotides by strand displacement, FEN1 cleaves the flap and DNA ligase I seals it. PARP1 and PARP2 sense breaks and make poly(ADP-ribose) to recruit factors, PARG and ADPRS reverse it, and PARP inhibitors exploit this step.When a single added nucleotide leaves an end that cannot be ligated, repair continues by displacement. After AP endonuclease incision, a repair polymerase performs strand-displacement synthesis of roughly two to ten nucleotides, a flap endonuclease cleaves the displaced flap, and a ligase seals the nick. Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases detect the break and build the polymer that recruits and coordinates these factors; glycohydrolases reverse it to release them.—
NEIL3-mediated resolution of ICLs
originalInterstrand crosslinks covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription until they are removed. This route unhooks certain crosslinks directly, using the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 to cleave one of the two glycosidic bonds holding the lesion in place, converting the crosslink into a pair of more tractable single-strand lesions that base excision repair and downstream replication can handle. It acts on psoralen-induced crosslinks and on those arising spontaneously from abasic sites reacting with an opposing base, and it does so without the Fanconi anaemia machinery, so it avoids the double-strand break intermediates and incisions that nuclease-dependent crosslink repair requires. Acting at stalled replication forks, it offers cells a rapid, low-risk first option for crosslink removal, with the Fanconi anaemia route as backup when the lesion resists unhooking.
Interstrand crosslinks block replication and transcription. In this route the glycosylase NEIL3 unhooks certain crosslinks, such as psoralen- and abasic-site-derived ones, by cleaving one glycosidic bond, turning the crosslink into single-strand lesions manageable by base excision repair and replication. Acting at stalled forks without the Fanconi anaemia machinery, it avoids double-strand break intermediates and offers a rapid, low-risk first option, with Fanconi anaemia repair as backup.Interstrand crosslinks covalently tie the two strands together and block both replication and transcription. A glycosylase unhooks certain crosslinks directly, cleaving one of the two N-glycosidic bonds that anchor the lesion and converting it into a pair of single-strand lesions that base excision repair and replication can handle. Because no nuclease incision is needed, double-strand break intermediates are avoided; nuclease-dependent unhooking remains as backup.—
Recognition and association of DNA glycosylase with site containing an affected purine
originalOxidized and alkylated purines are the commonest chemical insults to DNA, and base excision repair begins when a damage-specific glycosylase finds one and cuts it out. Recognition and association of a DNA glycosylase with an affected purine site is that search-and-capture step: the enzyme scans the minor groove, kinks the backbone at the lesion, and flips the damaged base into an active-site pocket where the N-glycosidic bond is cleaved to leave an abasic site for downstream incision and resynthesis. Distinct enzymes cover distinct lesions — 8-oxoguanine by OGG1, adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine by MUTYH, alkylpurines by MPG, hydantoins by NEIL3 — and loss of this activity raises mutation rates, with MUTYH deficiency predisposing to colorectal adenomatous polyposis. Because the substrate is chromatin, nucleosomal histones are part of the context, and shelterin components place the same chemistry at telomeres, where oxidative purine damage threatens end protection.
Base excision repair of oxidised and alkylated purines begins when a specific glycosylase scans the minor groove, kinks the DNA and flips the damaged base into its active site, cleaving the N-glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site. OGG1 removes 8-oxoguanine, MUTYH removes adenine opposite it, MPG alkylpurines and NEIL3 hydantoins, within chromatin and at telomeres. Loss raises mutation rates, and MUTYH deficiency predisposes to colorectal adenomatous polyposis.A damage-specific glycosylase scans the minor groove, kinks the backbone at an oxidised or alkylated purine and flips the aberrant base into an active-site pocket, where the N-glycosidic bond is hydrolysed to leave an abasic site for downstream incision and resynthesis. Distinct enzymes capture distinct lesions, including oxidised guanine, alkylpurines, hydantoins and adenine mispaired opposite oxidised guanine. The search occurs on nucleosomal DNA.—

DNA Damage Bypass (6)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Translesion Synthesis by POLH
originalWhen a replication fork meets a UV-induced thymine dimer, the replicative polymerase stalls; DNA polymerase eta rescues it by copying directly across the lesion, inserting two adenines opposite the dimer with high fidelity. This translesion synthesis route is what keeps sunlight-damaged skin cells replicating accurately, and losing it causes the variant form of xeroderma pigmentosum, in which patients are extremely photosensitive and develop skin cancers early because the damage is bypassed by error-prone polymerases instead. Single-stranded DNA at the stalled fork is coated by the RPA complex, the clamp loader RFC loads PCNA, and monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits polymerase eta through its ubiquitin-binding domain. After a few nucleotides are added, the enzyme must be removed and the replicative polymerase restored: SPRTN and the VCP/p97 segregase with its UFD1-NPLOC4 cofactors, together with ubiquitin supplied by the polyubiquitin genes, drive that exchange.
When replication stalls at a UV-induced thymine dimer, DNA polymerase eta copies across it accurately, inserting two adenines; RPA coats the single strand, RFC loads PCNA, and monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits the polymerase. SPRTN and the VCP/p97 segregase with UFD1-NPLOC4, using ubiquitin, then remove the enzyme to restore replicative synthesis. Loss of polymerase eta causes variant xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme photosensitivity and early skin cancer from error-prone bypass.A replicative polymerase stalled at a cyclobutane dimer is replaced rather than restarted. Single-stranded DNA is coated by a trimeric binding protein, a clamp loader deposits the sliding clamp, and monoubiquitination of that clamp recruits a Y-family polymerase through its ubiquitin-binding domain, which inserts two adenines opposite the lesion. A protease and a ubiquitin-directed segregase then evict it, restoring processive replication.—
Translesion synthesis by POLK
originalWhen a replication fork meets a damaged base it stalls, and translesion synthesis by DNA polymerase kappa is one of the routes that lets replication continue past the lesion rather than collapse. POLK is a Y-family polymerase particularly suited to copying past oxidised bases such as thymine glycol and 8-oxoguanine and past bulky adducts formed by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, so it limits fork breakage and the chromosomal damage that follows, at the cost of introducing mutations. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader and marked using the ubiquitin pool encoded by UBB, UBC and the ribosomal fusion genes; RPA coats the exposed single strand. POLK acts with REV1 and the REV3L-MAD2L2 polymerase zeta complex, which extends the nucleotide inserted opposite the lesion, making this a damage-tolerance rather than a repair pathway.
Translesion synthesis by DNA polymerase kappa lets stalled forks continue past oxidised bases such as thymine glycol and 8-oxoguanine and past polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon adducts, preventing fork breakage at the cost of mutations. Recruitment needs RFC-loaded PCNA monoubiquitinated with ubiquitin from UBB, UBC and ribosomal fusion genes, plus RPA. POLK cooperates with REV1 and polymerase zeta (REV3L-MAD2L2), which extends past the lesion, making this damage tolerance rather than repair.A fork stalled at a damaged base is rescued by swapping in a Y-family polymerase whose open active site accommodates oxidised bases and bulky adducts. Recruitment requires monoubiquitination of the sliding clamp, loaded by the clamp loader onto coated template, and a scaffolding transferase with a two-subunit extension polymerase completes synthesis past the lesion. The route tolerates damage rather than removing it, at the cost of misincorporation.—
Termination of translesion DNA synthesis
originalTranslesion synthesis lets a replication fork copy past a damaged base, but the Y-family polymerases that do it are error-prone, so cells must switch back to accurate replication as soon as the lesion is passed. Terminating translesion DNA synthesis is that switch, and its failure raises the mutation burden carried forward into daughter cells, a route toward the mutational signatures seen in tumours. Monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits the bypass polymerases eta, iota, kappa and REV1; removing that ubiquitin mark, by deubiquitinases including USP10, evicts them and restores processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon loaded via replication factor C on RPA-coated template. An ISG15 arm, acting through UBA7, UBE2L6 and TRIM25, modifies PCNA and PCLAF to help disengage the bypass machinery, linking interferon-inducible conjugation to the fidelity of damage tolerance and to normal fork restart.
After error-prone Y-family polymerases bypass a lesion, translesion synthesis must be terminated to restore accurate replication and limit mutations carried into daughter cells. Deubiquitinases such as USP10 remove ubiquitin from PCNA, evicting polymerases eta, iota, kappa and REV1 so that polymerases delta and epsilon, loaded by RFC on RPA-coated template, resume. An ISG15 arm via UBA7, UBE2L6 and TRIM25 modifies PCNA and PCLAF, linking interferon-inducible conjugation to fork restart.Error-prone bypass polymerases are recruited by a monoubiquitinated sliding clamp, so synthesis reverts to high fidelity when that mark is removed. Deubiquitinases strip the ubiquitin, evicting the Y-family enzymes and allowing replicative polymerases reloaded by the clamp loader to resume processive synthesis on coated template. A parallel ubiquitin-like conjugation arm modifies the clamp and an accessory factor to help disengage the bypass machinery.—
Translesion synthesis by REV1
originalWhen a replication fork meets a lesion it cannot copy, such as an abasic site, replication would stall and collapse unless a specialised polymerase takes over. REV1-mediated translesion synthesis is one such bypass route: REV1 acts as a dCMP transferase that inserts a C opposite the damaged template position, and also as a scaffold that recruits the extension step. Monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader onto RPA-coated DNA, marks the damage site and stimulates REV1 recruitment. Handover then goes to DNA polymerase zeta, whose catalytic subunit REV3L pairs with MAD2L2 (REV7), the subunit that physically binds REV1. Polymerase zeta extends past the lesion with low fidelity and low processivity, so this pathway preserves replication and cell survival at the cost of point mutations, and contributes to damage tolerance and chemotherapy resistance.
REV1-mediated translesion synthesis allows replication past lesions such as abasic sites that would otherwise stall and collapse forks. REV1 inserts a C opposite the damage as a dCMP transferase and serves as a scaffold; monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by RFC onto RPA-coated DNA, promotes its recruitment. Polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2, which binds REV1) then extends past the lesion with low fidelity, preserving survival at the cost of point mutations.At a template position a replicative polymerase cannot copy, such as an abasic site, a deoxycytidyl transferase inserts a C opposite the lesion and simultaneously serves as a scaffold. Monoubiquitination of the sliding clamp, loaded by the clamp loader onto coated single-stranded DNA, marks the site and promotes that recruitment. A two-subunit extension polymerase, whose smaller subunit binds the scaffold, then extends past the lesion with low fidelity.—
Translesion synthesis by POLI
originalWhen a replication fork meets a damaged base it stalls, and DNA polymerase iota provides one way past the block: translesion synthesis by POLI lets replication continue across lesions that the high-fidelity polymerases cannot copy, trading accuracy for completion of the genome. This tolerance matters because unrescued stalled forks collapse into breaks and cell death, though the same error-prone copying contributes to mutation load. POLI is unusual in favouring Hoogsteen rather than Watson-Crick pairing, flipping template purines to a syn conformation so that adducted or edge-damaged G and A can still be read. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader onto RPA-coated DNA, together with REV1 as a scaffold. Because POLI extends poorly beyond the inserted nucleotide, polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2) carries out the extension step.
DNA polymerase iota lets stalled forks continue past lesions that replicative polymerases cannot copy, preventing fork collapse and cell death while adding mutations. POLI favours Hoogsteen pairing, flipping template purines into the syn conformation to read adducted or edge-damaged G and A. It is recruited by monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by RFC onto RPA-coated DNA, with REV1 as scaffold, and because it extends poorly, polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2) completes extension.One Y-family polymerase copies past lesions by favouring Hoogsteen rather than Watson-Crick geometry, rotating template purines into a syn conformation so that adducted or edge-damaged bases can still be read. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitination of the sliding clamp, loaded onto coated template, together with a transferase acting as scaffold. Because this enzyme extends poorly beyond the inserted nucleotide, a separate two-subunit polymerase performs extension.—
Recognition of DNA damage by PCNA-containing replication complex
originalDNA lesions block the replicative polymerases, and this step is how a stalled fork registers that fact and hands the template to a polymerase that can copy past damage. It matters because a fork arrested at a lesion will collapse into double-strand breaks unless replication is allowed to continue, and because the switch it triggers is inherently mutagenic, shaping the mutation spectra seen in tumours. The clamp loader complex and single-stranded DNA binding protein hold PCNA and polymerase delta or epsilon at the site; when synthesis stalls, RAD18 with its partner ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2B monoubiquitinates PCNA, weakening replicative polymerase binding and creating a mark read by the ubiquitin-binding motifs of Y-family translesion polymerases. A cullin-RING ligase with DDB1 and DTL also acts on PCNA, while the USP1-WDR48 deubiquitinase reverses the modification, limiting how long error-prone synthesis persists.
When replicative polymerases stall at DNA lesions, the fork signals this and switches to translesion polymerases, preventing collapse into double-strand breaks but introducing mutations seen in tumours. With PCNA and polymerase delta or epsilon held by the clamp loader and single-strand binding protein, RAD18-UBE2B monoubiquitinates PCNA, weakening replicative polymerase binding and recruiting Y-family polymerases. A DDB1-DTL cullin-RING ligase also modifies PCNA, and USP1-WDR48 deubiquitination limits error-prone synthesis.A fork arrested at a lesion must hand the template from a replicative to a damage-tolerant polymerase. While the clamp loader and a single-strand binding protein hold the sliding clamp and replicative polymerase in place, a ubiquitin ligase with its conjugating enzyme monoubiquitinates the clamp, weakening replicative polymerase binding and creating a mark read by ubiquitin-binding motifs of Y-family enzymes. A deubiquitinase reverses it, limiting how long bypass synthesis persists.—

Nucleotide Excision Repair (7)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Dual Incision in GG-NER
originalGlobal genome nucleotide excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts and chemical adducts from anywhere in the genome, and the dual incision step is the committed cut that releases them. Once the damage-verification factors XPA, RPA and the TFIIH helicases ERCC2/ERCC3 have opened a bubble around the lesion, the ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease cuts 5' to the damage and ERCC5 cuts 3', excising a roughly 27-30 nucleotide fragment. The resulting gap is immediately filled, so replication factor C, PCNA and DNA polymerases delta, epsilon and kappa are recruited as part of the same transaction. Damage recognition by the DDB1-DDB2 complex with cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase components, plus PARP1/PARP2, marks lesions in chromatin for this processing. Loss of these incision activities underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.
In global genome nucleotide excision repair, dual incision releases bulky lesions such as UV photoproducts after DDB1-DDB2 and PARP1/PARP2 mark the damage and XPA, RPA and TFIIH open a bubble. ERCC1-ERCC4 cuts 5' and ERCC5 cuts 3' of the lesion, excising a 27-30 nucleotide fragment, and RFC, PCNA and polymerases delta, epsilon and kappa fill the gap. Defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum with sun sensitivity and skin cancer.Bulky, helix-distorting lesions are removed by a dual incision. After verification factors, a single-strand binding trimer and the helicase subunits of a general transcription factor open a bubble around the lesion, one structure-specific endonuclease cuts 5' of it and another 3', releasing a fragment of roughly 27-30 nucleotides. A clamp loader, sliding clamp and repair polymerases immediately refill the resulting gap.—
Gap-filling DNA repair synthesis and ligation in TC-NER
originalWhen RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky, helix-distorting lesion, transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair removes the damaged strand; this final stage refills and seals the resulting single-stranded gap so transcription can resume. Loss of the pathway underlies Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, where neurons and other non-dividing cells accumulate transcription-blocking damage and degenerate. After dual incision, RPA coats the gap, the clamp loader RFC deposits PCNA, and DNA polymerases delta or epsilon, or the translesion polymerase kappa, synthesize the repair patch; ligase I or ligase III with its partner XRCC1 then seals the nick. The stalled polymerase complex, the CSA and CSB proteins with UVSSA and a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, and the TFIIH helicases provide the damage-recognition and unwinding context, linking genome maintenance directly to ongoing gene expression.
The final stage of transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair fills and seals the gap left after a lesion stalling RNA polymerase II is excised, so transcription can resume. RPA coats the gap, RFC loads PCNA, polymerases delta, epsilon or kappa synthesise the patch, and ligase I or ligase III-XRCC1 seals it, with CSA, CSB, UVSSA and TFIIH present. Loss causes Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes with degeneration of non-dividing cells.After dual incision has removed a transcription-blocking lesion, the single-stranded gap is refilled and sealed. A trimeric binding protein coats the gap, a clamp loader deposits the sliding clamp, and replicative or translesion polymerases copy the intact strand to synthesise the repair patch. A ligase, alone or bound to a scaffold protein, then seals the remaining nick, restoring a continuous duplex.—
DNA Damage Recognition in GG-NER
originalBulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts must be found before they can be cut out, and damage recognition in global genome nucleotide excision repair is the search step that scans the entire genome rather than only transcribed strands. Two sensors cooperate: an XPC complex with RAD23A or RAD23B and centrin-2 probes for destabilised base pairing and binds the undamaged strand, while the UV-DDB ubiquitin ligase built on DDB2, DDB1, a cullin-4 scaffold and RBX1 engages the lesion itself and helps retain XPC there. Ubiquitin transfer, modulated by the COP9 signalosome, and PARP1/PARP2 activity mark the site, and INO80 chromatin remodelling opens nucleosomal DNA for access. Loss of these factors underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer, placing this step upstream of the incision and resynthesis stages of repair.
Damage recognition in global genome nucleotide excision repair scans the whole genome for bulky lesions such as UV photoproducts. XPC with RAD23A/B and centrin-2 detects destabilised pairing, while the UV-DDB ligase (DDB2, DDB1, cullin-4, RBX1) binds the lesion and retains XPC; COP9-modulated ubiquitination, PARP1/2 and INO80 remodelling make the site accessible. This step precedes incision and resynthesis, and its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum with sun sensitivity and skin cancer.Bulky, helix-distorting lesions are located by two cooperating sensors. One complex probes for destabilised base pairing and binds the undamaged strand opposite the lesion, while a cullin-based ubiquitin ligase engages the lesion itself and helps retain the first sensor there. Ubiquitin transfer, poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation and ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling mark the site and open chromatin, positioning it for incision.—
Dual incision in TC-NER
originalWhen RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky lesion in a transcribed strand, transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair removes the damage so that gene expression can resume; the dual incision step is where the damaged oligonucleotide is actually cut out. Loss of this route causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with photosensitivity, developmental failure and neurodegeneration rather than the cancer predisposition typical of the global-genome branch. Stalled polymerase must first backtrack to expose the lesion, aided by ERCC6 and ERCC8-dependent remodelling and ubiquitination, UVSSA, TCEA1-stimulated nascent RNA cleavage, and the helicase subunits of TFIIH. The ERCC1:ERCC4 endonuclease then incises 5' of the lesion and ERCC5 3' of it, on a substrate stabilised by XPA and the RPA trimer, leaving a gap that replicative polymerases with PCNA and clamp loader refill.
Dual incision in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair cuts out a bulky lesion that has stalled RNA polymerase II. The polymerase first backtracks, aided by ERCC6, ERCC8-dependent ubiquitination, UVSSA, TCEA1-stimulated RNA cleavage and TFIIH helicases; then ERCC1-ERCC4 incises 5' and ERCC5 3' of the lesion on a substrate stabilised by XPA and RPA, leaving a gap refilled by PCNA-dependent polymerases. Loss causes Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes with photosensitivity and neurodegeneration.A stalled RNA polymerase must backtrack to expose the lesion, assisted by remodelling and ubiquitination of the elongation complex, cleavage of the nascent transcript, and the helicase subunits of a general transcription factor. One structure-specific endonuclease then cuts 5' of the damage and another 3' of it, on a substrate stabilised by a verification factor and a single-strand binding trimer, leaving a gap for resynthesis.—
Formation of Incision Complex in GG-NER
originalBulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV photoproducts are removed anywhere in the genome by global genome nucleotide excision repair, and this step builds the machinery that actually cuts them out. Once damage-sensing proteins XPC with its partners and the UV-DDB complex mark the site, the transcription factor TFIIH is recruited; its helicase subunits ERCC2 and ERCC3 open a bubble around the lesion while XPA verifies that real damage is present and RPA coats the undamaged strand to shield it. The endonucleases ERCC5 and the ERCC1-ERCC4 heterodimer then dock to form the incision complex that excises the damaged oligonucleotide. Assembly is tuned by PARP1/PARP2, ubiquitin ligase activity of CUL4-DDB1-RBX1, and SUMO conjugation with SUMO-targeted ubiquitylation. Loss of these factors underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.
Global genome nucleotide excision repair assembles an incision complex to excise bulky lesions such as UV photoproducts. After XPC and UV-DDB mark the damage, TFIIH is recruited, its ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases open a bubble, XPA verifies the lesion and RPA protects the undamaged strand; ERCC5 and ERCC1-ERCC4 then dock to cut. PARP1/2, CUL4-DDB1-RBX1 and SUMO modification tune assembly, and defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum with skin cancer.Once sensors have marked a helix-distorting lesion, a multisubunit transcription factor is recruited and its two helicase subunits open a bubble around the damage, while a verification protein confirms a genuine lesion and a trimeric binding protein shields the undamaged strand. Two structure-specific endonucleases then dock to form the incision complex. Assembly is tuned by poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation, cullin-RING ubiquitylation and SUMO conjugation.—
Formation of TC-NER Pre-Incision Complex
originalWhen RNA polymerase II stalls at a lesion in the transcribed strand, cells assemble the pre-incision complex of transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, the step that verifies the damage and opens the DNA before cutting. This route clears bulky, transcription-blocking lesions from active genes, and its loss causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with premature ageing, neurodegeneration and failure to resume transcription after UV rather than cancer predisposition. ERCC6 (CSB) recognises the stalled polymerase and brings in ERCC8 (CSA) within a CUL4A/CUL4B-DDB1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase regulated by the COP9 signalosome; UVSSA delivers the deubiquitinase USP7 to protect ERCC6 from degradation. XPA arrives with the ten-subunit TFIIH complex, whose ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases unwind the damaged duplex, while the XAB2 complex and the elongation factor TCEA1 help the polymerase backtrack so repair proteins can reach the lesion.
In transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, a pre-incision complex forms at RNA polymerase II stalled on a lesion to verify damage and open DNA. ERCC6 (CSB) recruits ERCC8 (CSA) in a CUL4-DDB1-RBX1 ligase regulated by the COP9 signalosome, UVSSA brings USP7 to stabilise ERCC6, and XPA with TFIIH helicases unwinds DNA while XAB2 and TCEA1 aid polymerase backtracking. Loss causes Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes with neurodegeneration rather than cancer.A translocase recognises the stalled elongation complex and recruits a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase whose activity is tuned by a signalosome, while an adaptor delivers a deubiquitinase that protects the translocase from degradation. A verification factor then arrives with a ten-subunit transcription factor whose two helicases unwind the damaged duplex, and accessory elongation factors help the polymerase backtrack so repair proteins can reach the lesion.—
Gap-filling DNA repair synthesis and ligation in GG-NER
originalThe final stage of global genome nucleotide excision repair restores an intact duplex after a bulky, helix-distorting lesion such as a UV photoproduct has been cut out. Dual incision leaves a gap of roughly 27-30 nucleotides held by replication protein A; the clamp loader RFC deposits PCNA, and DNA polymerase delta, epsilon or the Y-family polymerase kappa copies the undamaged strand to refill it. LIG1 seals the remaining nick during replicative repair, while LIG3 in complex with the scaffold XRCC1 performs ligation in non-cycling cells, giving the step two routes depending on proliferative state. Ubiquitin contributed by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes supports PCNA modification and turnover of repair factors. Without this gap-filling and sealing, incision leaves persistent single-strand breaks, and defective nucleotide excision repair underlies xeroderma pigmentosum and its extreme sunlight-induced cancer risk.
The last stage of global genome nucleotide excision repair restores intact DNA after a bulky lesion is excised. The 27-30 nucleotide gap is held by RPA, RFC loads PCNA, and polymerase delta, epsilon or kappa refills it; LIG1 seals nicks in replicating cells, whereas LIG3-XRCC1 does so in non-cycling cells, with ubiquitin supporting PCNA modification. Without it single-strand breaks persist, and repair defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum and sunlight-induced cancer.Dual incision leaves a gap of roughly 27-30 nucleotides held by a single-strand binding trimer. A clamp loader deposits the sliding clamp and a replicative or Y-family polymerase copies the intact strand to refill it, after which a ligase seals the remaining nick; a second ligase bound to a scaffold protein provides an alternative route when replicative ligase activity is low. Ubiquitin supports clamp modification and factor turnover.—

DNA Double-Strand Break Repair (10)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Presynaptic phase of homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange
originalRepair of a double-strand break by homologous recombination requires a search for an intact sister template, and this presynaptic step builds the tool that performs the search. Resection nucleases and helicases acting with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and CtIP generate long 3' single-stranded tails, which RPA coats to remove secondary structure. BRCA2, working with BRCA1-BARD1 and licensed by checkpoint kinase signalling through ATM, ATR and CHEK1, then loads RAD51 onto that ssDNA in place of RPA, nucleating the helical nucleoprotein filament that will invade duplex DNA. Paralogue complexes containing RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D and XRCC2 stabilise the filament. The same events sustain the damage checkpoint via the 9-1-1 clamp and its loader. Loss of these factors causes error-prone repair, chromosomal instability and hereditary breast, ovarian and Fanconi-type cancer predisposition, and underlies sensitivity to PARP inhibition.
During homologous recombination, the presynaptic step builds the RAD51 nucleoprotein filament that searches for a sister template. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP and other nucleases resect breaks into RPA-coated 3' tails; BRCA2 with BRCA1-BARD1, under ATM, ATR and CHEK1 signalling, replaces RPA with RAD51, and RAD51 paralogues stabilise the filament while the 9-1-1 clamp sustains checkpoint signalling. Loss causes chromosomal instability, hereditary breast, ovarian and Fanconi-type cancer predisposition, and PARP-inhibitor sensitivity.Repair by homologous recombination needs a filament that can search duplex DNA. Nucleases and helicases acting with a sensor complex resect the broken ends into long 3' single-stranded tails, which a trimeric binding protein coats. Mediator proteins, licensed by checkpoint kinase signalling, then exchange that coat for a recombinase, nucleating the helical nucleoprotein filament; paralogue complexes stabilise it.—
Resolution of D-loop Structures through Synthesis-Dependent Strand Annealing (SDSA)
originalHomologous recombination repair of a double-strand break can end without exchanging chromosome arms, and synthesis-dependent strand annealing is the route that achieves it. After the invading strand has been extended using the sister chromatid as template, the extended strand is displaced from the D-loop and reanneals with its original partner, so repair restores sequence without generating a crossover — the outcome that protects cells from loss of heterozygosity and gross rearrangement. Upstream components carry out end resection and filament assembly: the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex with CtIP, EXO1, DNA2 and the BLM–TOP3A–RMI1–RMI2 dissolvasome, then BRCA1–BARD1, PALB2 and BRCA2 loading RAD51 and its paralogues. The helicase RTEL1 promotes D-loop disassembly, remaining gaps are filled by polymerase-mediated synthesis, and nicks are ligated. Loss of these factors underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition and sensitivity to crosslinking agents.
Synthesis-dependent strand annealing lets homologous recombination repair a double-strand break without crossover: after extension on the sister template, the invading strand is displaced from the D-loop by RTEL1 and reanneals with its partner, avoiding loss of heterozygosity. Upstream, MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1, DNA2 and the BLM dissolvasome resect ends, and BRCA1-BARD1, PALB2 and BRCA2 load RAD51; gaps are filled and ligated. Defects cause breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.After a recombinase filament invades a homologous duplex and the invading 3' end is extended, the displacement loop is taken apart rather than cleaved. A helicase disassembles the loop, the extended strand is released and reanneals with the second end of the break, so sequence is restored without a crossover; remaining gaps are filled by polymerase synthesis and the nicks are ligated.—
HDR through MMEJ (alt-NHEJ)
originalMicrohomology-mediated end joining, also called alternative nonhomologous end joining, is a mutagenic backup route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that operates when high-fidelity repair is saturated or genetically compromised. It matters clinically because tumours deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, lean on it to survive, which is why polymerase theta and PARP are drug targets there. Repair begins with limited end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex together with CtIP, generating 3' single-stranded overhangs that are not licensed for recombination. PARP1 or PARP2 and DNA polymerase theta then align the two ends through short microhomologous tracts, POLQ extends by strand-displacement synthesis, FEN1 trims the displaced 5' flaps, and LIG3 with XRCC1 seals the remaining nicks. The outcome is invariably a deletion spanning the sequence between microhomologies, plus frequent base substitutions and occasional chromosomal translocations.
Microhomology-mediated end joining is a mutagenic backup for double-strand break repair, relied on by homologous recombination-deficient tumours such as BRCA-mutant cancers, making polymerase theta and PARP drug targets. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP performs limited resection; PARP1/2 and POLQ align ends at short microhomologies, POLQ extends them, FEN1 trims flaps and LIG3-XRCC1 seals nicks. Products always carry deletions, often base substitutions and occasionally translocations.Limited nucleolytic resection exposes short 3' single-stranded overhangs that are not licensed for recombination. A poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase and a specialised polymerase then align the two ends through short complementary microhomology tracts and extend them by strand-displacement synthesis; a flap endonuclease removes the displaced 5' flaps and a ligase-scaffold complex seals the nicks, deleting the intervening sequence.—
Negative Regulation of DNA Double Strand Break Response
originalRepair of DNA double-strand breaks must be switched off as well as on, and this pathway describes how the break response is damped by destroying the proteins that organize it. The BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer, which drives homologous recombination and end resection, is polyubiquitinated by Cullin4-RBX1-DDB1 ubiquitin ligase complexes using DCAF8L1 or DCAF8L2 as substrate receptors, and the tagged proteins are then degraded by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle, ATPase and lid subunits is represented here along with ubiquitin itself. Limiting BRCA1-BARD1 levels restrains recombination, influences the choice between repair routes, and tunes how long checkpoint signalling persists after damage. Because BRCA1-BARD1 loss underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, ubiquitin-dependent turnover of these factors also shapes genome stability and the sensitivity of tumour cells to agents that create double-strand breaks.
Double-strand break responses are damped by degrading the BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer, which drives homologous recombination and resection. Cullin4-RBX1-DDB1 ligases with DCAF8L1 or DCAF8L2 as substrate receptors polyubiquitinate BRCA1-BARD1, which the 26S proteasome then degrades. This turnover restrains recombination, influences repair pathway choice and limits checkpoint duration; because BRCA1-BARD1 loss causes hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, it also affects genome stability and tumour sensitivity to break-inducing agents.A heterodimeric ubiquitin ligase that organises end resection is itself destroyed to switch the break response off. Cullin-RING ligase complexes, using interchangeable substrate receptors, transfer polyubiquitin chains onto the heterodimer, which is then unfolded and hydrolysed by the 26S proteasome. Lowering the available pool limits recombinase loading, shifts the balance between repair routes, and shortens the duration of checkpoint signalling.—
Recruitment and ATM-mediated phosphorylation of repair and signaling proteins at DNA double strand breaks
originalA DNA double-strand break must be converted into a signal that stops the cell cycle and marshals repair machinery, and this is the step that builds that signal at the break. The MRN complex (MRE11:RAD50:NBN) senses broken ends and activates ATM, which phosphorylates histone H2AX on serine 139; the resulting gamma-H2AX mark spreads over flanking chromatin and docks MDC1, creating ionizing radiation-induced foci. Ubiquitin ligases RNF8 and RNF168, with HERC2 and ubiquitin conjugating enzymes, modify histones to retain downstream factors, recruiting UIMC1/RAP80 and the BRCA1-A complex, while removal of the KDM4A/KDM4B demethylases and NSD2-dependent H4K20 methylation license 53BP1 binding. ATM then phosphorylates BRCA1:BARD1, 53BP1 and CHEK2, enforcing checkpoint arrest via TP53 and biasing repair toward homologous recombination or end joining. Loss of these components underlies radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
A double-strand break is converted into a checkpoint and repair signal when MRN senses ends and activates ATM, which phosphorylates H2AX; gamma-H2AX spreads and docks MDC1 to form foci. RNF8, RNF168 and HERC2 ubiquitinate histones to recruit RAP80 and BRCA1-A, while KDM4A/B removal and NSD2-mediated H4K20 methylation allow 53BP1 binding. ATM phosphorylates BRCA1-BARD1, 53BP1 and CHEK2, driving TP53 arrest; defects cause radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and breast and ovarian cancer.A sensor complex binds the broken ends and activates a kinase that phosphorylates histone H2AX on serine 139; the mark spreads through flanking chromatin and docks a scaffold protein, nucleating large foci. Ubiquitin ligases and conjugating enzymes then modify histones to retain downstream factors, while changes in histone methylation license further readers. The same kinase phosphorylates effectors that enforce cycle arrest and bias repair pathway choice.—
Resolution of D-loop Structures through Holliday Junction Intermediates
originalHomologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks begins with strand invasion, and the branched D-loop that results must be taken apart before chromosomes can segregate. How it is dismantled determines the genetic outcome: the BLM-TOP3A-RMI1-RMI2 helicase-topoisomerase complex dissolves double Holliday junctions to give non-crossover products and suppresses sister chromatid exchange, while nucleolytic resolvases such as GEN1 and the SLX1A-SLX4 partnership with MUS81-EME1/EME2 cleave them and yield crossovers. Crossovers in mitotic cells risk loss of heterozygosity, exposing recessive mutations in tumour suppressors, so the choice between routes is a genome-stability decision. The upstream context is present too: MRE11-RAD50-NBN and CtIP-driven resection with EXO1 and DNA2, ATM signalling, BRCA1-BARD1 and BRCA2-PALB2 loading of RAD51 with its paralogues, and SPIDR with FIGNL1-FIRRM biasing recombination toward the non-crossover path. Mutation of these factors underlies Bloom syndrome and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
D-loops and double Holliday junctions formed in homologous recombination must be removed before segregation, and the route decides the genetic outcome. BLM-TOP3A-RMI1-RMI2 dissolves junctions into non-crossovers, whereas GEN1, SLX1A-SLX4 and MUS81-EME1/EME2 cleave them into crossovers that risk loss of heterozygosity. Upstream resection, ATM signalling and RAD51 loading by BRCA1-BARD1 and BRCA2-PALB2 provide context, with SPIDR and FIGNL1-FIRRM favouring non-crossovers; mutations underlie Bloom syndrome and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.The branched joint molecule formed by strand invasion must be taken apart before segregation, and how it is taken apart sets the genetic outcome. A helicase-topoisomerase complex can dissolve double Holliday junctions to give non-crossover products, whereas nucleolytic resolvases cleave them and yield crossovers. Upstream resection, checkpoint signalling and recombinase loading build the junction, and accessory factors bias the choice toward the non-crossover route.—
Sensing of DNA Double Strand Breaks
originalA double-strand break is the most dangerous lesion a genome can sustain, and this pathway is the first step by which a cell notices one. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex binds the broken ends and holds them together, and its recruitment converts a physical break into a signal: the acetyltransferase KAT5 acetylates ATM, which autophosphorylates and switches from an inactive dimer to an active monomeric kinase. Active ATM then phosphorylates the substrates that arrest the cell cycle and assemble repair factors at the lesion, so detection and the damage response are coupled at their origin. Import of components into the nucleus depends on karyopherin-mediated transport. Loss of this sensing step underlies ataxia-telangiectasia and the related Nijmegen breakage and MRE11-deficiency syndromes, with radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency, chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition.
This first step of double-strand break detection begins when MRE11-RAD50-NBN binds and tethers broken ends, triggering KAT5 to acetylate ATM, which autophosphorylates and converts from inactive dimer to active monomer. Active ATM then phosphorylates targets that arrest the cell cycle and recruit repair factors, coupling detection to the damage response, with karyopherins importing components into the nucleus. Defects cause ataxia-telangiectasia, Nijmegen breakage and MRE11-deficiency syndromes with immunodeficiency and cancer predisposition.A trimeric sensor complex binds and tethers the two broken ends, and its recruitment converts a physical break into a chemical signal: an acetyltransferase modifies the apical checkpoint kinase, which autophosphorylates and dissociates from an inactive dimer into active monomers. The kinase then phosphorylates substrates that halt cycle progression and assemble repair factors, coupling detection to response; nuclear import of components depends on karyopherin-mediated transport.—
Nonhomologous End-Joining (NHEJ)
originalDouble-strand breaks are the most dangerous lesions a genome can suffer, and nonhomologous end joining is the route that repairs them by re-ligating the two ends directly, without a homologous template. It works throughout the cell cycle, dominates in G1, and is the mechanism that seals the programmed breaks of antigen receptor gene rearrangement — loss of its ligase or nuclease components causes radiosensitivity and severe combined immunodeficiency. Break recognition by the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex activates ATM, which phosphorylates H2AX; ubiquitin signalling through RNF8, RNF168 and UBE2N builds the foci that recruit 53BP1 with RIF1 and PAXIP1, blocking end resection and steering repair away from homologous recombination. The Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer with DNA-PKcs synapses the ends, ARTEMIS trims overhangs, TDP1 and TDP2 clear blocking adducts, polymerases mu and lambda fill short gaps, and XRCC4–LIG4 with XLF completes ligation, sometimes with small deletions.
Nonhomologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks by direct religation without a template, functions throughout the cycle especially in G1, and seals V(D)J recombination breaks; defects cause radiosensitivity and severe combined immunodeficiency. MRN activates ATM, H2AX phosphorylation and RNF8/RNF168/UBE2N signalling recruit 53BP1 with RIF1 and PAXIP1 to block resection. Ku70/Ku80 with DNA-PKcs synapses ends, ARTEMIS, TDP1 and TDP2 process them, polymerases mu and lambda fill gaps, and XRCC4-LIG4-XLF ligates.Broken ends are re-ligated directly, without a homologous template. End binding activates an apical kinase that phosphorylates H2AX, and ubiquitin signalling builds foci that recruit factors blocking resection and steering repair away from recombination. A ring-shaped heterodimer with an associated kinase synapses the ends, a nuclease trims overhangs, phosphodiesterases clear blocking adducts, polymerases fill short gaps, and a ligase complex completes joining.—
Processing of DNA double-strand break ends
originalBefore a broken chromosome can be repaired using a sister chromatid as template, the two DNA ends must be trimmed back to leave long single-stranded 3' tails, and this end-processing step is what commits a double-strand break to homology-directed repair rather than to blunt-end joining. Resection proceeds in two stages: the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1 initiates trimming, then EXO1 or DNA2 working with the BLM or WRN helicases extends it over kilobases. CDK2-cyclin A activity restricts initiation to S and G2 phases when a sister chromatid exists, while ATM-dependent phosphorylation and ubiquitin and SUMO marks laid on chromatin histones by RNF8, RNF168 and associated ligases organise factor recruitment around the break. RPA-coated overhangs then recruit ATR-ATRIP with TOPBP1, RAD17-RFC and the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp to activate CHEK1 checkpoint signalling. Loss of these steps underlies chromosomal instability and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.
End resection commits a double-strand break to homology-directed repair by producing long 3' single-stranded tails. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1 initiate trimming, and EXO1 or DNA2 with BLM or WRN extend it; CDK2-cyclin A limits this to S and G2, while ATM and RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin and SUMO marks organise recruitment. RPA-coated tails activate ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1, RAD17-RFC and 9-1-1 to signal through CHEK1; defects cause instability and breast and ovarian cancer.Commitment to homology-directed repair requires the broken ends to be trimmed into long 3' single-stranded tails. A nuclease complex with its activating partners initiates short-range trimming, then an exonuclease or a helicase-nuclease pair extends resection over kilobases. Cyclin-dependent kinase activity restricts initiation to phases when a duplicated template exists, ubiquitin and SUMO marks on chromatin organise recruitment, and the coated tails activate checkpoint kinase signalling.—
HDR through Single Strand Annealing (SSA)
originalSingle strand annealing is a mutagenic route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that falls back on direct pairing of repeated sequences rather than faithful copying from a homologous template. It matters because it salvages breaks that cannot be repaired accurately, at the cost of deleting one repeat and everything between them, and because its use reshapes genomes in tumours where accurate recombination is compromised. Breaks first activate ATM and are extensively resected by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1, then by EXO1 or DNA2 with the BLM and WRN helicases, generating long 3' single-stranded tails that RPA coats and that trigger ATR-TOPBP1-9-1-1 checkpoint signalling. RAD52 heptamers, phosphorylated by ABL1, anneal homologous repeats in opposing tails and simultaneously block invasive RAD51 filament formation, committing the break away from homologous recombination. The ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease trims displaced 3' flaps before ligation seals the product.
Single strand annealing is a mutagenic double-strand break repair route that pairs repeated sequences, deleting one repeat and the intervening DNA, reshaping tumour genomes when recombination fails. ATM activation and extensive resection by MRN with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1, then EXO1 or DNA2 with BLM and WRN, create RPA-coated tails that trigger ATR checkpoint signalling. ABL1-phosphorylated RAD52 anneals the repeats and blocks RAD51, ERCC1-ERCC4 trims flaps, and ligation completes repair.This route rejoins a break by pairing direct repeats rather than copying a homologous template. Extensive resection by a nuclease complex and then an exonuclease or helicase-nuclease pair generates long 3' tails that a binding trimer coats and that trigger checkpoint signalling; a phosphorylated heptameric annealing protein pairs homologous repeats in opposing tails while blocking recombinase filament formation. A structure-specific endonuclease trims displaced 3' flaps before ligation.—

Transcriptional regulation by RUNX1 (12)

RUNX1 and FOXP3 control the development of regulatory T lymphocytes (Tregs)
originalRegulatory T cells keep immune responses from turning on self tissue, and their identity is set by a transcriptional circuit in which RUNX1 and FOXP3 control Treg development. RUNX1, acting with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, drives transcription of FOXP3 itself; FOXP3 protein then binds back to the RUNX1:CBFB complex and redirects it. Inflammatory effector genes such as IL2 and IFNG, which RUNX1 would otherwise switch on, are repressed, while the surface hallmarks of the suppressive lineage are induced: the IL-2 receptor alpha chain, CTLA4 and GITR, with NFATC2 cooperating at these promoters. RUNX1:CBFB also activates the complement receptor CR1, whose appearance on activated T cells favours Treg generation. Loss of FOXP3 abolishes this programme and produces fatal multi-organ autoimmunity, and weakened Treg output underlies autoimmune disease and allergy more broadly.
Regulatory T cell identity is set by a circuit in which RUNX1 with CBFB drives FOXP3 transcription, and FOXP3 then binds RUNX1:CBFB to redirect it. The complex represses effector genes such as IL2 and IFNG while inducing IL-2 receptor alpha, CTLA4 and GITR with NFATC2, and activates CR1, which favours Treg generation. Loss of FOXP3 causes fatal multi-organ autoimmunity, and weakened Treg output contributes to autoimmunity and allergy.A heterodimeric transcription factor, whose non-DNA-binding subunit is required for stable DNA contact, activates transcription of a forkhead factor; the forkhead protein then binds back to that same heterodimer and redirects its output. Inflammatory cytokine genes the complex would otherwise induce are repressed, while surface receptor genes of a suppressive programme are activated, with a calcineurin-responsive factor cooperating at those promoters.—
RUNX1 regulates genes involved in megakaryocyte differentiation and platelet function
originalPlatelets arise from megakaryocytes, and the transcription factor RUNX1 with its partner CBFB sets the gene programme that makes them. The complex is induced as progenitors commit to the megakaryocytic lineage and switched off as they turn erythroid, and it cooperates with GATA1 and its partner ZFPM1 at megakaryocyte promoters. Which coregulators are recruited decides the outcome: arginine methylation by PRMT1 favours an activating complex with the acetyltransferases EP300 and KAT2B and WDR5-containing methyltransferase complexes, whereas unmethylated RUNX1 binds SIN3A/SIN3B with HDAC1 and PRMT6 to repress. Targets include the integrin ITGA2B and GP1BA for adhesion and aggregation, THBS1, the alpha-granule chemokine PF4, MYL9, PRKCQ, NFE2 and NR4A3, plus MIR27A, which feeds back on RUNX1 translation. Loss of RUNX1 function causes familial platelet disorder with thrombocytopenia and predisposition to leukaemia.
RUNX1 with CBFB drives the megakaryocyte gene programme that produces platelets, being induced on megakaryocytic commitment, silenced in erythroid cells and cooperating with GATA1-ZFPM1. PRMT1 arginine methylation favours activation with EP300, KAT2B and WDR5 complexes, whereas unmethylated RUNX1 represses with SIN3A/B, HDAC1 and PRMT6. Targets include ITGA2B, GP1BA, THBS1, PF4, MYL9, PRKCQ, NFE2, NR4A3 and MIR27A, which feeds back on RUNX1; loss causes familial platelet disorder and leukaemia predisposition.Whether this heterodimeric transcription factor activates or represses its targets depends on which coregulators it recruits, and arginine methylation sets that choice. The methylated factor assembles with acetyltransferases and a WDR5-containing methyltransferase complex to activate, whereas the unmethylated form binds corepressor scaffolds with a histone deacetylase and a different methyltransferase to repress. Targets include adhesion receptors, secreted granule proteins and a microRNA that feeds back on its own translation.—
Regulation of RUNX1 Expression and Activity
originalRUNX1 is the master transcription factor of definitive blood formation, and the many layers that set its abundance and activity determine whether hemogenic endothelium yields hematopoietic stem cells and whether progenitors mature into T cells, megakaryocytes and other lineages; dosage matters so much that haploinsufficiency causes familial platelet disorder with leukemia predisposition, and translocations disrupting the gene drive acute myeloid leukemia. Transcription proceeds from two alternative promoters used differently across development, while a panel of microRNAs including miR-17, miR-20a, miR-18a and miR-27a engage the 3'UTR through Argonaute and TNRC6 silencing complexes to limit translation. Protein activity is then tuned by partners and modifications: heterodimerization with CBFB is required for DNA binding and transactivation, D-type cyclins and CDK6 antagonize that step, SRC-family tyrosine phosphorylation is reversed by the phosphatase PTPN11, and PML directs subnuclear localization.
RUNX1, master regulator of definitive haematopoiesis, is controlled at many layers that determine stem cell emergence and lineage maturation; haploinsufficiency causes familial platelet disorder and translocations drive acute myeloid leukaemia. It is transcribed from two alternative promoters, and microRNAs such as miR-17, miR-20a, miR-18a and miR-27a limit translation via Argonaute-TNRC6. Activity then depends on heterodimerisation with a non-DNA-binding subunit required for DNA binding, antagonism by D-type cyclins with their kinase, tyrosine phosphorylation reversed by a phosphatase, and subnuclear localisation directed by a scaffold.—
RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in WNT signaling
originalRUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, is a lineage-defining transcription factor best known in blood development, and part of what it does is set the level of WNT signalling by transcribing WNT pathway components directly. This matters because the strength of WNT input decides whether progenitors self-renew or differentiate, and because RUNX1 is a recurrent target of translocation and mutation in leukaemia and a modifier of breast cancer behaviour. Two targets illustrate opposite arms of the same control. With the regulatory T cell factor FOXP3 as cofactor, the complex drives RSPO3, a secreted R-spondin that potentiates WNT receptor signalling and has oncogenic activity in breast tissue. With ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha, it instead induces AXIN1, a scaffold of the destruction complex that restrains beta-catenin. Hormonal and immune context therefore determines whether RUNX1 amplifies or dampens WNT output.
RUNX1 with CBFB, a blood lineage regulator often altered in leukaemia, directly transcribes WNT pathway components and so sets WNT signalling strength, which governs self-renewal versus differentiation. With FOXP3 as cofactor it induces RSPO3, a WNT-potentiating R-spondin with oncogenic activity in breast; with ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha it induces AXIN1, a destruction-complex scaffold restraining beta-catenin. With a forkhead cofactor it drives a secreted R-spondin that potentiates receptor signalling; with a ligand-activated nuclear receptor it instead induces a scaffold of the cytoplasmic destruction complex that restrains the pathway's transcriptional effector. Cofactor availability therefore decides whether output is amplified or damped.—
RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in BCR signaling
originalB cells need a functioning antigen receptor signalling apparatus, and part of that apparatus is put in place transcriptionally before any antigen is ever seen. Here RUNX1 controls transcription of genes acting in B cell receptor signalling, most directly the B lymphoid tyrosine kinase BLK, which propagates receptor engagement into the intracellular kinase cascades that drive B cell development, differentiation and antibody responses. RUNX1 works as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, which stabilises DNA binding, and cooperates at the BLK promoter with the ETS-family factors ELF1 and ELF2 and with PAX5, the transcription factor that commits and maintains the B lymphoid lineage. This convergence of lineage-determining and general ETS regulators on a single kinase gene illustrates how haematopoietic transcription factors specify signalling competence; RUNX1 itself is a recurrent target of leukaemic translocation and mutation.
Part of the B cell receptor signalling apparatus is set up transcriptionally before antigen exposure, as RUNX1 with CBFB activates genes such as BLK, a kinase propagating receptor engagement into cascades driving B cell development, differentiation and antibody responses. At the BLK promoter RUNX1 cooperates with ETS factors ELF1 and ELF2 and with the B lineage factor PAX5. This shows how haematopoietic transcription factors specify signalling competence.A heterodimeric transcription factor, stabilised on DNA by its non-DNA-binding subunit, transcribes a gene encoding a Src-family tyrosine kinase that propagates antigen receptor engagement into intracellular kinase cascades. At that promoter it cooperates with two ETS-family factors and with a paired-box lineage-determining factor. Signalling competence is therefore established transcriptionally, before any receptor engagement occurs.—
RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in interleukin signaling
originalThe transcription factor RUNX1, working with its obligate partner CBFB, directs the haematopoietic gene programme, and part of that programme is the cell's ability to send and receive interleukin-family signals. Through this arm of its output RUNX1 turns on the gene for the leukemia inhibitory factor receptor, which transmits signals from an interleukin-6 family cytokine and contributes to blood cell production, embryo implantation, placental development and neural differentiation. Together with the ETS-family co-activator ELF1, the RUNX1:CBFB heterodimer also drives transcription of interleukin-3, a growth factor for multipotent progenitors and myeloid lineages. Because cytokine responsiveness and proliferative signalling are set here, disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB — as happens in familial platelet disorder and in the recurrent translocations of acute leukaemia — leaves progenitors with a miscalibrated response to interleukin cues.
RUNX1 with CBFB shapes haematopoietic cytokine responsiveness by inducing the leukemia inhibitory factor receptor, which transmits IL-6 family signals involved in blood production, implantation, placental development and neural differentiation. With the ETS coactivator ELF1 it also drives interleukin-3, a growth factor for multipotent and myeloid progenitors. Disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB in familial platelet disorder and acute leukaemia translocations leaves progenitors with miscalibrated responses to interleukin cues.A heterodimeric transcription factor transcribes genes for cytokine signalling. It activates the gene encoding the receptor for an interleukin-6-family cytokine, which transduces that signal into intracellular kinase cascades, and, together with an ETS-family coactivator, drives transcription of an interleukin growth factor itself. Both responsiveness to and production of these cytokines are therefore set transcriptionally by one complex.—
RUNX1 regulates estrogen receptor mediated transcription
originalEstrogen-responsive gene expression in breast epithelium is shaped not only by the hormone receptor itself but by the transcription factors it recruits, and RUNX1 acting on estrogen receptor mediated transcription is one such partnership. RUNX1, together with its obligate cofactor CBFB, binds directly to ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha and co-occupies the regulatory regions of a subset of estrogen target genes, among them the glycerolipid synthesis enzyme GPAM, the substrate adaptor KCTD6, and the Wnt pathway scaffold AXIN1. This gives RUNX1 a say in which genes respond to estrogen, linking hormone signalling to lipid metabolism and Wnt regulation rather than to proliferation alone. The relationship matters clinically: RUNX1 is a recurrently altered tumour suppressor in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, and high GPAM expression tracks with better overall survival.
RUNX1 with CBFB binds ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha in breast epithelium and co-occupies regulatory regions of a subset of estrogen targets, including GPAM, KCTD6 and AXIN1. This gives RUNX1 influence over which genes respond to estrogen, connecting hormone signalling to lipid metabolism and Wnt regulation beyond proliferation. Which genes respond to the hormone is therefore partly decided by this partnership, linking receptor signalling to lipid synthesis and pathway scaffolding rather than to proliferative targets alone.—
RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in differentiation of myeloid cells
originalMyeloid progenitors in the bone marrow must be instructed to become granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes or platelet-producing megakaryocytes, and RUNX1 is the transcription factor that issues much of that instruction. Acting as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, it occupies target promoters and recruits the acetyltransferase CREBBP to open chromatin and drive transcription. Among the genes switched on are CSF2, encoding GM-CSF, a cytokine that supports growth, survival and maturation across several myeloid lineages; LGALS3, whose galectin-3 product rises as myeloid cells mature; and PRKCB, a protein kinase C isoform governing myeloid cell apoptosis. Because this programme sets the balance between progenitor self-renewal and differentiation, loss or translocation of RUNX1 or CBFB stalls maturation and is a recurrent cause of acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorders.
RUNX1 with CBFB instructs myeloid progenitors toward granulocyte, monocyte, erythroid and megakaryocyte fates, recruiting CREBBP to open chromatin at target promoters. Targets include CSF2 (GM-CSF), supporting myeloid growth, survival and maturation; LGALS3, whose galectin-3 rises with maturation; and PRKCB, regulating myeloid apoptosis. Because this programme balances self-renewal and differentiation, RUNX1 or CBFB loss or translocation stalls maturation and causes acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorders.Acting as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner, this transcription factor occupies target promoters and recruits an acetyltransferase that opens chromatin and drives transcription. Its targets encode a secreted colony-stimulating cytokine supporting growth, survival and maturation, a beta-galactoside-binding lectin that accumulates with maturation, and a protein kinase C isoform governing apoptosis, so the complex sets the balance between self-renewal and differentiation.—
RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in differentiation of keratinocytes
originalSkin epithelium must balance stem cell maintenance against terminal differentiation, and the transcription factor RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, tilts that balance in keratinocytes by repressing a small set of target genes. One is the protease inhibitor SERPINB13, which restrains cathepsin-family proteases such as cathepsin L and V that participate in epidermal differentiation and desmosomal remodelling; its loss is common in head and neck cancers. RUNX1 also represses SOCS3 and SOCS4, the negative feedback inhibitors of JAK-STAT signalling, so removing them raises STAT3 activity. Sustained STAT3 output favours proliferation and self-renewal in hair follicle and epithelial stem cell compartments, which is why this circuit is implicated in tumour initiation and in squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. The pathway thus links lineage-specific transcriptional repression to cytokine signalling strength and protease balance in stratified epithelium.
In keratinocytes, RUNX1 with CBFB shifts the balance between stem cell maintenance and differentiation by repressing a few targets. It represses SERPINB13, an inhibitor of cathepsins L and V acting in epidermal differentiation and often lost in head and neck cancer, and SOCS3 and SOCS4, raising STAT3 activity. Elevated STAT3 promotes proliferation and self-renewal in hair follicle and epithelial stem cells, implicating this circuit in skin squamous cell carcinoma.Here the heterodimeric transcription factor acts as a repressor at a small set of promoters. RUNX1 interacts with co-factors whose precise effect on RUNX1 targets is not known
originalRUNX1, partnered with CBFB, is the master transcription factor of definitive blood formation, and its output depends heavily on which chromatin co-factors it brings to a promoter. Here RUNX1 is shown engaging partners whose net effect on target genes remains ambiguous, a state of affairs that matters because the same complex can activate or silence the same promoter depending on context. HIPK2 phosphorylates both RUNX1 and the acetyltransferase EP300 bound to the complex, and leukemia-associated CBFB mutations disrupt this modification. RUNX1:CBFB also associates with polycomb repressive complex 1 subunits, including RING1/RNF2 with CBX and PHC proteins, found at many RUNX1 targets acting as co-activators or co-repressors. Direct contacts with SWI/SNF subunits such as SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and ARID1A recruit nucleosome remodelling. Casein kinase 2 subunits add further phosphorylation input, tying hematopoietic gene control to chromatin state.
RUNX1 with CBFB, master regulator of definitive haematopoiesis, recruits chromatin co-factors whose net effect on targets can be activating or repressive depending on context. HIPK2 phosphorylates RUNX1 and bound EP300, a step disrupted by leukaemia-associated CBFB mutations.
