RUNX1 regulates expression of components of tight junctions
originalTight junctions seal the space between adjacent endothelial and epithelial cells and set how much solute can cross a barrier; here that barrier programme is placed under transcriptional control by RUNX1. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX1 binds the promoters of the genes for ZO-1, occludin and claudin-5 and raises their expression, so the scaffolding protein and the two integral junctional membrane proteins that form the seal are produced together. The relevance is barrier permeability: in brain endothelium these three products are core constituents of the blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier, and loss of RUNX1 output, as occurs when the microRNA miR-18a represses it, loosens the junctions and increases passage across the barrier in glioma. This links a transcription factor best known in haematopoiesis to endothelial barrier integrity and to the problem of drug delivery into tumours.
RUNX1 with CBFB binds the promoters of ZO-1, occludin and claudin-5 and increases their expression, coordinating production of the scaffold and membrane proteins that form endothelial and epithelial tight junctions. In brain endothelium these form the blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier, and when miR-18a represses RUNX1 in glioma, junctions loosen and permeability rises. This links a haematopoietic transcription factor to endothelial barrier integrity and drug delivery to tumours.With its obligate non-DNA-binding partner, this transcription factor binds the promoters of genes encoding a junctional scaffolding protein and two integral junctional membrane proteins, raising their expression together. Because those three products form the seal between adjacent cells, output here sets paracellular permeability, and repression of the factor by a microRNA loosens the junctions and increases solute passage across the barrier.—
RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in differentiation of HSCs
originalBlood formation requires stem cells to stop renewing themselves and commit to a lineage, and RUNX1, acting with its partner CBFB, is one of the transcription factors that makes that decision. Its best-defined target here is SPI1 (PU.1): RUNX1 brings the histone methyltransferase KMT2A to the SPI1 promoter and upstream regulatory element, depositing activating H3K4 trimethylation, and the resulting PU.1 expression restrains stem cell self-renewal while enabling myeloid and lymphoid commitment. RUNX1 also sits within a TAL1-containing complex with LMO1/LMO2, LDB1, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives MYB transcription, a configuration that in T-ALL promotes proliferation and blocks apoptosis. Proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes reflect the degradation that limits RUNX1 levels, ITCH and CDK7-containing kinase activity among its regulators. Loss or translocation of RUNX1 underlies familial platelet disorder and acute myeloid leukemia.
RUNX1 with CBFB helps blood stem cells commit to lineages, notably by recruiting KMT2A to the SPI1 promoter to deposit H3K4 trimethylation, inducing PU.1, which limits self-renewal and enables myeloid and lymphoid commitment. RUNX1 also joins a TAL1 complex with LMO1/LMO2, LDB1, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives MYB, promoting proliferation and survival in T-ALL. ITCH and proteasomal degradation limit RUNX1, whose loss causes familial platelet disorder and AML.This heterodimer recruits a histone methyltransferase to the promoter and upstream regulatory element of a gene encoding an ETS-family transcription factor, depositing activating H3K4 trimethylation; the product then restrains self-renewal and permits lineage commitment. The same factor also sits in a complex with a helix-loop-helix factor, LIM-domain adaptors, a bridging protein, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives transcription of a proliferative factor. Ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation limits its level.—

Transcriptional regulation by RUNX3 (9)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
RUNX3 regulates RUNX1-mediated transcription
originalRUNX family transcription factors cross-regulate one another, and here RUNX3 acts on the RUNX1 gene itself: bound with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX3 occupies Runx response elements in the distal P1 promoter of RUNX1 and represses its transcription. This negative feedback sets the balance between two related master regulators whose combined output shapes haematopoietic stem cell emergence, lymphocyte and megakaryocyte differentiation, and gut epithelial homeostasis. Because neither factor binds DNA efficiently alone, the shared non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB determines how much of either complex is available, and shifting occupancy of the P1 promoter changes which RUNX1 isoform predominates. Loss of this restraint matters clinically: RUNX1 dosage is sensitive, its disruption underlies familial platelet disorder and recurrent leukaemic translocations, while RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric and other epithelial cancers.
RUNX3, with its partner CBFB, binds Runx elements in the distal P1 promoter of RUNX1 and represses it, forming negative cross-regulation between two master regulators of haematopoietic stem cell emergence, lymphocyte and megakaryocyte differentiation and gut epithelial homeostasis. Because both need CBFB, its availability and P1 occupancy determine RUNX1 isoform use. RUNX1 disruption causes familial platelet disorder and leukaemia; RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric cancers.One member of a transcription factor family, bound to its obligate non-DNA-binding partner, occupies response elements in the distal promoter of a paralogue's gene and represses its transcription. This negative feedback sets the relative output of two related master regulators that share the same partner subunit, so how much partner is available determines how much of either complex can form. Shifting promoter occupancy also changes which isoform predominates.—
RUNX3 regulates YAP1-mediated transcription
originalThe Hippo pathway effectors YAP1 and its paralogue WWTR1 (TAZ) drive growth-promoting transcription by partnering with TEAD family DNA-binding factors, and one of their canonical outputs is CCN2 (connective tissue growth factor), a matricellular protein that fuels proliferation, matrix production and fibrosis. RUNX3 acts here as a brake: by binding the TEAD:YAP1 complex it blocks its loading onto the CCN2 promoter, damping transcription of this growth factor. The interaction links a classical tumour-suppressor RUNX transcription factor to organ-size and contact-inhibition control, and helps explain why loss or silencing of RUNX3, common in gastric and other epithelial cancers, permits unrestrained YAP-driven target gene expression. The balance set at TEAD-bound enhancers thus determines whether epithelial cells proliferate and remodel their surroundings or remain quiescent, placing this regulation at the intersection of Hippo signalling, tissue repair and tumour suppression.
Hippo effectors YAP1 and TAZ partner with TEAD factors to activate growth genes including CCN2, a matricellular protein promoting proliferation, matrix production and fibrosis. RUNX3 binds the TEAD:YAP1 complex and prevents it loading onto the CCN2 promoter, damping transcription. This links RUNX3 tumour suppression to organ-size and contact-inhibition control, explaining why RUNX3 loss in gastric and other epithelial cancers releases YAP-driven expression.Two paralogous coactivators relieved of inhibitory kinase signalling partner with TEAD-family DNA-binding factors to transcribe a matricellular growth factor gene. A Runt-domain transcription factor acts as a brake by binding the coactivator-TEAD complex and blocking its loading onto that promoter, damping transcription. The balance struck at TEAD-occupied enhancers therefore decides whether growth-promoting and matrix-remodelling transcription proceeds or is held off.—
RUNX3 regulates p14-ARF
originalThis is a tumour-suppressive transcriptional switch in which RUNX3, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, turns on p14-ARF from the CDKN2A locus and so raises the barrier to oncogenic transformation. p14-ARF sequesters MDM2 and stabilises p53, meaning that loss of this arm allows cells carrying activating lesions such as mutant KRAS to proliferate instead of arresting or dying; RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric and other epithelial cancers. The control is acetylation-dependent: the acetyltransferase p300 modifies RUNX3, acetylated RUNX3 is read by the bromodomain protein BRD2, and this complex drives p14-ARF transcription. Cyclin D1 opposes the response by delivering the deacetylase HDAC4 to RUNX3, stripping the mark and muting induction, which couples the output to cell cycle state. TGF-beta signalling feeds into the same node, linking growth-inhibitory cues to p53 pathway activation.
RUNX3 with CBFB induces p14-ARF from CDKN2A, which sequesters MDM2 and stabilises p53, creating a barrier against oncogenic transformation by lesions such as mutant KRAS. Induction requires p300 acetylation of RUNX3 and recognition by the bromodomain protein BRD2, while cyclin D1 brings HDAC4 to deacetylate RUNX3 and mute the response, coupling it to the cell cycle. TGF-beta feeds into this node, and RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric cancers.A Runt-domain heterodimer activates transcription of an inhibitor of the ubiquitin ligase that would otherwise destabilise p53, and the switch is acetylation-dependent. An acetyltransferase modifies the transcription factor, a bromodomain protein reads the acetyl mark, and the resulting complex drives transcription. A cyclin opposes the response by delivering a deacetylase that strips the mark, coupling output to cycle state, while SMAD signalling feeds into the same node.—
RUNX3 regulates NOTCH signaling
originalThe transcription factor RUNX3 acts as a brake on NOTCH signalling, and losing that restraint is one route by which liver cells become tumorigenic. RUNX3 works at two points. It occupies the promoter of JAG1 and represses transcription of this NOTCH ligand, lowering the signal available to neighbouring cells. It also joins the coactivator complex assembled on cleaved NOTCH1 intracellular domain with RBPJ, Mastermind-like proteins and the acetyltransferases CREBBP/EP300 and KAT2A/KAT2B, and blocks activation of the target gene HES1. Because HES1 is a repressor that sustains progenitor states and blocks differentiation, this interference pushes cells toward differentiation and away from proliferation. RUNX3 silencing, common in hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer, releases NOTCH output and links its tumour suppressor function directly to developmental cell-fate signalling.
RUNX3 restrains NOTCH signalling, and losing this restraint helps liver cells become tumorigenic. It represses transcription of the NOTCH ligand JAG1, and joins the NICD1-RBPJ-Mastermind coactivator complex with CREBBP/EP300 and KAT2A/B to block activation of HES1, a repressor maintaining progenitor states. This pushes cells toward differentiation rather than proliferation; RUNX3 silencing in hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer releases NOTCH output, linking tumour suppression to cell-fate signalling.A Runt-domain transcription factor restrains a juxtacrine signalling pathway at two points. It occupies the promoter of a gene encoding one of the pathway's transmembrane ligands and represses it, lowering the signal presented to neighbouring cells. It also joins the coactivator complex assembled on the cleaved receptor intracellular domain with its DNA-binding partner, mastermind-like proteins and acetyltransferases, blocking activation of the complex's repressor target gene.—
RUNX3 regulates BCL2L11 (BIM) transcription
originalTGF-beta can instruct a cell to die rather than divide, and one route to that outcome is transcriptional induction of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. Here RUNX3 drives BCL2L11 transcription, acting on the gene's promoter together with receptor-activated SMAD3 and its partner SMAD4 and with the forkhead factor FOXO3. The BIM protein that results neutralises anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and promotes BAX/BAK-dependent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, committing the cell to the intrinsic apoptotic programme. This arm of TGF-beta signalling contributes to the cytokine's tumour-suppressive behaviour in epithelial and gastric tissue and to apoptotic culling in lymphocytes; RUNX3 silencing by promoter methylation, or loss of SMAD signalling, removes this death output and allows cells that should have been eliminated to survive. It links growth factor signal transduction directly to the apoptotic machinery.
TGF-beta can trigger apoptosis by inducing BIM: RUNX3 activates BCL2L11 transcription together with SMAD3, SMAD4 and FOXO3. BIM neutralises anti-apoptotic BCL2 proteins and promotes BAX/BAK-dependent mitochondrial permeabilisation, committing cells to intrinsic apoptosis. This contributes to TGF-beta tumour suppression in epithelial and gastric tissue and to lymphocyte culling, and RUNX3 methylation or SMAD loss lets cells survive that should be eliminated.A Runt-domain transcription factor drives transcription of a BH3-only gene, acting at its promoter together with receptor-activated SMAD proteins and a forkhead factor. The resulting BH3-only protein neutralises anti-apoptotic BCL2-family members and promotes pore formation in the mitochondrial outer membrane, committing the cell to the intrinsic apoptotic programme. This couples TGF-beta receptor signal transduction directly to the apoptotic machinery.—
Regulation of RUNX3 expression and activity
originalRUNX3 is a transcription factor that acts as a tumour suppressor in epithelial tissues and directs lymphocyte and dendritic cell differentiation, and the control of its expression and activity determines how much of it is available in the nucleus at any time. Its loss, most often through methylation of a CpG island at the internal promoter or through hypoxia-driven silencing, is a recurrent event in gastric and other solid tumours. Transcription responds to TGF-beta/SMAD input and to autoregulation; alternative promoter use and splicing yield isoforms differing in Runt-domain function. Once made, RUNX3 must heterodimerise with CBFB to bind DNA and recruits the acetyltransferase EP300 to activate targets such as CDKN2A. Activity is curtailed by SRC-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation, which blocks nuclear entry, and by polyubiquitination via MDM2, SMURF1 and SMURF2 followed by proteasomal degradation, the reason the 26S proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes feature here.
RUNX3, an epithelial tumour suppressor directing lymphocyte and dendritic cell differentiation, is regulated at several levels; CpG methylation or hypoxia silences it in gastric tumours. Transcription responds to TGF-beta/SMAD and autoregulation, with alternative promoters and splicing giving distinct isoforms. RUNX3 needs CBFB to bind DNA and EP300 to activate targets such as CDKN2A, while SRC phosphorylation blocks nuclear entry and MDM2 and SMURF ligases drive its degradation.How much of a Runt-domain transcription factor is active in the nucleus is set at several steps. Transcription responds to SMAD input and to autoregulation, promoter CpG methylation can silence the gene, and alternative promoters and splicing yield isoforms differing in Runt-domain function. The protein must heterodimerise with a non-DNA-binding subunit to bind DNA and recruits an acetyltransferase, while tyrosine phosphorylation blocks nuclear entry and polyubiquitination directs proteasomal degradation.—
RUNX3 regulates CDKN1A transcription
originalGrowth arrest imposed by TGF-beta depends on turning on the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, and RUNX3-driven transcription of CDKN1A is one route by which that happens. It matters most in gastric and other epithelia, where loss of this control removes a brake on proliferation: mice lacking Runx3 become insensitive to TGF-beta and develop gastric epithelial hyperplasia, and RUNX3 silencing is a recurrent event in gastric cancer. Mechanistically, TGFB1 signalling activates a SMAD3:SMAD4 complex that RUNX3 binds and cooperates with at the CDKN1A promoter; the RUNX3 heterodimer also engages the tumour suppressor ZFHX3 to reinforce induction. RUNX3 can additionally act as a co-factor for TP53, boosting p53-dependent target genes including CDKN1A, linking this transcriptional node to both cytokine-driven and damage-driven cell cycle arrest.
TGF-beta growth arrest requires p21, and RUNX3 induces CDKN1A by binding and cooperating with TGFB1-activated SMAD3:SMAD4 at its promoter, reinforced by ZFHX3. This is especially important in gastric epithelium: Runx3-deficient mice are TGF-beta-insensitive and develop gastric hyperplasia, and RUNX3 silencing recurs in gastric cancer. RUNX3 also coactivates TP53, boosting p53 targets including CDKN1A and linking cytokine- and damage-driven cell cycle arrest.Cytokine-driven growth arrest requires transcription of a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor gene. Receptor signalling activates a SMAD complex that a Runt-domain transcription factor binds and cooperates with at that promoter, and the heterodimer also engages a large zinc-finger protein to reinforce induction. The same factor can act as a cofactor for p53, boosting p53-dependent transcription of the inhibitor, so cytokine- and damage-driven arrest converge on one node.—
RUNX3 regulates WNT signaling
originalRUNX3 acts as a brake on WNT-driven proliferation, and its loss helps explain why this transcription factor behaves as a tumour suppressor in gastrointestinal epithelium. When WNT signalling stabilises beta-catenin, the protein enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF factors such as TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2 and LEF1 to switch on growth-promoting target genes, chief among them cyclin D1 and MYC, which together push cells through the G1 restriction point. RUNX3 binds the beta-catenin:TCF/LEF complex directly and prevents it from occupying the CCND1 and MYC promoters, so the transcriptional output of the pathway is attenuated without blocking beta-catenin stabilisation itself. Silencing or mislocalisation of RUNX3 therefore leaves these complexes free to drive proliferation, linking this regulatory step to epithelial growth control and to carcinogenesis in the stomach and colon.
RUNX3 restrains WNT-driven proliferation, explaining its tumour suppressor role in gastrointestinal epithelium. Stabilised beta-catenin partners with TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2 and LEF1 to induce cyclin D1 and MYC, which drive G1 progression. RUNX3 binds the beta-catenin:TCF/LEF complex and prevents its occupancy of CCND1 and MYC promoters without affecting beta-catenin stabilisation, so RUNX3 silencing or mislocalisation promotes proliferation and gastric and colon carcinogenesis.When the pathway's transcriptional effector escapes cytoplasmic destruction it enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF DNA-binding factors to activate growth-promoting genes, chiefly a D-type cyclin and a helix-loop-helix factor that together drive passage through the G1 restriction point. A Runt-domain transcription factor binds that effector-TCF complex directly and prevents it occupying those promoters, attenuating output without blocking effector stabilisation itself.—
RUNX3 Regulates Immune Response and Cell Migration
originalRUNX3 is a transcription factor that shapes immune cell identity and the adhesion machinery leukocytes need to leave the bloodstream. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, it drives development of tissue-resident innate lymphoid cells of the ILC1 and ILC3 lineages, which guard mucosal surfaces against pathogens, by inducing the nuclear receptor RORC. In parallel it activates the integrin genes ITGAL (CD11a) and ITGA4 (CD49d), which mediate transendothelial migration during immune and inflammatory responses and provide co-stimulation to T cells. A shorter RUNX3 isoform lacking the DNA-binding Runt domain cannot transactivate these targets and accumulates as monocyte-derived dendritic cells mature, dampening inflammatory gene output. RUNX3 also raises expression of osteopontin (SPP1), a matrix protein that promotes invasiveness, linking this programme to pancreatic cancer progression as well as to normal mucosal immunity and leukocyte trafficking.
RUNX3 with CBFB shapes immune identity and leukocyte adhesion. It induces RORC to drive ILC1 and ILC3 development for mucosal defence, and activates ITGAL (CD11a) and ITGA4 (CD49d), which mediate transendothelial migration and T cell costimulation. A Runt-domain-lacking isoform accumulating in maturing monocyte-derived dendritic cells cannot transactivate these genes and dampens inflammation, and RUNX3 induction of osteopontin (SPP1) links this programme to pancreatic cancer invasiveness.With its obligate partner, this Runt-domain factor induces a nuclear receptor gene and activates two integrin subunit genes whose products mediate adhesion to endothelium and transmigration as well as providing costimulatory signalling. A shorter isoform lacking the DNA-binding Runt domain cannot transactivate these targets and accumulates during maturation, damping output. The factor also raises expression of a secreted matrix phosphoprotein that promotes invasiveness.—

FOXO-mediated transcription (5)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Regulation of localization of FOXO transcription factors
originalFOXO transcription factors drive programmes of stress resistance, autophagy, gluconeogenesis, apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and growth factor signalling switches those programmes off by moving the factors out of the nucleus. This is the main output of insulin and PI3K/AKT signalling onto metabolic and longevity gene expression: when insulin is present, hepatic glucose production and catabolic gene expression are suppressed, and when signalling is lost the factors return to chromatin. AKT1, AKT2 and AKT3 phosphorylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 at conserved sites, producing a conformational change that exposes a nuclear export signal; 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAB, YWHAZ and stratifin then bind the phosphorylated factors and hold them in the cytosol, away from their target promoters. FOXO6 lacks the export signal and stays nuclear, so phosphorylation instead dampens its transcriptional activity. Loss of this control contributes to insulin resistance and tumour suppression escape.
Insulin and PI3K/AKT signalling switch off FOXO programmes of stress resistance, autophagy, gluconeogenesis, apoptosis and arrest by exporting the factors from the nucleus. AKT1-3 phosphorylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, exposing a nuclear export signal, and 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAB, YWHAZ and stratifin retain them in the cytosol, suppressing hepatic glucose production; nuclear FOXO6 is instead inhibited directly. Losing this control contributes to insulin resistance and escape from tumour suppression.Phosphoinositide-dependent kinase signalling switches off a family of forkhead transcription factors by relocating them. Three related kinases phosphorylate conserved sites, producing a conformational change that exposes a nuclear export signal; dimeric phosphoserine-binding proteins then bind the modified factors and retain them in the cytosol, away from target promoters. One family member lacks the export signal, so phosphorylation instead directly lowers its transcriptional activity.—
FOXO-mediated transcription of oxidative stress, metabolic and neuronal genes
originalFOXO transcription factors act as the nuclear output of insulin and growth factor signalling, and this branch covers their direct control of oxidative stress defence, fuel metabolism and neuronal gene programmes. When insulin is low, as in fasting, PI3K/AKT no longer restrains FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6, which then drive hepatic gluconeogenesis through PCK1 and G6PC1 while repressing glucokinase via a SIN3A:HDAC corepressor complex and repressing SREBF1 to hold back lipogenesis; IGFBP1 and resistin further tune systemic insulin sensitivity. In hypothalamic neurons the same factors raise the orexigenic peptides NPY and AGRP and repress POMC, linking nutrient status to appetite. Antioxidant targets SOD2 and catalase, with contributions from cofactors such as PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and ataxin-3, limit superoxide and peroxide burden and support neuronal survival in neurodegeneration. FOXO6 also induces PLXNA4 during cortical radial glia migration, and FBXO32 and TRIM63 induction underlies starvation-induced muscle wasting.
When insulin is low, FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 escape AKT restraint and directly control metabolism, oxidative defence and neuronal programmes. They induce gluconeogenic PCK1 and G6PC1, repress glucokinase via SIN3A-HDAC and SREBF1, and tune IGFBP1 and resistin; in hypothalamus they raise NPY and AGRP and repress POMC. With PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and ataxin-3 they induce SOD2 and catalase, and drive FBXO32 and TRIM63 in muscle wasting.When phosphoinositide-dependent kinase signalling falls, forkhead factors occupy target promoters. They induce the gluconeogenic enzymes phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and glucose-6-phosphatase while repressing glucokinase through a corepressor-deacetylase complex and repressing a lipogenic transcription factor. They also activate antioxidant enzymes that lower superoxide and peroxide burden, with deacetylase and coactivator cofactors contributing, and induce two ubiquitin ligases that drive protein degradation.—
FOXO-mediated transcription of cell cycle genes
originalWhen growth factor and insulin signalling wane, FOXO transcription factors escape cytoplasmic sequestration and enter the nucleus to shut down proliferation, and their transcription of cell cycle genes is how that arrest is enacted. FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 induce the CDK inhibitors p21 (CDKN1A) and p27 (CDKN1B), the pocket protein RBL2/p130 that helps maintain quiescence, the anti-proliferative genes CCNG2 and BTG1, GADD45A, caveolin-1, and KLF4. The output is withdrawal into G0 rather than division, a brake on erythroid progenitors, lymphocytes and neuroepithelial progenitors of the developing telencephalon, where FOXG1 opposes this arrest. TGF-beta input converges here: activated SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 partners with FOXO to drive p21 and, in muscle, myostatin, coupling cytostasis to differentiation. Loss of this arm of FOXO activity removes a tumour-suppressive restraint on growth factor-driven proliferation and stem cell exhaustion.
When insulin and growth factor signals fall, nuclear FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 enforce quiescence by inducing p21, p27, RBL2/p130, CCNG2, BTG1, GADD45A, caveolin-1 and KLF4. This withdrawal into G0 restrains erythroid progenitors, lymphocytes and telencephalic neuroepithelial progenitors, where FOXG1 opposes it. SMAD2/3-SMAD4 from TGF-beta signalling partners with FOXO to induce p21 and, in muscle, myostatin, and loss of this arm removes a tumour-suppressive brake and promotes stem cell exhaustion.Relieved of kinase-driven cytoplasmic sequestration, forkhead factors enter the nucleus and transcribe genes that stop division: two cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, a pocket protein that maintains quiescence, several antiproliferative and growth-arrest genes, and a reprogramming factor. The result is withdrawal into a quiescent state rather than cycle progression. Receptor-activated SMAD complexes converge on the same promoters, partnering with the forkhead factors to drive inhibitor transcription.—
Regulation of FOXO transcriptional activity by acetylation
originalFOXO transcription factors decide whether a stressed cell mounts an antioxidant and repair response, arrests its cycle, or dies, and acetylation is one of the switches that sets that choice. Under oxidative stress the acetyltransferases CBP, p300 and PCAF add acetyl groups to FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, shifting which target promoters they favour and altering their nuclear retention in a way that can override the phosphorylation-driven nuclear exclusion imposed by insulin and growth factor signalling. The NAD-dependent deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT3 reverse these marks, linking FOXO output to cellular energy and redox state; thioredoxin and its inhibitor TXNIP tie the same factors to the thiol redox environment. Through this regulation FOXO proteins govern stress resistance, metabolic adaptation, muscle atrophy programmes and tumour suppression, and the axis is central to how longevity signalling is interpreted at the level of gene expression.
Acetylation helps determine whether stressed cells mount antioxidant and repair responses, arrest, or die via FOXO factors. Under oxidative stress CBP, p300 and PCAF acetylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, changing promoter preference and nuclear retention and potentially overriding insulin-driven exclusion; SIRT1 and SIRT3 deacetylate them, linking output to energy and redox state, with thioredoxin and TXNIP adding thiol control. This axis governs stress resistance, metabolism, muscle atrophy and tumour suppression.Acetylation is a switch on forkhead factor output. Under oxidative stress three acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to these factors, shifting which promoters they favour and altering nuclear retention in a way that can override the phosphorylation-driven nuclear exclusion imposed by kinase signalling. NAD-dependent deacetylases reverse the marks, tying output to energy and redox state, while a thiol oxidoreductase and its inhibitor couple the same factors to thiol redox state.—
FOXO-mediated transcription of cell death genes
originalWhen growth factor and insulin signalling falls silent, FOXO transcription factors move into the nucleus and switch on genes that kill the cell. This FOXO-driven transcription of cell death genes prunes neurons deprived of nerve growth factor, eliminates enteric nervous system precursors that lack RET signalling, and underlies much of the tumour-suppressive character of FOXO proteins; PI3K/AKT activity in cancer keeps FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 out of the nucleus and blocks it. The induced targets are the apoptotic machinery itself: the BH3-only proteins BIM and PUMA, the death ligand FASLG, the transcriptional repressor BCL6, plus PINK1 and the kinase STK11. Coactivators CREBBP and EP300 and the trimeric NF-Y complex work with FOXO at these promoters, while CITED2 and the stress-induced factor DDIT3 modulate the response, tying nutrient and stress sensing to a decision to die.
Without growth factor and insulin signalling, FOXO factors enter the nucleus and induce cell death genes, pruning NGF-deprived neurons, eliminating enteric precursors lacking RET signalling and underpinning FOXO tumour suppression, which PI3K/AKT activity in cancer blocks. Targets include BIM, PUMA, FASLG, BCL6, PINK1 and STK11. CREBBP, EP300 and NF-Y cooperate at these promoters while CITED2 and DDIT3 modulate the response, linking nutrient and stress sensing to cell death decisions.When kinase signalling falls silent, forkhead factors enter the nucleus and transcribe the apoptotic machinery itself: two BH3-only proteins, a death receptor ligand, a transcriptional repressor, a mitochondrial kinase and another serine-threonine kinase. Two acetyltransferase coactivators and a trimeric CCAAT-binding complex work with them at these promoters, while a coactivator and a stress-induced leucine zipper factor modulate the response, tying nutrient and stress sensing to a death decision.—

Transcriptional Regulation by MECP2 (5)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Regulation of MECP2 expression and activity
originalMECP2 reads methylated DNA and tunes neuronal gene expression, and the layers that set how much of it is present and what it does are the subject here. Loss or misdosage of MECP2 causes Rett syndrome, so the controls on its level and activity matter as much as the protein itself. Its mRNA is silenced post-transcriptionally by miR-132 acting through Argonaute-containing silencing complexes, placing MECP2 downstream of activity-dependent neurotrophin signalling. Activity also acts directly: calcium-dependent kinases including CaMK IV and PKA, along with HIPK2 and AURKB, phosphorylate MECP2 at distinct sites that shift its chromatin association and its choice of partner. Through those partners MECP2 can repress, via the NCoR/SMRT and SIN3A complexes with HDAC1/2, or activate together with CREB1. Interactions with FOXG1, huntingtin and the lamin B receptor further shape its function and nuclear positioning.
MECP2 reads DNA methylation to tune neuronal gene expression, and its level and activity are controlled at several layers, important because misdosage causes Rett syndrome. miR-132 silences MECP2 mRNA via Argonaute complexes downstream of activity-dependent neurotrophin signalling, and CaMK IV, PKA, HIPK2 and AURKB phosphorylate it to alter chromatin binding and partners. MECP2 represses through NCoR/SMRT and SIN3A-HDAC1/2 or activates with CREB1, and FOXG1 and huntingtin shape its function.A methyl-CpG-binding protein's abundance and behaviour are set at several layers. Its transcript is repressed post-transcriptionally by a microRNA loaded into an Argonaute-containing silencing complex, while calcium- and cyclic-AMP-dependent kinases and additional kinases phosphorylate the protein at distinct sites that alter its chromatin association and partner choice. Through those partners it either represses, with corepressor and deacetylase complexes, or activates alongside a cyclic-AMP-responsive factor.—
MECP2 regulates transcription factors
originalMECP2 is a methyl-CpG-binding nuclear protein that tunes neuronal gene expression, and one of its outputs is the level of other transcriptional regulators. By acting on the promoters of factors such as CREB1 and MEF2C, together with the splicing regulator RBFOX1 and the nuclear receptor PPARG, it sets the transcriptional tone for activity-dependent neuronal maturation, synapse refinement and dendritic complexity. MECP2 can both repress and activate these targets depending on context, so its loss does not silence a single gene but shifts a whole regulatory layer. That dependency explains why MECP2 mutation causes Rett syndrome, in which early development appears normal before acquired speech and motor skills regress, and why duplication of the locus is equally damaging. The PPARG link extends its reach beyond neurons to adipocyte differentiation and metabolic gene programmes.
MECP2, a methyl-CpG-binding nuclear protein, regulates other regulators, acting on promoters of CREB1, MEF2C, RBFOX1 and PPARG to set the tone of activity-dependent neuronal maturation, synapse refinement and dendritic complexity. Because it can repress or activate, its loss shifts a whole regulatory layer, explaining Rett syndrome, with regression after apparently normal early development, and equally damaging duplications. The PPARG connection extends its influence to adipocyte differentiation and metabolic programmes.A methyl-CpG-binding protein sets the level of other regulatory proteins by acting at their promoters, among them a cyclic-AMP-responsive factor, a MADS-box factor, a splicing regulator and a nuclear receptor. Depending on context it activates or represses these targets, so changing its dosage shifts an entire regulatory layer rather than silencing a single gene, altering downstream transcriptional and splicing programmes together.—
MECP2 regulates transcription of genes involved in GABA signaling
originalInhibitory neurotransmission depends on a steady supply of GABA, and the methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2 helps set that supply by directly and positively driving transcription of the two glutamate decarboxylase genes, GAD1 and GAD2, whose products convert glutamate to GABA. This link places MECP2, a reader of DNA methylation that tunes neuronal gene expression, upstream of the excitation-inhibition balance of cortical and subcortical circuits. Loss of MECP2 from GABA-releasing neurons lowers GABA content and reproduces much of the Rett syndrome phenotype, including breathing irregularity, stereotypies and motor and social deficits, while its loss specifically in parvalbumin interneurons blunts sensory-evoked responses and impairs motor learning along with maturation of interneuron membrane properties and expression of parvalbumin, GABA-A receptor subunits and potassium channels. The pathway thus connects epigenetic transcriptional control to inhibitory circuit function and neurodevelopmental disease.
MECP2 directly activates transcription of GAD1 and GAD2, whose enzymes convert glutamate to GABA, placing this methylation reader upstream of excitation-inhibition balance. MECP2 regulates neuronal receptors and channels
originalThe methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2 sets the transcriptional tone of maturing neurons, and one arm of that control is the direct regulation of the receptors, channels and transporters through which neurons sense and respond to their surroundings. Loss of MECP2 function causes Rett syndrome, in which apparently normal early development gives way to regression, and duplication of the gene is equally damaging, so the dosage of these target genes matters. Targets here include the AMPA receptor subunit GRIA2 and NMDA receptor subunits GRIN2A and GRIN2B, which shape excitatory synaptic transmission and its developmental switch; opioid receptors OPRK1 and OPRM1; the receptor tyrosine kinase MET and NOTCH1; the cation channel TRPC3 and glucose transporter SLC2A3. MECP2 acts with CREB1 and, through SIN3A and the histone deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, can repress as well as activate. MECP2 regulates transcription of neuronal ligands
originalMECP2 is the methyl-CpG-binding protein whose loss causes Rett syndrome, and much of its neuronal function comes down to setting the expression level of secreted signalling molecules that shape synapses and circuit activity. MECP2 can act in either direction at these promoters, recruiting the SIN3A corepressor with HDAC1 to deacetylate histones and dampen transcription, or cooperating with CREB1 to drive activity-dependent expression. Because ligand dosage rather than presence is what is tuned, both loss and duplication of MECP2 produce neurodevelopmental disease, linking chromatin readout of DNA methylation to synaptic and neuroendocrine output.

Transcriptional Regulation by NPAS4 (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
Regulation of NPAS4 mRNA translation
originalNPAS4 is an activity-dependent transcription factor made in neurons after depolarisation, where it shapes the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses onto a cell; because its protein must appear quickly and disappear again, how much of its mRNA is translated is tightly controlled. Here that control is exerted by microRNAs acting on the unusually conserved NPAS4 3'UTR, with miR-224 and miR-203 among the species shown to repress reporter expression through it. Silencing is carried out by the RNA-induced silencing complex: an Argonaute protein loaded with the guide microRNA, scaffolded by a GW182-family partner (TNRC6A, TNRC6B or TNRC6C) that recruits deadenylation and decay machinery, with the RNA helicase MOV10 assisting on structured targets. Loss of this restraint disturbs experience-driven synaptic scaling, memory formation and seizure thresholds.
NPAS4, an activity-induced neuronal transcription factor that balances excitatory and inhibitory synapses, must appear and disappear rapidly, so its translation is tightly regulated. MicroRNAs including miR-224 and miR-203 repress it through its conserved 3'UTR via the RNA-induced silencing complex: Argonaute bearing the guide, TNRC6 scaffolds recruiting deadenylation and decay machinery, and the helicase MOV10. Losing this restraint disrupts synaptic scaling, memory formation and seizure thresholds.Translation of a transcript is limited through conserved elements in its 3' untranslated region. Output is therefore set post-transcriptionally, allowing the encoded protein to appear and disappear quickly.—
NPAS4 regulates expression of target genes
originalNPAS4 is an activity-induced transcription factor that couples neuronal excitation to changes in gene expression, and through it to the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses on a stimulated neuron. It matters for experience-dependent plasticity, contextual memory formation, protection of neurons after seizure or ischaemic injury, and for insulin gene expression in stressed pancreatic beta cells. Because its basic helix-loop-helix domain cannot bind DNA alone, NPAS4 dimerizes with ARNT, ARNT2 or BMAL1 and recruits coactivators such as CREBBP, with MAPK1/MAPK3 signalling and nuclear export machinery shaping its activity and short half-life. Target genes span neuronal differentiation and maturation (CDK5 with its activator CDK5R1, RBFOX3, RET), synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission (BDNF, IQSEC3, PLK2, SYT10, FOS), and metabolic and circadian outputs including NAMPT. It is also expressed in endothelium, where it has been linked to angiogenesis.

Regulation of NPAS4 gene transcription
originalNPAS4 is a neuron-specific transcription factor induced within minutes of activity that tunes inhibitory synapse number onto excited neurons, and the control of NPAS4 gene transcription is how that homeostatic brake is set. Calcium entry during neuronal stimulation drives transcription, with SRF acting as an activity-dependent activator at the promoter and PI3K/AKT signalling contributing, while calcium-free KCNIP3 (DREAM) occupies the promoter and holds it silent in the resting state. REST keeps the gene off in non-neuronal cells and can act in either direction in neurons, limiting the duration of the response. Stress imposes a second layer: glucocorticoid-bound NR3C1 binds upstream response elements and represses induction, and histone deacetylase activity and promoter CpG methylation state further gate the locus. Loss of this regulation disturbs excitatory-inhibitory balance, memory formation, and stress-related and neurodegenerative processes in the hippocampus.

Transcriptional regulation by RUNX2 (5)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
RUNX2 regulates genes involved in cell migration
originalRUNX2 is the master transcription factor of osteoblast differentiation, but the same factor also drives a migratory and invasive gene programme in bone and in tumour cells that colonise it. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 turns on ITGA5, which mediates attachment to fibronectin and helps breast cancer cells adhere within bone, ITGBL1, which modulates TGF-beta signalling and contributes to RUNX2-driven bone metastasis, and MMP13, a collagenase that degrades fibrillar collagen during skeletal remodelling and permits immune cells and cancer cells to move through matrix. AKT kinases phosphorylate RUNX2 and raise its transcriptional output, linking growth factor and PI3K signalling to this migratory programme. The same targets support endothelial cell movement during retinal angiogenesis and stem cell migration, so the pathway spans normal tissue morphogenesis and metastatic invasion.
Beyond osteoblast differentiation, RUNX2 with CBFB drives a migratory and invasive programme in bone and in tumour cells colonising it. It activates ITGA5 for fibronectin attachment, ITGBL1, which modulates TGF-beta and aids bone metastasis, and the collagenase MMP13, which lets immune and cancer cells traverse matrix. RUNX2 regulates genes involved in differentiation of myeloid cells
originalThe transcription factor RUNX2, best known for driving osteoblast commitment, also acts on genes of the myeloid programme, and this arm of its activity is captured by its control of galectin-3. Together with its paralogue RUNX1 and the shared non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, which stabilises RUNX binding to DNA and is required for its transcriptional output, RUNX2 stimulates transcription of LGALS3. Galectin-3 is present in myeloid progenitors and accumulates as those cells mature, contributing to adhesion, phagocyte behaviour and inflammatory responses. Because the same RUNX-CBFB module governs haematopoietic differentiation more broadly, misregulation here links lineage-specifying transcription to disease: galectin-3 is abundantly expressed in pituitary tumours and glioma, and RUNX1-CBFB disruption is a recurrent event in leukaemia. The pathway therefore connects a core developmental transcription complex to the maturation state and secreted lectin output of myeloid cells.

Regulation of RUNX2 expression and activity
originalRUNX2 is the master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation and bone formation, and this pathway covers how much of it is made and how active it is once made. The dosage matters clinically: loss of one functional copy causes cleidocranial dysplasia, with defective clavicles and delayed cranial suture closure, while sustained activity drives skeletal mineralization and chondrocyte maturation. Transcription is driven from two alternative promoters, stimulated by estrogen receptor alpha, the homeodomain factors DLX5 and DLX6, and TWIST1, and repressed by the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, MSX2 and NKX3-2; estrogen-related receptor alpha switches between activation and repression depending on whether PGC1-alpha or PGC1-beta is bound. Protein-level control adds heterodimerization with CBFB and cooperation with cofactors, cytoplasmic sequestration by unphosphorylated STAT1, and polyubiquitination by SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2-containing cullin-RING ligases followed by proteasomal degradation.

RUNX2 regulates osteoblast differentiation
originalOsteoblasts are made, not born, and RUNX2 acting with its partner CBFB is the transcriptional switch that commits mesenchymal progenitors to the bone-forming lineage and drives the genes that build mineralized matrix. Loss of this programme gives cleidocranial dysplasia and failed ossification, while its output — type I collagen, osteocalcin, and the cartilage-associated matrix protein UCMA — defines the skeleton's organic scaffold and its endocrine activity. RUNX2 cooperates with SP7 (Osterix) and SATB2 at target promoters, and is tuned by a dense layer of regulation: MAPK phosphorylation and SRC/YES1-dependent YAP1 binding respectively promote and restrain activity at the osteocalcin promoter, activated androgen receptor and HDAC recruitment block DNA binding, Notch effectors HEY1 and HES1 and the zinc finger ZNF521 repress it, and ubiquitin-dependent turnover limits its abundance. The pathway sits at the junction of skeletal development, hormonal signalling and matrix production.

RUNX2 regulates chondrocyte maturation
originalLong bones form by endochondral ossification, in which cartilage is progressively replaced by bone, and the step at which chondrocytes stop proliferating and become hypertrophic is controlled by RUNX2. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 drives transcription of Indian hedgehog and of markers of the hypertrophic state such as type X collagen, coupling chondrocyte maturation to the parathyroid hormone-related peptide feedback loop that sets growth plate length. GLI2 transduces the hedgehog signal, while HDAC4 restrains RUNX2 activity and so delays hypertrophy; loss of this brake causes premature ossification, and loss of RUNX2 function blocks maturation and limb elongation. The same factor governs osteoblast differentiation, making it the shared switch for skeletal patterning, and its haploinsufficiency underlies cleidocranial dysplasia.

Transcriptional regulation by the AP-2 (TFAP2) family of transcription factors (6)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
TFAP2 (AP-2) family regulates transcription of growth factors and their receptors
originalThe AP-2 transcription factors TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C control a battery of growth factor and receptor genes, and through them the proliferative behaviour of epithelial and placental cells. Their targets read as a map of breast cancer biology: the estrogen receptor ESR1, the receptor tyrosine kinases ERBB2, EGFR and KIT, and the ligand TGFA are all directly stimulated, while VEGFA transcription is repressed, linking these factors to angiogenic output as well as to mitogenic signalling. Cooperating partners modulate the response, with YY1 association raising the rate of ERBB2 transcription and the bromodomain coactivator ATAD2 contributing to target gene activation. In placenta the same factors drive both chorionic gonadotropin subunits, supporting trophoblast hormone production. Overexpression of TFAP2C in estrogen-receptor-positive breast and endometrial tumours makes this circuitry a determinant of hormone-responsive tumour phenotype.
The AP-2 factors TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C regulate growth factor and receptor genes that govern epithelial and placental proliferation. They activate ESR1, ERBB2, EGFR, KIT and TGFA but repress VEGFA, with YY1 enhancing ERBB2 transcription and ATAD2 aiding activation, and in placenta they drive both chorionic gonadotropin subunits. TFAP2C overexpression in estrogen-receptor-positive breast and endometrial tumours makes this circuitry a determinant of hormone-responsive tumour phenotype.Three paralogous dimeric transcription factors directly stimulate transcription of a nuclear hormone receptor, several receptor tyrosine kinase genes and a growth factor ligand, while repressing a secreted angiogenic factor. Partner proteins tune the response: association with a zinc-finger factor raises the transcription rate at one receptor gene, and a bromodomain coactivator contributes to target activation, so the same factors can act in opposite directions at different promoters.—
TFAP2A acts as a transcriptional repressor during retinoic acid induced cell differentiation
originalRetinoic acid pushes cells out of cycle and into differentiation, and part of how it does so is by shutting down genes that support growth. In this arm of the response, the transcription factor TFAP2A accumulates after retinoic acid treatment and acts as a repressor rather than an activator, partnering with the nucleolar chaperone nucleophosmin (NPM1) at target promoters. The repressed targets are growth- and proliferation-associated: the mitochondrial chaperonin HSPD1, the rRNA methyltransferase NOP2, and the cell cycle transcription factor MYBL2, the latter two used as proliferation markers. Repression is thought to work through NPM1-dependent recruitment of the histone deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, deacetylating promoter chromatin. The complex also occupies the NPM1 promoter itself, consistent with the fall in NPM1 levels after treatment, giving a self-limiting loop that links retinoid signalling to withdrawal from proliferation.

The complex also occupies the chaperone's own promoter, creating a self-limiting loop.—
Activation of the TFAP2 (AP-2) family of transcription factors
originalThe AP-2 family of transcription factors controls gene programmes in neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and placental development, and their loss produces recognizable malformation syndromes — branchio-oculo-facial syndrome from TFAP2A mutation, Char syndrome from TFAP2B — while TFAP2C is a driver of trophoblast and germ cell identity and is co-amplified with HER2 in breast cancer. Activation of these factors begins with dimerization through the helix-span-helix motif and binding of a basic region to palindromic GC-rich elements, though individual members prefer variant sites. Transactivation depends on partners: CITED family co-factors, CITED2 most avidly, dock on the helix-span-helix domain and bring in the acetyltransferase co-activators EP300 and CREBBP, and YEATS4 raises TFAP2B DNA binding, whereas WWOX sequesters AP-2 proteins and dampens their output. Mouse CITED2 loss recapitulates neural crest, cardiac and adrenal defects expected from failed AP-2 activation.

TFAP2 (AP-2) family regulates transcription of other transcription factors
originalAP-2 transcription factors act high in developmental hierarchies, and one of their outputs is the control of other transcription factors that pattern the embryo. Here TFAP2A and TFAP2C, as homodimers and possibly heterodimers, cooperate with the transcriptional coactivator CITED2 to stimulate expression of PITX2, a homeodomain factor that establishes left-right asymmetry and directs outflow tract and valve formation in the developing heart. Because PITX2 sits downstream, loss of this input reproduces laterality defects and congenital cardiac malformations seen when CITED2 or the AP-2 factors are disrupted; TFAP2A mutation in humans also causes branchio-oculo-facial syndrome, reflecting the family's wider role in neural crest and craniofacial development. The relationship illustrates how a coactivator-dependent dimeric factor converts positional signals into a downstream regulatory programme rather than directly into structural gene expression.

TFAP2 (AP-2) family regulates transcription of cell cycle factors
originalAP-2 transcription factors set how strongly a cell brakes its own division by controlling the p21 cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor gene. Because p21 restrains CDK-cyclin complexes at the G1/S transition and is a principal effector of growth arrest and senescence, the balance struck here determines whether cells proliferate or pause, and it is frequently skewed in tumours. Two closely related family members act in opposition at the same locus: TFAP2A binds the CDKN1A promoter and activates it, while TFAP2C represses it, recruiting MYC together with the histone demethylase KDM5B, which strips activating methylation from promoter histones to shut transcription down. The result is a switch in which the relative abundance of the two paralogues, rather than an external signal, dictates p21 levels, linking developmental transcription factor programmes to cell cycle entry and to differentiation-associated exit from the cycle.

Negative regulation of activity of TFAP2 (AP-2) family transcription factors
originalAP-2 family transcription factors drive programmes of neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and mammary development, and their output must be restrained as well as switched on; this pathway covers the mechanisms that damp AP-2 activity. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the AP-2 transactivation domain and block transcriptional activation, a brake whose loss in KCTD1 mutation causes scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects. SUMO conjugation through the E2 enzyme UBE2I attaches SUMO1 to TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, converting them into weaker activators and influencing epithelial differentiation and cancer stem cell traits in breast tumours. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C outside the nucleus, preventing it from reaching its targets. Together these controls set the dosage of AP-2 signalling, which matters because both excess and deficiency distort embryonic patterning and epithelial gene expression.

Batch 10 · under "negative regulation of immune system process"

negative regulation of leukocyte migration (6)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of macrophage chemotaxis
originalMacrophages are recruited to tissues by chemotactic gradients, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven, or inflammatory infiltrate persists and causes collateral tissue damage. Negative regulation of macrophage chemotaxis covers the signals that slow or stop that directed migration, restraining how many macrophages arrive at a site of injury or infection and how far they move once there. The genes involved act at several levels: secreted cytokine-like mediators and their receptor engagement, a complement component whose cleavage products are themselves chemoattractants and therefore a point of gradient control, a matrix metalloproteinase implicated in limiting macrophage recruitment, a signalling adaptor, and an immune-cell surface receptor of the SLAM family. An estrogen-synthesising enzyme links steroid hormone status to the strength of the response, one route by which sex hormones shape inflammation and the resolution phase of wound healing.
Macrophage chemotaxis toward injury or infection must be damped so inflammatory infiltrates do not persist and cause collateral tissue damage. Negative regulators limit how many macrophages arrive and how far they move, acting through secreted cytokine-like mediators, a complement component whose cleavage products are chemoattractants, a matrix metalloproteinase, a signalling adaptor and a SLAM-family receptor. An estrogen-synthesising enzyme links sex hormone status to inflammation and wound-healing resolution.Directed migration up a chemoattractant gradient is damped as well as driven. A steroid-synthesising enzyme links hormone levels to response strength.—
negative regulation of neutrophil migration
originalNeutrophils are the first cells recruited to infection or injury, and the braking mechanisms that damp their migration determine whether that response resolves or becomes tissue-destroying. Negative regulation of neutrophil migration covers signals that reduce the rate and extent of chemotactic movement out of the vasculature and through tissue, limiting collateral damage in conditions such as acute lung injury, ischemia-reperfusion and chronic inflammatory disease. The genes here act at several levels: SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to repel chemotaxing neutrophils and stabilise their cytoskeleton, C5AR2 serves as a non-canonical receptor for the complement fragment C5a that tempers signalling through the classical C5a receptor, TNFAIP6 modifies hyaluronan-rich matrix to interfere with adhesion and extravasation, and the microRNA MIR223 restrains myeloid activation transcriptionally. Together they represent the resolution side of innate immune recruitment rather than its initiation.

SLIT2 acts through Robo receptors to repel neutrophils and stabilise their cytoskeleton, C5AR2 tempers classical C5a receptor signalling, TNFAIP6 modifies hyaluronan matrix to hinder adhesion and extravasation, and MIR223 restrains myeloid activation.
