negative regulation of cellular extravasation
originalLeukocytes leave the bloodstream by adhering to endothelium and squeezing between cells, and this biology restrains that step, limiting how many cells extravasate into tissue. Damping cellular extravasation keeps inflammation proportionate: without such brakes, neutrophils and monocytes accumulate in tissue and drive collateral injury, as seen in sepsis, arthritis and atherosclerotic vessel walls. The restraint comes from several directions. Chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21, CCL25 and CCL28 pattern where cells are held or directed, and in some contexts their signalling retains cells rather than recruiting them. Prostaglandin E2 acting through the EP4 receptor raises cyclic AMP in leukocytes and endothelium to suppress adhesion, MIR146A dampens NF-κB-driven inflammatory output, and phospholipase C beta and a cytokine receptor subunit tune the downstream signalling that converts chemotactic cues into firm arrest and diapedesis.
Restraining leukocyte extravasation keeps inflammation proportionate, preventing neutrophil and monocyte accumulation that damages tissue in sepsis, arthritis and atherosclerosis. Chemokines CXCL12, CCL21, CCL25 and CCL28 pattern cell positioning and can retain cells, prostaglandin E2 acting through EP4 raises cAMP to suppress adhesion, and MIR146A dampens NF-kB output. Phospholipase C beta and a cytokine receptor subunit tune signalling that converts chemotactic cues into firm arrest and diapedesis.Adhesion to endothelium and passage between endothelial cells is actively restrained. Chemokines pattern where migrating cells are held rather than recruited, so the same receptor signalling can retain instead of attract. A prostaglandin acting through one of its G-protein-coupled receptors raises cyclic AMP to suppress adhesion, a microRNA dampens NF-kappaB-driven transcription, and a phospholipase C isoform and a cytokine receptor subunit tune the conversion of chemotactic cues into firm arrest.—
negative regulation of granulocyte chemotaxis
originalGranulocytes are recruited to infected or damaged tissue by chemotactic gradients, and this recruitment must be braked so that neutrophil and eosinophil influx resolves rather than destroying the tissue it is meant to protect. The processes grouped here dampen granulocyte chemotaxis, and their loss favours persistent neutrophilic inflammation of the kind seen in sepsis, arthritis and chronic lung disease. The mechanisms are varied: a decoy-like receptor for complement-derived anaphylatoxins tempers signalling through the classic C5a receptor; a cell-surface peptidase trims chemokines and neuropeptides, altering their potency; a secreted guidance cue better known from axon pathfinding repels migrating leukocytes; a hyaluronan-binding inflammatory protein modifies the matrix and limits transmigration; and a myeloid microRNA restrains the granulocyte differentiation and activation programme itself. Together they place inflammation resolution alongside chemokine signalling and directed cell migration.
Granulocyte chemotaxis must be braked so neutrophil and eosinophil influx resolves rather than destroying tissue, since failure favours persistent neutrophilic inflammation in sepsis, arthritis and chronic lung disease. Mechanisms include a decoy-like anaphylatoxin receptor tempering C5a receptor signalling, a surface peptidase trimming chemokines and neuropeptides, a secreted axon guidance cue repelling leukocytes, a hyaluronan-binding protein limiting transmigration, and a myeloid microRNA restraining differentiation and activation.Chemotactic recruitment along gradients is damped by several unrelated mechanisms: a decoy-like receptor for complement-derived anaphylatoxins tempers signalling through the classical receptor, a cell-surface peptidase trims chemokines and neuropeptides and alters their potency, a secreted guidance cue repels migrating cells, a hyaluronan-binding protein modifies matrix and limits transmigration, and a microRNA restrains the differentiation and activation programme itself.—
negative regulation of T cell migration
originalT cells only reach the right tissue if their motility is switched off at the right moment, and this is the braking side of that decision — processes that reduce the rate or extent of T cell migration. Restraining movement matters for retaining activated cells in lymph nodes, limiting infiltration of inflamed or immunoprivileged tissue, and preventing autoimmune damage; the same brakes, exploited by tumours, keep effector cells out of the tumour bed. CD69 is an early activation marker whose surface expression blocks egress from lymphoid tissue, while CD200 engaging its receptor CD200R1 delivers an inhibitory signal from tissue cells to myeloid and lymphoid cells. RIPOR2 and LRCH1 act inside the cell on Rho-family GTPase signalling to dampen chemokine-driven adhesion and polarisation, linking receptor input to cytoskeletal output.
Braking T cell migration retains activated cells in lymph nodes, limits infiltration of inflamed or immunoprivileged tissue and prevents autoimmune damage, though tumours exploit it to exclude effector cells. CD69, an early activation marker, blocks egress from lymphoid tissue, CD200 engaging CD200R1 delivers inhibitory signals to myeloid and lymphoid cells, and RIPOR2 and LRCH1 act on Rho-family GTPase signalling to dampen chemokine-driven adhesion and polarisation.Motility is reduced by signals acting at the surface and inside the cell. One early activation glycoprotein appears at the membrane and blocks egress by interfering with the receptor that senses a lipid gradient, while a surface ligand engaging its inhibitory receptor delivers a negative signal between neighbouring cells. Intracellularly, two Rho-family effectors dampen GTPase signalling, weakening chemokine-driven adhesion and polarisation so receptor input no longer produces movement.—
negative regulation of monocyte chemotaxis
originalMonocytes are recruited out of the bloodstream toward chemokine gradients at sites of injury and infection, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven; damping it is what negative regulation of monocyte chemotaxis does. Restraining monocyte influx limits the tissue damage of prolonged inflammation and shapes how atherosclerotic lesions, fibrotic scars and healing wounds develop, since each depends on how many monocyte-derived macrophages arrive. The activities represented here work at different levels: secreted matricellular and BMP-antagonist proteins such as CCN3, NBL1 and GREM1 act in the extracellular milieu, the repulsive guidance cue SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to block directed migration of myeloid cells, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases to cut short inflammatory signalling, and the immune receptor SLAMF8 tempers macrophage responses. Together they set a brake on innate immune cell trafficking rather than on chemokine production alone.
Negative regulation of monocyte chemotaxis damps recruitment from blood toward chemokine gradients, limiting prolonged inflammatory damage and shaping atherosclerotic lesions, fibrotic scars and wound healing through the number of monocyte-derived macrophages arriving. Secreted CCN3, NBL1 and GREM1 act extracellularly, SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to block directed myeloid migration, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases to curtail inflammatory signalling, and SLAMF8 tempers macrophage responses.Directed migration along chemokine gradients is damped by activities working at different levels. Secreted matricellular proteins and BMP antagonists act in the extracellular milieu; a repulsive guidance ligand signals through Robo receptors to block directed movement; a dual-specificity phosphatase dephosphorylates MAP kinases and so cuts short inflammatory signalling; and a surface immunoreceptor tempers activating responses. The brake is applied to the migratory response itself rather than to chemokine production.—

negative regulation of hemopoiesis (8)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of granulocyte differentiation
originalGranulocyte production from myeloid progenitors must be held in check as well as driven, and this set covers the braking side: processes that slow or block commitment of progenitors to the neutrophil and eosinophil lineages. Restraint matters because unchecked granulopoiesis distorts the balance between granulocytes, monocytes and dendritic cells, and loss of these controls contributes to myeloid leukaemias and to inflammatory tissue damage. The transcriptional arm includes RUNX1 and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose fusion in acute promyelocytic leukaemia freezes cells at the promyelocyte stage, alongside PRDM16 and ZBTB46, the latter marking classical dendritic cells rather than granulocytes. Signalling and degradation components contribute too: the inositol phosphatase INPP5D dampens phosphoinositide-dependent growth factor responses, TRIB1 directs turnover of myeloid transcription factors, and CUL4A supplies ubiquitin ligase activity. Together they set lineage output and the pace of emergency granulopoiesis.
Granulopoiesis must be braked as well as driven, since unchecked neutrophil and eosinophil production distorts myeloid balance and contributes to leukaemia and inflammatory damage. Transcriptional restraint involves RUNX1, RARA, whose fusion in acute promyelocytic leukaemia arrests promyelocytes, PRDM16 and the dendritic cell factor ZBTB46. INPP5D dampens growth factor phosphoinositide signalling, TRIB1 drives turnover of myeloid transcription factors and CUL4A provides ubiquitin ligase activity, together setting lineage output and emergency granulopoiesis.Commitment along one differentiation programme is restrained rather than promoted here. The transcriptional arm includes a Runt-domain factor, a retinoic acid receptor and two zinc-finger factors that impose alternative programmes. Signalling and degradation components add further restraint: an inositol polyphosphate phosphatase dampens phosphoinositide-dependent growth factor responses, a pseudokinase directs turnover of lineage transcription factors, and a cullin supplies ubiquitin ligase activity, together setting the pace of lineage output.—
negative regulation of immature T cell proliferation in thymus
originalThymocyte expansion must be curbed as well as driven, and this pathway covers the signals that dampen proliferation of immature T cells in the thymus. Restraining the progenitor pool sets the size and timing of successive developmental stages, allowing selection to operate on a controlled number of cells; loss of such brakes contributes to thymocyte hyperplasia and lymphoid malignancy. The genes involved span secreted morphogens and cell-intrinsic cell cycle control: bone morphogenetic protein and hedgehog ligands produced by thymic stroma act on developing thymocytes to limit their expansion, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor encoded at the INK4A locus enforces cell cycle arrest, and a transmembrane regulator of Wnt responsiveness tempers proliferative signalling. Together they illustrate how niche-derived cues and intracellular checkpoints converge to balance proliferation against differentiation during T cell development.
Proliferation of immature thymocytes must be curbed so that developmental stages proceed with controlled cell numbers for selection, and loss of these brakes contributes to thymic hyperplasia and lymphoid malignancy. Stromal bone morphogenetic protein and hedgehog ligands limit thymocyte expansion, an INK4A-locus CDK inhibitor enforces arrest, and a transmembrane Wnt regulator tempers proliferative signals. Niche cues and intracellular checkpoints thus balance proliferation and differentiation during T cell development.Proliferation at an early developmental stage is damped by a combination of secreted morphogens and intrinsic cycle control. Bone morphogenetic protein and hedgehog family ligands released by neighbouring cells act on the dividing precursors to limit expansion, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor enforces cycle arrest, and a transmembrane regulator of Wnt responsiveness tempers proliferative signalling. Niche-derived cues and intracellular checkpoints therefore converge to balance proliferation against differentiation.—
negative regulation of osteoclast development
originalBone mass is maintained by holding osteoclast formation in check, and this braking arm of osteoclast development limits how many bone-resorbing multinucleated cells arise from myeloid precursors. When the restraint fails, resorption outpaces formation and bone is lost, as in osteoporosis, inflammatory erosion and other high-turnover skeletal disease; excessive restraint instead gives dense, poorly remodelled bone. The genes involved act at several levels: a claudin tight-junction protein whose loss in the stomach alters systemic signals to bone, an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that sequesters TGF-beta family ligands and so tunes precursor differentiation, an F-box ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor that targets osteoclastogenic transcription factors for degradation, an inhibitory leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor that dampens ITAM-driven costimulation, and lactoferrin, an iron-binding secreted protein that suppresses precursor commitment while favouring osteoblasts. Together they place skeletal remodelling under immune, endocrine and matrix control.
Restraining osteoclast formation from myeloid precursors preserves bone mass; when it fails, resorption exceeds formation in osteoporosis and inflammatory erosion, while excess restraint gives dense, poorly remodelled bone. Contributors include a claudin whose gastric loss alters systemic signals to bone, a matrix glycoprotein sequestering TGF-beta family ligands, an F-box substrate receptor degrading osteoclastogenic factors, an inhibitory leukocyte receptor dampening ITAM costimulation, and lactoferrin, which favours osteoblasts.Entry into this differentiation and fusion programme is held in check at several levels: a tight-junction claudin that alters systemic signalling, a secreted matrix glycoprotein that sequesters TGF-beta family ligands and so tunes how much differentiation signal precursors receive, an F-box substrate receptor that targets the lineage-determining transcription factors for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, an inhibitory immunoglobulin-like receptor that dampens ITAM-driven costimulation, and an iron-binding secreted protein that suppresses commitment.—
negative regulation of monocyte differentiation
originalMyeloid progenitors must be held back from becoming monocytes if the marrow is to retain proliferating precursors and generate other lineages, and this restraint on monocyte differentiation is how that balance is kept. It matters because loss of the brake shifts output toward monocytes and macrophages, while its inappropriate persistence blocks maturation, a pattern seen in myeloid leukaemias where differentiation arrest accompanies continued proliferation. The genes involved act at several levels: cell cycle and growth regulators such as CDK6 and MYC keep progenitors cycling rather than maturing, a homeobox factor and the dendritic-cell-restricted factor ZBTB46 impose alternative transcriptional programmes, the inositol phosphatase INPP5D dampens signalling downstream of growth factor and immune receptors, and a microRNA tunes the same decision post-transcriptionally. The result is a checkpoint on lineage commitment within haematopoiesis and innate immune cell supply.
Holding myeloid progenitors back from monocyte differentiation preserves proliferating precursors and other lineages; losing the brake shifts output toward monocytes and macrophages, while its persistence blocks maturation as in myeloid leukaemias. CDK6 and MYC keep progenitors cycling rather than maturing, a homeobox factor and the dendritic cell factor ZBTB46 impose alternative programmes, INPP5D dampens growth factor and immune receptor signalling, and a microRNA tunes the decision post-transcriptionally.Commitment to this differentiation programme is actively opposed, keeping precursors proliferating and available for alternative fates. A cyclin-dependent kinase and a helix-loop-helix transcription factor sustain cycling rather than maturation, a homeobox factor and a zinc-finger factor impose alternative transcriptional programmes, an inositol polyphosphate phosphatase dampens signalling downstream of growth factor and immune receptors, and a microRNA tunes the same decision post-transcriptionally.—
negative regulation of B cell differentiation
originalB cell output has to be capped, and this is the braking side of that decision: processes that slow or block progenitors from committing to and maturing along the B lineage. Restraint matters because unchecked B cell production skews the marrow toward lymphoid output at the expense of other lineages and enlarges the pool of cells that must later be screened for self-reactivity. The genes act mostly by opposing the transcriptional and signalling inputs that drive commitment — ID2 sequesters E-protein transcription factors such as E2A that would otherwise turn on the B cell programme, the activin and inhibin subunits provide TGF-beta family signals that suppress lymphoid differentiation, SFRP1 dampens Wnt signalling in the marrow niche, and HMGB3 keeps progenitors in a less committed state. Complement receptor CR1 links the pathway to immune complex feedback on B cells.
Restraining B lineage commitment and maturation prevents marrow output skewing toward lymphoid cells and enlarges less the pool needing screening for self-reactivity. ID2 sequesters E-proteins such as E2A that would activate the B cell programme, activin and inhibin subunits supply TGF-beta family signals suppressing lymphoid differentiation, SFRP1 dampens Wnt signalling in the niche, and HMGB3 keeps progenitors uncommitted, while complement receptor CR1 links immune complex feedback to B cells.Commitment along this lineage programme is opposed rather than driven. A helix-loop-helix inhibitor sequesters E-protein transcription factors that would otherwise activate the programme, activin and inhibin subunits provide TGF-beta family signals that suppress differentiation, a secreted frizzled-related protein dampens Wnt signalling in the surrounding niche, and an HMG-box protein holds precursors in a less committed state. A complement receptor links the pathway to immune complex feedback.—
negative regulation of regulatory T cell differentiation
originalRegulatory T cells restrain immune responses, so the pathways that hold back their differentiation set how much suppression a response is allowed to accumulate. Damping Treg output favours effector T cell expansion and is needed for effective responses to pathogens and tumours, while excessive suppression of Treg development tips the balance toward autoimmunity and tissue damage. Several routes converge here: the OX40 ligand encoded by TNFSF4 signals to conventional T cells and opposes the induced Treg programme, checkpoint receptors such as CTLA4 and LAG3 and the transcription factor IRF1 shape the cytokine and costimulatory environment in which FOXP3 is or is not induced, the growth factor midkine skews differentiation away from the regulatory fate, and microRNAs including miR-21 tune the same decision. Proteasome subunits, including the immunoproteasome catalytic subunits, contribute by degrading lineage-determining factors and controlling antigen presentation.
Restraining regulatory T cell differentiation limits accumulated suppression, favouring effector expansion against pathogens and tumours, while excessive restraint risks autoimmunity. TNFSF4 (OX40 ligand) signals to conventional T cells and opposes the induced Treg programme, CTLA4, LAG3 and IRF1 shape the environment in which FOXP3 is induced, midkine skews differentiation away from the regulatory fate, and microRNAs such as miR-21 tune it; proteasome subunits degrade lineage factors and affect antigen presentation.Differentiation into the suppressive programme is opposed by several converging routes. A TNF-family ligand signals to responder cells and counteracts induction of the programme, checkpoint receptors and an interferon regulatory factor shape the cytokine and costimulatory environment in which the lineage-specifying forkhead factor is or is not induced, a secreted growth factor skews differentiation toward alternative fates, and microRNAs tune the same decision; proteasomal degradation of lineage factors contributes.—
negative regulation of dendritic cell differentiation
originalDendritic cells are the antigen-presenting cells that prime naive T cells, and restraining their differentiation from myeloid progenitors sets how much of that priming capacity a tissue has. Holding this brake in place favours tolerance: fewer, less mature dendritic cells mean weaker T cell activation against self and against transplanted or fetal tissue, while loss of restraint contributes to autoimmunity and unwanted inflammation. The genes involved act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors bearing ITIM motifs, including the IgG receptor FCGR2B, the C-type lectin CLEC12A and the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor LILRB1, recruit phosphatases that dampen activating signals; HLA-G is a non-classical MHC class I ligand for such receptors and a mediator of immune privilege. The related membrane proteins TMEM176A and TMEM176B act intracellularly to hold cells in an immature state, and ZBTB46 is a transcription factor marking the classical dendritic cell lineage while limiting its activation.
Restraining dendritic cell differentiation from myeloid progenitors limits T cell priming capacity and favours tolerance to self, transplanted and fetal tissue, while losing restraint contributes to autoimmunity. ITIM-bearing inhibitory receptors FCGR2B, CLEC12A and LILRB1 recruit phosphatases dampening activating signals, and HLA-G is a non-classical ligand mediating immune privilege. TMEM176A and TMEM176B act intracellularly to maintain immaturity, and ZBTB46 marks classical dendritic cells while limiting their activation.Progression along this differentiation programme is held back by brakes at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors bearing tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs, including an immunoglobulin G receptor, a C-type lectin and a leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor, recruit phosphatases that dampen activating signals, and a non-classical MHC class I molecule serves as ligand for such receptors. Two related membrane proteins act intracellularly to hold cells immature, and a zinc-finger transcription factor limits activation.—
negative regulation of macrophage differentiation
originalMonocytes and myeloid progenitors do not become macrophages by default; this is the restraining side of that decision, holding back macrophage differentiation so that progenitors remain available or commit to other fates. Its output matters for the balance of myeloid populations in tissue: too little restraint and inflammatory macrophage numbers expand, which contributes to atherosclerotic plaque growth and adipose tissue inflammation. The mechanisms represented are heterogeneous. Transcriptional control comes from GATA2, which sustains earlier progenitor programmes, and from ZBTB46, which marks and enforces the conventional dendritic cell alternative rather than the macrophage one. Secreted inhibin and activin subunits act on progenitors from outside, and adipocyte-derived adiponectin dampens macrophage development and activation. Post-transcriptional and signalling brakes include the RNA-binding protein QKI and the phosphatase PTPN2, which limits cytokine receptor signalling driving myeloid maturation.
Holding back macrophage differentiation keeps progenitors available or directs them to other fates, and too little restraint expands inflammatory macrophages, contributing to atherosclerotic plaque growth and adipose inflammation. GATA2 sustains earlier progenitor programmes and ZBTB46 enforces the conventional dendritic cell alternative; secreted inhibin and activin subunits and adipocyte-derived adiponectin act from outside; and the RNA-binding protein QKI and the phosphatase PTPN2 limit cytokine receptor signalling driving maturation.Commitment to this differentiation programme is actively opposed. Transcriptional restraint comes from a zinc-finger factor that sustains earlier progenitor programmes and from another that enforces an alternative lineage programme. Secreted inhibin and activin subunits and a secreted adipokine act on precursors from outside to dampen differentiation, while an RNA-binding protein and a tyrosine phosphatase that limits cytokine receptor signalling provide post-transcriptional and signalling-level brakes.—

negative regulation of immune effector process (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of mast cell degranulation
originalMast cells release histamine, proteases and other preformed mediators within seconds of activation, so restraining that release sets the threshold for allergic and anaphylactic reactions. Negative regulation of mast cell degranulation keeps resting mast cells quiescent and limits mediator output once IgE crosslinks the high-affinity IgE receptor, protecting tissues from unnecessary bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and itch; loss of this brake underlies atopic disease and mast cell hyperreactivity. The inhibitory arm works partly through surface immunoreceptors carrying tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs, such as CD300A, which counter activating signals at the membrane, and partly through lectin-mediated engagement of mast cell surface receptors by galectin-9. Intracellularly, RABGEF1 restrains signalling downstream of receptor engagement, and its absence produces spontaneous skin inflammation in mice. The pathway sits within innate immune tolerance and the control of type I hypersensitivity rather than in mediator synthesis itself.
Negative regulation of mast cell degranulation keeps resting cells quiescent and limits release of histamine and proteases after IgE crosslinking, setting the threshold for allergy and anaphylaxis and preventing bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and itch. Inhibitory immunoreceptors such as CD300A counter activating signals, galectin-9 engages surface receptors, and intracellular RABGEF1 restrains downstream signalling, its absence causing spontaneous skin inflammation in mice. Failure contributes to atopic disease and mast cell hyperreactivity.Release of preformed granule contents triggered by antigen crosslinking of a high-affinity immunoglobulin receptor is actively restrained. Part of the brake is applied at the membrane by surface immunoreceptors bearing tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs, which recruit phosphatases to counter activating signals, and by lectin engagement of surface glycoproteins. Intracellularly, a Rab guanine nucleotide exchange factor restrains signalling downstream of receptor engagement, raising the threshold for exocytosis.—
negative regulation of immunoglobulin production
originalAntibody output has to be capped as well as switched on, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that stop or reduce immunoglobulin production by B cells. Without such restraint, plasma cell differentiation and class switching run unchecked, contributing to hypergammaglobulinaemia, autoantibody formation and allergic IgE responses. The genes here act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CD22 and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B raise the threshold for B cell activation and deliver negative signals from immune complexes, while complement receptor CR1 tunes complement-dependent stimulation. BCL6 holds germinal centre B cells in a proliferative, differentiation-blocked state, opposing terminal plasma cell commitment. FOXP3 marks regulatory T cells that suppress the helper signals B cells require, and NDFIP1 promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation of lymphocyte responses. Cytokine-side components, including an IL-33 and decoy IL-13 receptor pairing, link tissue signals to restraint of type 2 antibody responses.
Immunoglobulin production by B cells must be capped, or plasma cell differentiation and class switching cause hypergammaglobulinaemia, autoantibodies and allergic IgE. Inhibitory receptors CD22 and FCGR2B raise activation thresholds, CR1 tunes complement-dependent stimulation, BCL6 holds germinal centre B cells undifferentiated, FOXP3 marks regulatory T cells suppressing helper signals, and NDFIP1 promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation; IL-33 and decoy IL-13 receptor components link tissue signals to restraint of type 2 responses.Immunoglobulin output is capped by brakes at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors, including a sialic-acid-binding lectin and a low-affinity immunoglobulin G receptor, recruit phosphatases to raise the activation threshold and deliver negative signals from immune complexes, while a complement receptor tunes complement-dependent stimulation. A BTB-domain repressor holds cells in a proliferative, differentiation-blocked state, an adaptor promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation of responses, and cytokine receptor pairings add further restraint.—
negative regulation of macrophage cytokine production
originalMacrophages amplify inflammation by secreting cytokines, and this braking arm keeps that output proportionate, limiting collateral tissue damage and allowing resolution once a threat is cleared. Loss of such restraint underlies septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and fibrosis, while excessive restraint leaves macrophages tolerant and poorly responsive to infection. The negative regulation of macrophage cytokine production operates at two levels represented here: an intracellular checkpoint on Toll-like receptor signalling, where IRAK3 acts as a catalytically inactive decoy kinase that blocks downstream NF-κB activation, and CUEDC2 dampens inflammatory transcriptional responses; and secreted control, where the three TGF-beta ligands act on macrophages in an autocrine and paracrine fashion to suppress pro-inflammatory gene expression and push cells toward a reparative, immunosuppressive state. Together these mechanisms set the threshold and duration of innate immune activation.
Negative regulation of macrophage cytokine production keeps inflammation proportionate and allows resolution; its loss underlies septic shock, chronic inflammation and fibrosis, while excess leaves macrophages tolerant. Intracellularly IRAK3 acts as a catalytically inactive decoy kinase blocking NF-kB activation downstream of Toll-like receptors and CUEDC2 dampens inflammatory transcription; extracellularly the three TGF-beta ligands act in autocrine and paracrine fashion to suppress pro-inflammatory genes and promote a reparative state.Cytokine output is damped at two levels. Intracellularly, a catalytically inactive decoy kinase occupies the Toll-like receptor signalling complex and blocks downstream NF-kappaB activation, and a CUE-domain protein dampens inflammatory transcription. Extracellularly, three TGF-beta ligands act through their receptors in autocrine and paracrine fashion to suppress pro-inflammatory gene expression and shift the transcriptional programme toward a reparative, suppressive one, setting the threshold and duration of activation.—

negative regulation of cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signaling pathway (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of cGAS/STING signaling pathway
originalCytosolic DNA sensing by cGAS and its adaptor STING triggers type I interferon and inflammatory gene expression, and this pathway describes the brakes that keep that response proportionate and self-limiting. Restraint matters because unchecked activation by the cell's own DNA drives interferonopathies, lupus-like autoimmunity and sterile inflammation, while excessive signalling during infection is itself damaging. The brakes act at every step: nucleases such as TREX1 degrade cytosolic DNA before it is sensed, cGAS itself is held in check by kinase- and acyltransferase-mediated modification and by nuclear tethering to chromatin via BANF1, the second messenger cGAMP is hydrolysed extracellularly, and adaptor turnover through autophagy factors and ubiquitin-ligase adaptors such as SPSB3 limits signalling duration. Phosphatase activity and DNA-damage-response proteins including PARP1 and PRKDC further couple genome surveillance to dampened interferon output.
Brakes on cGAS-STING signalling keep cytosolic DNA-triggered type I interferon and inflammatory responses proportionate, preventing interferonopathies, lupus-like autoimmunity and damaging inflammation. TREX1 degrades cytosolic DNA, cGAS is inhibited by kinase and acyltransferase modifications and by BANF1-mediated chromatin tethering, extracellular cGAMP is hydrolysed, and autophagy factors and adaptors such as SPSB3 limit adaptor lifespan. Phosphatases and DNA-damage proteins PARP1 and PRKDC further connect genome surveillance to reduced interferon output.Cytosolic double-stranded DNA sensing by a nucleotidyltransferase and its endoplasmic reticulum adaptor is braked at every step. Exonucleases degrade cytosolic DNA before it is sensed, the sensor is held in check by phosphorylation, acylation and tethering to chromatin, the cyclic dinucleotide second messenger is hydrolysed extracellularly, and adaptor turnover through autophagy and ubiquitin-ligase adaptors limits signalling duration. Phosphatase activity and damage-response proteins add further restraint.—
negative regulation of toll-like receptor 9 signaling pathway
originalToll-like receptor 9 detects unmethylated CpG DNA inside endosomes and drives type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine output, particularly from plasmacytoid dendritic cells; braking that response keeps recognition of self DNA from tipping into autoimmunity. Negative regulation of TLR9 signalling gathers the mechanisms that limit how strongly and how long the receptor fires, and its loss is associated with interferon-driven disease such as lupus. The genes here act at distinct points: a plasmacytoid dendritic cell surface immunoreceptor delivers an inhibitory signal that dampens interferon production, a small GTPase controls endosomal and lysosomal trafficking of the receptor and so limits its residence in the signalling compartment, and a receptor phosphatase and a lysosomal thioesterase further restrain downstream activation. Together they set the threshold for innate sensing of DNA and enforce tolerance to host nucleic acids.
TLR9 senses endosomal unmethylated CpG DNA and drives type I interferon and cytokine production, especially from plasmacytoid dendritic cells, so its signalling must be restrained to avoid autoimmunity such as lupus. A plasmacytoid dendritic cell inhibitory receptor dampens interferon output, a small GTPase limits receptor residence in signalling endosomes, and a receptor phosphatase and lysosomal thioesterase restrain downstream activation, together setting the threshold for DNA sensing and self-tolerance.Endosomal recognition of unmethylated CpG DNA by a Toll-like receptor, and the interferon and cytokine transcription it drives, are limited at distinct points. A surface immunoreceptor delivers an inhibitory signal that dampens interferon output, a small GTPase controls endosomal and lysosomal trafficking of the receptor and so limits its residence in the signalling compartment, and a receptor phosphatase and a lysosomal thioesterase further restrain downstream activation.—
negative regulation of RIG-I signaling pathway
originalDetection of cytoplasmic viral RNA by RIG-I triggers interferon production, and this braking machinery keeps that alarm proportionate and self-limiting, preventing sustained type I interferon output and the autoinflammatory or interferonopathy-like damage that follows unchecked sensing. The regulators act at several points: a RIG-I-like helicase relative, LGP2 (DHX58), competes with and modulates recognition of duplex RNA; mitochondrial proteins such as NLRX1 and C1QBP restrain the adaptor MAVS at the outer membrane; RNF125 ubiquitinates RIG-I to drive its degradation; and the NPLOC4-UFD1 partners of the p97 segregase feed sensor and adaptor components into proteasomal turnover. Together they set the threshold and duration of antiviral innate signalling, so that interferon-stimulated gene expression resolves once infection is cleared. Loss of this negative control tips the balance toward chronic inflammation, while viruses exploit the same nodes to blunt host defence.
Brakes on RIG-I sensing of cytoplasmic viral RNA keep interferon production proportionate and self-limiting, preventing sustained output and autoinflammatory damage. LGP2 (DHX58) competes with and modulates duplex RNA recognition, NLRX1 and C1QBP restrain MAVS at the mitochondrial membrane, RNF125 ubiquitinates RIG-I for degradation, and NPLOC4-UFD1 with the p97 segregase feeds components to the proteasome. Loss favours chronic inflammation, and viruses exploit the same nodes.Recognition of cytoplasmic double-stranded RNA by a DExD/H-box helicase sensor is braked at several points. A related helicase lacking the signalling domain competes with and modulates duplex RNA recognition; mitochondrial proteins restrain the outer-membrane adaptor; a RING-domain ligase ubiquitinates the sensor to drive its degradation; and cofactors of an AAA-ATPase segregase feed sensor and adaptor components into proteasomal turnover, setting the threshold and duration of signalling.—
negative regulation of NLRP3 inflammasome complex assembly
originalThe NLRP3 inflammasome converts danger signals into caspase-1 activation, IL-1β and IL-18 release, and pyroptotic death, so cells need brakes on its assembly to avoid self-damaging inflammation. Restraining that assembly is what keeps sterile injury, crystal deposition and infection from tipping into chronic inflammatory disease; loss of these brakes underlies periodic fever syndromes and contributes to gout, atherosclerosis and neuroinflammation. The restraint works at several levels: ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM31 and FBXL2 target NLRP3 for degradation, autophagy machinery including IRGM and LAMP2-dependent chaperone-mediated autophagy clears the sensor, pyrin-domain-only proteins PYDC1 and PYDC2 act as decoys that block adaptor recruitment, and depalmitoylases together with kinases and SIRT2 tune NLRP3 through reversible lipid and post-translational modification. Other NLR and pyrin-domain proteins, and the microglial receptor TREM2, provide additional inhibitory input, setting the threshold for innate immune activation.
Brakes on NLRP3 inflammasome assembly prevent caspase-1 activation, IL-1beta and IL-18 release and pyroptosis from tipping into chronic inflammation; their loss underlies periodic fever syndromes and contributes to gout, atherosclerosis and neuroinflammation. TRIM31 and FBXL2 ubiquitinate NLRP3 for degradation, IRGM and LAMP2-dependent autophagy clear it, PYDC1 and PYDC2 act as pyrin-domain decoys, and depalmitoylases, kinases and SIRT2 tune it; other NLRs and TREM2 add inhibitory input.Assembly of this sensor-adaptor-caspase platform is restrained at several levels. Ubiquitin ligases target the sensor for degradation, autophagy machinery including chaperone-mediated autophagy clears it, pyrin-domain-only proteins act as decoys that block adaptor recruitment, and depalmitoylases, kinases and an NAD-dependent deacetylase tune the sensor through reversible lipid and other post-translational modification. Related NLR and pyrin-domain proteins and an inhibitory surface receptor add further input.—

negative regulation of immune response (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of acute inflammatory response to antigenic stimulus
originalAcute inflammation triggered by antigen must be actively damped, or immune complexes and mast cell activation drive tissue injury, anaphylaxis and autoantibody-driven disease; the genes here restrain that response rather than initiate it. The clearest example is the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, the only inhibitory Fc gamma receptor, which carries an inhibitory signalling motif and raises the threshold for B cell, mast cell and phagocyte activation by immune complexes; loss of its function predisposes to systemic autoimmunity. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors links neural output to immune tone, illustrating neuroimmune brake on local inflammatory responses, while sialophorin (SPN, CD43) shapes leukocyte adhesion and contact-dependent activation. Other members contribute cytokine receptor signalling and endoplasmic reticulum stress handling. Collectively this is the negative arm of hypersensitivity control, setting how strongly and how long an antigen-provoked inflammatory episode proceeds.
Antigen-triggered acute inflammation must be actively damped to prevent immune complex injury, anaphylaxis and autoimmunity. The inhibitory Fc gamma receptor FCGR2B raises the activation threshold of B cells, mast cells and phagocytes, and its loss predisposes to systemic autoimmunity. negative regulation of response to type II interferon
originalInterferon-gamma drives macrophage activation, antigen presentation and Th1 immunity, and this braking arm keeps that response proportionate so that inflammation resolves rather than damaging tissue. Damping the cellular reaction to type II interferon limits classical macrophage polarisation and helps preserve an alternative, tissue-repair phenotype; when the brake fails, chronic IFN-gamma signalling contributes to autoimmunity and inflammatory pathology, while excessive braking favours tumour immune evasion and poor control of intracellular pathogens. The mechanisms are varied: a phosphatase dephosphorylates JAK kinases and STAT1 to terminate receptor signalling, nuclear receptors including the two liver X receptors and the adipogenic and anti-inflammatory PPARG transcriptionally oppose interferon-induced gene programmes, an ADP-ribosyltransferase of the macrodomain family biases signalling toward Th2/STAT6 output, and arginase 1 consumes arginine that inducible nitric oxide synthase would otherwise use for antimicrobial killing.

negative regulation of T-helper 1 type immune response
originalTh1 responses drive interferon-gamma-dependent defence against intracellular pathogens, but unchecked they cause tissue damage and autoimmunity, so they must be actively restrained; this pathway covers the brakes applied to T-helper 1 type immunity. Several mechanisms appear together. IL-27, formed from EBI3 with its partner chain and signalling through IL27RA with the shared IL6ST subunit, limits Th1 and Th17 differentiation and promotes regulatory programmes. The checkpoint receptor HAVCR2 (TIM-3) engaged by galectin-9 (LGALS9) triggers exhaustion or death of interferon-gamma-producing effector T cells. A soluble binding protein sequesters IL-18, neutralising a cytokine that would otherwise amplify interferon-gamma output, while IL-33 acting through IL1RL1 skews responses toward type 2 immunity. Loss of such restraint underlies chronic inflammatory disease, whereas its excess in tumours blunts protective antitumour T cell activity.

negative regulation of type I interferon-mediated signaling pathway
originalType I interferon signalling must be shut off once a viral threat is cleared, and this braking programme is what limits it. Sustained interferon output damages tissue and drives autoinflammatory disease: loss of the cytosolic exonuclease TREX1 or the dNTP triphosphohydrolase SAMHD1 leaves self nucleic acids to trigger chronic interferon production, as in Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, while ADAR-mediated RNA editing marks endogenous double-stranded RNA as self so it is not read as viral. Downstream, USP18 removes ISG15 conjugates and independently blocks JAK-STAT engagement at the receptor, and the phosphatase PTPN2 dephosphorylates JAK-STAT components. Additional restraint comes from m6A-dependent decay of interferon transcripts through METTL3 and the YTHDF readers, deadenylation by CNOT7, and translational repression via the EIF4E2-GIGYF2 module. Together these set the amplitude and duration of antiviral gene expression and preserve tolerance to self nucleic acids.

cellular response to chemical stress (11)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
cellular response to salt stress
originalCells exposed to changing extracellular salt must defend their volume and internal ion balance or lose enzyme function and membrane integrity; the cellular response to salt stress is the set of adjustments that follow such a change. It matters most in tissues that routinely face osmotic swings, above all the kidney medulla, where interstitial sodium and urea reach concentrations that would kill most cells. The genes here span the main arms of that defence: aldose reductase generates sorbitol as a compatible osmolyte, aquaporin-1 provides regulated water flux, a potassium-chloride cotransporter and the sodium pump gamma subunit tune ion movement, and the mechanosensitive channel TRPV4 reports cell swelling. Mitochondrial calcium uptake components and LETM1 link osmotic and ionic stress to organelle homeostasis, while transcript-stability and DNA-repair factors handle the downstream consequences of hypertonic damage.

cellular response to nitrosative stress
originalWhen nitric oxide or peroxynitrite accumulates, proteins become S-nitrosylated and tyrosine-nitrated and DNA is damaged; the cellular response to nitrosative stress is the set of adaptations that let a cell survive or die cleanly under those conditions. It matters most in inflamed tissue and in neurons, where sustained nitric oxide output from activated glia contributes to neurodegeneration, and it is one reason macrophage-derived NO is toxic to bystander cells. The genes here connect several arms of that defence: PARK7/DJ-1 acts as a redox-sensitive protector whose loss causes early-onset parkinsonism, DNAJA1 provides chaperone support for misfolded and modified proteins, autophagic turnover through ATG5 clears damaged cargo, ATM couples nitrosative DNA lesions to checkpoint signalling, and DDIT3/CHOP links persistent stress to apoptotic commitment. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of proteostasis, genome surveillance and inflammatory injury.

cellular response to hydroperoxide
originalHydroperoxides, the monosubstituted relatives of hydrogen peroxide, arise from lipid and membrane oxidation, and cells must sense them and respond by changing gene expression, redox enzyme output, survival signalling or growth arrest. The cellular response to hydroperoxide covers that adaptation, which sets the threshold between tolerated oxidative stress and oxidant-driven death, and is relevant to atherosclerosis, where oxidised lipoproteins taken up by scavenger receptors such as CD36 deliver the oxidant load. Detoxification capacity is supplied by glutathione transferase activity in membranes, while oxidation resistance factors and p53-induced stress genes bias the outcome toward antioxidant defence or apoptosis. Kinases including PRKCD and DAPK1 transduce the oxidant signal into death and cytoskeletal programmes, and chromatin corepressor activity links it to transcriptional reprogramming. Together these place peroxide handling at the junction of lipid metabolism, redox homeostasis and stress-induced cell fate decisions.

cellular response to hyperoxia
originalOxygen above normal tension is toxic, and cells respond to hyperoxia with a defined programme of stress signalling, antioxidant and clearance responses, and, when damage exceeds repair, death. This matters most in the lung, where supplemental oxygen given to preterm infants and ventilated patients injures alveolar epithelium and endothelium, contributing to bronchopulmonary dysplasia and acute lung injury. Raised oxygen drives reactive species production, with NADPH oxidase activity adding superoxide to the burden, while the FOXO1 transcription factor redirects gene expression toward stress resistance and apoptosis. Death receptor signalling through FAS commits irreversibly damaged cells to apoptosis, and autophagy machinery requiring ATG7 clears oxidised proteins and damaged mitochondria, a response that can protect or contribute to cell loss. Caveolin-1 links the membrane compartment to these decisions. The balance between adaptation and death determines tissue outcome.

cellular hyperosmotic response
originalCells exposed to a solute concentration higher than their own shrink as water leaves, and the cellular hyperosmotic response is how they sense that loss and restore volume and ionic balance. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where interstitial osmolality is extreme by design, and its failure leaves cells with concentrated intracellular salt, protein damage and DNA breaks. Two arms dominate the gene list. A kinase cascade in which WNK1 and WNK3 activate the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39 switches on electroneutral cation-chloride transport to reaccumulate ions, while the transcription factor NFAT5 drives expression of organic osmolyte machinery, including aldose reductase for sorbitol synthesis, so that volume can be regained without raising intracellular ionic strength. Aquaporin-mediated water flux, glucose uptake, mitochondrial calcium and magnesium handling, and cytoskeletal remodelling through ARHGEF2 accompany the adaptation.

cellular response to hydrogen peroxide
originalHydrogen peroxide is both a by-product of aerobic metabolism and a deliberate second messenger, and this pathway covers how a cell senses it and reshapes its behaviour in response. The outcome ranges from restored redox balance to inflammation, growth arrest and regulated death, so it sits at the heart of oxidative stress biology in ageing, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration. Detoxification and thiol buffering by catalase, thioredoxin and PARK7 limit the signal, while NFE2L2 drives the antioxidant transcriptional programme and SIRT1 and histone-modifying enzymes tune the longer-term response. Peroxide-sensitive kinases including SRC, ABL1, PRKCD and MAP3K5 relay the stimulus, RELA links it to cytokine output such as IL6, and TRPM2 and TRPA1 convert it into calcium and sensory signals. When damage exceeds repair, autophagy, mitochondrial permeability transition and RIPK1/RIPK3 necroptosis are engaged instead.

cellular hypotonic response
originalCells placed in a hypotonic environment take up water and swell, and the cellular hypotonic response is how they sense that swelling and restore volume before the membrane or cytoskeleton is damaged. It matters for epithelial fluid secretion, corneal and lens transparency, renal water handling and nociceptor mechanosensitivity; loss of its components causes corneal endothelial dystrophy, neuropathy and skeletal dysplasias. Mechanism begins with detection of membrane stretch and dilution, notably through the stretch-sensitive cation channel TRPV4 and water flux via aquaporin channels, and continues as solutes leave the cell through chloride and potassium-chloride cotransport pathways such as CLCN2 and SLC12A6, driving regulatory volume decrease. The WNK-activated kinases OXSR1 and STK39 with their scaffold CAB39 set cotransporter phosphorylation according to tonicity, while myosin light chain kinase links volume change to cytoskeletal tension.

negative regulation of hydrogen peroxide-mediated programmed cell death
originalHydrogen peroxide generated during oxidative stress can push cells past a threshold into programmed death, and this pathway describes the braking mechanisms that keep them alive. It matters wherever cells face chronic oxidant load: cardiomyocytes after ischaemia, dopaminergic neurons, and tissues undergoing regeneration, where premature death would mean irreplaceable loss. Survival signalling through the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET converges on AKT1 to suppress apoptotic commitment, while the scaffold RACK1 and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrain death machinery at the organelle. PARK7 and PINK1, both mutated in recessive parkinsonism, protect mitochondria from oxidative damage and support removal of damaged ones, linking failure of this protection to neurodegeneration. Several microRNAs, including miR-21 and members of the miR-17/92 and let-7 families, tune the same survival programmes post-transcriptionally, and carbonic anhydrase 3 contributes antioxidant buffering in muscle.

regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to hydrogen peroxide
originalHydrogen peroxide generated during oxidative stress can permeabilize mitochondria and commit a cell to death, and this pathway covers the controls that set how readily that happens. Tuning it decides whether a transient burst of peroxide is buffered or converted into caspase activation, which matters for neuronal survival, muscle and cardiac tolerance of ischaemia, and the resistance of tumour cells to oxidative therapy. Most of the components act as brakes: AKT1 signalling promotes survival, PARK7 and PINK1 protect mitochondria against oxidative damage and their loss causes recessive Parkinson's disease, and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrains permeabilization. RACK1 scaffolds the kinases involved, carbonic anhydrase III contributes antioxidant thiol capacity, and two microRNAs add post-transcriptional regulation. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of redox homeostasis and the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis rather than within either alone.

positive regulation of hydrogen peroxide-mediated programmed cell death
originalHydrogen peroxide accumulating inside a cell can either be detoxified or read as a death signal, and this pathway covers the inputs that push the balance toward death, increasing the rate and extent of peroxide-triggered programmed cell death. It matters wherever oxidative stress decides cell fate: ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiomyocyte loss, and the removal of cells whose redox damage exceeds repair. The regulators involved act at different levels. FOXO3 is a stress-responsive transcription factor that drives pro-apoptotic and redox target genes, PAWR acts as a pro-apoptotic effector partner, and the mitochondrial nuclease endonuclease G is released to fragment nuclear DNA in a caspase-independent branch of cell death. A microRNA and a forkhead-family transcriptional repressor add post-transcriptional and transcriptional tuning, so sensitivity to peroxide is set by gene expression as much as by the oxidant burden itself.

osmosensory signaling pathway
originalCells must sense changes in external osmolarity and respond before they swell or shrink past tolerance, and osmosensory signaling is the route from that physical cue to a corrective response. It matters for systemic water balance, blood pressure control and the volume regulation of every epithelium, and in the kidney and brain it underlies the thirst and vasopressin responses to hypertonicity. Mechanosensitive and osmotically gated cation channels of the TRPV family provide an entry point for calcium, while the WNK-OXSR1 kinase module couples tonicity to phosphorylation of cation-chloride cotransporters and thus to ion and water movement; a sodium channel subunit implicated in sodium-level sensing acts in the same context. Hypotonic or hypertonic stress also converges on the NLRP3 inflammasome with ASC and caspase-1, linking cell volume disturbance to interleukin-1 processing and inflammatory signalling.

cellular senescence (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of cellular senescence
originalCellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle triggered by telomere erosion, oncogene activation or persistent damage, and this pathway covers the mechanisms that hold it off so that proliferating and stem-like cells retain their capacity to divide. Telomerase components, including the catalytic subunit TERT and its RNA template TERC, together with the telomere-protective factor TERF2, prevent chromosome ends from being read as damage; the sirtuins SIRT1 and SIRT6 act as NAD-dependent deacetylases restraining damage and stress responses at chromatin. Transcriptional repressors such as BCL6, TBX2 and TWIST1 suppress the p16/p21 arrest programme, while CDK6 and cell-cycle regulators drive continued proliferation and several microRNAs damp senescence-promoting transcripts. Losing this restraint contributes to tissue ageing and stem cell exhaustion; its excess allows damaged cells to escape the senescence barrier to tumour formation.
These mechanisms hold off cellular senescence, the permanent cell cycle exit triggered by telomere erosion, oncogene activation or persistent damage. stress-induced premature senescence
originalCells exposed to oxidative or genotoxic insult — hydrogen peroxide, irradiation — can exit the cycle permanently rather than repair and divide, and stress-induced premature senescence is that irreversible arrest. It limits the propagation of damaged genomes and so acts as a barrier to tumour formation, but the accumulation of such arrested cells in tissues contributes to ageing phenotypes and chronic inflammation. The route runs through p38 MAPK and its downstream kinase relaying stress signals to p53, which induces the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 to lock the cell out of S phase. Modifiers set the threshold: the deacetylase SIRT1 restrains p53 activity and is protective against oxidative arrest, while a secreted WNT contributes to the paracrine phenotype of senescent cells. A circadian transcription factor links the response to metabolic and redox rhythms.

positive regulation of cellular senescence
originalCellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle imposed on damaged, stressed or oncogene-activated cells, and this pathway covers the inputs that push cells into that state. It acts as a barrier to tumour formation — mutant KRAS signalling, for example, triggers senescence rather than transformation unless the programme is disabled — while its chronic activation drives tissue ageing and the inflammatory secretory phenotype of aged tissue. TP53 sits at the centre, supported by effectors such as YPEL3 and PAWR, and by cytosolic DNA sensing through CGAS, which links damaged chromatin fragments to an interferon-flavoured arrest. Several microRNAs, notably MIR34A and MIR22, reinforce the decision by silencing proliferative and survival targets, and SIRT1 appears here as a deacetylase whose modulation tunes the p53 response. The output is durable growth arrest with altered secretion and immune visibility.

oncogene-induced cell senescence
originalWhen a cell acquires a strongly activating oncogenic lesion, such as mutant HRAS, one outcome is not transformation but a permanent proliferative arrest, and oncogene-induced senescence is that outcome. It acts as a barrier to tumour initiation: cells bearing a driver mutation withdraw irreversibly from the cell cycle, adopt a flattened secretory phenotype, and are often cleared by immune surveillance, so its loss is a recognised step in progression from benign lesion to carcinoma. Arrest is enforced through cell cycle inhibitors including p21, while PML bodies act as organising sites for senescence-associated signalling and architectural HMGA proteins help remodel chromatin into the heterochromatic foci that lock down proliferative genes. Lineage factors such as SPI1 connect the state to transcriptional reprogramming. The programme overlaps replicative and stress-induced senescence but is triggered by oncogenic signalling rather than telomere attrition.

cellular response to starvation (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
cellular response to leucine starvation
originalCells monitor leucine because it is the amino acid that most strongly licenses growth, and the cellular response to leucine starvation is how they stand down anabolism when it runs short. When leucine is abundant, sestrins release the GATOR2 complex and leucyl-tRNA synthetase and the Rag GTPases permit mTORC1 to dock at the lysosome; withdrawal reverses this, mTORC1 activity falls, protein synthesis and ribosome biogenesis are curtailed, and autophagy is de-repressed to recover amino acids from bulk cytoplasm. In parallel, uncharged tRNA accumulation drives a transcriptional arm through ATF4 and ATF2 that induces amino acid transporters, synthetases and stress-adaptive genes, including the sestrins themselves as a feedback loop. This surveillance couples nutrient supply to cell size, muscle protein balance and immune cell activation, and is the route by which leucine and its analogues influence mTOR-dependent growth control.

When it is abundant, sestrins release a pentameric regulatory complex, and a tRNA synthetase and small GTPases allow the growth kinase complex to dock on the lysosomal surface; withdrawal reverses this, so kinase activity falls, protein synthesis and ribosome biogenesis are curtailed, and autophagy is de-repressed to recover amino acids. Uncharged tRNA accumulation also drives a transcriptional arm inducing transporters and synthetases.—
cellular response to glucose starvation
originalWhen glucose runs low, cells must switch from growth and biosynthesis to conservation and self-digestion, and this starvation response is what makes that switch. It preserves ATP levels and viability during ischaemia, exercise and nutrient-poor tumour microenvironments, and its failure leaves cells unable to survive metabolic stress. Falling energy charge activates the AMP-activated kinase complex through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, which restrains anabolic signalling and licenses autophagy via the class III PI3-kinase complex containing beclin 1, VPS34 and ATG14. In parallel, the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response drives ATF4 to induce amino-acid supply enzymes such as asparagine synthetase, while sestrins, FOXO3, p53 and SIRT1 reinforce catabolic and antioxidant programmes. Glucose and amino acid transporters, GATOR/KICSTOR components and lipid droplet perilipins tie nutrient sensing to mTORC1 control and to mobilisation of internal fuel stores.

Nutrient transporters and lipid droplet coat proteins tie sensing to internal fuel mobilisation.—
cellular response to zinc ion starvation
originalZinc is required as a cofactor by hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, so cells monitor its availability and remodel transport and gene expression when it runs short. This response to zinc ion starvation adjusts uptake at the cell surface and rewires transcription to preserve the most zinc-dependent functions. Intestinal zinc acquisition depends on SLC39A4, whose loss-of-function causes acrodermatitis enteropathica with dermatitis, diarrhoea and impaired growth, while SLC39A5 contributes to serosal zinc handling and has been linked to myopia and to systemic zinc balance. Downstream, the zinc-finger transcription factor SP1 and the immediate-early factor FOS alter target gene output, including osteoblast products such as osteocalcin and the osteoclast receptor RANK, connecting zinc supply to bone formation and remodelling as well as to epithelial integrity and immune competence.

regulation of cellular response to stress (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of hypoxia-induced intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway
originalWhen oxygen falls, mitochondria are primed to release apoptogenic factors, and this set describes the braking mechanisms that block that hypoxia-induced intrinsic apoptotic route so cells survive ischaemia rather than die. It matters in tissues that routinely experience low oxygen or transient ischaemia — heart, brain, kidney — where such restraint limits infarct size, and in solid tumours, where the same protection lets hypoxic cells persist and resist therapy. The mechanisms are varied: survival signalling through PI3K and MEK sustains anti-apoptotic gene expression, an ARC-type inhibitor blocks caspase activation, an ER stress-inducible chaperone and a transmembrane BAX inhibitor buffer calcium release and mitochondrial permeabilisation, and PINK1 preserves mitochondrial quality control and membrane integrity. Metabolic adaptation is part of the response as well, linking glycolytic enzyme function to survival under oxygen limitation.
These braking mechanisms block hypoxia-induced intrinsic apoptosis so cells survive ischaemia, limiting infarct size in heart, brain and kidney while letting hypoxic tumour cells persist and resist therapy. Glycolytic adaptation supports survival.—
positive regulation of cellular response to hypoxia
originalCells sense falling oxygen and respond by remodelling metabolism, survival and gene expression; this pathway covers inputs that amplify that response, making the hypoxic programme stronger or longer-lasting than the oxygen signal alone would produce. Such positive regulation matters in ischaemic tissue, in the hypoxic cores of solid tumours, and in pulmonary and neuronal adaptation to low oxygen, where the size of the response determines whether a cell adapts or dies. The contributing genes are heterogeneous rather than a single complex: a de novo DNA methyltransferase links hypoxia to epigenetic reprogramming, a two-pore potassium channel and a metabotropic glutamate receptor connect membrane excitability and neurotransmitter signalling to oxygen stress, and two microRNAs tune the downstream transcript pool. Together they act as modifiers upstream of hypoxia-inducible transcription and its metabolic, angiogenic and apoptotic outputs.
These inputs amplify the hypoxic response, making metabolic, survival and transcriptional remodelling stronger or longer-lasting than the oxygen signal alone, which matters in ischaemic tissue, hypoxic tumour cores and pulmonary and neuronal adaptation. regulation of SREBP signaling pathway
originalCells must match their output of cholesterol and fatty acids to demand, and this regulatory layer sets how strongly SREBP transcription factors are allowed to drive that lipogenic programme. Control is exerted mainly on the precursor's escape from the endoplasmic reticulum: INSIG1 and INSIG2 retain the SREBP cleavage-activating protein complex in the ER when sterols are abundant, blocking transport to the Golgi where proteolytic activation occurs, while SPRING1 and scaffolding proteins such as PAQR3 and TMED2 influence trafficking and complex assembly. Additional restraint comes after activation, with the ubiquitin ligase machinery including AMFR and FBXW7 promoting turnover of the mature nuclear form, and microRNA and transcriptional inputs tuning component levels. Loss of this restraint drives unchecked de novo lipogenesis and cholesterol accumulation, linking the pathway to hepatic steatosis, hyperlipidaemia and the lipid supply of proliferating tumour cells.

tube formation (8)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
otic vesicle formation
originalThe inner ear begins as a thickened patch of surface ectoderm, the otic placode, which invaginates and pinches off to form the otic vesicle; otic vesicle formation is that transition, and everything downstream depends on it. The vesicle is the transient epithelial sac from which the cochlea, vestibular organs, endolymphatic duct and the sensory hair cells and neurons of the auditory-vestibular system are later patterned, so disruption at this stage produces profound congenital deafness and balance defects. Fibroblast growth factor signalling through FGF8 and FGF10 acting on FGFR2 induces and shapes the placode, while transcription factors including SOX9, PROX1 and HESX1 drive the epithelial morphogenesis and regional identity that make closure possible. Ciliary and structural contributions, such as CEP290, link this morphogenesis to broader syndromic disorders in which hearing loss accompanies retinal and renal disease.
The otic placode, a thickened patch of surface ectoderm, invaginates and pinches off to form the otic vesicle, from which the cochlea, vestibular organs, hair cells and auditory neurons later arise. FGF8 and FGF10 acting on FGFR2 induce the placode, while SOX9, PROX1 and HESX1 drive its morphogenesis. Ciliary and structural proteins support the cell-shape changes that allow the vesicle to close and separate.Inner ear development in the vertebrate embryo, when the earliest precursor of the hearing and balance organs forms from surface tissue of the head. Because the cochlea, vestibular organs and their sensory cells all derive from it, disruption at this stage causes profound congenital deafness and balance defects, sometimes within syndromes that also affect the retina and kidney.
ureteric bud formation
originalThe kidney begins when an outgrowth emerges from the Wolffian duct toward the metanephric mesenchyme; ureteric bud formation covers that first protrusion, from the moment epithelium bulges out of the duct until a distinct bud exists. Everything downstream depends on it — the bud branches into the collecting duct system and its tips induce nephron progenitors, so failure or ectopic budding produces renal agenesis, hypoplasia, duplex kidneys and vesicoureteric reflux. Mesenchymal GDNF is the inductive signal, its production controlled by SIX1 and SIX4 and its reception restricted in position by GATA3 within the duct epithelium. Sulfation of heparan sulfate by HS2ST1 shapes how that signal is presented, while BMP antagonists such as GREM1 and NOG relieve BMP4 inhibition so that budding occurs at one site and one time.
Ureteric bud formation is the first outgrowth from the Wolffian duct toward metanephric mesenchyme; the bud later branches into the collecting system and induces nephrons. Mesenchymal GDNF, controlled by SIX1 and SIX4 and positionally restricted by GATA3, is the inductive signal, shaped by HS2ST1 heparan sulfation and the BMP antagonists GREM1 and NOG. tube lumen cavitation
originalSome tubes in the body are not built by wrapping cells around a space but by hollowing out an already solid cord of cells, and tube lumen cavitation is that clearing step. It matters wherever a duct must connect a secretory organ to a surface: sweat and salivary glands, mammary ducts, and the airways all depend on converting a cord into a patent conduit, and failure leaves a blind or occluded duct with loss of secretion. Ectodysplasin signalling through its receptor drives the process in skin appendage ducts, and mutations in this ligand-receptor pair cause hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, in which sweat glands fail to form usable lumens. Hedgehog signalling and an NFI-family transcription factor supply epithelial patterning and branching context, while transglutaminase activity remodels the surrounding matrix. The step links epithelial morphogenesis to programmed cell clearance and cell rearrangement.

positive regulation of epithelial tube formation
originalEpithelial tubes are the structural basis of kidney nephrons, airways, glands and blood vessels, and this pathway covers the signals that promote their formation rather than the tube-building itself. Growth factors dominate: GDNF drives ureteric bud outgrowth and branching in kidney development, while EGF, FGF2 and VEGFA stimulate epithelial and endothelial cells to proliferate, migrate and organise into lumenised cords. These cues converge on intracellular signalling, with PI3K catalytic subunits relaying receptor activation to cytoskeletal and survival responses. Transcription factors act upstream and in parallel: SIX1 and SIX4 specify nephrogenic mesenchyme and sustain GDNF expression, and GATA3 is required for ureteric epithelium identity. Matrix components such as MMRN2 contribute to the extracellular environment guiding tube formation. Loss of these inputs causes renal agenesis or hypoplasia, branchio-oto-renal syndrome, and defective vascular and glandular tubulogenesis.

neural fold formation
originalNeural fold formation is the shaping step that converts the flat neural plate into a U-shaped groove: the plate edges thicken and elevate, bringing the prospective dorsal margins toward each other so that they can later fuse into the neural tube. Without it, closure fails and the result is a neural tube defect such as exencephaly, anencephaly or spina bifida. The genes here span the signals and the machinery that execute the bending. BMP family ligands and NODAL provide dorsoventral patterning cues from surrounding tissue, while cofilin-mediated actin filament severing and other cytoskeletal regulators generate the apical constriction and cell shape changes that hinge the epithelium. A chromatin remodelling component and transcriptional regulators couple these signals to gene expression in surface ectoderm and neuroepithelium, linking morphogenesis to the patterning of the early central nervous system.

nephric duct formation
originalThe nephric duct is the tube that drains the primitive kidney, and its initial formation sets up the plumbing from which the ureter, collecting system and, in males, parts of the reproductive tract derive. Epithelialisation of the intermediate mesoderm into a patent duct that extends caudally to insert into the cloaca depends on a small transcriptional and signalling module: PAX2 and GATA3 specify and maintain the nephric duct epithelium and guide its caudal extension, HNF1B shapes tubular epithelial identity, and BMP4 and WNT9B provide the surrounding instructive signals, with WNT9B later inducing metanephric mesenchyme. Failure or misrouting at this stage produces congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, including renal agenesis, duplex or ectopic ureters and vesicoureteral reflux, and mutations in these regulators cause inherited renal-coloboma and renal cyst syndromes.

metanephric tubule formation
originalMetanephric tubule formation is the step at which mesenchymal cells of the kidney-forming metanephros first organize into an epithelial tube, the precursor of the nephron's proximal tubule, loop and distal segments that will later filter and reabsorb from the blood. Failure of this step leaves nephrons unformed, producing renal hypoplasia, dysplasia or agenesis and the reduced nephron endowment that predisposes to later kidney disease. The paired box factors PAX2 and PAX8 act partly redundantly to specify and maintain the nephric epithelial state, SOX8 and SOX9 contribute transcriptional input to progenitor behaviour, and WNT9B from the ureteric epithelium induces WNT4 in surrounding cap mesenchyme, which drives mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition. The biology thus links inductive Wnt signalling between adjacent tissues to lineage specification and epithelial tube morphogenesis during organogenesis.

tube closure
originalTurning a flat epithelial sheet into a sealed tube — most consequentially the neural tube, but also the optic fissure and palate — requires the edges of an epithelial fold to bend, meet and fuse, creating the central lumen. Failure produces some of the commonest human birth defects: spina bifida, anencephaly and craniorachischisis, which is why folate metabolism genes such as MTHFR, MTHFD1 and the receptor FOLR1 sit alongside the morphogenetic machinery here. Closure depends on planar cell polarity components (VANGL2, CELSR1, PRICKLE1, FZD3/6, SCRIB) to drive convergent extension, on actin regulators such as PFN1, VASP and COBL to constrict apical surfaces, and on hedgehog, BMP and WNT signalling — with NOG and SFRPs as antagonists — to pattern the dorsal neuroepithelium. Ciliary and intraflagellar transport proteins tune that signalling, and apoptotic caspases remodel the fusing seam.

formation of primary germ layer (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
regulation of endodermal cell differentiation
originalEndoderm is the germ layer that gives rise to gut, liver, pancreas and lung epithelium, and the differentiation of cells into it must be timed and positioned correctly during gastrulation or organ primordia form in the wrong place or not at all. The genes here act as modulators rather than core effectors of that fate decision: a secreted Wnt antagonist tunes the Wnt/nodal signalling gradients that partition mesoderm from endoderm, a bHLH transcription factor of the nascent mesoderm helps set the boundary between the two lineages, a histone variant that marks facultative heterochromatin constrains which lineage programmes remain accessible, and fibrillar collagen V contributes to the extracellular matrix through which migrating cells receive positional cues. Together they illustrate how signalling, chromatin state and matrix context converge to raise or lower the rate at which cells adopt endodermal identity.
Endoderm gives rise to gut, liver, pancreas and lung epithelium, and its differentiation during gastrulation must be correctly timed and positioned. Correct timing and placement matter because errors leave organ primordia mispositioned or missing. The influences involved tune how often cells take this route rather than dictate it, shaping the size and placement of the future digestive and respiratory organs.
regulation of mesodermal cell fate specification
originalDuring gastrulation, epiblast cells must decide whether to become mesoderm, and this regulatory layer sets how many do so, where, and when. The outcome determines the heart, blood, skeleton and muscle that later derive from mesoderm, and misregulation produces axis duplication, failed primitive streak formation or absent cardiac progenitors. Control is exerted largely by extracellular signals and their tuning: WNT3A drives streak formation while the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain WNT signalling to limit the mesodermal domain, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A patterns posterior and extraembryonic mesoderm, and FGFR1 is required for cells to ingress through the streak and adopt mesodermal identity. Downstream, the transcription factor MESP1 marks and specifies nascent cardiovascular mesoderm. The same signalling logic is exploited to steer pluripotent stem cells toward mesodermal lineages in culture.
During gastrulation, signals control how many epiblast cells become mesoderm, and where and when, shaping heart, blood, skeleton and muscle; misregulation causes axis duplication or absent cardiac progenitors. WNT3A drives primitive streak formation, DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain it, BMPR1A patterns posterior mesoderm and FGFR1 enables ingression, while MESP1 specifies cardiovascular mesoderm.
