endodermal cell fate specification
originalEndodermal cell fate specification is the step at which a cell in the early embryo becomes competent to differentiate into endoderm on its own, though the commitment is still reversible and can be overridden by other signals. It sets aside the germ layer that gives rise to gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid, so failures here compromise the entire digestive and respiratory lineage, and the same programme is exploited to make definitive endoderm from pluripotent stem cells in culture. Pluripotency factors such as POU5F1 and NANOG provide the starting state, SOX2 must be extinguished as SOX17 comes on, and EOMES acts with nodal signalling to drive endoderm rather than mesoderm, an alternative marked by MESP1. HNF1B carries the decision forward into gut tube patterning, while DKK1 antagonises Wnt to bias regional identity.
Endodermal specification makes early embryonic cells competent, though still reversibly, to become endoderm, the source of gut, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid, and is used to derive definitive endoderm from stem cells. POU5F1 and NANOG set the starting state, SOX2 gives way to SOX17, and EOMES with nodal favours endoderm over MESP1-marked mesoderm; HNF1B and DKK1 carry regional patterning forward.Cells become competent to differentiate as endoderm, though the commitment remains reversible. The same programme is used to derive definitive endoderm from pluripotent stem cells in culture, which matters for regenerative medicine.
paraxial mesoderm formation
originalParaxial mesoderm is the band of tissue flanking the neural tube that later segments into somites and gives rise to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis, so its initial formation sets up the segmented body plan of the trunk. During gastrulation, cells emerging from the primitive streak must be allocated to a paraxial rather than lateral or intermediate fate, and Wnt ligands acting through canonical and non-canonical routes drive both that allocation and the collective movement of the cells into position; LEF1 transduces the canonical arm to target genes. The forkhead factors FOXC1 and FOXC2 act redundantly to maintain paraxial identity and subsequent somite formation, and their loss produces axial skeletal and vascular defects. Vesicle trafficking through the exocyst contributes the membrane delivery that polarized migration and convergent extension require.

This band later segments and gives rise to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis, establishing the segmented trunk. somitogenesis (4)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
regulation of somitogenesis
originalSomitogenesis carves the presomitic mesoderm into paired blocks that later give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis, and this set concerns the inputs that set how fast and how regularly those segments form. Notch signalling supplies the oscillatory clock: the ligand DLL1 and receptor NOTCH1 couple neighbouring cells, while the glycosyltransferase LFNG modifies Notch to modulate ligand sensitivity and keep the oscillation periodic and phase-locked across the field. Caudal-type homeobox factors CDX1 and CDX2 pattern posterior axial identity and maintain the progenitor pool from which new somites are added, and DMRT2 acts in the forming somite to fix segment polarity and myogenic competence. Disturbance of this timing produces irregular, fused or asymmetric segments, the developmental basis of congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis.
Somitogenesis segments the presomitic mesoderm into blocks that form vertebrae, ribs, muscle and dermis, and these genes set its pace and regularity. somite rostral/caudal axis specification
originalEach somite is polarised into rostral and caudal halves before any morphological boundary appears, and this patterning is what later dictates where sclerotome cells condense, where vertebrae segment relative to muscle, and along which corridor migrating neural crest cells and motor axons may travel. Loss of the polarity produces fused and malformed vertebrae and disordered spinal nerve segmentation, as seen in congenital spine disorders. The bHLH factors MESP1 and MESP2 are induced in the rostral presomitic mesoderm as segmentation clock and Notch signals converge, with TBX6 licensing their expression and NRARP tuning Notch output; RIPPLY1 and RIPPLY2 then feed back to extinguish TBX6 and MESP activity, sharpening the boundary. LHX1 and nodal-type signalling through GDF3 and SMAD4 contribute upstream, while EPB41L5 links the resulting polarity to epithelialisation of the forming somite.

MESP1 and MESP2, licensed by TBX6 and tuned by Notch via NRARP, are then shut off by RIPPLY1 and RIPPLY2 feedback, with LHX1, GDF3, SMAD4 and EPB41L5 contributing. somite specification
originalSomite specification is the step in vertebrate trunk development at which each newly formed block of paraxial mesoderm acquires its own positional and segmental identity, fixing which vertebra, rib and body-wall muscle group will derive from it. Getting this wrong produces fused or malformed vertebrae and rib defects of the kind seen in congenital segmentation disorders of the spine. The genes here act at the boundary between the segmentation clock and stable somite patterning: Notch ligand signalling through DLL1 provides the oscillatory and boundary-forming cue, RIPPLY1 acts as a repressor that terminates that cue and sharpens the rostral-caudal subdivision of each somite, and the MEOX transcription factors specify sclerotome and dermomyotome fates within the segment. The pathway therefore links periodic patterning of the presomitic mesoderm to the axial skeleton and skeletal muscle that later form from it.

axis elongation involved in somitogenesis
originalVertebrate embryos build their trunk and tail progressively from a caudal progenitor zone, and axis elongation during somitogenesis is the growth that extends the head-to-tail axis so that successive somites can be laid down behind the advancing tail bud. Without it the axis is truncated, somite number is reduced, and the vertebrae, ribs and axial muscles derived from those segments are correspondingly incomplete. The genes here point to WNT signalling as the driver: WNT3A ligand from the posterior growth zone maintains presomitic mesoderm progenitors, SFRP1 sequesters Wnt ligands and NKD1 acts as an induced negative feedback regulator, tuning pathway output rather than simply switching it on. A Mediator complex subunit links the pathway to transcriptional output, and a protein phosphatase 2A regulatory subunit contributes phosphorylation-dependent control. The result couples posterior progenitor renewal to the segmentation clock that times somite formation.
Axis elongation extends the trunk and tail from a caudal progenitor zone so somites can form progressively; failure truncates the axis and reduces vertebrae, ribs and axial muscle. secondary heart field specification
originalSpecification of the secondary heart field sets aside a pool of lateral mesoderm distinct from the first heart field, and its descendants build most of the right ventricle together with the outflow tract at the arterial pole and part of the inflow tract at the venous pole. Because these are precisely the structures malformed in conotruncal and right-heart congenital heart disease, the delineation step underlies tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle and persistent truncus arteriosus. Mesodermal progenitors marked by MESP1 are directed into this territory by BMP4 and by non-canonical WNT5A and WNT11 signalling, with canonical Wnt output tuned through AXIN2 and Notch input relayed by RBPJ. ISL1 identifies the undifferentiated progenitor state, while MEF2C and the chromatin-remodelling subunit SMARCD3 drive the transcriptional programme that commits these cells to cardiomyocyte fate and later cardiac morphogenesis.
The secondary heart field is a lateral mesoderm pool that builds most of the right ventricle and the outflow and inflow tracts, so its specification underlies conotruncal defects such as tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus. trachea formation
originalTrachea formation covers the earliest events that carve a single cartilage-supported airway tube out of the anterior foregut, separating it from the esophagus and connecting it to the branching bronchi below. Getting this right determines whether an infant can breathe and swallow independently; failure produces tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, tracheal agenesis or stenosis, and the tracheomalacia seen when the cartilage rings are malformed. The genes involved place the process at the intersection of BMP and TGF-beta signalling from the surrounding splanchnic mesenchyme, canonical Wnt signalling through beta-catenin in the foregut endoderm, and the MEK1/MEK2-ERK1/ERK2 kinase cascade that relays growth factor input into proliferation and dorsoventral patterning of the tube. Epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk of this kind decides where respiratory identity begins and where cartilage and smooth muscle differentiate around it.

organ induction
originalOrgans do not arise from single cells acting alone; they form where one tissue signals to a neighbour and changes its fate. Organ induction describes these reciprocal interactions, typically between epithelium and adjacent mesenchyme, that commit a field of cells to build a kidney, limb, lung, heart or gonad. The signalling currencies are few and reused: fibroblast growth factors and their receptor and adaptor components, bone morphogenetic proteins, and WNT ligands acting through beta-catenin, with DKK1 and SPRY1 restraining WNT and FGF output so induction stays spatially bounded. Transcription factors such as SIX1, GATA5, MESP1 and posterior HOX proteins read these cues and fix regional identity, while GDNF-driven signalling initiates ureteric branching. Loss or misplacement of these inductive signals produces organ agenesis, hypoplasia and congenital malformation, linking the pathway to embryonic patterning and branching morphogenesis.
Organ induction is the signalling between neighbouring tissues, usually epithelium and mesenchyme, that commits cells to form kidney, limb, lung, heart or gonad. regulation of prostatic bud formation
originalThe prostate begins as buds of epithelium that emerge from the fetal urogenital sinus, and this pathway covers the signals that set how many buds form, where, and how far they grow. Androgen receptor signalling in the surrounding mesenchyme licenses budding in males, and the epithelial-mesenchymal dialogue that follows determines prostate size and branching architecture; failure of these controls gives prostatic agenesis or hypoplasia, while the same signalling axes are reactivated in benign hyperplasia and prostate cancer. Hedgehog signalling from the budding epithelium and WNT5A from mesenchyme position and restrain outgrowth, BMP4 and BMP7 act largely as inhibitors that limit bud number, and the extracellular sulfatase SULF1 tunes availability of heparan sulfate-bound growth factors. Together these define an androgen-dependent branching morphogenesis programme.

regulation of secondary heart field cardioblast proliferation
originalThe second heart field is a pool of committed but still dividing cardiac precursors that supplies the right ventricle, the outflow tract and the inflow region, and how long those cardioblasts keep proliferating before differentiating sets the size of these structures. Control of that proliferative window matters clinically: too little expansion of the field underlies conotruncal and outflow tract malformations, including persistent truncus arteriosus and double outlet right ventricle, and contributes to hypoplasia of right-sided chambers. The regulators here combine progenitor identity with growth signalling — ISL1 marks the undifferentiated second heart field state, a SIX1–EYA1 transcriptional pair and the Notch effector HES1 restrain or sustain division, HAND2 and TBX5 pattern the cardiac lineage, and beta-catenin couples Wnt input to precursor expansion. The pathway thus sits at the junction of cardiac fate commitment and cell cycle control during cardiac morphogenesis.

acrosome assembly
originalAcrosome assembly is the step in spermiogenesis that converts Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles into the single large cap covering the anterior sperm nucleus, the secretory organelle whose hydrolases and adhesion proteins let a sperm penetrate the zona pellucida and fuse with the egg. Without it spermatozoa are globozoospermic — round-headed, acrosome-less and infertile — a recognised cause of male infertility treatable only by assisted fertilisation. The genes here cover vesicle trafficking and tethering from the Golgi, a Rab GAP and Golgi-associated tethering factors, membrane fusion and docking, and the acroplaxome/acrosome–acroplaxome anchoring machinery built on actin-related proteins that also couples the acrosome to nuclear shaping and manchette function. Transcriptional regulators active in round spermatids drive the haploid programme, while zona-binding and sperm–egg interaction proteins are the cargo whose correct packaging is the point of the whole process.
During spermiogenesis, Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles assemble into the acrosome, the cap over the sperm nucleus whose enzymes and adhesion proteins enable zona penetration and egg fusion. central nervous system myelin formation
originalOligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord extend processes that spiral around axons and compact their membrane into myelin, the insulating sheath that permits fast saltatory conduction and supports long-term axonal integrity. Central nervous system myelin formation sets conduction velocity in white matter tracts, and its failure or breakdown underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis. The genes here act at several stages: recognition and adhesion between the glial membrane and the axon surface through myelin-associated glycoprotein and contactin, lipid handling and intracellular trafficking needed to build a membrane of unusual composition, and regulators that control oligodendrocyte differentiation and process outgrowth. The pathway therefore links glial cell fate and membrane biogenesis to axon-glia communication, and connects to broader programmes of neural development and white matter maintenance.

cardiac myofibril assembly
originalCardiac myofibril assembly builds the ordered sarcomeric apparatus that lets heart muscle cells contract, taking nascent actin bundles in the developing myocardium through to mature, aligned myofibrils. Without it the embryonic heart cannot generate organized force, and in the adult heart defective assembly or maintenance of sarcomeric components underlies dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies. Cardiac actin and the ventricular myosin light chain supply the contractile core, while titin acts as the molecular ruler spanning the sarcomere and telethonin anchors its Z-disc end; formin-family FHOD3 and nebulin-related proteins organize and length-regulate the thin filaments, and myosin light chain kinase 3 tunes contractility. Z-disc proteins such as CSRP3 couple mechanical strain to signalling. Transcriptional inputs from NKX2-5, SRF, PROX1 and SMAD4, together with PDGF receptor signalling, link cardiomyocyte differentiation and growth cues to the sarcomeric gene programme.

skeletal muscle thin filament assembly
originalSkeletal muscle contracts only if its actin-based thin filaments are built to a defined length and anchored correctly within each sarcomere, and this assembly programme is what produces them. Skeletal alpha-actin polymerises into the filament core, with cardiac actin contributing in developing and regenerating fibres; leiomodin-3 nucleates new actin filaments and sets thin filament length, and its loss causes nemaline myopathy with disorganised, rod-containing fibres and severe congenital weakness. Titin spans the sarcomere as a molecular ruler and elastic element, and telethonin binds its Z-disc end to help anchor the filament lattice. The transcription factor PROX1 contributes to the myogenic gene programme that establishes fibre-type-appropriate sarcomeric components. Together these activities link myofibrillogenesis during muscle development and repair to the force-generating geometry that thick-thin filament sliding requires.

positive regulation of sarcomere organization
originalMuscle cells generate force only when actin and myosin are packed into sarcomeres, the repeating contractile units bounded by Z discs, and this pathway covers the signals that promote and accelerate that assembly. It matters most in the heart, where myofibril growth accompanies cardiomyocyte maturation and the hypertrophic response to load; failure of sarcomere assembly and alignment underlies dilated cardiomyopathy and thin, poorly contractile ventricular walls. The genes here act as upstream instructions rather than structural components: a cardiac-restricted growth factor of the BMP family and the vasoactive peptide endothelin-1 act as paracrine cues, a myosin light chain kinase and a protein kinase C-related kinase phosphorylate targets that set filament assembly and Z-disc gene expression, a transcription factor contributes to chamber and conduction patterning, and a muscle-enriched microRNA tunes the output. Together they link extracellular signalling to the building of the contractile apparatus.
These signals promote sarcomere assembly in muscle, especially in the heart, where myofibril growth accompanies cardiomyocyte maturation and hypertrophy; failure underlies dilated cardiomyopathy. paranodal junction assembly
originalSaltatory conduction depends on a tight seal where the myelin sheath meets the axon at each end of a node of Ranvier, and paranodal junction assembly builds that seal. The septate-like contacts formed there anchor the myelin loops to the axolemma, separate the sodium channels clustered at the node from the potassium channels of the juxtaparanode, and act as a diffusion barrier for the periaxonal space. A neurexin-family axonal adhesion protein, CNTNAP1, partners with contactin to engage glial neurofascin, while a band 4.1-like protein links the complex to the underlying cytoskeleton and a tetraspanin contributes to membrane organization. Galactolipid synthesis by UGT8 and ether lipid synthesis by GNPAT supply the myelin lipids on which junction integrity depends. Disruption causes conduction slowing, disorganized nodes and severe congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy.

regulation of cell projection assembly (3)

pathwayneutralprocess onlycontext only
negative regulation of ruffle assembly
originalMembrane ruffles are transient actin-rich folds that form when branched actin polymerisation pushes the plasma membrane forward; suppressing their assembly is how a cell limits spreading, lamellipodium formation and migration when it should stay put. The genes here act at several points in that restraint. ARHGAP24 is a GTPase-activating protein that lowers Rac signalling toward the actin nucleation machinery, KANK1 constrains talin-dependent adhesion and actin coupling at the cell edge, ABI3 participates in the WAVE regulatory complex without promoting ruffling, and EVL and PFN2 shape filament elongation and available actin monomer rather than allowing unchecked branching. The net effect is control of cell shape, adhesion turnover and motility, with relevance to how epithelial and immune cells balance movement against stable contact, and to invasive behaviour when negative regulation of ruffle assembly is lost.
Membrane ruffles are actin-rich folds driven by branched polymerisation, and suppressing them lets a cell limit spreading and migration. ARHGAP24 lowers Rac activity, KANK1 restrains talin-dependent adhesion, ABI3 sits in the WAVE complex without promoting ruffling, and EVL and PFN2 shape filament elongation. This control balances motility against stable contact in epithelial and immune cells and opposes invasive behaviour.Formation of transient actin-rich membrane folds, driven by branched actin polymerisation pushing the plasma membrane forward, is suppressed. This balance between moving and maintaining stable contacts matters for epithelial and immune cells. When the restraint is lost, cells can become inappropriately motile and invasive, a feature of tumour spread.
negative regulation of lamellipodium assembly
originalMigrating cells push forward by building lamellipodia, thin sheets of branched actin at the leading edge; restraining that assembly is how a cell stops spreading, changes direction, or holds still. Negative regulation of lamellipodium assembly limits protrusion and so shapes axon guidance, wound repair, angiogenesis and the invasiveness of tumour cells. The genes act at several levels: cofilin severs and depolymerises actin filaments to turn over the network, an ABI family member dampens WAVE-complex-driven Arp2/3 nucleation, and repulsive guidance cues acting through plexin and Slit receptors collapse protrusions by reducing Rac-dependent actin polymerisation. Histidine-rich glycoprotein contributes an extracellular anti-angiogenic, anti-migratory influence, and two microRNAs tune the same output post-transcriptionally. Loss of such restraint gives persistent, poorly directed motility, as seen when guidance signalling fails during neural wiring or when carcinoma cells acquire migratory freedom.
Restraining lamellipodium assembly lets migrating cells stop, turn or remain still, shaping axon guidance, wound repair, angiogenesis and tumour invasion. negative regulation of filopodium assembly
originalFilopodia are the thin, finger-like actin bundles that motile cells and axonal growth cones push out to sample their surroundings, and their assembly must be restrained as well as driven; this pathway covers the braking side, limiting how many protrusions form and how fast. Restraint shapes neuronal morphology in particular: by slowing filopodial emergence, it sets the pace of dendritic spine maturation and the timing of synapse formation, and the human-specific paralogue SRGAP2C acts by antagonising ancestral SRGAP2 function, a change linked to the protracted spine development characteristic of human cortex. Other members contribute Rho-family GTPase regulation through a GAP domain, membrane deformation and small GTPase-dependent membrane traffic, and kinase signalling, while presynaptic adhesion molecule neurexin-1 ties the process to synaptic contact. Loss of such control yields excess protrusions and miswired connectivity.
This pathway restrains filopodia formation, limiting how many protrusions cells and growth cones produce. In neurons it paces spine maturation and synapse formation, and human-specific SRGAP2C antagonises SRGAP2, linked to prolonged spine development in human cortex. In the cortex this restraint sets the pace of dendritic spine maturation and synapse formation; a human-specific gene duplication slows this pace and is linked to the prolonged spine development characteristic of the human brain. Loss of control gives excess projections and miswired connectivity.

negative regulation of autophagosome assembly
originalAutophagosome formation has to be held in check when nutrients are plentiful or when unrestrained self-digestion would damage a cell, and this pathway covers the brakes applied to that step. Suppressing autophagosome assembly keeps basal turnover matched to demand, and its loss shifts cells toward excessive sequestration of cytoplasm and organelles; conversely, too much suppression blocks clearance of damaged mitochondria and aggregated proteins, a defect linked to neurodegeneration through LRRK2 and PINK1. Inhibitory inputs act at several levels: chromatin and transcriptional regulators such as EHMT2 and NUPR1 limit expression of autophagy genes, PHF23 restrains the initiation machinery centred on BECN1, FEZ1 and FEZ2 interfere with early assembly, and membrane-trafficking components including SEC22B, SCFD1 and TMEM39A govern how much lipid and cargo reaches the nascent phagophore. Together these constitute the negative arm of autophagy initiation control.
This pathway restrains autophagosome formation when nutrients are plentiful, matching self-digestion to demand; too little restraint causes excess sequestration, while too much blocks clearance of damaged mitochondria and aggregates, linked to neurodegeneration via LRRK2 and PINK1. That clearance failure is linked to neurodegeneration, notably familial Parkinson disease.
negative regulation of centriole replication
originalCells must build exactly one new centriole per existing one per cycle, and the restraints that block extra rounds of centriole replication are what keep centrosome number at two. Losing them produces supernumerary centrioles, multipolar spindles, chromosome missegregation and the aneuploidy typical of tumours, which is why several of these genes behave as tumour suppressors. The brakes act at different points: BRCA1 restrains centrosome amplification through ubiquitin ligase activity, TRIM37 degrades pericentriolar assembly factors and suppresses ectopic centriolar structures, CDK5RAP2 organises pericentriolar material and couples centrosome integrity to mitotic fidelity, while MDM1 and RBM14 block inappropriate elongation or de novo assembly of centriolar cartwheels. The acetyltransferases KAT2A and KAT2B contribute through chromatin and non-histone acetylation that limits duplication licensing. Mutations in this circuitry underlie microcephalic dwarfism syndromes and predispose to cancer.
Restraints on centriole replication keep each cell to one new centriole per existing one; their loss causes centrosome amplification, multipolar spindles and the aneuploidy typical of tumours. Losing this control produces extra centrosomes, abnormal division and chromosome imbalance, a hallmark of tumours, which is why several factors involved behave as tumour suppressors, including one linked to hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. Defects also underlie microcephalic dwarfism syndromes.
regulation of cytoplasmic stress granule assembly
originalWhen cells meet oxidative, heat or nutrient stress, stalled translation initiation complexes and their mRNAs condense into cytoplasmic stress granules, and this regulatory layer sets how readily those granules form and how large they grow. The decision matters because granule assembly sequesters mRNA away from ribosomes, buys time for repair, and tunes signalling and survival; persistent or aberrant condensation is the entry point to pathological aggregation in neurodegeneration. Scaffolding RNA-binding proteins such as UBAP2L, CAPRIN1 and IGF2BP1 promote condensation, while USP10 acts with G3BP-family scaffolds to restrain it, and the catalytic subunits of AMP-activated protein kinase couple granule dynamics to energy stress. Autophagy components ATG5 and BECN1 tie granule turnover to bulk degradative clearance, linking this process to the broader stress response and to mRNA storage and triage.

regulation of mitotic spindle assembly
originalBefore a cell can divide accurately it must build a bipolar microtubule array, and the processes that tune mitotic spindle assembly set how fast and how faithfully that array forms. Getting this wrong produces multipolar or misoriented spindles, lagging chromosomes and aneuploidy, which is why several members are studied as mitotic drug targets. The ESCRT-III machinery is prominent here — the CHMP proteins with the VPS4B ATPase and the ALIX adaptor — linking membrane remodelling activity at the nuclear envelope and midbody to spindle organisation. PLK1 provides the master mitotic kinase input, RCC1 generates the chromatin-associated RanGTP gradient that releases spindle assembly factors near chromosomes, and CEP97 restrains centriole and cilium behaviour so centrosomes act as poles. Additional microtubule- and RNA-binding components, including EML3 and HNRNPU, contribute to spindle microtubule stability and chromosome alignment.
These processes tune how quickly and accurately the bipolar mitotic spindle forms; errors cause multipolar spindles, lagging chromosomes and aneuploidy, and some members are drug targets. regulation of inhibitory synapse assembly
originalInhibitory synapses set the balance between excitation and inhibition in neural circuits, and this pathway governs how many of them form and how quickly. The genes act at the point of contact between a GABAergic or glycinergic terminal and its target, biasing nascent contacts toward an inhibitory identity rather than an excitatory one. Secreted and transmembrane organizers bridge the cleft and recruit postsynaptic scaffolds: LHFPL4 is required to cluster gephyrin and GABA-A receptors at inhibitory postsynaptic sites, calsyntenin-3 and cerebellin family ligands engage presynaptic adhesion partners, and semaphorin signalling through plexin receptors tunes contact formation. Shifting this regulation changes inhibitory tone, and loss of inhibitory synapse number is associated with epilepsy and with neurodevelopmental disorders in which circuits become hyperexcitable. The biology sits within synaptogenesis and activity-dependent circuit refinement.
This pathway governs how many inhibitory GABAergic or glycinergic synapses form, setting the excitation-inhibition balance of neural circuits. regulation of synaptic assembly at neuromuscular junction
originalMotor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres must build a synapse precisely where they meet, and this regulatory programme sets how much and how fast that neuromuscular junction is assembled. Its output is reliable neuromuscular transmission: nerve-derived agrin acting through the muscle receptor tyrosine kinase MuSK drives clustering of acetylcholine receptors beneath the nerve terminal, while a collagen-tailed subunit anchors acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft so that transmitter is cleared after each impulse. Transcription factors of the SIX family contribute to the muscle differentiation context in which the postsynaptic apparatus forms, and scaffolding and ubiquitin-ligase components tune synaptic protein localisation and terminal growth. Loss of agrin-MuSK signalling, or autoantibodies against it, produces congenital myasthenic syndromes and myasthenia gravis, with fatigable weakness from failed postsynaptic organisation.

negative regulation of bicellular tight junction assembly
originalEpithelial and endothelial sheets seal their paracellular space with tight junctions, and this pathway covers the signals that hold that sealing back or take it apart, lowering barrier resistance and permitting permeability. Such negative regulation of tight junction assembly is normal during wound repair, morphogenetic rearrangement and leukocyte transit, but sustained it produces the leaky gut and blood-brain barrier of inflammatory disease and the loss of polarity seen in tumour invasion and metastasis. Inflammatory input through TNF and the IKK-NF-kB arm disassembles junctional complexes, while the Rho effector kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 drive actomyosin contraction that pulls on junction anchors rather than allowing them to mature. Small RNAs including miR-105 and miR-142 act by repressing junction proteins post-transcriptionally, linking microRNA control to barrier integrity and to the vascular permeability that precedes metastatic seeding.
These signals inhibit or dismantle tight junctions, increasing paracellular permeability in epithelia and endothelia; this is normal during wound repair and leukocyte transit but, when sustained, drives leaky gut, blood-brain barrier failure and tumour invasion. regulation of postsynapse assembly
originalExcitatory and inhibitory synapses are built largely on the receiving side, where receptor scaffolds, actin and adhesion molecules are gathered into a functional postsynaptic specialization; this pathway covers the signals that tune how fast and how extensively that assembly proceeds. Its output is dendritic spine number and shape, and hence synaptic strength, learning and the balance of circuit excitability, with defects contributing to intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia risk. Much of the control converges on Rho-family GTPase signalling: Rac1 and Rac3 with their DOCK-family activators and ARHGAP-family inactivators remodel the spine actin cytoskeleton, while RhoG and GNA13 feed in upstream cues. Trans-synaptic adhesion and guidance receptors including neurexin, nectin-3, LRP4 and the Nogo receptor position nascent contacts, and neddylation enzymes, retromer trafficking and translational repressors such as CPEB3 and PUM2 set the local supply of postsynaptic components.

negative regulation of synapse assembly
originalSynapse number is set not only by signals that build contacts but by signals that restrain them, and this negative regulation of synapse assembly covers the brakes. Limiting synaptogenesis matters for refining circuits during development and for keeping excitatory drive within bounds in the mature brain; loss of such restraint is associated with excess spine density, aberrant connectivity and epileptiform activity. The genes here act largely at the cell surface: secreted Wnt-pathway ligands and the Wnt antagonist DKK1 suppress spine and synapse formation, Slit ligands with their Robo receptor and an Eph receptor deliver repulsive guidance cues that discourage contact, cerebellin and calsyntenin act as trans-synaptic organizers whose activity can curb assembly, and immune-linked TLR2 signalling and the adhesion molecule NEGR1 modulate neurite and synapse number. Together they represent the inhibitory side of synaptic connectivity and pruning.

regulation of synaptic vesicle priming
originalBefore a synaptic vesicle can release neurotransmitter it must be made fusion-competent, and this pathway tunes how many vesicles reach that primed, release-ready state. Because priming sets the size of the readily releasable pool, its regulation determines release probability, short-term plasticity and the fidelity of fast synaptic transmission; loss of the machinery produces severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathies and movement disorders. Regulation acts on assembly of the SNARE complex that docks vesicle and presynaptic membranes: syntaxin-1A and -1B provide the plasma membrane SNARE, Munc18-1 chaperones syntaxin and is required for its productive engagement, a Munc13 isoform catalyses transition to the primed state, and tomosyn restrains priming by forming a non-fusogenic SNARE complex. NSF-associated alpha- and beta-SNAP recycle SNAREs for further rounds, while synaptophysin and synaptogyrin shape the vesicle membrane, and a presynaptic kinase adds phosphorylation-dependent control.

pointed-end actin filament capping
originalActin filaments grow and shrink at both ends, and capping the pointed (minus) end fixes filament length by blocking subunit addition or loss there. This is how sarcomeric thin filaments acquire and keep their uniform length: tropomodulins sit at the minus end of each actin filament, working together with tropomyosin, while the leiomodins are related proteins that instead nucleate new filaments and can compete for the same site. The balance between them sets thin filament length in cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle, and also stabilises the short actin filaments of the erythrocyte membrane skeleton and neuronal cytoskeleton. Loss of the skeletal muscle isoform LMOD3 causes nemaline myopathy with disorganised, poorly formed thin filaments, and TMOD1 loss disrupts myofibril assembly, tying pointed-end capping directly to contractile function and cell shape.
Capping the pointed end of actin filaments blocks subunit exchange there and fixes filament length. regulation of barbed-end actin filament capping
originalActin filaments elongate almost exclusively at their barbed ends, so proteins that cap those ends decide whether a growing network extends or stalls. Regulation of barbed-end capping tunes that decision, and through it the speed of lamellipodial protrusion, cell migration, and the remodelling of cortical actin during adhesion and immune cell function. Most of the regulators here act on capping protein itself: the CARMIL family binds it and lowers its affinity for filament ends, allowing uncapping and renewed growth, while myotrophin (MTPN) similarly sequesters or antagonises it, and a WASH complex subunit couples capping control to branched nucleation on endosomes. Cofilin contributes by severing and turning over filaments, creating new ends. Loss of such control is seen in CARMIL2 deficiency, where T cell activation and actin-dependent immune responses fail.

negative regulation of NLRP3 inflammasome complex assembly
originalThe NLRP3 inflammasome converts danger signals into caspase-1 activation, IL-1β and IL-18 release, and pyroptotic death, so cells need brakes on its assembly to avoid self-damaging inflammation. Restraining that assembly is what keeps sterile injury, crystal deposition and infection from tipping into chronic inflammatory disease; loss of these brakes underlies periodic fever syndromes and contributes to gout, atherosclerosis and neuroinflammation. The restraint works at several levels: ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM31 and FBXL2 target NLRP3 for degradation, autophagy machinery including IRGM and LAMP2-dependent chaperone-mediated autophagy clears the sensor, pyrin-domain-only proteins PYDC1 and PYDC2 act as decoys that block adaptor recruitment, and depalmitoylases together with kinases and SIRT2 tune NLRP3 through reversible lipid and post-translational modification. Other NLR and pyrin-domain proteins, and the microglial receptor TREM2, provide additional inhibitory input, setting the threshold for innate immune activation.

negative regulation of microtubule polymerization
originalMicrotubules are only useful if they can shorten as well as grow, and this pathway covers the activities that suppress tubulin polymerization or limit how far a plus end extends. Restraining assembly sets microtubule length and turnover, allows spindles and growth cones to remodel rather than freeze, and frees tubulin dimers for reuse. The clearest effectors here are the stathmins, which sequester soluble tubulin dimers and promote catastrophe, with STMN2 acting in neurons where axonal microtubule dynamics govern growth and regeneration; MAPRE1 tracks growing plus ends, and MAP2 and tubulin cofactors tune the polymer that results. Kinase input from DYRK1A and phosphorylation of stathmin link the balance to developmental and signalling cues. Because neurons depend on precisely dynamic microtubules, loss of this restraint contributes to axonal degeneration, and alpha-synuclein ties it to synucleinopathy.

regulation of SNARE complex assembly
originalMembrane fusion requires SNARE proteins on two bilayers to zipper into a four-helix bundle, and this pathway covers the factors that promote or restrain that assembly step, setting where and when fusion happens. It matters most in neurons, where the rate of SNARE pairing governs synaptic vesicle priming and neurotransmitter release: STXBP1 chaperones syntaxin-1 into a fusion-ready conformation and its loss causes severe infantile epilepsy, while PRRT2 mutations produce paroxysmal dyskinesia and alpha-synuclein can both nucleate and, in excess, derange SNARE complex formation. A second arm is endolysosomal, with the HOPS and CORVET tethering subunits (VPS11, VPS16, VPS18, VPS33A, VPS39, VPS41, VPS8) coupling Rab-dependent tethering to SNARE engagement for late endosome and lysosome fusion. Other members, including LRRK2 and STXBP6, act as modulators that tune assembly rather than catalyse it, linking this control point to both neurotransmission and lysosomal delivery.

regulation of protein oligomerization
originalMany proteins only work once they assemble into dimers or larger complexes, and this pathway covers the control points that determine whether, how fast, and to what extent that assembly happens. Setting oligomerization thresholds matters because the same chemistry that builds functional complexes also produces pathological aggregates, as in the misfolded protein deposits that accumulate when clearance and chaperone routes fail. The genes here act through varied routes: acetylation and deacetylation of substrates by a transcriptional coactivator acetyltransferase and by a cytoplasmic deacetylase that also handles aggregate clearance via the aggresome; oxygenase-mediated modification; ubiquitin-like ISG15 conjugation and a tripartite-motif ubiquitin ligase; and retromer-dependent endosomal sorting through VPS35, which determines the fate of membrane cargo. Together they link post-translational modification, trafficking and protein quality control to the assembly state of client proteins.
This pathway controls whether and how fast proteins assemble into dimers and larger complexes, which matters because the same chemistry can produce pathological aggregates when quality control fails. negative regulation of complement activation
originalComplement is a rapidly amplifying proteolytic cascade, and restraining it is what keeps that amplification aimed at pathogens rather than at host tissue. Negative regulation of complement activation is carried out by soluble and membrane-bound inhibitors that block cascade initiation, dismantle the C3 and C5 convertases, and prevent assembly of the lytic membrane attack complex. C1 inhibitor holds the classical and lectin initiation proteases in check; C4b-binding protein and CD46 act as cofactors for factor I-mediated cleavage of C4b and C3b; CD55 accelerates convertase decay, and CD59 stops terminal pore formation on self membranes. Loss of these brakes produces recognisable disease — hereditary angioedema when C1 inhibitor is deficient, and complement-mediated haemolysis when erythrocytes lack CD55 and CD59. The same regulators mark host cells as off-limits, shaping immune tolerance, clearance of apoptotic debris and inflammation in kidney, eye and blood.

originalNaive CD4 T cells choose among helper fates, and this is the brake on the Th2 option — the programme that restrains differentiation toward the IL-4/IL-5/IL-13-producing lineage. prepulse inhibition
originalPrepulse inhibition is the reflex-damping phenomenon in which a weak warning stimulus shortly before a loud one blunts the startle response, and it serves as a readout of sensorimotor gating: the brain's ability to filter redundant sensory input so that a response is not mounted to everything at once. Loss of this gating is a robust correlate of schizophrenia, autism and Tourette syndrome, and it is the standard assay for antipsychotic action. The genes involved point to the circuitry responsible: dopamine D2 and D3 receptors and the dopamine transporter set striatal dopaminergic tone, adenosine A2A receptors oppose it, and glutamatergic components including an NMDA receptor subunit and a delta-type receptor supply excitatory drive. Synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins such as CNTNAP2 and MDGA1, together with chromatin and signalling regulators like CHD8 and PTEN, connect the trait to neurodevelopmental wiring of these pathways.

originalGrowing axons are steered as much by being told where not to go as by attraction, and this pathway covers the repulsive arm of guidance: signals that halt or slow extension of a growth cone so that it turns away, stalls, or prunes an inappropriate branch. originalEndothelial cells migrate toward chemotactic cues when new vessels are needed, and this pathway describes the braking signals that hold that migration in check. originalMonocytes are recruited out of the bloodstream toward chemokine gradients at sites of injury and infection, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven; damping it is what negative regulation of monocyte chemotaxis does. originalMacrophages are recruited to tissues by chemotactic gradients, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven, or inflammatory infiltrate persists and causes collateral tissue damage. negative regulation of IRE1-mediated unfolded protein response
originalThe IRE1 arm of the unfolded protein response senses misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum and, through XBP1 mRNA splicing and stress kinase signalling, expands ER capacity or commits a cell to death; dampening that arm is how cells end the response once folding homeostasis returns and avoid the apoptotic output of chronic signalling. The balance set here determines whether ER stress resolves adaptively or progresses to cell death, a switch relevant to secretory cell function, metabolic disease, and neurodegeneration.

originalWhen misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response halts most translation and drives a stress transcriptional programme; dampening that arm is how cells recover protein synthesis and avoid committing to apoptosis when stress is transient or resolved. Golgi disassembly
originalBefore a cell divides it must take apart its Golgi apparatus so that the stacks can be partitioned between daughters and rebuilt, and Golgi disassembly is that mitotic breakdown step, which underlies Golgi inheritance. Loss of the process blocks progression into mitosis in some settings, because Golgi fragmentation is itself monitored as a checkpoint, and it leaves membrane and secretory cargo unequally distributed at division. The mechanism is largely mitotic phosphorylation: cyclin-dependent kinase 1 together with polo-like and VRK kinases modify structural and trafficking components, notably the golgin GM130 encoded by GOLGA2, the SNARE syntaxin 5 and the Arf activator GBF1. Phosphorylation severs golgin-mediated tethering between cisternae and suspends vesicle fusion, converting stacked ribbon into dispersed tubules and vesicles. It links cell cycle control directly to secretory pathway organisation and organelle biogenesis.

originalThe Golgi ribbon's stacked, pericentrosomal architecture is not self-maintaining; it is actively set and reset, and regulation of Golgi organization covers the inputs that determine how compact, how positioned and how connected the cisternae are. This matters for directional secretion, glycosylation fidelity and for the ordered disassembly and reassembly of the Golgi at mitosis, when ribbon unlinking is coupled to cell cycle progression. Rab GTPases including RAB33B and RAB43 direct intra-Golgi and retrograde traffic, and SNAREs STX5 and STX18 execute the membrane fusion that keeps cisternae continuous. originalWhen a cell divides, the Golgi ribbon fragments and is partitioned between daughters; Golgi reassembly is the reformation of stacked, functional cisternae from those fragments, and it is what allows each daughter cell to resume secretion, glycosylation and polarised membrane traffic without rebuilding the organelle from scratch. It is therefore part of organelle inheritance rather than of trafficking as such. Membrane fusion is the central step: a deubiquitinating enzyme acting on p97/VCP-associated substrates reverses the ubiquitin marks that keep mitotic membranes apart, while a 14-3-3 adaptor and the CCM3-STK25 kinase module link Golgi architecture to cell polarity and stress signalling. originalMembrane traffic arriving at the Golgi only delivers its cargo when the transport vesicle's bilayer merges with the target cisterna, and this fusion step is what sustains secretion, glycosylation and the flow of newly made proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell surface. Tethering precedes fusion: a long coiled-coil tether captures incoming vesicles at a distance and holds them against the Golgi membrane, after which SNARE proteins on the two bilayers zipper into a four-helix bundle that forces lipid mixing. Members of the SNARE machinery here serve distinct arrival routes, with some pairing at the cis-Golgi for ER-derived vesicles and others at the trans-Golgi for endosomal traffic. originalIn mammalian cells the individual Golgi stacks are laterally linked into a single continuous ribbon positioned near the centrosome, and this pathway covers the tethering and cytoskeletal machinery that builds and maintains that arrangement. Ribbon organisation matters for orderly anterograde traffic, for uniform glycosylation of secreted and surface proteins, and for directing secretion toward one face of a migrating or polarised cell; the ribbon is also deliberately dismantled at mitosis so that Golgi membranes partition between daughters. Ribbon fragmentation is a recurring feature of neurodegeneration and of cells under stress.

peripheral nervous system myelin maintenance
originalMyelin in peripheral nerves must be actively maintained long after it is first wrapped, and this upkeep of mature Schwann cell myelin keeps internodes intact, compacted and able to support fast saltatory conduction. When it fails, the result is demyelinating neuropathy with slowed conduction, distal weakness and sensory loss, the clinical picture of several inherited Charcot-Marie-Tooth and related forms. The genes involved act largely in the Schwann cell rather than the axon: periaxin anchors the abaxonal membrane to the basal lamina through its dystroglycan complex, SH3TC2 and NDRG1 handle membrane trafficking and turnover in the myelinating cell, plectin provides cytoskeletal linkage, and fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies hydroxylated sphingolipids that stabilise the lipid-rich sheath. Akt signalling sustains the trophic and metabolic state needed for continual renewal, linking myelin maintenance to growth factor input and to axonal survival.

originalA dying cell must advertise itself, and exposure of phosphatidylserine on the apoptotic cell surface is that advertisement. nuclear membrane reassembly
originalAt the end of mitosis each daughter cell must rebuild a sealed nuclear envelope around its decondensing chromosomes, and nuclear membrane reassembly is the step that accomplishes this. Without it the nucleus remains leaky, chromatin fragments can be left outside, and micronuclei and DNA damage follow. originalTail-anchored proteins carry their single transmembrane segment at the extreme C-terminus, so it emerges from the ribosome only after translation has finished and cannot use the co-translational targeting route. originalThe peripheral endoplasmic reticulum is not a uniform bag but a polygonal network of narrow tubules, and this pathway builds and maintains the membrane of that network. regulation of endoplasmic reticulum tubular network organization
originalThe endoplasmic reticulum is not a uniform sheet: much of it is a branching network of tubules whose junctions, curvature and extent must be actively set, and this pathway governs how much tubular network the cell builds and maintains. Tubule shape determines where the ER contacts mitochondria, endosomes and the plasma membrane, and how lipids and calcium are distributed, so control of it feeds into organelle communication and membrane traffic. Curvature-stabilising reticulon-like and hairpin membrane proteins such as ARL6IP1 and TMEM33 tune the propensity of the membrane to bend, while LNPK stabilises the three-way junctions that keep the network polygonal, and the RAB3GAP1-RAB3GAP2 complex links tubular organisation to Rab-dependent regulation. Loss of these activities in humans causes hereditary spastic paraplegia and Warburg micro syndrome, pointing to long axons and neurodevelopment as especially dependent on correct ER geometry.

endoplasmic reticulum tubular network formation
originalThe peripheral endoplasmic reticulum is not a uniform sac: much of it is a branching network of narrow tubules whose membranes are strongly curved, and forming that network is what this process does. The tubular ER is where contacts with mitochondria, endosomes and the plasma membrane are made, where lipid transfer and calcium handling occur, and along which the ER is dragged as cells extend processes. Reticulon family proteins and ARL6IP1 insert wedge-like hydrophobic domains into the bilayer to generate and stabilise high curvature, restricting themselves to tubules and the edges of sheets, while protrudin links ER membrane to microtubule-based extension of new tubules. Mutations in several of these genes cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, implying that long motor axons depend particularly on maintaining a properly shaped ER.

endoplasmic reticulum membrane fusion
originalThe endoplasmic reticulum is a single continuous membrane network, and that continuity has to be actively maintained by fusing tubules together wherever they meet. This homotypic membrane fusion builds and repairs the polygonal ER tubular network, allowing lumenal contents, calcium and newly made proteins to diffuse throughout the cell and permitting the ER to be remodelled during growth and after division. The atlastin GTPases ATL1, ATL2 and ATL3 drive the fusion step directly, tethering apposed tubule tips and merging their bilayers through GTP-dependent conformational change, while accessory factors including a SNARE-associated component and a deubiquitinating enzyme contribute to membrane joining and its regulation. Mutations in ATL1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, and ATL3 defects cause sensory neuropathy, linking ER shape to the maintenance of long axons.

regulation of endosome organization
originalEndosomes must be shaped, matured and positioned correctly for material taken into a cell to reach lysosomes, be recycled to the surface, or be handed to autophagic membranes; regulation of endosome organization covers the inputs that set how fast and how far that remodelling goes. The genes here act at different points on that theme: a small GTPase that marks late endosomes and licenses their fusion with lysosomes, a lysosomal membrane protein needed for delivery of a glucocerebrosidase, a phosphoinositide phosphatase that controls membrane lipid identity during vesicle uncoating, an adaptor that engages ubiquitinated cargo and autophagic machinery, and a ubiquitin ligase linked to damaged-organelle clearance. Several are mutated in Parkinson disease and related neurodegeneration, reflecting how strongly neurons depend on accurate endosomal maturation and cargo sorting for synaptic vesicle recycling and protein turnover.

endosome membrane tubulation
originalCargo leaving an endosome must first be concentrated into a tubular extension that can be pinched off as a recycling carrier, and endosome membrane tubulation is the deformation step that makes those carriers possible. Without it, receptors and transporters that should return to the plasma membrane or the Golgi are instead delivered to lysosomes and degraded, so surface levels of nutrient receptors, adhesion molecules and signalling receptors fall. Sorting nexins with BAR domains provide the curvature-sensing scaffold, SNX1 and SNX2 pairing with SNX5 or SNX6 to form dimers that read the membrane shape and select cargo; TMCC1 acts at endoplasmic reticulum contacts where tubules are constricted and severed. Actin dynamics and Rab-directed traffic contribute through a coronin family actin regulator and a MICAL-family effector, tying tubule formation to the cytoskeleton and to polarised recycling routes.

multivesicular body organization
originalMultivesicular body organization is how a late endosome converts itself into a sorting station: patches of the limiting membrane bud inward, capturing ubiquitinated membrane proteins into intralumenal vesicles that are then delivered to lysosomes for degradation or released as exosomes. This is the route by which activated growth factor and cytokine receptors are permanently switched off, so its failure leaves signalling receptors recycling at the surface and contributes to tumour growth and to neurodegeneration. The machinery is the ESCRT series acting in order: a ubiquitin-recognizing complex built on HGS and STAM, TSG101 with VPS28 and VPS37 subunits, the VPS25/VPS36/SNF8 module, and CHMP proteins that polymerize to constrict and sever the bud neck. The AAA-ATPase VPS4, with VTA1, disassembles these filaments for reuse. The same membrane-scission chemistry serves cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope resealing and viral budding.

endosomal lumen acidification
originalEndosomes must become progressively acidic as they mature, and the pumping of protons into the endosomal lumen is what makes that gradient. The low pH releases ligands from internalized receptors, allows iron to leave transferrin, activates hydrolases, and is exploited by viruses and toxins that need an acidic trigger to penetrate the membrane; without it, receptor recycling, cargo sorting and eventual lysosomal degradation all fail. Most of the work is done by the vacuolar H+-ATPase, whose membrane-embedded V0 subunits form the proton channel and whose cytosolic V1 subunits hydrolyse ATP, with accessory factors such as ATP6AP1, ATP6AP2 and TMEM9 needed for assembly and targeting. Because pumping charge alone would stall the pump, a chloride transporter, CLCN3, provides counterion shunt conductance. The same acidification supports secretory and lytic vesicle function, including delivery of FASLG to the cell surface.
